section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A patient sustains a penetrating injury resulting in complete, permanent loss of vision in the right eye; the left eye remains normal. Months later the patient reports trouble with certain depth judgments. Which depth cue is the patient now unable to use?
rationale: Retinal disparity is a binocular cue: the brain compares the two slightly different retinal images to compute depth. With one eye there is no second image, so it is lost. Every other option is monocular.
why: Interposition is monocular — one eye suffices to see a near object occlude a far one.
Correct. Disparity needs two eyes producing two images.
Relative size is monocular.
Motion parallax is monocular — differential sweep of near vs. far objects during self-motion.
takeaway: Only two cues are binocular: retinal disparity and convergence. A one-eyed patient loses exactly those two.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: As an object moves toward a person's face, both eyes rotate inward toward the nose, and the brain reads the muscular rotation to gauge distance. This cue is best classified as:
rationale: Convergence is the inward rotation of both eyes to fixate a near object; because it depends on both eyes it is binocular. The distractor to beat is accommodation — the other oculomotor cue — which is monocular.
why: Accommodation is oculomotor but is the ciliary muscle changing lens shape in one eye — monocular, and not the rotation described.
Correct. Both eyes rotating inward = binocular oculomotor cue.
Disparity is binocular but refers to the difference between the two images, not muscular rotation.
Motion parallax is object motion during observer movement, not eye rotation, and is monocular.
takeaway: Accommodation = lens shape, MONOcular; convergence = eyes rotating inward, BINocular. Both signal 'near.'

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A passenger gazing out the side window of a moving train sees fence posts beside the track streak past rapidly, while distant mountains drift by slowly. The cue producing this depth impression is:
rationale: Motion parallax: objects at different distances appear to move at different speeds as the observer moves — near fast, far slow. Monocular, and it requires observer motion.
why: Linear perspective is apparent convergence of parallel lines in a static scene.
Texture gradient is a static change in surface grain with distance.
Correct. Differential apparent speed during self-motion.
Convergence is an oculomotor cue, unrelated to external object motion.
takeaway: Observer moving + near things moving faster than far things = motion parallax, the one monocular cue that needs motion.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
tag: Pictorial cues · what a flat canvas can't do
stem: A painter wants a convincing illusion of depth on a flat canvas. Which cue is the painter fundamentally unable to employ?
rationale: A flat canvas presents essentially the same image to both eyes, so it cannot generate retinal disparity (which needs a real 3-D scene giving each eye a different image). The others are pictorial/monocular cues.
why: Linear perspective is a pictorial cue.
Interposition is a pictorial cue.
Correct. Disparity needs a true 3-D scene; a flat image can't produce it.
Relative size is a pictorial cue.
takeaway: 'Pictorial cues' ARE the monocular cues — those that survive on a 2-D surface. Binocular cues are exactly what a flat image loses.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: At the edge of a cobblestone plaza, an observer sees stones look large and distinct near their feet but progressively smaller, finer, and denser toward the far side. The primary monocular cue here is:
rationale: A continuous surface whose texture becomes finer and denser with distance is a texture gradient. The cue is the graded change in one uniform surface's grain, not a comparison of separate objects.
why: Relative size compares separate objects of known size; here it's one continuous surface.
Correct. Progressive fining of a surface = texture gradient.
Interposition needs one object overlapping another; nothing is occluded.
Relative height concerns vertical position near the horizon, not texture density.
takeaway: Texture gradient = one continuous surface getting finer with distance. Relative size = separate known objects imaged smaller.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In a photograph, a car partially blocks a building behind it, and the viewer judges the car to be closer. Which cue is operating, and what is its key limitation vs. binocular cues?
choices: Interposition; it yields only relative depth order, not absolute distance
Retinal disparity; it yields precise absolute distance
Linear perspective; it requires input from both eyes
Accommodation; it operates only for objects several meters away
rationale: Interposition: an occluding object is seen as nearer. It reliably tells you the order of objects but not how far apart they are — relative, not absolute, depth. Monocular.
why: Correct. Overlap establishes near/far ordering only.
The cue described is overlap, not disparity; disparity is binocular.
Linear perspective is monocular and isn't described here.
Accommodation is monocular and works for near objects, opposite of the claim.
takeaway: Interposition ranks objects front-to-back without quantifying the gap. Disparity is prized because it approaches absolute depth up close.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A sociologist studies two attributes of a person: the caste they were born into, and the profession they later entered through training. These are best described, respectively, as:
choices: An ascribed status and an achieved status
An achieved status and an ascribed status
rationale: An ascribed status is assigned at birth or involuntarily (caste, sex, race). An achieved status is earned through one's own actions (a profession entered via training).
why: Caste is ascribed, but a trained profession is earned.
Correct. Caste = ascribed; trained profession = achieved.
Reversed.
Caste is not achieved; it's assigned at birth.
takeaway: Ascribed = given to you (birth, involuntary). Achieved = earned. Occupation and education are the classic achieved statuses.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A society allows essentially no movement between strata; position is fixed at birth and endogamy is enforced. Compared with a class system, this caste system is best characterized as:
choices: An open system with high social mobility
A closed system with little to no social mobility
A meritocracy based on achieved status
A system defined primarily by economic capital
rationale: A caste system is closed: strata are fixed at birth, mobility is essentially impossible, membership is ascribed. A class system is open, permitting mobility partly on achieved status.
why: Open, mobile systems are class systems.
Correct. Caste = closed, ascribed, minimal mobility.
Meritocracy rewards achieved status; caste is ascribed.
Caste is defined by birth-ascribed rank, not primarily economic capital.
takeaway: Caste = closed/ascribed/no mobility. Class = open/allows mobility. 'Closed vs. open' is the core contrast.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A first-generation student is comfortable with academic norms, formal speech, and cultural references that ease their way through elite institutions, despite modest family income. This asset is best labeled:
rationale: Cultural capital is the non-financial social assets — education, tastes, speech, cultural knowledge — that promote mobility and ease within institutions. Distinct from money (economic) and networks (social).
why: Economic capital is financial resources; the stem specifies modest income.
Correct. Norms, speech, cultural fluency = cultural capital.
Social capital is the value of one's networks, not cultural fluency.
Human capital (skills for labor markets) is close, but the stem describes cultural fluency — Bourdieu's cultural capital.
takeaway: Bourdieu: economic = money; cultural = knowledge/tastes; social = networks. 'Fits in at elite institutions' → cultural capital.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A woman born to working-class parents becomes a physician. Over her own career she is later promoted from resident to department chief. These two changes illustrate, respectively:
rationale: Working-class parents to physician is intergenerational mobility (relative to the prior generation). Resident to chief within her own working life is intragenerational.
why: Reversed.
Correct. Between generations first, then within her own lifetime.
Both moves are vertical (upward).
Structural mobility refers to whole groups moving due to societal change.
takeaway: Intergenerational = across generations (parent→child). Intragenerational = within one lifetime/career.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: During rapid industrialization, a large share of a nation's population moves from agricultural labor into factory and clerical jobs as the occupational structure shifts. This population-level upward movement is best termed:
rationale: Structural mobility is movement of many people caused by changes in society's structure (industrialization creating new job categories), not individual effort.
why: The stem describes a society-wide shift, not individual merit.
Correct. Economy-driven movement of many people.
Horizontal mobility is same-rank change; this is upward.
The movement is upward, not downward.
takeaway: Structural mobility = society changes and moves whole groups. Contrast with individual mobility from personal effort.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A theorist argues that schools transmit the dominant group's cultural capital, so children of advantaged families are rewarded for norms they already possess, quietly reproducing the class structure across generations. This reflects:
choices: The Davis–Moore (functionalist) view that stratification is beneficial
Symbolic interactionism at the societal level
rationale: Social reproduction — associated with conflict theory and Bourdieu — holds that institutions like schools transmit advantage across generations, perpetuating inequality rather than rewarding pure merit.
why: Davis–Moore argues stratification is functional; this stem critiques inequality.
Correct. Institutions reproducing class advantage = social reproduction.
The argument is that merit is NOT what's rewarded — it opposes meritocracy.
Symbolic interactionism is micro-level meaning-making, not macro reproduction.
takeaway: Social reproduction = inequality perpetuated through institutions (esp. schools). Conflict-theory idea; contrast Davis–Moore.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A loud sound triggers a small muscle in the ear to contract and dampen the vibrations reaching the inner ear (the acoustic reflex). Because this reflex takes up to a fraction of a second to engage, it:
choices: Protects hearing during sustained loud noise, like a concert, but not a sudden gunshot
Protects against a sudden gunshot but not sustained noise
Works equally well for sudden and sustained sounds
Makes the ear more sensitive to loud sounds
rationale: The acoustic reflex is too slow to react to an abrupt, impulsive sound like a gunshot, but it can dampen sustained loud noise once engaged — which is why a prolonged concert is attenuated while a sudden blast is not.
why: Correct. Slow onset → useless for an instantaneous blast, useful for prolonged loud sound.
Reversed — the delay means it can't protect against a sudden gunshot.
Its latency makes it selective for sustained sound, not equal for both.
It dampens vibration to protect the ear; it doesn't increase sensitivity.
takeaway: The acoustic reflex is protective but slow — it guards against sustained loud noise, not sudden impulse sounds like a gunshot.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After a few minutes in a room with a strong smell, a person stops noticing it even though the odor concentration is unchanged and the olfactory receptors in the nose are desensitizing over time. This fading perception is best described as:
rationale: Sensory adaptation is the reduced responsiveness of the receptors themselves to a constant stimulus — exactly the olfactory desensitization described.
why: Correct. The receptors desensitize to the ongoing odor — receptor-level adaptation.
Habituation is a learned, central decrease in behavioral response to a repeated stimulus, not receptor desensitization.
Sensitization is an increase in response — the opposite.
The absolute threshold is the minimum detectable stimulus; it isn't what changes as receptors adapt to a strong, ongoing odor.
takeaway: Sensory adaptation = the receptors themselves fire less to a CONSTANT stimulus. Habituation = a learned, central drop in response to a REPEATED stimulus.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Stepping outdoors into bright sunlight, a person is briefly dazzled, then vision normalizes as the pupils constrict and the photoreceptors become less responsive to light. This rapid adjustment is:
rationale: In bright light the eye down-regulates sensitivity: the pupil constricts to admit less light and the photoreceptors desensitize. This is light adaptation, and it's fast.
why: Correct. Bright light → pupil constriction + photoreceptor desensitization = light adaptation.
Dark adaptation is the opposite — increasing sensitivity in dim conditions.
Sensitization would increase responsiveness; here the receptors become less responsive.
Rhodopsin regenerates during dark adaptation; in bright light it's bleached.
takeaway: Light adaptation = down-regulate: pupils constrict, photoreceptors desensitize (fast). Dark adaptation = up-regulate: pupils dilate, pigment regenerates (slow).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Entering a dark theater, a person can barely see at first but gradually regains vision over about 20–30 minutes as the pupils dilate and the rods synthesize light-sensitive molecules. The slow phase of this dark adaptation is mainly due to:
choices: Regeneration of photopigment (rhodopsin) in the rods, raising sensitivity
rationale: Dark adaptation's slow phase is the regeneration of rhodopsin in the rods (bleached in the prior bright light), which steadily increases sensitivity. Pupil dilation helps but is fast; the 20–30-minute course is the pigment rebuilding.
why: Correct. Rods resynthesize light-sensitive pigment, and sensitivity climbs over ~20–30 min.
Pupils dilate in the dark; and that's a fast effect, not the slow phase.
Sensitivity increases during dark adaptation — the rods become more, not less, responsive.
Rods and cones are separate receptors; one doesn't convert into the other.
takeaway: Dark adaptation (up-regulation): pupils dilate + rods regenerate rhodopsin → sensitivity rises over ~20–30 min.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A volunteer wears goggles that flip the visual field upside-down. Disoriented at first, after several days they navigate normally and the world even begins to look upright again. This illustrates that the nervous system:
choices: Adapts to persistently altered sensory input by recalibrating perception
Permanently loses the ability to perceive true orientation
Increases the absolute threshold for vision
Stops transducing visual signals at the retina
rationale: Given continuously altered input, the brain recalibrates — perceptual adaptation — so behavior and eventually perception normalize. Remove the goggles and there's a brief after-effect until it recalibrates back.
why: Correct. Sustained altered input → the nervous system adapts and re-normalizes perception.
It's reversible — removing the goggles produces a temporary after-effect, then normal perception returns.
Absolute threshold (minimum detectable light) isn't what's changing; orientation processing is recalibrating.
The retina keeps transducing normally; the adaptation is central/perceptual.
takeaway: Perceptual adaptation: with sustained altered input (inverting goggles), the brain recalibrates so perception normalizes — and shows an after-effect when the input is removed.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A hot bath feels almost unbearably hot for the first few seconds, then comfortable within a minute — even though the water temperature hasn't changed. The fading of the intense heat sensation is best explained by:
choices: Adaptation of temperature receptors to the constant stimulus
A drop in the water's temperature
An increase in the difference threshold
rationale: The thermoreceptors adapt to the constant temperature, reducing their firing so the sensation fades — classic sensory adaptation to an unchanging stimulus.
why: Correct. Constant temperature → thermoreceptors reduce firing → the sensation fades.
The stem states the water temperature is unchanged; the change is in the receptors, not the water.
Sensitization would intensify the sensation, the opposite of what happens.
The difference threshold (smallest detectable change) isn't what drives the fading of a constant sensation.
takeaway: Temperature receptors adapt to constant warmth or cold — why a hot bath or a cold pool feels extreme at first, then normal.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: You feel a shirt when you first put it on, but minutes later you don't, though the fabric still touches you. In terms of receptor regulation, this sensory adaptation is:
choices: Down-regulation — the receptor reduces its response to a constant stimulus
rationale: Sensory adaptation is down-regulation: the receptor fires less to a constant, unchanging stimulus.
why: Up-regulation would increase the response — the opposite of adaptation.
Correct. Adaptation is down-regulation: a receptor progressively reduces its firing to an unchanging stimulus.
Amplification strengthens a signal; adaptation weakens the response.
Transduction is converting a stimulus to a neural signal, not the fading response.
takeaway: Sensory adaptation = down-regulation (reduced response to a constant stimulus).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: One reason sensory adaptation is useful is that it:
choices: Amplifies weak signals for the brain
Filters out constant, unchanging stimuli — and can protect receptors from damaging overexcitation
rationale: Adaptation filters out unchanging stimuli so we notice change, and protects receptors from damaging overexcitation.
why: Amplification (up-regulation) does that — not adaptation.
Adaptation decreases, not increases, response to a constant stimulus.
Adaptation modulates the ongoing response; it doesn't stop transduction.
Correct. Adaptation lets us ignore constant, uninformative input and spares receptors from overexcitation (persistent intense signaling can damage cells).
takeaway: Adaptation = ignore constant stimuli + protect receptors from overexcitation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The opposite of sensory adaptation — in which a signal is strengthened rather than reduced — is called:
rationale: Amplification = up-regulation: the signal is strengthened, the opposite of adaptation's down-regulation.
why: Correct. Amplification is up-regulation — strengthening a signal — the opposite of adaptation's down-regulation.
Habituation is a learned decrease in response, not signal strengthening.
Down-regulation is adaptation, the opposite of amplification.
Accommodation is the lens focusing in the eye, unrelated.
takeaway: Amplification = up-regulation (strengthen the signal). Adaptation = down-regulation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: How can a single photoreceptor firing produce a much stronger signal by the time it reaches the brain?
choices: The receptor keeps firing forever on its own
Adaptation boosts the signal along the way
One activated cell can excite several downstream cells, which each excite more — amplifying the signal
The stimulus physically grows stronger inside the eye
rationale: Amplification works by divergence: one cell activates several downstream cells, each activating more — so the signal grows before reaching the brain.
why: Receptors don't fire indefinitely; amplification is about spreading the signal.
Adaptation reduces responses; it doesn't boost the signal.
Correct. Signal amplification comes from divergence: one cell activates several, which each activate more, so the signal grows en route to the brain.
The stimulus doesn't grow — the neural signal is amplified by divergence.
takeaway: Amplification = one cell activates many downstream (divergence) → signal grows.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person can just detect the difference between a 2.0 lb and a 2.2 lb weight. Assuming Weber's law holds, the smallest weight reliably distinguishable from a 5.0 lb weight is about:
rationale: Weber's law says the JND is a constant fraction of the baseline: k = ΔI/I = 0.2/2 = 0.1. At 5.0 lb, ΔI = kI = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 lb → about 5.5 lb.
why: 5.2 assumes a constant absolute JND (0.2 lb), exactly the misconception Weber's law corrects.
Correct. ΔI = 0.1 × 5 = 0.5 → 5.5 lb.
5.05 uses far too small a change; the JND grows with the baseline.
7.0 (a 2 lb change) is much larger than the proportional JND requires.
takeaway: JND is a constant proportion of the baseline (ΔI = kI), not a fixed amount. Heavier start → larger absolute change to notice.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: According to Weber's law, as the intensity of a baseline stimulus increases, the just-noticeable difference (JND):
choices: Grows in absolute terms while staying a constant proportion of the baseline
Stays the same fixed absolute amount
rationale: The JND is a fixed ratio (ΔI/I = k). A bigger baseline means a bigger absolute JND, but the same fraction.
why: Correct. Constant fraction → the absolute JND grows as the baseline rises.
A fixed absolute JND is precisely the misconception Weber's law corrects.
The absolute JND grows, not shrinks, with baseline.
It never reaches zero — there's always some detectable proportional change.
takeaway: Weber's law: the JND is a constant fraction of the stimulus, so the absolute difference needed grows with intensity.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Weber's law can be written ΔI = kI, where ΔI is the difference threshold and I is the background intensity. A graph of ΔI (y-axis) against I (x-axis) is:
choices: A straight line through the origin with slope k
A curve that levels off at high I
rationale: ΔI = kI is linear through the origin: as background intensity rises, the difference threshold rises proportionally. The ratio ΔI/I is constant (k) — but the plotted line itself is not flat; it climbs with slope k.
why: Correct. ΔI = kI → straight line, through the origin, slope k.
A flat line would mean a constant absolute JND regardless of intensity — the opposite of Weber's law. It's the ratio that's constant, not ΔI itself.
A leveling curve resembles Fechner's log relationship for perceived magnitude, not Weber's difference threshold.
ΔI is a function of I, so the relationship isn't vertical.
takeaway: ΔI = kI plots as a straight line through the origin (slope k). The constant thing is the RATIO ΔI/I — not the value of ΔI.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Two sensory dimensions have Weber fractions of k = 0.02 and k = 0.10. A smaller Weber fraction indicates:
choices: Greater sensitivity — a smaller proportional change can be detected
rationale: k is the fraction of the baseline needed to notice a change. A smaller k means a smaller relative change is detectable — finer discrimination, greater sensitivity.
why: Correct. k = 0.02 means a 2% change is noticeable; k = 0.10 needs 10% — the 0.02 dimension is more sensitive.
Smaller k is more sensitive, not less.
The Weber fraction concerns the difference threshold, not the absolute threshold.
The two fractions differ fivefold in sensitivity.
takeaway: Smaller Weber fraction (k) = finer discrimination = more sensitive to proportional change.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Weber's law describes the difference threshold. This is distinct from the absolute threshold, which is:
choices: The minimum stimulus intensity a person can detect 50% of the time
The largest change a person can tolerate
The point at which receptors stop adapting
rationale: The absolute threshold is the smallest amount of a stimulus detectable 50% of the time. Weber's law instead concerns the difference threshold (JND) — how much change is needed to notice a difference.
why: Correct. Absolute threshold = minimum detectable intensity (50% detection).
ΔI/I = k is Weber's law itself (the difference threshold), not the absolute threshold.
Weber's law isn't about tolerance limits.
That describes sensory adaptation, a different concept.
takeaway: Absolute threshold = can you detect it at all (minimum intensity). Difference threshold / JND (Weber's law) = can you tell two stimuli apart.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Adding 1 candle to a room lit by 10 candles produces a just-noticeable increase in brightness. To produce a just-noticeable increase in a room lit by 100 candles, one must add about:
rationale: k = ΔI/I = 1/10 = 0.1. At 100 candles, ΔI = kI = 0.1 × 100 = 10 candles — the same proportional change is required.
why: Correct. 0.1 × 100 = 10 candles.
1 candle worked at 10 candles (10%); at 100 candles it's only 1% — below the JND.
2 candles is 2% of 100 — still below the 10% needed.
100 candles is far more than the proportional JND requires.
takeaway: Same Weber fraction across intensities: 1/10 at ten candles = 10/100 at a hundred. The proportional change is what's fixed.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The absolute threshold of sensation is best defined as:
choices: The minimum stimulus intensity a person can detect 50% of the time
The smallest detectable difference between two stimuli
The maximum intensity a person can tolerate
The intensity at which a stimulus becomes painful
rationale: The absolute threshold is the minimum intensity of a stimulus needed to detect it 50% of the time. Detection is probabilistic, so it's pinned to the 50% point, not an all-or-nothing cutoff.
why: Correct. Minimum intensity detected on half of trials.
That's the difference threshold (JND) — a related but distinct concept.
Absolute threshold is the lower limit of detection, not an upper tolerance limit.
Pain onset is a separate phenomenon, not the absolute threshold.
takeaway: Absolute threshold = the minimum intensity detectable 50% of the time. The '50%' is the whole point — detection is probabilistic.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: When percent-correct detections are plotted against stimulus intensity, the result is an S-shaped (sigmoidal) curve rather than a sharp step. This shape reflects that:
choices: Detection is probabilistic — near threshold, the same faint stimulus is sometimes detected and sometimes missed
The absolute threshold is a fixed, unvarying value
Stronger stimuli are detected less often
Detection is impossible below the threshold and certain above it
rationale: Near the threshold, a faint stimulus is detected on some trials and missed on others (and it varies across people), so detection rises gradually with intensity — an S-curve. The threshold is defined at the 50%-detection point.
why: Correct. Trial-to-trial and person-to-person variability makes detection gradual, not all-or-nothing.
A fixed value would give a sharp step, not an S-curve.
Stronger stimuli are detected more often — the curve rises.
A true step function (impossible below, certain above) is exactly what the gradual S-curve contradicts.
takeaway: Detection near threshold is probabilistic → a sigmoidal curve. The threshold is the 50% point, not a hard cutoff.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A quality-control worker must (1) notice whether a faint tone is present at all, and (2) tell whether one tone is slightly louder than another. These two tasks measure, respectively:
rationale: Detecting whether a stimulus is present at all = absolute threshold. Detecting a change or difference between two stimuli = difference threshold (JND).
why: Correct. Present-or-not = absolute; tell-them-apart = difference.
Reversed.
The second task discriminates two stimuli — a difference threshold.
The first task detects presence — an absolute threshold.
takeaway: Absolute threshold = can you detect it at all? Difference threshold (JND) = can you tell two stimuli apart?

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person waiting anxiously for an important text notices a faint phone buzz they would normally miss. This best illustrates that the absolute threshold:
choices: Is not fixed — it's influenced by psychological states like expectation and motivation
Is a constant, unchanging property of the sensory receptors
Has been permanently lowered by the experience
Is the same thing as the difference threshold
rationale: Absolute thresholds shift with expectation, motivation, experience, and alertness. Anticipating the text makes the person more likely to detect a faint signal — the threshold is state-dependent, not fixed.
why: Correct. Expectation and motivation lower the effective threshold in the moment.
If it were fixed at the receptor level, the buzz wouldn't be noticed only when anticipated.
The shift is temporary and state-dependent, not a permanent recalibration.
That's a different concept — detecting a change between two stimuli.
takeaway: Absolute threshold isn't a fixed number — expectation, motivation, experience, and alertness move it.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Two people have identical hearing, but the one told to expect a faint tone reports detecting it far more often than the one who isn't. Signal detection theory explains this by proposing that detection depends on:
choices: Both sensory sensitivity and a decision criterion shaped by expectation and motivation
A fixed absolute threshold with no role for expectation
The difference threshold between the two listeners
rationale: Signal detection theory holds that detecting a weak signal depends on sensitivity plus a response criterion — how much evidence you require before saying 'yes.' Expectation and motivation shift the criterion, so identical ears give different detection rates.
why: Correct. Detection = sensitivity + a criterion influenced by expectation, motivation, and payoffs.
Sensitivity alone can't explain it — their hearing is identical.
A fixed threshold with no role for expectation is exactly what signal detection theory replaces.
The difference threshold is unrelated; this is about detecting a single faint signal.
takeaway: Signal detection theory: detecting a weak signal = sensory sensitivity + a decision criterion (shifted by expectation, motivation, rewards). It's why the absolute threshold isn't fixed.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A stimulus presented below a person's absolute threshold of sensation is described as:
choices: Subliminal — below the level of conscious detection
rationale: By definition, a subliminal stimulus falls below the absolute threshold — it isn't consciously detected (whether it can influence behavior is a separate, debated question).
why: Correct. Subliminal = below the absolute threshold, not consciously perceived.
Supraliminal is above threshold — consciously detectable.
The difference threshold concerns telling two stimuli apart, not detecting one faint stimulus.
The JND is the difference threshold, not a below-detection stimulus.
takeaway: Subliminal = below the absolute threshold (not consciously detected). Supraliminal = above it.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A drowsy night-shift worker repeatedly fails to notice a faint alarm that they easily detect when fully alert. This shift illustrates that the absolute threshold is influenced by:
rationale: The absolute threshold isn't fixed — alertness (with expectation, motivation, and experience) shifts it. A drowsy observer needs a stronger signal to reach the 50%-detection point.
why: The difference threshold concerns telling two stimuli apart, not detecting a faint one.
Correct. Arousal/alertness is one of the psychological states that shift the absolute threshold.
Wavelength is a property of the stimulus, not the reason detection changed with drowsiness.
Adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus; here detection varies with the worker's state.
takeaway: Alertness moves the absolute threshold: drowsy = higher threshold, alert = lower.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A new parent wakes to their own baby's faintest cry but sleeps through louder, unfamiliar street noise. Detecting the faint but familiar sound reflects the influence of what on the absolute threshold?
rationale: Experience and familiarity (a top-down factor) lower the absolute threshold for meaningful stimuli — why a parent detects their own baby's faint cry over louder but irrelevant noise.
why: The JND is a difference threshold, not the detection of one faint sound.
Weber's constant governs difference thresholds, not this effect.
Correct. Familiarity with a meaningful stimulus lowers the effective threshold for detecting it.
Pure bottom-up processing can't explain why a familiar, meaningful sound is favored — that's top-down influence.
takeaway: Familiar, meaningful stimuli are detected at lower intensities — experience shifts the absolute threshold (top-down).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In classic psychophysics, the absolute threshold for vision is often illustrated as a candle flame seen from about 30 miles away on a clear, dark night. This figure represents:
choices: The maximum light a person can tolerate
The smallest change in brightness detectable
The point of complete dark adaptation
The minimum light intensity detectable 50% of the time
rationale: The candle-at-30-miles figure classically illustrates the absolute threshold — the minimum stimulus intensity detectable 50% of the time.
why: Absolute threshold is a lower limit of detection, not an upper tolerance.
That's the difference threshold (JND), not the absolute threshold.
Dark adaptation is a separate process; the candle example illustrates the detection floor.
Correct. A vivid illustration of an absolute threshold — the least intense stimulus detectable half the time.
takeaway: Absolute threshold = the faintest detectable stimulus (50% of the time), e.g., a candle ~30 miles off on a dark night.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A stimulus presented so briefly that a viewer cannot consciously report seeing it still slightly biases a later choice. The stimulus was:
choices: Subliminal — below the absolute threshold, yet capable of weak priming effects
rationale: A subliminal stimulus is below the absolute threshold — not consciously perceived — yet may produce weak, short-lived priming. Contrast supraliminal: consciously detected.
why: Supraliminal means consciously detected — but the viewer couldn't report seeing it.
Correct. Below the absolute (conscious) threshold = subliminal; such stimuli can produce limited priming effects without awareness.
The difference threshold concerns discriminating two stimuli, not conscious detection of one.
'Terminal threshold' is the upper limit of sensation, unrelated here.
takeaway: Subliminal = below conscious detection (can weakly prime). Supraliminal = consciously perceived.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person can sense the position of their arm in space without looking at it. This submodality of somatosensation is:
rationale: Proprioception is the sense of the position and movement of the body in space — how you know where your arm is with your eyes closed.
why: Nociception is the sense of pain, not body position.
Thermoception senses temperature, not position.
Correct. Proprioception is the sense of body and limb position.
Mechanoreception senses pressure and touch, not limb position.
takeaway: Somatosensory submodalities: temperature = thermoception, pressure/touch = mechanoreception, pain = nociception, body position = proprioception.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In the somatosensory system, the intensity of a stimulus is encoded primarily by:
choices: The neuron's firing rate — faster firing signals a more intense stimulus
The location on the body where it occurs
How long the receptor takes to adapt
rationale: Stimulus intensity is rate-coded: a more intense stimulus makes the sensory neuron fire more rapidly. Slow firing = low intensity, fast firing = high intensity.
why: Receptor type encodes the modality (touch vs. pain vs. temperature), not intensity.
Correct. Intensity is signaled by firing rate — stronger stimulus, faster firing.
Location tells the brain where, not how intense.
Adaptation encodes timing (onset/offset), not intensity.
takeaway: Intensity = firing RATE (faster = stronger). Modality = which receptor. Location = where. Timing = adaptation pattern.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A fast-adapting mechanoreceptor fires a burst when a stimulus begins, falls silent during steady stimulation, then fires again when the stimulus is removed. This makes it best suited to detect:
choices: Changes in stimulation — its onset and its offset
The constant intensity of a sustained stimulus
The exact temperature of an object
The body location of an injury
rationale: Fast-adapting receptors fire at the onset and again at the offset of a stimulus, staying silent in between — ideal for detecting change rather than steady state (feeling a watch go on and come off, but not while it sits still).
why: Correct. Firing at onset and offset makes it a change detector — it flags when stimulation starts and stops.
A constant, sustained stimulus is exactly what a fast-adapting receptor stops responding to.
Temperature is thermoception; a fast-adapting mechanoreceptor isn't a thermometer.
Localizing injury depends on dermatomes and pain pathways, not adaptation pattern.
takeaway: Fast-adapting = change detector: fires when a stimulus starts and when it stops, silent during steady stimulation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Proprioceptors must continuously report joint position, and nociceptors must keep signaling ongoing injury. For these functions, the most useful firing pattern is:
choices: Fast-adapting, firing only at onset and offset
Rapidly adapting to silence within milliseconds
Firing only once the stimulus is removed
Non-adapting — steady firing that tracks the ongoing stimulus
rationale: Functions that must be monitored continuously — joint position, ongoing tissue damage — are best served by non-adapting (tonic) receptors that keep firing for as long as the stimulus lasts.
why: Fast-adapting would go silent during the sustained stimulus — you'd lose track of position or ongoing pain.
Rapid adaptation to silence is the opposite of what continuous monitoring needs.
Firing only at offset gives no signal during the stimulus itself.
Correct. Non-adapting (tonic) firing continuously reports the ongoing stimulus — essential for position sense and persistent pain.
takeaway: Non-adapting (tonic) keeps firing throughout → good for things you must track continuously (position, ongoing pain). Fast-adapting = change only.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The nervous system localizes where on the body a touch occurred largely because each spinal nerve carries sensation from a specific region of skin. These regions are called:
rationale: The body surface is divided into dermatomes — each a strip of skin whose sensory input travels through a single spinal nerve. This organization lets the brain localize where a stimulus occurred.
why: Myotomes are the muscle groups innervated by a spinal nerve — the motor analog, not the skin map.
Correct. A dermatome is the area of skin whose sensation is carried by one spinal nerve.
The homunculus is the body map in the cortex, not the skin regions of spinal nerves.
Not a standard term; dorsal root ganglia house cell bodies but aren't the skin map.
takeaway: Dermatome = skin region mapped to one spinal nerve (sensory). Myotome = muscle analog. Homunculus = cortical body map.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A somatosensory neuron fires strongly when a stimulus begins, gradually reduces its firing during continued stimulation, but keeps firing at a lower rate for as long as the stimulus is present. This timing pattern is:
rationale: Slow-adapting receptors respond strongly at onset, then reduce firing but continue at a lower rate for the stimulus's duration — between non-adapting (constant) and fast-adapting (onset/offset only).
why: Non-adapting fires at a constant rate — it wouldn't gradually decline.
Fast-adapting goes silent during steady stimulation, then fires again at offset — not a maintained lower rate.
Correct. Slow-adapting fires strongly at onset, then declines but continues while the stimulus lasts.
The neuron is clearly responding, so 'non-responsive' is wrong.
takeaway: Three timing classes: non-adapting (constant), slow-adapting (declines but continues), fast-adapting (onset + offset only, silent between).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person can tell two closely spaced points apart on a fingertip but feels only one point when the same two are applied to the back. This difference in spatial acuity is because the fingertip has:
choices: A lower absolute threshold for pain
A higher density of receptors with smaller receptive fields
rationale: Spatial acuity (the two-point threshold) depends on receptor density and receptive-field size: fingertips have dense receptors with small fields → fine discrimination; the back has the opposite.
why: Adaptation speed governs timing, not spatial resolution.
Pain threshold is unrelated to two-point spatial acuity.
Receptor adaptation class doesn't set spatial resolution.
Correct. Fingertips pack many receptors with small receptive fields (fine discrimination); the back has sparse receptors with large fields.
takeaway: Two-point discrimination is finest where receptors are dense with small receptive fields (fingertips, lips), poorest where sparse (back).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Whether a somatosensory stimulus is felt as warmth, pressure, or pain is determined primarily by:
choices: Which type of receptor and pathway is activated (a 'labeled line')
Where on the body it occurs
How long the receptor takes to adapt
rationale: The modality (warmth vs. pressure vs. pain) is set by which receptor type and pathway is activated — the 'labeled line' principle.
why: Firing rate codes intensity, not which modality is felt.
Correct. Modality is coded by which receptor/pathway carries the signal — a labeled line.
Location codes where, not what kind of sensation.
Adaptation codes timing, not modality.
takeaway: Somatosensory coding: modality = which receptor (labeled line), intensity = firing rate, location = dermatome, timing = adaptation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Grasping a hot mug and later an ice cube activates different receptors for each. This reflects that thermoreception uses:
choices: A single receptor that encodes temperature by firing rate alone
Separate populations of warm and cold receptors
rationale: Thermoreception relies on separate warm and cold receptor populations tuned to different ranges (with nociceptors signaling painful extremes) — not one receptor rate-coding all temperatures.
why: Temperature isn't handled by one rate-coding receptor; there are separate warm and cold types.
Nociceptors signal painful extremes, but normal warm/cold sensing uses dedicated thermoreceptors.
Correct. Distinct warm and cold thermoreceptors respond to different temperature ranges.
Proprioceptors sense body position, not temperature.
takeaway: Temperature is sensed by distinct warm and cold receptors; painful heat/cold additionally recruits nociceptors.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Proprioceptive information about muscle length and limb position comes largely from specialized receptors located in:
choices: The muscles and tendons (e.g., muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs)
rationale: Proprioception draws on receptors within muscles and tendons — muscle spindles (stretch/length) and Golgi tendon organs (tension) — to report limb position and movement.
why: Skin receptors handle touch/temperature/pain, not muscle length.
The cochlea is for hearing.
Otolithic organs sense head linear acceleration (vestibular), not limb proprioception.
Correct. Muscle spindles (length/stretch) and Golgi tendon organs (tension) supply proprioceptive signals.
takeaway: Proprioceptors live in muscle/tendon: muscle spindles (length/stretch) + Golgi tendon organs (tension).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person shakes their head "no," rotating it side to side. Which structure detects this rotational movement?
choices: The otolithic organs, via calcium carbonate crystals
The semicircular canals, as shifting endolymph bends hair cells
The cochlea, via the basilar membrane
rationale: The semicircular canals detect rotational (angular) acceleration. As the head rotates, the endolymph inside lags behind, bending hair cells and signaling the direction and speed of rotation.
why: Otolithic organs detect linear acceleration and head tilt, not rotation.
Correct. The canals sense rotation: head rotation makes the endolymph lag and bend hair cells.
The cochlea is for hearing, not balance.
The saccule detects linear (vertical) acceleration, not rotation.
takeaway: Semicircular canals = ROTATION (angular acceleration), sensed by endolymph movement bending hair cells.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A car suddenly accelerates forward, pressing you back into the seat. Which structures detect this linear acceleration?
choices: The otolithic organs (utricle and saccule), via CaCO₃ crystals pulling on hair cells
The cochlea, via hair cells on the basilar membrane
rationale: The otolithic organs — the utricle and saccule — detect linear acceleration and head tilt. They contain calcium carbonate crystals (otoliths) in a gel; when you accelerate or tilt, the crystals shift and pull on hair cells, triggering action potentials.
why: Correct. Otolithic organs sense linear acceleration and head position; their CaCO₃ otoliths shift and pull on hair cells.
Semicircular canals sense rotation, not straight-line acceleration.
The cochlea handles hearing, not acceleration.
Dermatomes are skin regions for touch localization, unrelated to acceleration.
takeaway: Otolithic organs (utricle + saccule) = LINEAR acceleration + head tilt, via CaCO₃ otoliths pulling hair cells.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Which correctly pairs the vestibular structures with what they sense?
choices: Semicircular canals → linear acceleration; otolithic organs → rotation
Semicircular canals → rotational acceleration; otolithic organs → linear acceleration and head tilt
rationale: Division of labor: the semicircular canals detect rotational (angular) acceleration, while the otolithic organs detect linear acceleration and head position relative to gravity.
why: Reversed — canals do rotation, otolithic organs do linear.
The otolithic organs detect linear acceleration, not rotation.
Correct. Canals = rotation; otolithic organs = linear acceleration + tilt.
The semicircular canals detect rotation, not linear acceleration.
takeaway: Canals = rotation. Otoliths = linear + tilt. That split is the core of the vestibular system.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The otolithic organs depend on gravity pulling their calcium-carbonate crystals against hair cells. In the microgravity of orbit, an astronaut would most likely experience:
choices: Failure of the semicircular canals to sense rotation
Impaired sensing of head position and linear acceleration, causing spatial disorientation
rationale: Otoliths work because gravity pulls the dense CaCO₃ crystals against the hair cells. In microgravity there's no such pull, so head-position and linear-acceleration sensing is degraded — a major cause of space-related spatial disorientation. The rotation-sensing canals, which rely on fluid inertia, still function.
why: Hearing (cochlea) isn't affected this way by microgravity.
Balance is impaired, not improved, without gravity acting on the otoliths.
The semicircular canals sense rotation via endolymph inertia and still work in microgravity.
Correct. Without gravity to pull the otoliths, head-position and linear-acceleration cues degrade → disorientation.
takeaway: Otoliths need gravity; microgravity degrades linear/tilt sensing → disorientation. Semicircular canals (fluid inertia) still work.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After spinning rapidly on a chair and abruptly stopping, a person feels as if they are still spinning. The best explanation is that:
choices: The endolymph in the semicircular canals keeps moving after the head stops, signaling rotation that is no longer occurring
The otoliths detached from the hair cells
The cochlea was overstimulated by the spinning
Gravity reversed on the otolithic organs
rationale: Endolymph has inertia: when you suddenly stop spinning, the fluid keeps moving for a moment, continuing to bend the hair cells. The brain reads this as ongoing rotation — the post-rotatory dizziness/vertigo effect.
why: Correct. Endolymph continues to move briefly after you stop, bending hair cells and falsely signaling rotation.
Otoliths don't detach; and they sense linear acceleration, not spinning.
The cochlea is for hearing and isn't the source of spinning dizziness.
Gravity doesn't reverse; the effect is endolymph inertia.
takeaway: Post-spin dizziness = endolymph keeps moving after you stop, so the canals falsely signal rotation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The inner ear houses both the vestibular organs and one structure devoted to hearing rather than balance. That structure is the:
rationale: The cochlea is the organ of hearing. The semicircular canals, utricle, and saccule are all vestibular (balance) structures. They share the inner ear but serve different senses.
why: The utricle is a vestibular (balance) organ — linear acceleration and tilt.
Correct. The cochlea is the auditory organ; the others are vestibular (balance).
The semicircular canals are vestibular — rotational sensing.
The saccule is a vestibular organ — vertical linear acceleration.
takeaway: Inner ear: cochlea = HEARING; semicircular canals + utricle + saccule = BALANCE (vestibular).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Within the otolithic organs, the utricle and saccule specialize for different directions of linear acceleration. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Utricle → horizontal acceleration; saccule → vertical acceleration
rationale: The otolithic organs split linear motion by axis: the utricle detects horizontal acceleration and head tilt; the saccule detects vertical acceleration (like an elevator).
why: Reversed.
Correct. The utricle senses horizontal linear acceleration (and head tilt); the saccule senses vertical (e.g., an elevator).
Rotation is the semicircular canals' job, not the otolithic organs'.
They cover different axes — one horizontal, one vertical — not both vertical.
takeaway: Utricle = horizontal linear acceleration + tilt. Saccule = vertical linear acceleration (elevator).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Both the semicircular canals and the otolithic organs convert motion into neural signals using the same basic mechanism:
choices: Release of calcium carbonate into the blood
Bending of hair-cell stereocilia opens ion channels, depolarizing the cell
rationale: The vestibular system uses hair cells as its transducer: whether by endolymph (canals) or shifting otoliths, the stereocilia bend, opening ion channels and depolarizing the cell to fire action potentials.
why: Photopigment bleaching is vision (photoreceptors), not the vestibular system.
Otoliths are CaCO₃ crystals that pull on hair cells; they aren't released into blood.
Correct. In both, fluid or otolith movement bends hair-cell stereocilia, opening channels and depolarizing the cell → APs.
Pupil constriction is a visual reflex, unrelated to vestibular transduction.
takeaway: Vestibular transduction = bending hair-cell stereocilia → depolarization. Same mechanism in canals and otolith organs.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Each ear has three semicircular canals oriented roughly perpendicular to one another. The functional reason is to:
choices: Detect rotation in any plane (all three axes of head movement)
rationale: The three semicircular canals sit in roughly orthogonal planes, so together they detect rotational acceleration about any axis — however the head turns, some canal registers it.
why: Sound amplification is the middle ear/cochlea, not the canals.
Linear acceleration is the otolithic organs' job.
The canals don't 'regenerate' endolymph; the geometry is about sensing all rotational planes.
Correct. Three orthogonal canals let the system register rotation about any axis — nodding, shaking, tilting.
takeaway: Three orthogonal canals per ear → rotation in any plane can be sensed (yaw, pitch, roll).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Reading a book in a moving car often causes nausea. The leading explanation is that:
choices: The vestibular system senses motion while the eyes, fixed on the page, signal stillness — a sensory conflict
The semicircular canals have stopped working
rationale: Motion sickness is best explained by sensory conflict: the vestibular organs sense the car's motion while the eyes, fixed on a page, signal stillness. The mismatch produces nausea.
why: Otoliths don't detach; the problem is conflicting sensory information.
Correct. Motion sickness arises from a mismatch: the vestibular system reports movement, but vision reports a stationary page.
The cochlea (hearing) isn't the source of car sickness.
The canals are working fine — they're what report the motion the eyes don't.
takeaway: Motion sickness = vestibular–visual sensory conflict (inner ear says moving, eyes say still).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A radiologist reports a tumor on a scan that is in fact completely normal (no tumor present). In signal detection terms, this outcome is a:
rationale: A false alarm is responding 'signal present' when no signal actually exists (signal absent + 'yes').
why: A hit is a 'yes' when the signal is present — but here no tumor was present.
A miss is a 'no' when the signal is present — but she responded 'yes.'
Correct. Signal absent (no tumor) + responded 'yes' = false alarm.
A correct rejection is a 'no' when no signal is present — she said 'yes,' so it isn't this.
takeaway: Four outcomes: Hit = yes/present, Miss = no/present, False alarm = yes/absent, Correct rejection = no/absent.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An airport screener fails to flag a bag that actually contains a prohibited item. This outcome is a:
rationale: A miss is responding 'no signal' when the signal is actually present (signal present + 'no').
why: Correct. Signal present (prohibited item) + responded 'no' (didn't flag) = miss.
A false alarm is flagging a bag that's actually safe — the opposite.
A hit would be correctly flagging the dangerous bag; here it was missed.
A correct rejection is correctly not flagging a safe bag; this bag was dangerous.
takeaway: Miss = the signal was there and you said no. In screening, misses are the dangerous errors.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In signal detection theory, d′ reflects the separation between the signal and noise distributions. A larger d′ means:
choices: The observer has become more conservative
The signal is easier to distinguish from noise — greater sensitivity
The observer will make more false alarms
rationale: d′ (sensitivity) is the distance between the means of the noise and signal distributions. A bigger d′ means the two are farther apart and easier to tell apart — independent of the observer's decision strategy.
why: That describes the criterion (c), not d′. d′ is independent of strategy.
Correct. Larger d′ = greater separation of signal and noise = easier discrimination (higher sensitivity).
False-alarm rate depends on the criterion, not d′.
Shifting the criterion is a change in c, not d′.
takeaway: d′ = sensitivity (how separable signal is from noise). Bigger d′ = easier detection. It's separate from the criterion.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An observer adopts a conservative strategy, saying "signal present" only when absolutely certain. Compared with a liberal strategy, this produces:
choices: More false alarms but fewer misses
More hits and more false alarms
Fewer false alarms but more misses
rationale: A conservative criterion (say 'yes' only when very sure) minimizes false alarms but increases misses. A liberal criterion (say 'yes' readily) does the reverse. The criterion sets the trade-off between the two error types.
why: That's the liberal pattern — a conservative criterion reduces false alarms.
Saying 'yes' rarely produces fewer hits and false alarms, not more.
Shifting the criterion trades one error type for the other, so both change.
Correct. A high (conservative) criterion means few false alarms but more misses.
takeaway: Conservative criterion → fewer false alarms, more misses. Liberal → more hits/false alarms, fewer misses.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A radiologist is told that missing a tumor is far worse than a false alarm, so she starts flagging even faint, ambiguous spots. In signal detection terms, she has:
choices: Shifted her criterion to be more liberal, without changing her sensitivity (d′)
Eliminated the possibility of a miss
rationale: This is the central SDT insight: sensitivity (d′) and decision criterion (c) are separable. Rewards, costs, expectations, and motivation shift the criterion without changing how well the observer can actually discriminate signal from noise.
why: Correct. Payoffs shifted her decision criterion (toward liberal); her perceptual sensitivity (d′) is unchanged.
Her ability to distinguish tumor from normal tissue (d′) hasn't improved — only her willingness to say 'yes.'
d′ isn't decreasing either; the change is in criterion, not sensitivity.
A liberal criterion reduces misses but doesn't eliminate them.
takeaway: Payoffs/motivation move the CRITERION (bias), not d′. Detection = sensitivity + a separable decision criterion.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: On a foggy night, a driver correctly decides not to brake when there is in fact no red light ahead. This correct "no signal" judgment is a:
rationale: A correct rejection is correctly responding 'no signal' when the signal is genuinely absent (signal absent + 'no').
why: A miss is failing to respond to a signal that is present — but here there was no red light.
Correct. Signal absent (no red light) + responded 'no' (didn't brake) = correct rejection.
A hit is a correct 'yes' to a present signal; there was no signal here.
A false alarm is braking for a red light that isn't there — the opposite of what happened.
takeaway: Correct rejection = nothing was there and you correctly said no. The 'good' outcome on the signal-absent side.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A sonar operator correctly reports “enemy submarine present” when there genuinely is one. In signal detection terms, this is a:
rationale: A hit is correctly responding 'signal present' when the signal truly is present (present + 'yes').
why: A false alarm is a 'yes' when nothing is there.
A correct rejection is a 'no' when nothing is there.
Correct. Signal present + responded 'yes' = hit.
A miss is a 'no' when the signal is present.
takeaway: Hit = the signal was there and you correctly said yes — the good outcome on the signal-present side.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In signal detection theory, “noise” refers to:
choices: Only loud sounds in the environment
The intensity of the true signal
Background stimulation and internal variability that can be mistaken for the signal
rationale: Noise is the background activity — external stimulation plus internal (neural) variability — that is always present. Detection is telling a real signal apart from fluctuating noise.
why: 'Noise' is any interfering background, not just literal sound.
The criterion is the decision rule, not the background noise.
That describes the signal, not the noise it must be distinguished from.
Correct. Noise is the ever-present background (external and internal/neural) the signal must be told apart from.
takeaway: Noise = the ever-present background (external + internal) the signal must be distinguished from.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An anxious airport screener flags nearly every bag that looks even slightly unusual, rarely letting anything questionable pass. This liberal criterion will produce:
choices: Many hits but also many false alarms
Few hits and few false alarms
rationale: A liberal criterion means saying 'signal present' on little evidence: it maximizes hits (few misses) at the cost of many false alarms — the mirror of a conservative criterion.
why: Saying 'yes' readily produces fewer misses, not more.
Correct. A liberal criterion (say 'yes' readily) catches most real threats (hits) but flags many harmless bags (false alarms).
A liberal criterion increases both hits and false alarms.
Flagging readily guarantees more false alarms, not zero.
takeaway: Liberal criterion → more hits and more false alarms, fewer misses. Conservative → the reverse.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After months of training, a radiologist gets genuinely better at telling real tumors from normal tissue — her hit rate rises while her false-alarm rate falls. In signal detection terms, she has:
rationale: When both hits rise and false alarms fall, the signal and noise distributions are better separated for the observer — a rise in sensitivity (d′). A pure criterion shift only trades one error for the other.
why: A liberal criterion would raise hits but also raise false alarms, not lower them.
A conservative criterion would lower false alarms but also lower hits.
Correct. Raising hits while lowering false alarms means better discrimination — a higher d′.
This is about discriminating signal from noise (d′), not a simple detection-floor shift.
takeaway: Criterion shift trades hits↔false alarms. Improving BOTH at once = a genuine rise in sensitivity (d′), e.g., from training.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A person encounters a completely novel object they have never seen and builds a perception of it purely from its edges, colors, and shapes, with no prior expectation. This is:
rationale: Bottom-up processing begins with the stimulus: perception is assembled from incoming sensory features, without preconceived constructs. Data-driven.
why: Top-down processing relies on prior knowledge and expectation — absent here for a novel object.
Correct. Building perception from the raw stimulus features, with no prior expectation, is bottom-up (data-driven) processing.
A perceptual set is a readiness to perceive based on expectation — a top-down influence.
The stimulus-first build is a processing direction, not a form of logical reasoning.
takeaway: Bottom-up = start with the stimulus, build perception from features. Data-driven, no prior expectation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Searching a crowded “Where’s Waldo?” page, you use your knowledge of Waldo’s red-striped shirt and glasses to guide your search. This reliance on prior knowledge to direct perception is:
rationale: Top-down processing uses background knowledge, context, and expectation to shape perception — like using a mental template of Waldo to guide your search.
why: Bottom-up would build perception from the raw image with no prior template.
Sensory adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus — unrelated to guided search.
Correct. Using stored knowledge and expectation to guide what you look for is top-down (concept-driven) processing.
Feature detection is the bottom-up analysis of basic features, not the knowledge-guided search described.
takeaway: Top-down = prior knowledge/expectation guides perception (Where's Waldo, reading in context). Concept-driven.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The key difference between bottom-up and top-down processing is that:
choices: Bottom-up is data-driven (built from the stimulus), while top-down is concept-driven (guided by prior knowledge and expectation)
Bottom-up is concept-driven, while top-down is data-driven
Both begin with the observer's expectations
Neither makes any use of sensory input
rationale: Bottom-up = data-driven (stimulus → perception). Top-down = concept-driven (knowledge/expectation → how the stimulus is interpreted).
why: Correct. Bottom-up starts with the sensory data; top-down starts with concepts, knowledge, and expectations.
Reversed — bottom-up is data-driven and top-down is concept-driven.
Bottom-up specifically does not begin with expectation; it begins with the stimulus.
Both ultimately involve sensory input; they differ in how much prior knowledge guides its interpretation.
takeaway: Bottom-up = data-driven (stimulus first). Top-down = concept-driven (knowledge first).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In the Kanizsa illusion, viewers perceive the edges of a shape (such as a cube or triangle) that is not actually drawn, because the brain fills it in from context. This “seeing what isn’t there” is an example of:
rationale: The Kanizsa illusion is a classic top-down effect: expectation and context lead the brain to construct contours that aren't physically present — which is why top-down perception can be fooled.
why: Pure bottom-up processing would register only the marks actually present, not the illusory edges.
The absolute threshold is about detecting a faint stimulus, not filling in missing contours.
Transduction is converting a stimulus into neural signals, not constructing an illusory shape.
Correct. Filling in edges that aren't in the stimulus, based on context, is top-down processing — and shows top-down can yield perceptions the raw data don't fully support.
takeaway: Illusory contours (Kanizsa) = top-down filling-in. Top-down can produce perceptions the stimulus doesn't actually contain.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A sloppily written word is illegible on its own but easily read inside a full sentence, because the surrounding words create an expectation. This use of context to interpret ambiguous input is:
rationale: When context and expectation let you interpret otherwise ambiguous input, that's top-down processing — the same mechanism behind reading messy handwriting fluently in a sentence.
why: Bottom-up would rely only on the ambiguous marks themselves, which were illegible in isolation.
Correct. Using surrounding context and expectation to interpret ambiguous input is top-down processing.
Rate coding is how intensity is signaled by firing frequency — unrelated.
A difference threshold is about telling two stimuli apart, not using context to read a word.
takeaway: Context/expectation resolving ambiguous input = top-down processing.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Which statement about bottom-up and top-down processing is most accurate?
choices: Everyday perception usually combines both — sensory input (bottom-up) is interpreted using prior knowledge (top-down)
Perception uses only one of the two at any time
Bottom-up processing is immune to all perceptual error
Top-down processing ignores the actual stimulus entirely
rationale: Real perception is an interaction: bottom-up sensory data and top-down knowledge/expectation work together. Neither is used alone, and bottom-up isn't infallible.
why: Correct. Normal perception integrates both: raw sensory data and knowledge-driven interpretation operate together.
The two typically operate together, not in isolation.
Bottom-up processing can still be fooled by ambiguous or degraded stimuli — it isn't error-proof.
Top-down processing shapes interpretation of the stimulus but doesn't ignore it.
takeaway: Everyday perception = bottom-up + top-down together. Bottom-up isn't error-proof; top-down doesn't ignore the stimulus.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Watching a basketball game on television, you perceive a fluid, meaningful game rather than a grid of individual colored pixels. This tendency to perceive organized wholes rather than isolated parts is the central idea of:
rationale: The Gestalt principles describe how the mind organizes sensory parts into meaningful wholes — 'the whole is greater than the sum of its parts.'
why: Weber's law is about difference thresholds (JND), not perceptual grouping.
Signal detection theory concerns detecting a signal in noise, not organizing parts into wholes.
Correct. Gestalt psychology holds we perceive organized wholes — the whole is more than the sum of its parts.
Sensory adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus, unrelated to grouping.
takeaway: Gestalt = we perceive organized wholes, not isolated parts. The grouping laws describe how.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A display of alternating columns of squares and circles is automatically seen as vertical columns rather than horizontal rows, because like items group together. This is the Gestalt principle of:
rationale: Similarity: we group elements that resemble one another (shape, color, size) — why like-columns are seen together.
why: Correct. Grouping items that look alike (all squares, all circles) is similarity.
Proximity groups items by nearness in space, not by appearance.
Closure is filling in missing parts of a figure, not grouping like items.
Common fate groups items by shared motion, not by appearance.
takeaway: Similarity = group by looking alike. (Proximity = nearness; common fate = motion.)

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Dots that are physically closer to one another are perceived as belonging to the same cluster, while dots farther apart seem to form separate groups. This is the principle of:
rationale: Proximity: elements that are close together are grouped into the same unit.
why: Similarity groups by appearance, not distance.
Correct. Grouping elements by how near they are in space is proximity.
Continuity concerns perceiving smooth continuous paths, not clustering by nearness.
Prägnanz is the preference for the simplest overall interpretation, not spatial clustering.
takeaway: Proximity = group by nearness in space.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Three angled shapes are arranged so that viewers 'see' a complete triangle even though no triangle is actually drawn — the mind fills in the missing edges. This is the Gestalt principle of:
rationale: Closure: the mind fills in gaps to perceive a complete, whole object — e.g., 'seeing' a triangle whose edges aren't drawn.
why: Continuity is perceiving lines as following the smoothest continuous path, not completing a figure.
Symmetry is perceiving balanced forms around a center, not filling gaps.
Proximity groups elements by nearness, not by completing an outline.
Correct. Filling in missing information to perceive a complete figure is closure.
takeaway: Closure = fill in missing information to complete a figure (the illusory triangle).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: When two lines cross, we perceive each as a single continuous line following the smoothest path, rather than as four separate segments meeting at a point. This is the principle of:
rationale: Continuity (good continuation): elements on a line or curve are perceived as following the smoothest, most continuous path.
why: Correct. Perceiving elements as following the smoothest, most continuous path is continuity.
Closure completes missing parts of a figure; here nothing is missing — it's about smooth flow.
Similarity groups by appearance, not by smooth continuation.
Common fate groups by shared motion, not by continuous line.
takeaway: Continuity = perceive the smoothest continuous path (crossing lines seen as two flowing lines).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Shown a pattern of overlapping shapes, the brain interprets the Olympic logo as five simple interlocking rings rather than a set of complex irregular figures. This preference for the simplest, most stable interpretation is the law of:
rationale: Prägnanz (law of good figure/simplicity): perception defaults to the simplest, most stable form — five clean rings rather than complex shapes.
why: Proximity groups by nearness, not by choosing the simplest interpretation.
Common fate groups by shared motion.
Correct. The preference for the simplest, most orderly interpretation is Prägnanz.
Past experience uses prior learning; here it's about defaulting to the simplest form.
takeaway: Prägnanz = we default to the simplest, most stable interpretation (Olympic rings).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In a field of scattered, identical dots, those moving upward are perceived as one group and those moving downward as another. This grouping by shared motion is the law of:
rationale: Common fate: elements moving in the same direction are grouped together — even identical dots split into units by shared motion.
why: Similarity groups by appearance — but here the dots are identical; only motion differs.
Correct. Grouping elements that move together in the same direction is common fate.
Continuity concerns smooth continuous paths, not shared movement.
Closure is completing a figure, not grouping by motion.
takeaway: Common fate = group by shared motion/direction. (Similarity = group by appearance.)

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Two simple shapes placed side by side could be perceived as a single novel form or as two familiar letters; a fluent reader perceives the familiar letters. This influence of prior learning on grouping is the Gestalt law of:
rationale: Past experience: familiar patterns learned over time influence how we group and interpret stimuli — a reader sees letters where a non-reader sees shapes.
why: Correct. When prior learning shapes how elements are grouped, that's the law of past experience.
Prägnanz is about defaulting to the simplest form, not prior learning.
Proximity groups by spatial nearness, independent of experience.
Common fate groups by shared motion, not by learning.
takeaway: Past experience = prior learning guides grouping/interpretation (seeing familiar letters).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Looking at Rubin's famous image, a viewer sees either a white vase or two black faces in profile — but not both at once — depending on which region is taken as the object and which as the background. This is the Gestalt principle of:
rationale: Figure-ground organization separates a scene into a figure (the object) and the ground (background). Rubin's vase is reversible because either region can be taken as the figure.
why: Correct. Segmenting a scene into a figure (object of focus) and a ground (background) is figure-ground; the vase/faces image is reversible because either region can be the figure.
Closure fills in missing parts of a figure, not object-vs-background segmentation.
Similarity groups items by appearance, not figure vs. ground.
Common fate groups by shared motion.
takeaway: Figure-ground = separate the object (figure) from its background (ground). Rubin's vase = the classic reversible figure.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Presented with a scattered set of brackets, viewers group them into symmetrical pairs balanced around a center, perceiving orderly units rather than random marks. This is the Gestalt principle of:
rationale: Symmetry: the mind perceives objects as symmetrical forms balanced around a center point, favoring orderly, balanced units.
why: Proximity groups by nearness in space, not by symmetry.
Correct. Perceiving balanced, symmetrical forms organized around a center point is symmetry.
Continuity concerns smooth continuous paths, not balanced pairing.
Past experience uses prior learning, not symmetrical organization.
takeaway: Symmetry = perceive balanced, symmetrical forms around a center.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The ambiguous middle character in “A 13 C” is read as the letter “B,” but the identical mark in “12 13 14” is read as the number “13.” The surrounding items change how the same stimulus is perceived. This influence is best described as:
choices: A contextual effect on perceptual organization
rationale: Contextual effects: the surrounding context establishes how an ambiguous stimulus is organized — the same mark reads as 'B' among letters and '13' among numbers.
why: The absolute threshold is about detecting a faint stimulus, not context-driven interpretation.
Sensory adaptation is reduced response to a constant stimulus.
Correct. Context — the surrounding stimuli — determines how an ambiguous item is organized and interpreted.
Rate coding is how intensity is signaled by firing frequency.
