takeaway: LMN damage = atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia (all 'down'). UMN = 'up' (hyper).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The motor unit & lower motor neurons
stem: The small, involuntary muscle twitches seen with lower motor neuron damage are called:
rationale: Fasciculations = involuntary skeletal-muscle twitches — a hallmark lower-motor-neuron sign.
why: Retinal fibrillations aren't a thing; fasciculations are muscle twitches.
Correct. Fasciculations are visible involuntary twitches of skeletal muscle, a hallmark LMN sign.
Saccades are rapid eye movements, not muscle twitches from LMN damage.
Tonic-clonic seizures are a generalized seizure type, not LMN twitches.
takeaway: Fasciculations = involuntary muscle twitches (LMN sign).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The fast-adapting mechanoreceptor in the superficial skin that detects light touch and flutter with a small receptive field is the:
rationale: Meissner's corpuscle = fast-adapting, superficial, light touch/flutter, small receptive field.
why: Pacinian corpuscles are deep, fast-adapting receptors for vibration, with large receptive fields.
Correct. Meissner's corpuscles are fast-adapting, superficial receptors for light touch/flutter with small receptive fields (fine spatial detail, velocity).
Ruffini endings are slow-adapting stretch receptors.
Merkel discs are slow-adapting fine-touch/pressure receptors.
takeaway: Meissner = fast-adapting, light touch/flutter, small field (superficial).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The slow-adapting mechanoreceptor that senses sustained fine touch, pressure, and edges/detail with a small receptive field is the:
rationale: Merkel disc = slow-adapting, sustained fine touch/pressure, small receptive field (detail).
why: Pacinian corpuscles are fast-adapting vibration receptors.
Meissner's corpuscles are fast-adapting flutter receptors.
Ruffini endings sense skin stretch (slow-adapting, large field).
Correct. Merkel discs are slow-adapting receptors for sustained fine touch/pressure and fine spatial detail.
takeaway: Merkel = slow-adapting, fine touch/pressure/detail (sustained).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The deep, fast-adapting mechanoreceptor that detects vibration and deep pressure (responding to acceleration) with a large receptive field is the:
rationale: Pacinian corpuscle = deep, fast-adapting, vibration/deep pressure, large field. Mnemonic: 'Phone vibrates.'
why: Correct. Pacinian corpuscles are deep, fast-adapting receptors for vibration/deep pressure with large receptive fields (mnemonic: Pacinian = Phone vibrates).
Merkel discs are slow-adapting fine-touch receptors.
Meissner's corpuscles are superficial flutter receptors with small fields.
Ruffini endings are slow-adapting stretch receptors.
takeaway: Pacinian = deep, fast-adapting, vibration (Phone vibrates).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The slow-adapting mechanoreceptor in the deeper dermis that detects skin stretch, with a large receptive field, is the:
rationale: Ruffini ending = slow-adapting, skin stretch, large field. Mnemonic: Ruffini = stRetch.
why: Meissner's corpuscles sense flutter (fast-adapting, small field).
Pacinian corpuscles sense vibration (fast-adapting).
Correct. Ruffini endings are slow-adapting receptors for skin stretch (mnemonic: Ruffini = stRetch), with large receptive fields.
Merkel discs sense fine touch/pressure, not stretch.
takeaway: Ruffini = slow-adapting, skin stRetch, large field.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Sorted by adaptation, which pairing is correct?
choices: Fast-adapting: Merkel & Ruffini; slow-adapting: Meissner & Pacinian
Fast-adapting: Meissner & Pacinian (detect change/vibration); slow-adapting: Merkel & Ruffini (detect sustained pressure/stretch)
rationale: Fast-adapting = Meissner + Pacinian (change/vibration); slow-adapting = Merkel + Ruffini (sustained pressure/stretch).
why: Reversed — Merkel and Ruffini are the slow-adapting pair.
Correct. Fast-adapting (Meissner, Pacinian) signal change and vibration; slow-adapting (Merkel, Ruffini) signal sustained pressure and stretch.
Merkel and Ruffini are slow-adapting, not fast.
Meissner and Pacinian are fast-adapting, not slow.
takeaway: Fast-adapting: Meissner + Pacinian. Slow-adapting: Merkel + Ruffini.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Mechanoreceptors sense pressure/vibration/touch, nociceptors sense pain, and thermoreceptors sense temperature. Which stimulus–receptor pairing is correct?
rationale: Receptor classes: mechano (touch/pressure/vibration), noci (pain), thermo (temperature), photo (light), chemo (chemicals).
why: Chemoreceptors detect chemicals, not light.
Mechanoreceptors detect pressure/touch; thermoreceptors detect temperature.
Nociceptors detect pain/noxious stimuli, not sound.

Correct. Photoreceptors (rods/cones) detect light. Mechanoreceptors = pressure/touch/vibration; nociceptors = pain; thermoreceptors = temperature; chemoreceptors = chemicals (taste/smell, blood pH/CO₂).
takeaway: Mechano=touch, noci=pain, thermo=temp, photo=light, chemo=chemicals.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: Every reflex has two parts: an afferent limb and an efferent limb. These carry, respectively:
choices: The motor response and the sensory stimulus
The sensory stimulus (afferent) and the motor response (efferent)
rationale: A reflex = afferent (sensory stimulus in) + efferent (motor response out).
why: Reversed — afferent is sensory (in), efferent is motor (out).
A reflex arc has one sensory and one motor limb, not two sensory.
Correct. The afferent limb carries the sensory stimulus into the CNS; the efferent limb carries the motor response back out.
It has one sensory and one motor limb, not two motor.
takeaway: Reflex = afferent (stimulus in) + efferent (response out).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: The knee-jerk reflex — a muscle contracting after it's stretched, as a protective response — is the:
rationale: The muscle stretch reflex (knee-jerk) is ipsilateral and monosynaptic — a stretched muscle contracts protectively.
why: Correct. The muscle stretch (myotatic) reflex causes a stretched muscle to contract; afferent and efferent limbs are on the SAME side (ipsilateral), and it's monosynaptic.
The withdrawal reflex pulls a limb away from a painful stimulus, a different reflex.
The corneal reflex is the blink to eye stimulation.
The startle reflex is a whole-body response to a sudden stimulus.
takeaway: Muscle stretch reflex = stretched muscle contracts (ipsilateral, monosynaptic).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: The sensory receptors within a muscle that detect stretch and initiate the stretch reflex are the:
rationale: Muscle spindles detect stretch and send afferent signals that trigger the stretch reflex.
why: Pacinian corpuscles are skin vibration receptors, not muscle stretch sensors.
Merkel discs sense fine touch in skin, not muscle stretch.
Cochlear hair cells are for hearing.
Correct. Muscle spindles are the stretch-sensing proprioceptors whose afferent (somatosensory) neurons trigger the reflex.
takeaway: Muscle spindles = stretch sensors that trigger the reflex.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: For the stretch reflex to work, when the stretched muscle is excited to contract, the opposing (antagonist) muscle on the other side is:
rationale: Reciprocal inhibition: the antagonist muscle is inhibited while the agonist contracts — required for the reflex to move the limb.
why: If the antagonist also contracted, the limb couldn't move — it must be inhibited.
Correct. Reciprocal inhibition: the antagonist muscle is inhibited so the reflex movement isn't opposed — necessary for the reflex to occur.
The antagonist is inhibited, not destroyed.
It must be actively inhibited, not left unaffected.
takeaway: Reciprocal inhibition = antagonist muscle inhibited so the reflex can move the limb.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: In the autonomic nervous system, the sympathetic (fight-or-flight) division has a characteristic ganglionic pattern of:
choices: A long preganglionic then a short postganglionic axon
A single axon straight to the target
A short preganglionic axon (ganglia near the spine) then a long postganglionic axon
rationale: Sympathetic = short preganglionic (ganglia near spine) → long postganglionic. Parasympathetic = long then short.
why: That's the parasympathetic pattern (long then short).
The autonomic pathway is a two-neuron chain with a ganglion, not one axon.
Correct. Sympathetic: SHORT preganglionic (ganglia sit close to the spinal cord) → LONG postganglionic to the target. Parasympathetic is the reverse.
There is a ganglionic synapse; both divisions have ganglia.
takeaway: Sympathetic = short-then-long. Parasympathetic = long-then-short.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
idea: The muscle stretch reflex & autonomic pathways
stem: The sympathetic division originates from the middle of the spinal cord (thoracolumbar), while the parasympathetic division originates from:
choices: The brainstem and the bottom of the spinal cord (craniosacral)
The middle of the spinal cord as well
rationale: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle cord); parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral cord).
why: Correct. Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle); parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral cord).
That's the sympathetic origin; parasympathetic is craniosacral.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, not autonomic outflow origin.
Free nerve endings are sensory receptors, not autonomic origins.
takeaway: Sympathetic = thoracolumbar (middle). Parasympathetic = craniosacral (brainstem + sacral).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In the CNS, gray matter and white matter are distinguished by their contents:
choices: Gray matter = myelinated axons; white matter = somas
Gray matter = neuron cell bodies (somas); white matter = myelinated axons
rationale: Gray matter = neuron cell bodies; white matter = myelinated axons (myelin = white).
why: Reversed — gray = somas, white = myelinated axons.
Gray matter contains cell bodies, not only axons.
Correct. Gray matter holds most neuron somas; white matter is made of myelinated axon tracts (myelin gives the white color).
White matter is axons, not cell bodies.
takeaway: Gray matter = somas. White matter = myelinated axons.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The arrangement of gray and white matter differs between the spinal cord and the brain:
choices: In the spinal cord gray is inside and white outside; in the brain white is inside and gray (cortex) outside
Both have gray outside and white inside
Both have gray inside and white outside
The brain has no gray matter
rationale: Spinal cord: gray inside, white outside. Brain: white inside, gray (cortex) outside.
why: Correct. Spinal cord: gray inside (butterfly), white outside. Brain: gray outside (cortex), white inside (tracts).
The spinal cord has gray INSIDE, not outside.
The brain has gray OUTSIDE (cortex), not inside.
The brain's cortex is gray matter.
takeaway: Cord: gray in / white out. Brain: white in / gray out.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Somatosensory information travels in two broad tract categories. One carries position sense, vibration, and fine touch; the other carries:
choices: Pain, temperature, and gross (less precise) touch
rationale: Somatosensory tracts: (1) position/vibration/fine touch and (2) pain/temperature/gross touch.
why: Vision and hearing aren't somatosensory tracts.
These are sensory tracts, not motor.
These carry somatosensation, not autonomic outflow.
Correct. The two categories are (1) fine touch/vibration/proprioception and (2) pain/temperature/crude touch.
takeaway: Somatosensory tracts: fine touch/vibration/proprioception vs. pain/temp/gross touch.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Somatosensory pathways cross to the opposite side of the body (decussate). A key consequence is that:
choices: Each side of the brain serves the same side of the body
Injury to one side of the brain often impairs sensation on the opposite side of the body
Both sides of the brain serve only the left side
rationale: Somatosensory pathways decussate (cross) → one hemisphere represents the opposite side of the body (contralateral).
why: Sensory/motor representation is contralateral, not ipsilateral, due to crossing.
Correct. Because the pathways cross (decussate), one side of the brain represents the opposite side of the body — so a lesion affects the contralateral side.
Sensation does reach the brain via these tracts.
Each hemisphere serves the contralateral side, not both to one side.
takeaway: Sensory tracts cross → brain represents the opposite side of the body (contralateral).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Which sensations are carried by the dorsal-column (position/vibration/fine-touch) pathway?
choices: Proprioception (position sense), vibration, and fine discriminative touch
rationale: The dorsal-column pathway = fine touch + vibration + proprioception. Pain/temperature = the spinothalamic pathway.
why: Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic (not dorsal-column) pathway.
Crude touch travels with pain/temperature, not the fine-touch pathway.
Correct. The dorsal-column pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception; pain/temperature travel in the separate spinothalamic pathway.
Hearing and balance are separate senses, not somatosensory tracts.
takeaway: Dorsal column = fine touch, vibration, proprioception. Spinothalamic = pain, temperature.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An upper motor neuron (UMN) is a neuron that:
choices: Synapses directly on skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction
Carries sensory information from skin to brain
Originates in the cerebral cortex and synapses on lower motor neurons in the brainstem or spinal cord
Regulates hormone release from the pituitary
rationale: Upper motor neurons start in the cerebral cortex and command lower motor neurons; LMNs then drive the muscle.
why: That's a LOWER motor neuron — the LMN contacts muscle at the NMJ.
That describes an afferent (sensory) neuron.
Correct. UMNs live in the cerebral cortex and control LMNs (in the brainstem/cord); the LMNs are the ones that contact muscle directly.
That describes hypothalamic/pituitary control, not a UMN.
takeaway: UMN = cortex → controls LMNs (which drive muscle). UMN controls LMN.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The collection of upper-motor-neuron axons that travels from the cortex down to lower motor neurons in the spinal cord is the:
rationale: Corticospinal tract = UMN axons to the spinal cord. Corticobulbar tract = UMN axons to the brainstem.
why: Correct. The corticospinal tract carries UMN axons to the spinal cord (most decussate at the medulla). The corticobulbar tract instead goes to the brainstem.
The corticobulbar tract goes to the brainstem, not the spinal cord.
The dorsal column is a sensory (fine-touch) pathway.
The spinothalamic tract is a sensory (pain/temp) pathway.
takeaway: Corticospinal = UMN → spinal cord. Corticobulbar = UMN → brainstem.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Damage to an UPPER motor neuron produces which pattern of signs?
choices: Hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, and an extensor plantar (Babinski) response
rationale: UMN signs = 'up': hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, Babinski. LMN signs = 'down': atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia.
why: Those are LOWER motor neuron signs — the opposite pattern.
UMN damage clearly produces motor signs.
UMN lesions cause motor, not purely sensory, deficits.

Correct. UMN lesions cause 'up' signs: hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia/spasticity, and a Babinski (extensor plantar) response. LMN lesions cause the 'down' signs (atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia).
takeaway: UMN = up (hyperreflexia, clonus, hypertonia, Babinski). LMN = down (atrophy, fasciculations, hypotonia, hyporeflexia).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Rhythmic, involuntary contractions (e.g., the foot beating up and down when the ankle is dorsiflexed) — an upper-motor-neuron sign driven by hyperreflexia — are called:
rationale: Clonus = rhythmic involuntary contractions from hyperreflexia — an UMN sign.
why: Fasciculations are small twitches seen in LOWER motor neuron damage.
Correct. Clonus is rhythmic involuntary contraction from an exaggerated stretch reflex (hyperreflexia), a UMN sign.
A resting tremor is characteristic of Parkinson's (basal ganglia), not clonus.
Ataxia is uncoordinated movement, often cerebellar, not clonus.
takeaway: Clonus = rhythmic contractions from hyperreflexia (UMN sign).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: When the sole of the foot is scraped, the normal adult response is toe flexion (curling down). An extensor response — the big toe going UP — (the Babinski sign) indicates:
rationale: An extensor plantar (Babinski) response in an adult = upper motor neuron damage (normal response is toe flexion).
why: Toe flexion is the normal adult response; extension is abnormal.
The Babinski sign points to UMN, not specifically LMN, damage.
Correct. An extensor plantar (Babinski) response is abnormal in adults and signals UMN pathology (it's normal only in infants).
It reflects motor-pathway (UMN) damage, not a purely sensory issue.
takeaway: Babinski (toe up) in an adult = UMN damage. Normal adult = toes flex down.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Increased skeletal-muscle tone and resistance to stretch — an upper-motor-neuron sign — is called:
rationale: Hypertonia (increased tone/spasticity) = UMN sign. Hypotonia (decreased tone) = LMN sign.
why: Correct. Hypertonia (increased tone/spasticity) is a UMN sign; hypotonia (decreased tone) is a LMN sign.
Hypotonia (decreased tone) is a LOWER motor neuron sign.
Anhedonia is loss of pleasure, unrelated to muscle tone.
Hyporeflexia (reduced reflexes) is a LMN sign.
takeaway: Hypertonia = increased tone (UMN). Hypotonia = decreased tone (LMN).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The four lobes of the cerebral cortex (mnemonic F-POT) are the:
choices: Frontal, pontine, occipital, and thalamic lobes
Frontal, parietal, olfactory, and temporal lobes
Frontal, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes
Cerebellar, parietal, occipital, and temporal lobes
rationale: Four cortical lobes: Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal (F-POT).
why: The pons and thalamus are not cortical lobes.
There is no 'olfactory lobe' among the four; it's occipital.
Correct. F-POT = Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal.
The cerebellum is not a cortical lobe.
takeaway: Cortical lobes: Frontal, Parietal, Occipital, Temporal (F-POT).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The frontal lobe houses the motor cortex, the prefrontal cortex (executive function), and:
rationale: Frontal lobe = motor cortex + prefrontal cortex (executive) + Broca's area (speech production).
why: Correct. The frontal lobe contains the motor cortex, prefrontal cortex, and Broca's area (speech production).
The primary visual cortex is in the occipital lobe.
Wernicke's area is in the temporal lobe.
The somatosensory cortex is in the parietal lobe.
takeaway: Frontal = motor cortex, prefrontal (executive), Broca's (speech production).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The lobe containing the somatosensory cortex (touch, pressure, pain from the skin) and handling spatial manipulation is the:
rationale: Parietal lobe = somatosensory cortex (skin sensation) + spatial manipulation.
why: The occipital lobe processes vision.
The temporal lobe processes hearing.
The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function, not somatosensation.
Correct. The parietal lobe contains the somatosensory cortex and processes spatial orientation.
takeaway: Parietal = somatosensory cortex + spatial processing.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Vision, including the primary visual ('striate') cortex, is processed in the:
rationale: Occipital lobe = vision (primary visual / striate cortex).
why: The temporal lobe processes hearing.
Correct. The occipital lobe houses the primary visual (striate) cortex.
The parietal lobe processes somatosensation/space.
The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function.
takeaway: Occipital = vision (striate cortex).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Sound processing (auditory cortex) and Wernicke's area (language comprehension) are located in the:
rationale: Temporal lobe = hearing (auditory cortex) + Wernicke's area (comprehension).
why: The occipital lobe processes vision.
The parietal lobe processes somatosensation.
Correct. The temporal lobe contains the auditory cortex and Wernicke's area.
The frontal lobe handles motor/executive function and Broca's area.
takeaway: Temporal = auditory cortex + Wernicke's (comprehension).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The motor cortex and the somatosensory cortex sit on opposite sides of the central sulcus. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Motor cortex in the frontal lobe; somatosensory cortex in the parietal lobe
Motor cortex in the parietal lobe; somatosensory cortex in the frontal lobe
rationale: Motor cortex = frontal (precentral gyrus); somatosensory cortex = parietal (postcentral gyrus). They flank the central sulcus.
why: Correct. The motor cortex (precentral gyrus) is frontal; the somatosensory cortex (postcentral gyrus) is parietal — they flank the central sulcus.
Reversed — motor is frontal, somatosensory is parietal.
Both are near the central sulcus (frontal/parietal), not occipital.
Neither is in the temporal lobe.
takeaway: Motor cortex = frontal. Somatosensory cortex = parietal (across the central sulcus).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The bumps and grooves (gyri and sulci) that fold the cerebral cortex serve to:
choices: Increase the cortical surface area (and cellular mass) that fits in the skull
rationale: Cortical folding (gyri/sulci) increases surface area — more cortex/neurons in the same skull volume.
why: Folding increases, not decreases, neuronal capacity.
The folds aren't CSF reservoirs.
Folding isn't a myelin-generating structure.
Correct. Cortical folding packs more surface area (and neurons) into the limited skull volume.
takeaway: Cortical folds = more surface area (more neurons) in the skull.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: For movement and most senses, each cerebral hemisphere controls:
choices: The same (ipsilateral) side of the body
The opposite (contralateral) side of the body
rationale: The brain is contralateral: left hemisphere ↔ right body (and vice versa). Smell is the ipsilateral exception.
why: Control is contralateral, not ipsilateral (except smell).
Each hemisphere serves the opposite side, not both equally.
Correct. The brain is contralaterally organized — the left hemisphere controls the right body and vice versa (smell is the ipsilateral exception).
Hemispheric control extends to the whole contralateral body, not just head/neck.
takeaway: Contralateral control: left brain ↔ right body. Smell = ipsilateral exception.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: For the vast majority of people, the dominant hemisphere — handling language, math, and logic — is the:
rationale: Left hemisphere is dominant for most people: language, math, logic.
why: Correct. The left hemisphere is dominant for most people, specializing in language, math, and logical analysis.
The right hemisphere handles prosody, music, and spatial/holistic processing.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, not language dominance.
The brainstem handles vital functions, not language.
takeaway: Left hemisphere (dominant) = language, math, logic.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The non-dominant (usually right) hemisphere specializes in:
choices: Emotional tone (prosody), music, spatial processing, and big-picture/holistic thinking
rationale: Right (non-dominant) hemisphere: emotional prosody, music, spatial, big-picture/holistic thinking.
why: Grammar/vocabulary are left-hemisphere (language) functions.
Calculation is more left-hemisphere.
Speech production (Broca's) is left-hemisphere.
Correct. The right hemisphere handles the emotional tone of language (prosody), music, spatial processing, and holistic 'big-picture' thinking.
takeaway: Right hemisphere = prosody, music, spatial, big-picture.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Contralateral organization applies to most senses, but the exception — processed on the SAME (ipsilateral) side — is:
rationale: Smell is the ipsilateral exception (same-side); vision/hearing/touch are contralateral.
why: Vision is contralaterally organized.
Correct. Olfaction is ipsilateral — each nostril projects to the same-side hemisphere (it also bypasses the thalamus). Vision, hearing, and touch are contralateral.
Hearing is largely contralateral.
Touch is contralateral.
takeaway: Smell = ipsilateral exception. Vision/hearing/touch = contralateral.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The two cerebral hemispheres communicate and share information through the:
rationale: The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, letting them communicate.
why: The internal capsule carries tracts like the corticospinal, not interhemispheric fibers.
The reticular formation governs arousal, not hemisphere connection.
Correct. The corpus callosum is the large fiber bundle connecting the left and right hemispheres.
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
takeaway: Corpus callosum = connects/communicates between hemispheres.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The brainstem — which connects the brain to the spinal cord and carries the cranial nerves — consists of the:
rationale: The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla.
why: Those are higher structures, not the brainstem.
Those are cortical lobes, not the brainstem.
Correct. The brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla (mnemonic for the lower brainstem: Pons, Reticular formation, Medulla).
Those are limbic structures, not the brainstem.
takeaway: Brainstem = midbrain + pons + medulla.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The lower brainstem structure that controls vital involuntary functions — heartbeat and breathing — and is the crossover (decussation) point for many nerve tracts is the:
rationale: The medulla controls heartbeat and breathing (vital autonomic functions) and is a tract crossover point.
why: Correct. The medulla regulates heart rate and breathing and is a major decussation point for tracts.
The cerebellum coordinates movement, not heartbeat/breathing.
The thalamus is a sensory relay, not the vital-function center.
The hippocampus handles memory.
takeaway: Medulla = heartbeat + breathing (vital); tract crossover point.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The network of neurons running through the brainstem that governs arousal, alertness, and the sleep–wake cycle — and filters incoming sensory information — is the:
rationale: The reticular formation governs arousal, alertness, and the sleep–wake cycle (and filters sensory input).
why: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres, unrelated to arousal.
The basal ganglia handle motor control.
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
Correct. The reticular formation controls arousal/alertness and the sleep–wake cycle, filtering sensory input to the thalamus.
takeaway: Reticular formation = arousal/alertness + sleep–wake + sensory filtering.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The brainstem structure that acts as a bridge relaying signals, and plays a role in arousal and the sleep/REM cycle, is the:
rationale: The pons ('bridge') relays signals and contributes to arousal and the sleep/REM cycle.
why: The medulla controls heartbeat/breathing specifically.
Correct. The pons ('bridge') relays signals between brain regions and participates in arousal and sleep (including REM).
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
The amygdala handles fear/emotion.
takeaway: Pons = bridge/relay; arousal + sleep/REM.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The structure that coordinates voluntary movement and balance — receiving proprioceptive feedback, and notably impaired by alcohol — is the:
rationale: The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and balance (alcohol impairs it → poor coordination).
why: The medulla controls vital autonomic functions.
The thalamus is a sensory relay.
Correct. The cerebellum coordinates voluntary movement and balance; alcohol impairs it (why intoxication disrupts coordination/balance).
The corpus callosum connects hemispheres.
takeaway: Cerebellum = coordination + balance (alcohol impairs it).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Your notes describe the brain as 'building on itself.' In general, the deeper/older structures handle ______, while the superficial cortex handles ______.
choices: Basic survival functions (breathing, sleep); higher-order functions (cognition)
rationale: Deep/old brain = survival basics (breathing, sleep); superficial cortex = higher-order cognition.
why: Correct. Older, deeper structures manage survival basics (breathing, heartbeat, sleep); the newer, superficial cortex handles higher-order cognition.
Reversed — deep/old = survival, superficial/new = higher cognition.
The old/new distinction isn't vision vs. hearing.
It isn't a simple motor vs. sensory split.
takeaway: Old/deep brain = survival (breathing, sleep). New/superficial cortex = higher cognition.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Within the old brain, the structure that acts as the sensory relay station — routing eye/ear and other sensory info onward — is the:
rationale: The thalamus is the sensory relay station (all senses except smell).
why: The cerebellum coordinates movement, not sensory relay.
The pons is a bridge/relay for arousal and cross-signals, but the sensory relay station is the thalamus.
The medulla controls vital autonomic functions.
Correct. The thalamus relays incoming sensory information (all senses except smell) to the appropriate cortical areas.
takeaway: Thalamus = sensory relay (all senses but smell).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The subcortical nuclei that help refine and smooth voluntary movement (and also contribute to cognition and emotion), but contain NO upper motor neurons themselves, are the:
rationale: The basal ganglia refine/smooth voluntary movement (and aid cognition/emotion) — they modulate motor output, without UMNs of their own.
why: The corpus callosum connects hemispheres, not a motor-refining nucleus.
The reticular formation governs arousal.
Correct. The basal ganglia help motor areas produce smooth, proper movements (and aid cognition/emotion); they modulate rather than directly command via UMNs.
The olfactory bulb processes smell.
takeaway: Basal ganglia = smooth/refine movement (also cognition/emotion); no UMNs.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The subcortical white-matter structure that carries many important pathways — including the corticospinal tract — down from the cortex is the:
rationale: The internal capsule carries major pathways (including the corticospinal tract) from the cortex downward.
why: Correct. The internal capsule is a compact white-matter bundle carrying tracts (like the corticospinal) between the cortex and lower structures.
The corpus callosum connects the two hemispheres, a different bundle.
The basal ganglia are gray-matter nuclei, not the tract-carrying capsule.
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
takeaway: Internal capsule = white-matter bundle carrying the corticospinal tract.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Among the subcortical structures, the one connecting the right and left cerebral hemispheres is the:
rationale: The corpus callosum connects the right and left hemispheres.
why: The internal capsule carries corticospinal and other tracts, not the interhemispheric bridge.
The basal ganglia handle motor refinement.
The thalamus is the sensory relay.
Correct. The corpus callosum is the large commissure joining the two hemispheres.
takeaway: Corpus callosum = joins the two hemispheres.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The subcortical structure that controls the pituitary gland — the 'master gland' that regulates other endocrine glands — is the:
rationale: The hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland), bridging the nervous and endocrine systems.
why: The basal ganglia handle motor refinement, not endocrine control.
Correct. The hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland), linking the nervous and endocrine systems (and regulating hunger, thirst, temperature, etc.).
The cerebellum coordinates movement.
The corpus callosum connects hemispheres.
takeaway: Hypothalamus controls the pituitary (master gland).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Because the basal ganglia refine movement, dysfunction there is associated with movement disorders such as:
rationale: Basal-ganglia dysfunction → movement disorders (e.g., Parkinson's disease: resting tremor, rigidity).
why: Wernicke's aphasia is a temporal-lobe language disorder.
Anterograde amnesia is a hippocampal/memory disorder.
Correct. Basal-ganglia dysfunction (e.g., dopamine loss) produces movement disorders like Parkinson's disease.
Anosmia is loss of smell.
takeaway: Basal ganglia dysfunction → movement disorders (Parkinson's).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Learning is split into two broad types. Learning a link between two stimuli or between a behavior and its consequence is ______ learning; learning from repeated exposure to a single stimulus is ______ learning.
rationale: Associative learning links stimuli/behaviors (classical, operant); non-associative learning is response change to one repeated stimulus (habituation, sensitization).
why: Reversed — associative links stimuli, non-associative is single-stimulus.
Latent and observational aren't the associative/non-associative split.

Correct. Associative learning (classical/operant conditioning) links stimuli or behaviors to outcomes; non-associative learning (habituation, sensitization) is a change in response to a single repeated stimulus.
Insight/procedural aren't this dichotomy.
takeaway: Associative = link stimuli/consequences. Non-associative = single repeated stimulus.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Growing less responsive to a repeated, harmless stimulus — like ceasing to notice a ticking clock — is:
rationale: Habituation = decreased response to a repeated harmless stimulus (you tune it out).
why: Correct. Habituation is a decreased response to a repeated, non-threatening stimulus.
Sensitization is an INCREASED response, the opposite.
Acquisition is the initial learning of a conditioned association.
Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to a conditioned one.
takeaway: Habituation = tune out a repeated harmless stimulus (response decreases).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After you've habituated to a stimulus, a sudden change or new stimulus can restore the original response. This recovery is:
rationale: Dishabituation = a habituated response returns when a new or changed stimulus is introduced.
why: Sensitization is a heightened response to a strong stimulus, a different process.
Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response, a classical-conditioning term.
Discrimination is distinguishing a specific conditioned stimulus.
Correct. Dishabituation is the return of a habituated response when a new/changed stimulus appears.
takeaway: Dishabituation = habituated response comes back when the stimulus changes.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After a painful or intense stimulus, you become MORE responsive even to mild stimuli (jumpy after a scare). This is:
rationale: Sensitization = increased responsiveness after a strong/aversive stimulus (heightened reactivity).
why: Habituation is a DECREASED response, the opposite.
Correct. Sensitization is an increased response following a strong or noxious stimulus.
Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished conditioned response.
Shaping is reinforcing steps toward a target behavior (operant).
takeaway: Sensitization = more responsive after an intense stimulus (opposite of habituation).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Habituation differs from sensory adaptation in that habituation is:
choices: Purely a change in the sensory receptors
The same thing as sensory adaptation
A change in the central nervous system's response (learning), not a change in the sensory receptors themselves
A conscious decision to ignore a stimulus
rationale: Habituation = a learned CNS-level drop in response; sensory adaptation = receptor-level drop in sensitivity. Different mechanisms.
why: That's sensory adaptation (receptor-level), not habituation.
They're distinct: adaptation is receptor-level, habituation is a learned CNS response.
Correct. Habituation is a learned, CNS-level decrease in behavioral response; sensory adaptation is a receptor-level decrease in sensory signaling.
Habituation isn't a deliberate choice; it's a form of non-associative learning.
takeaway: Habituation = learned (CNS) response drop. Sensory adaptation = receptor-level. Not the same.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In Pavlov's work, food automatically makes a dog salivate. The food is the ______ and the salivation to food is the ______.
rationale: UCS = stimulus that naturally triggers a response (food); UCR = the automatic response (salivation to food). No learning required.
why: The food triggers salivation automatically (unconditioned), before any learning.
Food is not neutral — it naturally elicits the response.
Correct. Food naturally triggers salivation with no learning: food = unconditioned stimulus (UCS), salivation-to-food = unconditioned response (UCR).
Food is the unconditioned (not conditioned) stimulus.
takeaway: UCS = natural trigger (food). UCR = automatic response (salivate to food).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A bell initially produces no salivation. After being repeatedly paired with food, the bell alone makes the dog salivate. The bell has changed from a ______ into a ______.
rationale: A neutral stimulus (NS) becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) after repeated pairing with the UCS.
why: Correct. The bell starts neutral (no response), then through pairing with the UCS becomes a conditioned stimulus (CS) that elicits the response.
Reversed — it goes from neutral to conditioned, not the other way.
The bell is a stimulus that becomes conditioned, not a UCS/UCR pair.
The bell is a stimulus (CS), not a response.
takeaway: Bell: neutral stimulus → conditioned stimulus (after pairing with food).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After conditioning, the dog salivates to the bell alone. Salivation to the bell is the:
rationale: The conditioned response (CR) = the learned response to the conditioned stimulus (salivation to the bell).
why: The UCR is the response to the natural stimulus (food), not the bell.
The UCS is the natural stimulus (food), not a response.
A neutral stimulus is a stimulus, not a response.
Correct. Salivation triggered by the bell (the learned trigger) is the conditioned response (CR).
takeaway: CR = learned response to the CS (salivate to the bell).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The initial stage of classical conditioning — when the neutral stimulus and unconditioned stimulus are repeatedly paired until the association is learned — is:
rationale: Acquisition = the phase of learning the CS–UCS association (CS ideally just before UCS).
why: Extinction is the weakening of the response, not its establishment.
Correct. Acquisition is the phase where the CS–UCS association is established (works best when the CS slightly precedes the UCS).
Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished response.
Shaping is an operant-conditioning procedure, not classical acquisition.
takeaway: Acquisition = learning the CS–UCS pairing.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Classical conditioning is best characterized as learning that involves:
choices: Voluntary behaviors shaped by their consequences
Automatic, involuntary responses (reflexive) linked to a new stimulus
A single repeated stimulus with no pairing
rationale: Classical conditioning = automatic/reflexive responses linked to a new (conditioned) stimulus. Operant = voluntary behavior driven by consequences.
why: Voluntary behavior shaped by consequences is operant conditioning.
Learning by watching is observational learning.
Correct. Classical conditioning associates a new stimulus with an automatic, reflexive response (salivation, fear). Voluntary behaviors driven by consequences are operant conditioning.
A single repeated stimulus is non-associative learning.
takeaway: Classical = involuntary/reflexive responses. Operant = voluntary behavior + consequences.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Classical conditioning is generally most effective when the neutral stimulus:
choices: Comes just BEFORE the unconditioned stimulus (forward conditioning)
Comes well AFTER the unconditioned stimulus
Is never paired with the unconditioned stimulus
rationale: Conditioning is strongest when the CS precedes the UCS (the CS predicts the UCS).
why: Correct. Learning is strongest when the CS reliably precedes (predicts) the UCS — forward conditioning.
Presenting the NS after the UCS (backward conditioning) is weak/ineffective.
Pairing is required for classical conditioning to occur.
The NS becomes a signal for the UCS; it doesn't replace the response.
takeaway: Best conditioning: CS just before UCS (CS predicts UCS).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: If the bell (CS) is repeatedly presented WITHOUT the food (UCS), the dog gradually stops salivating to the bell. This weakening of the conditioned response is:
rationale: Extinction = the conditioned response fades when the CS is presented without the UCS.
why: Spontaneous recovery is the RETURN of the response after a rest, not its fading.
Acquisition is the initial learning of the association.
Correct. Extinction is the fading of the CR when the CS is presented repeatedly without the UCS.
Generalization is responding to similar stimuli.
takeaway: Extinction = CR fades when CS is shown without the UCS.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After a conditioned response has been extinguished, it suddenly reappears (weaker) following a rest period. This is:
rationale: Spontaneous recovery = an extinguished CR returns after a rest (the association was suppressed, not erased).
why: Correct. Spontaneous recovery is the reappearance of an extinguished CR after a pause — showing the association wasn't fully erased.
Extinction is the fading of the response, not its return.
Discrimination is distinguishing the specific CS from similar stimuli.
Habituation is a non-associative decrease in response.
takeaway: Spontaneous recovery = extinguished response comes back after a break.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: After being conditioned to salivate to a specific tone, the dog also salivates to similar tones. This is:
rationale: Stimulus generalization = the CR is elicited by stimuli similar to the original CS.
why: Discrimination is the opposite — responding only to the specific CS.
Extinction is the fading of the response.
Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.
Correct. Generalization is responding to stimuli similar to the original conditioned stimulus.
takeaway: Generalization = respond to stimuli SIMILAR to the CS.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: With further training, the dog salivates only to the exact tone that was paired with food, not to different tones. This is:
rationale: Stimulus discrimination = responding only to the specific CS, not to similar stimuli.
why: Generalization is responding to similar stimuli, the opposite.
Correct. Discrimination is learning to respond only to the specific CS and not to similar stimuli — the opposite of generalization.
Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished response.
Acquisition is the initial learning phase.
takeaway: Discrimination = respond ONLY to the specific CS (opposite of generalization).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Once a bell is a conditioned stimulus, pairing a NEW neutral stimulus (a light) with the bell can make the light elicit the response too. This is:
rationale: Higher-order conditioning: an established CS conditions a new neutral stimulus (light paired with an already-conditioned bell).
why: Extinction is the fading of a conditioned response.
Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.
Correct. Higher-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new neutral stimulus, without the original UCS.
Shaping is an operant procedure.
takeaway: Higher-order conditioning = an existing CS conditions a new stimulus.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Operant conditioning (Skinner, building on Thorndike's law of effect) is learning in which:
choices: Reflexive responses are paired with a new stimulus
Behavior changes from watching a model
Voluntary behavior is strengthened or weakened by its consequences
Response to a single stimulus declines with repetition
rationale: Operant conditioning: voluntary behavior is shaped by its consequences (Thorndike's law of effect; Skinner).
why: That's classical conditioning (reflexive responses + new stimulus).
That's observational learning.
Correct. Operant conditioning changes voluntary behavior through consequences (reinforcement increases it; punishment decreases it).
That's habituation (non-associative).
takeaway: Operant = voluntary behavior shaped by consequences (reinforcement/punishment).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In operant terms, reinforcement always ______ a behavior, and punishment always ______ a behavior.
rationale: Reinforcement increases a behavior; punishment decreases it (independent of add/remove).
why: Correct. Reinforcement increases the likelihood of a behavior; punishment decreases it — regardless of whether a stimulus is added or removed.
Reversed — reinforcement increases, punishment decreases.
Punishment decreases behavior, not increases.
Reinforcement increases behavior, not decreases.
takeaway: Reinforcement ↑ behavior. Punishment ↓ behavior.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In operant conditioning, 'positive' and 'negative' refer to:
choices: Whether the outcome is pleasant or unpleasant
Whether the behavior increases or decreases
Whether the learning is conscious or unconscious
Whether a stimulus is added (positive) or removed (negative) — not good vs. bad
rationale: In operant terms, positive = add a stimulus, negative = remove a stimulus (not good vs. bad).
why: Pleasant/unpleasant maps to reinforcement/punishment, not positive/negative.
Increase/decrease maps to reinforcement/punishment.
It refers to add/remove, not conscious/unconscious.
Correct. Positive = add a stimulus; negative = remove a stimulus. 'Good/bad' is captured by reinforcement vs. punishment, not by positive/negative.
takeaway: Positive = add stimulus. Negative = remove stimulus. (Not good/bad.)

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Giving a dog a treat when it sits, which makes it sit more often, is:
choices: Positive reinforcement (add a pleasant stimulus → behavior increases)
rationale: Positive reinforcement = add a pleasant stimulus → behavior increases (treat for sitting).
why: Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus, not adds a treat.
Correct. A pleasant stimulus is ADDED and the behavior INCREASES → positive reinforcement.
Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to decrease behavior.
Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to decrease behavior.
takeaway: Positive reinforcement = add something good → behavior increases.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A car beeps until you fasten your seatbelt; buckling STOPS the beep, so you buckle more. This is:
choices: Negative reinforcement (remove an aversive stimulus → behavior increases)
rationale: Negative reinforcement = remove an aversive stimulus → behavior increases (buckle to stop the beep). Not punishment!
why: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus to reduce behavior.
Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus to reduce behavior.
Correct. An aversive stimulus (beep) is REMOVED and the behavior (buckling) INCREASES → negative reinforcement. It is NOT punishment.
Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus.
takeaway: Negative reinforcement = remove something aversive → behavior increases (NOT punishment).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Adding a shock when a rat presses a lever, which makes it press less, is:
choices: Positive punishment (add an aversive stimulus → behavior decreases)
rationale: Positive punishment = add an aversive stimulus → behavior decreases (shock for lever-press).
why: Correct. An aversive stimulus is ADDED and the behavior DECREASES → positive punishment.
Negative punishment removes a pleasant stimulus.
Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase behavior.
takeaway: Positive punishment = add something aversive → behavior decreases.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Taking away a teen's phone for breaking curfew, which reduces curfew-breaking, is:
choices: Negative punishment (remove a pleasant stimulus → behavior decreases)
rationale: Negative punishment = remove a pleasant stimulus → behavior decreases (take the phone).
why: Positive punishment adds an aversive stimulus.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to INCREASE behavior.
Positive reinforcement adds a pleasant stimulus to increase behavior.
Correct. A pleasant stimulus (phone) is REMOVED and the behavior DECREASES → negative punishment.
takeaway: Negative punishment = remove something good → behavior decreases.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Teaching a complex behavior by reinforcing successive approximations — steps that get closer and closer to the target — is:
rationale: Shaping = reinforcing successive approximations toward a target behavior.
why: Extinction is the fading of a response.
Generalization is responding to similar stimuli (classical).
Correct. Shaping reinforces successive approximations toward a goal behavior.
Latent learning is learning that isn't shown until there's a reason to.
takeaway: Shaping = reinforce successive approximations toward the goal behavior.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A behavior reinforced only SOME of the time (partial/intermittent reinforcement), compared with every time (continuous), is:
choices: Faster to acquire but quickly extinguished
rationale: Partial (intermittent) reinforcement → more resistant to extinction (continuous → faster initial learning).
why: Correct. Continuous reinforcement produces faster initial learning, but partial (intermittent) reinforcement makes the behavior more resistant to extinction.
Continuous reinforcement gives faster acquisition; partial gives extinction resistance.
Partial reinforcement resists but doesn't prevent extinction entirely.
Reinforcement schedules are an operant, not classical, concept.
takeaway: Partial reinforcement = harder to extinguish. Continuous = faster to learn.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A factory worker paid for every 10 units produced is on which reinforcement schedule?
choices: Fixed-ratio (FR) — reinforcement after a set number of responses
rationale: Fixed-ratio (FR) = reinforcement after a set NUMBER of responses (high rate, post-reinforcement pause).
why: Fixed-interval reinforces the first response after a set TIME, not a set count.
Variable-ratio reinforces after an unpredictable NUMBER of responses.
Variable-interval reinforces after an unpredictable TIME.
Correct. Fixed-ratio delivers reinforcement after a set number of responses (every 10 units) — producing a high response rate with a brief post-reinforcement pause.
takeaway: Fixed-ratio = set number of responses (e.g., pay per 10 units).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A slot machine that pays out after an unpredictable number of pulls is which schedule — the one that produces the highest, steadiest response rate and greatest resistance to extinction?
rationale: Variable-ratio (VR) = reinforcement after an unpredictable NUMBER of responses → highest, steadiest rate, most resistant to extinction (gambling).
why: Fixed-ratio uses a set number of responses and has a post-reinforcement pause.
Correct. Variable-ratio reinforces after an unpredictable number of responses — the highest, steadiest rate and most extinction-resistant (why gambling is so persistent).
Fixed-interval reinforces after a set time (scalloped pattern).
Variable-interval reinforces after unpredictable time (slow, steady).
takeaway: Variable-ratio = unpredictable # of responses → highest rate, hardest to extinguish (gambling).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Reinforcing the first response after a set amount of TIME (e.g., a weekly paycheck) — producing a 'scalloped' pattern where responding speeds up near the deadline — is:
rationale: Fixed-interval (FI) = first response after a set TIME → scalloped pattern (responding accelerates near the deadline).
why: Variable-interval uses unpredictable time and gives a slow, steady rate.
Fixed-ratio is based on a set number of responses, not time.
Correct. Fixed-interval reinforces the first response after a fixed time; responding dips after reinforcement and accelerates as the interval ends (scalloped).
Variable-ratio is based on an unpredictable number of responses.
takeaway: Fixed-interval = set time → scalloped pattern (speed up near the deadline).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Checking your phone for a text that could arrive at any unpredictable time produces slow, steady responding. This is which schedule?
rationale: Variable-interval (VI) = first response after an unpredictable TIME → slow, steady responding.
why: Correct. Variable-interval reinforces the first response after an unpredictable time, producing a slow, steady response rate.
Fixed-interval uses a set (predictable) time and gives a scalloped pattern.
Variable-ratio is based on an unpredictable number of responses (high rate).
Fixed-ratio is based on a set number of responses.
takeaway: Variable-interval = unpredictable time → slow, steady responding.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
tag: Ratio vs. interval, fixed vs. variable
stem: Two general rules about schedules of reinforcement are:
choices: Interval schedules always beat ratio schedules for response rate
Fixed schedules always resist extinction better than variable ones
Schedule type has no effect on behavior
Ratio schedules produce higher response rates than interval schedules; variable schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones
rationale: Rules: ratio > interval for response rate; variable > fixed for extinction resistance.
why: Ratio schedules produce HIGHER rates than interval schedules.
VARIABLE schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones.
Schedule type strongly shapes response rate and persistence.
Correct. Ratio (response-based) schedules drive higher rates than interval (time-based) schedules; variable (unpredictable) schedules resist extinction better than fixed ones.
takeaway: Ratio > interval (response rate). Variable > fixed (extinction resistance).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Learning a behavior by watching and imitating others, rather than through direct reinforcement, is:
rationale: Observational learning = learning by watching/imitating a model (Bandura's social cognitive theory).
why: Classical conditioning pairs a stimulus with a reflexive response.
Operant conditioning shapes behavior through direct consequences.
Correct. Observational learning (modeling) is acquiring behavior by watching others — the basis of Bandura's social cognitive theory.
Habituation is a non-associative decrease in response.
takeaway: Observational learning = learn by watching/imitating a model.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The classic experiment showing children imitate aggression after watching an adult model attack a doll was conducted by:
rationale: Bandura's Bobo doll experiment demonstrated observational learning — children imitated modeled aggression.
why: Correct. Bandura's Bobo doll study demonstrated observational learning of aggression through modeling.
Pavlov studied classical conditioning (salivation), not modeling.
Skinner studied operant conditioning (reinforcement schedules).
Watson studied classical conditioning (Little Albert).
takeaway: Bobo doll = Bandura, observational learning of aggression.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In observational learning, the person whose behavior is watched and imitated is called the:
rationale: The model is the person observed and imitated in observational learning.
why: A conditioned stimulus is a classical-conditioning term.
A reinforcer is a consequence that increases behavior (operant).
A discriminative stimulus signals that reinforcement is available (operant).
Correct. The model is the individual being observed; imitating them is modeling.
takeaway: Model = the person you observe and imitate.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Seeing someone else get rewarded for a behavior makes you more likely to do it yourself. This is:
rationale: Vicarious reinforcement = you're influenced by seeing a model rewarded (or punished) for a behavior.
why: Direct reinforcement is a consequence delivered to you, not observed in another.
Correct. Vicarious reinforcement is learning from the consequences experienced by a model — a reward to the model makes the observer more likely to imitate.
Negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus to increase your own behavior.
Extinction is the fading of a learned response.
takeaway: Vicarious reinforcement = learning from what happens to the model (reward/punishment).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Bandura proposed observational learning requires attention, retention, reproduction, and motivation. A neural system often linked to imitation is the:
rationale: Observational learning needs attention, retention, reproduction, motivation; mirror neurons are linked to imitation.
why: The reticular activating system governs arousal, not imitation.
The vestibular system handles balance.

Correct. Mirror neurons — which fire both when performing and when observing an action — are often linked to imitation/observational learning. Bandura's four processes: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation.
The endocrine system releases hormones.
takeaway: Observational learning: attention, retention, reproduction, motivation. Mirror neurons = imitation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The finding that animals learn some associations far more easily than others — because of evolved predispositions — is called:
rationale: Biological constraints / preparedness: evolution makes some associations far easier to learn than others.
why: Latent learning is learning not shown until it's useful.
Higher-order conditioning uses an established CS to condition a new stimulus.
Correct. Biological constraints (preparedness) mean evolution readies organisms to learn certain associations more readily than others.
Shaping reinforces successive approximations.
takeaway: Biological constraints (preparedness) = some associations learned much more easily (evolved).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Getting sick hours after eating a food, then avoiding that food after a SINGLE pairing (even with a long delay), is:
choices: Standard classical conditioning requiring many trials
rationale: Conditioned taste aversion (Garcia effect) = one-trial learning with a long delay — evolved preparedness, breaking usual conditioning rules.
why: Correct. Conditioned taste aversion (Garcia) is learned in one trial despite a long delay — a biologically prepared exception to normal conditioning rules.
Ordinary classical conditioning needs repeated, closely-timed pairings; taste aversion needs neither.
It's a learned aversion (classical), not operant punishment.
Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.
takeaway: Taste aversion (Garcia) = one-trial, long-delay learning (biological preparedness).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: When trained animals drift back toward innate, instinctive behaviors that interfere with a conditioned response (the Brelands' raccoons), this is:
rationale: Instinctive drift = trained animals revert to instinctive behaviors — a biological limit on conditioning.
why: Spontaneous recovery is the return of an extinguished CR.
Generalization is responding to similar stimuli.
Latent learning is unexpressed learning.
Correct. Instinctive drift is the tendency to revert to instinctive behaviors, limiting what conditioning can achieve — another biological constraint.
takeaway: Instinctive drift = revert to instinctive behavior (biological constraint).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Learning to TERMINATE an aversive stimulus already present is escape learning; learning to PREVENT it before it starts is:
rationale: Escape learning ends an ongoing aversive stimulus; avoidance learning prevents it beforehand.
why: Escape learning terminates an ongoing aversive stimulus, not prevents it.
Correct. Escape learning ends an ongoing aversive stimulus; avoidance learning prevents it from occurring at all (typically via a warning signal).
Latent learning is unexpressed learning shown later.
Habituation is non-associative.
takeaway: Escape = end an ongoing aversive stimulus. Avoidance = prevent it beforehand.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A rat that explores a maze with no reward shows it learned the layout only later, when a reward is introduced and its performance jumps. This is:
rationale: Latent learning = learning that occurs without reinforcement and isn't shown until it's useful (Tolman's cognitive maps).
why: Observational learning is learning by watching a model.
Shaping reinforces successive approximations.
Correct. Latent learning is learning that occurs without reinforcement and stays hidden until there's a reason to demonstrate it (Tolman's cognitive maps).
Sensitization is a non-associative increase in response.
takeaway: Latent learning = learned without reward, revealed later when useful.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An innate, fixed behavior pattern present without learning (e.g., a spider spinning a web) is an instinct, whereas a conditioned response is:
rationale: Instinct = innate, unlearned behavior; a conditioned response is acquired through experience.
why: Correct. Instincts are innate, unlearned fixed action patterns; conditioned responses are acquired through experience.
A conditioned response is learned, not innate.
Conditioned responses can be modified (e.g., extinguished).
Instincts and conditioned responses differ in origin (innate vs. learned).
takeaway: Instinct = innate/unlearned. Conditioned response = learned through experience.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The theory that behavior is driven by innate, fixed, unlearned patterns (like a bird building a nest) is:
rationale: Instinct theory: behavior is motivated by innate, fixed, unlearned patterns.
why: Drive-reduction theory is about reducing physiological need states, not innate instincts.
Correct. Instinct theory attributes motivation to innate, species-typical fixed action patterns.
Incentive theory explains motivation by external rewards.
Cognitive theory explains motivation by expectations and value.
takeaway: Instinct theory = innate, fixed, unlearned behavior patterns.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Drive-reduction theory proposes that a physiological need creates an aroused tension (a drive) that motivates us to:
choices: Act to reduce the drive and restore homeostasis
rationale: Drive-reduction theory: a need → a drive (tension) → behavior that reduces it, restoring homeostasis.
why: Drive-reduction is about reducing tension, not seeking novelty for its own sake.
It seeks to reduce, not endlessly increase, arousal.
Imitating a model is observational learning, not drive reduction.
Correct. A need (e.g., hunger) produces a drive that pushes behavior to satisfy the need and return the body to homeostatic balance.
takeaway: Drive-reduction = need creates a drive → act to reduce it (restore homeostasis).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In drive-reduction theory, hunger and thirst are ______ drives, while the desire for money or approval are ______ drives.
rationale: Primary drives = innate biological (hunger, thirst); secondary drives = learned (money, approval).
why: Correct. Primary drives are innate biological needs (hunger, thirst); secondary drives are learned (money, approval).
Reversed — biological needs are primary, learned ones secondary.
Extrinsic/intrinsic describe reward source, not primary/secondary drives.
Those aren't the drive categories here.
takeaway: Primary drives = biological (hunger). Secondary drives = learned (money).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Arousal theory of motivation states that we are motivated to:
choices: Maintain an optimal level of arousal — seeking stimulation when under-aroused and calm when over-aroused
rationale: Arousal theory: motivation to reach an optimal arousal level (moderate) — performance peaks there (inverted-U).
why: We don't seek zero arousal — too little prompts stimulation-seeking.
We don't endlessly maximize arousal — too much impairs performance.
Correct. Arousal theory: people seek an optimal (moderate) arousal level; performance peaks there (Yerkes-Dodson inverted-U).
Arousal theory isn't limited to biological drives.
takeaway: Arousal theory = seek an optimal (moderate) arousal level.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Incentive theory explains motivation as behavior driven by:
choices: External rewards that pull us toward a goal (rather than internal drives pushing us)
Only the reduction of biological needs
rationale: Incentive theory: external rewards pull behavior toward goals (vs. drives that push).
why: That's instinct theory, not incentive theory.
Correct. Incentive theory emphasizes external incentives (rewards) that 'pull' behavior, complementing the internal 'push' of drives.
That's drive-reduction; incentive theory adds external rewards.
That describes cognitive dissonance, not motivation by incentives.
takeaway: Incentive theory = external rewards pull behavior (drives push, incentives pull).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Doing an activity for its own inherent satisfaction is ______ motivation; doing it for an external reward or to avoid punishment is ______ motivation.
rationale: Intrinsic motivation = for its own sake; extrinsic = for external reward/consequences.
why: Reversed — intrinsic is internal, extrinsic is external.
Primary/secondary are drive types, not the intrinsic/extrinsic split.
Central/peripheral are persuasion routes, not motivation types.
Correct. Intrinsic motivation comes from internal satisfaction; extrinsic motivation comes from external rewards/consequences.
takeaway: Intrinsic = internal satisfaction. Extrinsic = external reward.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Rewarding someone for an activity they already enjoy can REDUCE their intrinsic motivation for it. This is the:
rationale: Overjustification effect: an external reward can undermine existing intrinsic motivation.
why: Correct. The overjustification effect: an external reward can undermine pre-existing intrinsic motivation (the person re-attributes their behavior to the reward).
Yerkes-Dodson relates arousal to performance, not reward undermining interest.
Foot-in-the-door is a compliance technique, not about intrinsic motivation.
Drive-reduction is about need states, not reward undermining interest.
takeaway: Overjustification = rewarding an already-enjoyed activity lowers intrinsic motivation.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Maslow's hierarchy of needs, from the base upward, is:
rationale: Maslow (base→top): physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization.
why: That's the reverse order.
Correct. The pyramid rises: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization.
Physiological needs are the base, below esteem and love.
Physiological needs come before safety, and love before esteem.
takeaway: Maslow: physiological → safety → love/belonging → esteem → self-actualization.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A central claim of Maslow's hierarchy is that:
choices: Higher needs must be met before lower ones
All needs are pursued equally at once
Only physiological needs ever motivate people
Lower (more basic) needs must be reasonably met before higher needs strongly motivate behavior
rationale: Maslow: lower needs are generally satisfied first, then higher needs motivate behavior.
why: Reversed — basic needs generally come first.
The hierarchy implies a general priority order, not equal simultaneous pursuit.
Higher needs (esteem, self-actualization) also motivate once basics are met.
Correct. Maslow proposed a prepotent hierarchy: basic needs generally take priority until reasonably satisfied, then higher needs emerge.
takeaway: Maslow: meet basic needs first, then higher needs motivate.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The need at the top of Maslow's pyramid — realizing one's full potential and becoming the most one can be — is:
rationale: Self-actualization = the top need: realizing your full potential.
why: Correct. Self-actualization is the highest need: fulfilling one's unique potential.
Safety is a lower (deficiency) need.
Esteem sits below self-actualization.
Physiological needs are the base of the pyramid.
takeaway: Self-actualization = realize your full potential (top of the pyramid).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In Maslow's model, the lower four levels are called ______ needs, while self-actualization is a ______ need.
rationale: Maslow: the lower four are deficiency needs; self-actualization is a growth need.
why: Reversed — the lower four are deficiency needs.
Primary/secondary are drive terms, not Maslow's categories.
Correct. The lower four (physiological, safety, love, esteem) are deficiency needs; self-actualization is a growth (being) need.
Intrinsic/extrinsic describe motivation source, not Maslow's need types.
takeaway: Maslow: lower four = deficiency needs; self-actualization = growth need.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In Maslow's hierarchy, the need for achievement, competence, recognition, and respect from others is the level of:
rationale: Esteem needs = achievement, competence, recognition, respect (just below self-actualization).
why: Physiological needs are basic biological requirements.
Correct. Esteem needs — achievement, status, respect — sit just below self-actualization.
Safety needs concern security and stability.
Self-actualization is the top level, above esteem.
takeaway: Esteem needs = achievement, respect, recognition.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The brain region that regulates hunger and satiety — integrating signals about energy needs — is the:
rationale: The hypothalamus regulates hunger and satiety.
why: The cerebellum coordinates movement.
Correct. The hypothalamus regulates hunger and satiety (and other homeostatic drives).
The occipital lobe processes vision.
The hippocampus handles memory.
takeaway: Hunger/satiety = hypothalamus.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Within the hypothalamus, the lateral region acts as a hunger 'on' switch, while the ventromedial region acts as the:
rationale: Lateral hypothalamus = hunger 'on'; ventromedial hypothalamus = satiety 'off.'
why: The ventromedial region signals satiety, not more hunger.
It regulates satiety, not only thirst.
It signals fullness, distinct from temperature regulation.
Correct. Lateral hypothalamus = hunger ('eat'); ventromedial hypothalamus = satiety ('stop'). Damage to the ventromedial region can cause overeating.
takeaway: Lateral hypothalamus = hunger (on). Ventromedial = satiety (off).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Two appetite hormones work in opposition: one from fat cells suppresses appetite, the other from the stomach stimulates it. These are, respectively:
rationale: Leptin (fat) suppresses appetite; ghrelin (stomach) stimulates it. Mnemonic: Ghrelin = Go eat.
why: Correct. Leptin (from adipose tissue) reduces appetite; ghrelin (from the stomach) increases it.
Reversed — leptin suppresses, ghrelin stimulates.
Insulin/cortisol aren't the leptin/ghrelin appetite pair.
Melatonin and gustducin aren't appetite hormones.
takeaway: Leptin (fat) = suppress appetite. Ghrelin (stomach) = stimulate appetite (Go eat).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The idea that the body defends a relatively stable weight by adjusting hunger and metabolism when weight drifts from that level is:
rationale: Set-point theory: the body defends a stable weight by adjusting hunger and metabolism.
why: Drive-reduction is a broad motivation theory, not the weight set-point specifically.
Incentive theory concerns external rewards.
Correct. Set-point theory: the body has a 'thermostat' for weight and adjusts hunger/metabolism to defend it.
The overjustification effect concerns intrinsic motivation.
takeaway: Set-point theory = body defends a stable weight (adjusts hunger/metabolism).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Sexual motivation is best described as influenced by:
choices: Purely biological hormones with no cultural influence
Both biological factors (e.g., sex hormones) and sociocultural factors
Purely learned cultural norms with no biology
rationale: Sexual motivation is biopsychosocial: biological (hormones) + sociocultural factors.
why: Culture clearly shapes sexual behavior alongside biology.
Correct. Sexual motivation reflects both biology (hormones like testosterone/estrogen) and sociocultural learning — like hunger, it's biopsychosocial.
Biology (hormones) contributes alongside culture.
Both biology and environment influence it.
takeaway: Sexual motivation = biology (hormones) + sociocultural factors.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Attitudes are commonly described as having three components (the ABC model):
rationale: Attitudes (ABC): Affective (feelings), Behavioral (actions), Cognitive (beliefs).
why: Those aren't the three attitude components.
Correct. The ABC model: Affective (emotional), Behavioral (action tendency), Cognitive (belief/thought) components.
Those aren't the ABC attitude components.
Those aren't the ABC attitude components.
takeaway: Attitude ABC: Affective (feelings), Behavioral (actions), Cognitive (beliefs).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Feeling anxious at the sight of a spider reflects which component of the attitude toward spiders?
rationale: The affective component = the feelings/emotions in an attitude.
why: The cognitive component is beliefs/thoughts, not feelings.
The behavioral component is action tendencies.
'Arousal' isn't one of the three attitude components.
Correct. The affective component is the emotional/feeling aspect of an attitude.
takeaway: Affective component = feelings/emotions.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Believing that 'spiders are dangerous' reflects which component of an attitude?
rationale: The cognitive component = the beliefs/thoughts in an attitude.
why: Correct. The cognitive component is the thoughts/beliefs that make up an attitude.
The affective component is feelings, not beliefs.
The behavioral component is action tendencies.
'Peripheral' is a persuasion route, not an attitude component.
takeaway: Cognitive component = beliefs/thoughts.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Avoiding a room because a spider is in it reflects which component of an attitude?
rationale: The behavioral component = how an attitude shows up in actions.
