takeaway: Primacy = first info wins. Recency = latest info wins.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The belief that the world is fair, so people generally get what they deserve (leading to victim-blaming), is the:
rationale: Just-world hypothesis: people get what they deserve (→ victim-blaming).
why: Correct. The just-world hypothesis assumes fairness in outcomes, which can lead to blaming victims for their misfortune.
The halo effect is a global-impression bias.
The self-serving bias concerns one's own successes/failures.
The looking-glass self concerns self-image formation.
takeaway: Just-world = the world is fair, people deserve their fate (victim-blaming).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A powerfully negative social label that devalues a person and marks them as different or discredited is a:
rationale: Stigma = a devaluing social label that discredits and sets a person apart.
why: A reference group is a comparison standard.
A folkway is a mild social norm.
Correct. Stigma (Goffman) is a mark of social disgrace that sets a person apart and reduces their status.
A halo is a positive-impression bias.
takeaway: Stigma = a devaluing 'mark' that discredits a person.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Simply being repeatedly exposed to a person or stimulus tends to increase liking for it. This is the:
rationale: Mere exposure effect: repeated exposure → increased liking (familiarity breeds liking).
why: The halo effect is a global-impression bias.
The reciprocity norm is returning favors, not exposure-based liking.
The bystander effect concerns helping in groups.
Correct. The mere exposure effect: familiarity from repeated exposure increases liking (a driver of proximity-based attraction).
takeaway: Mere exposure = the more you see it, the more you like it.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A major, well-documented predictor of who becomes friends or partners — largely because it increases exposure — is:
rationale: Proximity predicts attraction — it raises exposure and interaction.
why: Similarity, not dissimilarity, predicts attraction.
Correct. Proximity increases the chance of interaction and exposure, strongly predicting attraction/relationship formation.
Attractiveness (not unattractiveness) increases initial attraction.
Isolation reduces the exposure that fosters attraction.
takeaway: Proximity → attraction (more exposure/interaction).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Contrary to 'opposites attract,' research shows relationships more often form and last between people who are:
choices: Similar in attitudes, values, and background
rationale: Similarity (attitudes/values/background) predicts attraction — 'birds of a feather.'
why: Opposites-attract is largely a myth; similarity predicts attraction.
Attraction requires interaction, not permanent strangeness.
Correct. Similarity (attitudes, values, background) is a strong, reliable predictor of attraction and relationship stability.
Large value differences tend to reduce, not increase, attraction.
takeaway: Similarity predicts attraction (not 'opposites attract').

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Harlow's experiments with infant monkeys and wire vs. cloth 'mothers' demonstrated that attachment depends heavily on:
rationale: Harlow: infant monkeys chose the cloth 'mother' — attachment depends on contact comfort, not just food.
why: Monkeys chose comfort over the food-providing wire mother.
Attachment wasn't reducible to food-based conditioning.
Harlow's work highlighted contact comfort, not imprinting.
Correct. Infant monkeys preferred the soft cloth 'mother' for comfort even when the wire 'mother' provided food — contact comfort drives attachment.
takeaway: Harlow = contact comfort drives attachment (cloth > wire mother).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An infant who explores freely when a caregiver is present, is distressed at separation, and is comforted on reunion shows ______ attachment.
rationale: Secure attachment: uses caregiver as a safe base; comforted on reunion.
why: Avoidant infants show little distress and avoid the caregiver on reunion.
Correct. Secure attachment: the caregiver is a safe base; the child seeks and is soothed by them on reunion.
Anxious-ambivalent infants are highly distressed and hard to soothe.
Disorganized attachment shows confused, contradictory behavior.
takeaway: Secure attachment = safe base, soothed on reunion.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Ainsworth's Strange Situation identified insecure styles including avoidant and:
rationale: Insecure attachment styles: avoidant and anxious-ambivalent (plus disorganized).
why: Secure is the non-insecure category.
Authoritative is a parenting style, not an attachment style.
Correct. Insecure styles include avoidant and anxious-ambivalent (resistant); later work added disorganized.
'Assimilated' isn't an attachment style.
takeaway: Insecure attachment = avoidant + anxious-ambivalent (+ disorganized).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Helping others at a cost to oneself, with no expectation of personal reward, is:
rationale: Altruism = helping others at a cost to yourself, without expecting reward.
why: Aggression is behavior intended to harm.
Egoism is self-interested motivation, the opposite of altruism.
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in a group.
Correct. Altruism is selfless prosocial behavior benefiting others at a cost to the self.
takeaway: Altruism = selfless helping at a cost to yourself.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Helping close genetic relatives — which can promote the survival of shared genes — is explained by:
rationale: Kin selection: helping relatives promotes shared genes (inclusive fitness).
why: Reciprocal altruism involves helping non-kin who may repay later.
Correct. Kin selection: favoring relatives boosts inclusive fitness by aiding the survival of shared genes.
The bystander effect concerns helping in groups.
Social loafing is reduced effort in groups.
takeaway: Kin selection = help relatives (shared genes / inclusive fitness).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Helping an unrelated individual with the implicit expectation that the favor may be returned later is:
rationale: Reciprocal altruism: help non-kin who may return the favor later.
why: Kin selection involves genetic relatives.
Aggression is intended harm.
Correct. Reciprocal altruism: helping non-kin who may reciprocate, benefiting both over time.
The mere exposure effect concerns familiarity and liking.
takeaway: Reciprocal altruism = you scratch my back, I'll scratch yours (non-kin).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Aggression is best understood as arising from:
choices: Biological, psychological, and social factors interacting (e.g., amygdala, testosterone, frustration, learning)
Only conscious choice with no biology
rationale: Aggression = biology (amygdala, testosterone) + situational (frustration) + learning, interacting.
why: Correct. Aggression is multiply determined: neural (amygdala), hormonal (testosterone), situational (frustration), and learned (modeling).
No single gene determines aggression.
Biology (amygdala, hormones) clearly contributes.
Learning contributes, but so do biology and situational factors.
takeaway: Aggression = biology + situation + learning (multiply determined).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Goffman's view that people manage social interaction like actors performing on a stage — with 'front stage' and 'back stage' behavior — is the:
rationale: Dramaturgical approach (Goffman): social life as theater (front stage vs. back stage).
why: The looking-glass self is Cooley's concept of self-image from others.
The just-world hypothesis concerns deserved outcomes.
Social exchange theory frames relationships as cost–benefit trades.
Correct. The dramaturgical approach (Goffman) frames social life as theatrical performance with front- and back-stage regions.
takeaway: Dramaturgy = life as a stage; front stage vs. back stage (Goffman).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The process of consciously or unconsciously controlling how others perceive us is:
rationale: Impression management = controlling how others perceive you (self-presentation).
why: Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in a group.
Correct. Impression management is the effort to shape the impressions others form of us (self-presentation).
Cognitive dissonance is attitude–behavior inconsistency.
Reciprocal determinism is Bandura's interaction model.
takeaway: Impression management = curate how others see you.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Tension among the demands of a SINGLE role is ______; tension between the demands of TWO OR MORE different roles is ______.
rationale: Role strain = conflict WITHIN one role; role conflict = clash BETWEEN roles.
why: Reversed — strain is within one role, conflict is between roles.
Role exit/role set are different concepts.
Correct. Role strain = conflicting demands within one role; role conflict = demands across different roles clash.
Status inconsistency is a different concept.
takeaway: Role strain = within one role. Role conflict = between roles.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Discrimination carried out by individuals is 'individual'; discrimination built into the policies and practices of organizations and society is:
rationale: Institutional discrimination = unequal treatment built into institutional policies/practices.
why: Correct. Institutional discrimination is embedded in the rules/practices of institutions, operating even without individual prejudice.
Personal prejudice is an individual attitude, not institutional practice.
Ethnocentrism is judging other cultures by one's own.
Stereotype threat is a performance-impairing phenomenon.
takeaway: Institutional discrimination = baked into policies/systems (not just individuals).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An organism's total genetic contribution to future generations — including offspring AND the effect of aiding relatives — is:
rationale: Inclusive fitness = own offspring + effect on relatives' reproduction (drives kin selection).
why: Reproductive isolation prevents interbreeding between species.
Genetic drift is random allele-frequency change.
Density dependence is a population-regulation concept.
Correct. Inclusive fitness counts an individual's own reproduction plus its effect on relatives' reproduction (basis of kin selection).
takeaway: Inclusive fitness = your genes via offspring + helping relatives reproduce.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Behaviors like a bee's waggle dance signaling a food source illustrate that animal communication often functions to:
choices: Convey information that benefits survival/reproduction (e.g., food location)
rationale: Animal communication (e.g., the bee waggle dance) conveys adaptive information like food location.
why: Such signaling is adaptive, not purposeless.
Correct. Animal communication (e.g., the honeybee waggle dance) transmits adaptive information such as food location.
Many animals communicate, not only humans.
Effective communication generally increases, not reduces, fitness.
takeaway: Animal communication = adaptive signaling (e.g., bee waggle dance = food).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Evolutionary game theory (e.g., the prisoner's dilemma, tit-for-tat) helps explain how ______ can be stable even among self-interested individuals.
rationale: Evolutionary game theory explains how cooperation can be stable among self-interested agents (tit-for-tat).
why: Game theory explains cooperation's stability, not just aggression.
It models strategic, not random, behavior.
Correct. Game theory shows cooperative strategies (like tit-for-tat) can be evolutionarily stable, explaining reciprocal altruism.
Reproductive isolation is a speciation concept, unrelated.
takeaway: Game theory = how cooperation stays stable (tit-for-tat, prisoner's dilemma).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The macro-sociological perspective that views society as a system of interdependent parts each serving a function to maintain stability is:
rationale: Functionalism: society = interdependent parts working to maintain stability (Durkheim).
why: Conflict theory emphasizes power struggles over resources, not consensus/stability.
Symbolic interactionism is micro-level, focused on meaning in interaction.
Correct. Functionalism (Durkheim) sees society as an integrated system whose parts contribute to overall stability and solidarity.
Rational choice theory models behavior as cost–benefit calculation.
takeaway: Functionalism = society's parts work together for stability.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The perspective (rooted in Marx) that focuses on power, inequality, and competition among groups over scarce resources is:
rationale: Conflict theory (Marx): society shaped by power struggles and inequality over resources.
why: Correct. Conflict theory sees society as an arena of inequality and struggle between groups with competing interests.
Functionalism emphasizes consensus and stability, not struggle.
Symbolic interactionism is a micro perspective on meaning.
Exchange theory focuses on cost–benefit in relationships.
takeaway: Conflict theory = power struggles over resources (Marx).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The MICRO-level perspective focused on how people create and interpret shared meanings and symbols in everyday interaction is:
rationale: Symbolic interactionism = micro-level meaning-making through symbols in interaction.
why: Functionalism is a macro perspective on stability.
Conflict theory is a macro perspective on power.
Feminist theory analyzes gender-based inequality.
Correct. Symbolic interactionism (Mead, Blumer) is a micro perspective on meaning-making in face-to-face interaction.
takeaway: Symbolic interactionism = micro; shared meanings/symbols in interaction.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The view that many social realities (e.g., money, race, gender roles) exist because people collectively agree to treat them as real is:
rationale: Social constructionism: social realities exist through collective human agreement.
why: Functionalism concerns the functions of social parts, not construction of meaning.
Correct. Social constructionism holds that social categories/institutions are created and maintained through shared human agreement.
Rational choice models individual cost–benefit decisions.
Positivism is an epistemology emphasizing observable facts.
takeaway: Social constructionism = society builds its 'realities' by agreement.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The theory that individuals act to maximize benefits and minimize costs, and that relationships persist when rewards exceed costs, is:
rationale: Rational choice / exchange theory: people maximize rewards and minimize costs.
why: Functionalism is a macro stability perspective.
Symbolic interactionism focuses on meaning, not cost–benefit.
Correct. Rational choice/exchange theory models behavior and relationships as cost–benefit calculations.
Feminist theory analyzes gender inequality.
takeaway: Rational choice/exchange = maximize rewards, minimize costs.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Family, education, religion, government, and the economy are examples of:
rationale: Social institutions = enduring structures (family, education, religion, government, economy) meeting society's needs.
why: Reference groups are comparison standards, not society-wide structures.
A subculture is a group within a culture, not an institution.
Correct. Social institutions are enduring structures that organize and meet a society's basic needs.
A total institution is a specific controlling setting (e.g., prison).
takeaway: Social institutions = family, education, religion, government, economy.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The process by which non-medical problems (e.g., shyness, aging) come to be defined and treated as medical conditions is:
rationale: Medicalization = defining/treating non-medical issues as medical conditions.
why: Correct. Medicalization brings human conditions under medical definition and control (a key concept in health/medicine as an institution).
Secularization is the declining influence of religion.
Assimilation is adopting a dominant culture.
Urbanization is population shift to cities.
takeaway: Medicalization = turning life problems into medical conditions.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Beyond academics, schools transmit norms, values, and social expectations (punctuality, obedience, competition) through the:
rationale: The hidden curriculum = implicit norms/values schools teach beyond academics.
why: The formal syllabus is the explicit content, not the hidden lessons.
Demographic transition is a population model.
The looking-glass self concerns self-image formation.
Correct. The hidden curriculum is the implicit socialization schools provide alongside formal instruction.
takeaway: Hidden curriculum = the unwritten social lessons of school.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Physical objects a society creates (tools, buildings, art) are ______ culture; its ideas, beliefs, values, and norms are ______ culture.
rationale: Material culture = physical objects; nonmaterial culture = beliefs, values, norms.
why: Reversed — objects are material, ideas are nonmaterial.
Folk/popular is a different cultural distinction.
Correct. Material culture = physical artifacts; nonmaterial culture = intangible beliefs, values, and norms.
Dominant/sub describes culture prominence, not material vs. ideas.
takeaway: Material culture = objects. Nonmaterial = ideas/beliefs/norms.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A group with distinct values within a larger culture is a ______; one that actively OPPOSES the dominant culture's values is a ______.
rationale: Subculture = distinct within the mainstream; counterculture = opposes dominant values.
why: Correct. A subculture differs from but coexists with the mainstream; a counterculture rejects/opposes dominant values.
Reversed — the opposing group is the counterculture.
In-group/out-group is about belonging, not cultural opposition.
Folkway/more are norm types.
takeaway: Subculture = differs within; counterculture = opposes the mainstream.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Disorientation from encountering an unfamiliar culture is culture ______; the delay between a change in material culture (e.g., new tech) and society's adaptation is culture ______.
rationale: Culture shock = disorientation in a new culture; culture lag = norms trailing tech change.
why: Reversed — shock is the disorientation, lag is the delayed adaptation.
Diffusion/assimilation are different processes.
Relativism/ethnocentrism are cultural attitudes.
Correct. Culture shock = disorientation in a new culture; culture lag = nonmaterial culture lagging behind material/technological change.
takeaway: Culture shock = disorientation abroad. Culture lag = norms lag behind tech.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Understanding and evaluating another culture by ITS OWN standards, rather than one's own, is:
rationale: Cultural relativism = evaluate a culture by its own standards (opposite of ethnocentrism).
why: Ethnocentrism judges others by one's own culture.
Correct. Cultural relativism judges a culture on its own terms — the opposite of ethnocentrism.
Assimilation is adopting a dominant culture.
Xenocentrism is preferring another culture over one's own.
takeaway: Cultural relativism = judge a culture on its own terms.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Max Weber's 'ideal bureaucracy' is characterized by hierarchy, division of labor, explicit rules, and:
rationale: Weber's ideal bureaucracy: hierarchy, division of labor, rules, impersonality, merit.
why: Bureaucracy replaces favoritism with impersonal rules.
Explicit rules are a defining feature, not their absence.
Correct. Weber's ideal-type bureaucracy features hierarchy, specialization, formal rules, impersonality, and merit-based advancement.
Bureaucratic authority is rational-legal, not charismatic.
takeaway: Ideal bureaucracy = hierarchy + rules + impersonality + merit (Weber).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Ritzer's term for society adopting the efficiency, calculability, predictability, and control of fast-food restaurants is:
rationale: McDonaldization (Ritzer): efficiency, calculability, predictability, control spread through society.
why: Correct. McDonaldization describes the spread of bureaucratic rationalization (efficiency, calculability, predictability, control) across institutions.
Secularization is the decline of religious influence.
Globalization is worldwide interconnection.
Gentrification is neighborhood change by wealthier residents.
takeaway: McDonaldization = efficiency/calculability/predictability/control everywhere.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Studying large-scale social structures and institutions is ______ sociology; studying small-scale, face-to-face interaction is ______ sociology.
rationale: Macrosociology = large structures; microsociology = face-to-face interaction.
why: Reversed — macro is large-scale, micro is face-to-face.
Functionalism/conflict are theories, not the scale distinction.
Etic/emic are research-perspective terms.
Correct. Macrosociology examines broad structures; microsociology examines everyday interaction.
takeaway: Macro = big structures. Micro = face-to-face interaction.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The model describing a society's shift from high birth AND death rates to low birth and death rates as it industrializes is the:
rationale: The demographic transition: high→low birth and death rates as a society industrializes.
why: The Malthusian view predicts population outstripping resources, a different idea.
Social reproduction is the passing of inequality across generations.
Correct. The demographic transition traces falling death rates then falling birth rates as societies industrialize.
Gentrification is neighborhood change by wealthier residents.
takeaway: Demographic transition = high→low birth/death rates with industrialization.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In migration, conditions driving people to LEAVE an area (war, poverty) are ______ factors; conditions attracting them to a destination (jobs, safety) are ______ factors.
rationale: Push factors drive people to leave; pull factors attract them to a destination.
why: Correct. Push factors drive out-migration; pull factors attract in-migration.
Reversed — push drives leaving, pull attracts arriving.
Fertility/mortality are population rates, not migration factors.
Emigration/immigration are directions of migration, not the causal factors.
takeaway: Push = reasons to leave. Pull = reasons to come.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In demography, ______ refers to biological/anatomical differences, while ______ refers to socially constructed roles and identities.
rationale: Sex = biological; gender = socially constructed roles/identity.
why: Reversed — sex is biological, gender is social.
Fertility/fecundity are reproduction measures.
Race/ethnicity is a different distinction.
Correct. Sex is biological; gender is the socially constructed set of roles, behaviors, and identities.
takeaway: Sex = biology. Gender = social roles/identity.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The population shift from rural to urban areas is ______; the growing worldwide interconnection of economies and cultures is ______.
rationale: Urbanization = rural→urban shift; globalization = worldwide interconnection.
why: Reversed — urbanization is city growth, globalization is worldwide interconnection.
Correct. Urbanization is rural-to-urban migration/city growth; globalization is increasing worldwide interconnection.
Gentrification/suburbanization are narrower spatial processes.
Assimilation/diffusion are cultural processes.
takeaway: Urbanization = move to cities. Globalization = worldwide interconnection.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Lacking the resources to meet basic survival needs (food, shelter) is ______ poverty; having far less than the typical standard of one's society is ______ poverty.
rationale: Absolute poverty = can't meet basic needs; relative poverty = far below the societal standard.
why: Reversed — absolute is survival-level, relative is compared to others.
Correct. Absolute poverty is deprivation of basic necessities; relative poverty is disadvantage compared to the societal standard.
Structural/cyclical describe causes, not this definition pair.
Chronic/acute describe duration, not this pair.
takeaway: Absolute poverty = survival deprivation. Relative poverty = below society's standard.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The process by which social inequality is transmitted across generations (e.g., through unequal schooling and inherited capital) is:
rationale: Social reproduction = inequality passed down across generations (via schooling, capital).
why: Social mobility is movement between social positions, not the transmission of inequality.
Meritocracy is the (often idealized) idea that position reflects merit.
Assimilation is adopting a dominant culture.
Correct. Social reproduction is how structures of inequality are passed from one generation to the next.
takeaway: Social reproduction = inequality inherited across generations.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Being systematically shut out of full participation in society's economic, political, and social life is:
rationale: Social exclusion = systematic barring from full participation in society.
why: Correct. Social exclusion is the systematic denial of resources and participation to certain groups.
Social facilitation is a performance effect, unrelated.
Upward mobility is rising in social position.
Cultural relativism is judging a culture on its own terms.
takeaway: Social exclusion = shut out of society's economic/political/social life.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Marx's term for a group's awareness of its shared position and interests is ______; a group's mistaken beliefs that work against its own interests is ______.
rationale: Class consciousness = awareness of shared class interests; false consciousness = beliefs against one's own interests (Marx).
why: Reversed — class consciousness is accurate awareness, false consciousness is the mistaken beliefs.
Anomie/solidarity are Durkheimian concepts, not this Marxian pair.
Correct. Class consciousness = awareness of shared class interests; false consciousness = beliefs contrary to one's real interests.
Stigma/prestige are status concepts.
takeaway: Class consciousness = aware of class interests. False consciousness = beliefs against them.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Systematic, avoidable differences in health outcomes linked to social disadvantage (race, class, geography) are:
rationale: Health disparities = systematic, avoidable health differences tied to social disadvantage.
why: They are systematic and socially patterned, not random.
Correct. Health disparities are preventable differences in health that track with social and economic disadvantage.
The demographic transition is a population model.
The hidden curriculum concerns implicit school socialization.
takeaway: Health disparities = unfair, patterned health gaps by social group.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The physical separation of groups (often by race or income) into different neighborhoods, concentrating disadvantage, is:
rationale: Residential segregation = groups separated into different neighborhoods, concentrating (dis)advantage.
why: Gentrification is the influx of wealthier residents into a lower-income area.
Suburban sprawl is low-density outward city growth.
Globalization is worldwide interconnection.
Correct. Residential segregation clusters groups into separate areas, concentrating advantage or disadvantage (a form of spatial inequality).
takeaway: Residential segregation = separated neighborhoods concentrate disadvantage.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The principle that no group should bear a disproportionate share of environmental hazards (pollution, toxic sites) is:
rationale: Environmental justice = fair distribution of environmental hazards across groups.
why: Correct. Environmental justice addresses the unequal distribution of environmental harms across social groups.
Cultural relativism concerns evaluating cultures on their own terms.
Medicalization is defining problems as medical.
Social facilitation is a performance effect.
takeaway: Environmental justice = no group bears unfair environmental harm.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Epidemiology consistently finds a 'social gradient': as socioeconomic status rises, health tends to:
choices: Improve steadily across the whole SES range
rationale: The social gradient: health improves stepwise as SES rises (at every level).
why: Health improves, not worsens, with higher SES.
Health varies by SES; it isn't identical across levels.
Correct. The social gradient: health improves stepwise with rising SES — not just poor vs. rich, but at every level.
Social factors, not genetics alone, drive the gradient.
takeaway: Social gradient = higher SES → better health, all the way up.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The framework (Crenshaw) recognizing that overlapping identities (race, gender, class) combine to create UNIQUE, compounded experiences of disadvantage is:
rationale: Intersectionality (Crenshaw): overlapping identities combine into unique, compounded (dis)advantage.
why: Assimilation is adopting a dominant culture.
Correct. Intersectionality analyzes how multiple social identities intersect to shape compounded, distinctive experiences of privilege or oppression.
Meritocracy is the idea that position reflects merit.
The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve.
takeaway: Intersectionality = overlapping identities compound disadvantage.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The uneven distribution of resources and opportunity BETWEEN nations — not just within them — is:
rationale: Global inequality = uneven resources/opportunity between nations.
why: Structural mobility is society-wide position change from economic shifts.
Culture lag is norms trailing technological change.
Deindividuation is loss of self-awareness in groups.
Correct. Global inequality concerns disparities in wealth, power, and well-being across countries.
takeaway: Global inequality = disparities between countries.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Wallerstein's world-systems theory divides the global economy into wealthy, dominant ______ nations and exploited, resource-supplying ______ nations.
rationale: World-systems (Wallerstein): wealthy core nations dominate; peripheral nations supply cheap labor/resources.
why: Correct. World-systems theory: core nations dominate and profit; peripheral nations supply cheap labor/resources (semi-periphery is intermediate).
Reversed — core nations are the wealthy dominant ones.
Urban/rural is a within-country distinction, not the world-systems pair.
Push/pull are migration factors.
takeaway: World-systems: core = wealthy/dominant, periphery = exploited/supplying.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: The key feature that makes a study EXPERIMENTAL — and allows causal conclusions — is that the researcher:
choices: Only observes variables without manipulating them
Manipulates an independent variable and uses random assignment
rationale: Experiments manipulate an IV + use random assignment → can infer causation. Observational studies only measure.
why: That describes an observational study, which can't establish causation.
Sample size alone doesn't make a study experimental.
Correct. An experiment manipulates the IV and randomly assigns subjects to conditions, supporting causal inference. Observational studies only measure what already exists.
Measuring a correlation is observational, not experimental.
takeaway: Experiment = manipulate IV + random assignment → causation. Observational = just measure.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In an experiment testing whether sleep affects test scores, the amount of sleep (manipulated) is the ______ variable and the test score (measured) is the ______ variable.
rationale: IV = manipulated (cause); DV = measured (effect).
why: Correct. The independent variable is manipulated (the presumed cause); the dependent variable is measured (the presumed effect).
Reversed — the manipulated variable is independent, the measured one is dependent.
Confounding/control describe other variable roles, not the manipulated/measured pair.
Continuous/discrete describe data types, not IV/DV roles.
takeaway: IV = manipulated (cause). DV = measured (effect).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: An extraneous variable that is related to BOTH the independent and dependent variables — offering an alternative explanation for the results — is a:
rationale: A confounding variable is tied to both IV and DV, giving an alternative explanation for results.
why: The dependent variable is the measured outcome, not an alternative explanation.
An operational definition specifies how a variable is measured.
A placebo is an inert treatment used as a control.
Correct. A confound is linked to both the IV and DV and can create a spurious apparent relationship; controlling confounds is essential for valid causal claims.
takeaway: Confound = 3rd variable tied to both IV and DV (alternative explanation).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Randomly placing participants into experimental groups supports ______; randomly selecting participants from a population supports ______.
rationale: Random assignment → internal validity (causation); random sampling → external validity (generalizability).
why: Reversed — assignment aids causation, sampling aids generalizability.
Correct. Random ASSIGNMENT balances groups (internal validity/causation); random SAMPLING makes the sample representative (external validity/generalizability).
These concern validity types, not the reliability/validity distinction directly.
They are distinct procedures serving different goals.
takeaway: Assignment = causal validity. Sampling = generalizability.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A measure that yields consistent results on repeated use is ______; a measure that actually captures what it intends to measure is ______.
rationale: Reliability = consistent results; validity = measures what it's supposed to. Reliable ≠ valid.
why: Reversed — consistency is reliability, accuracy is validity.
Random/systematic describe error/bias types, not this pair.
Correct. Reliability = consistency/repeatability; validity = accuracy (measuring the intended construct). A measure can be reliable but not valid.
Descriptive/inferential describe statistics types.
takeaway: Reliable = consistent. Valid = accurate. (Can be reliable but not valid.)

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A correlational study finds ice-cream sales and drowning rise together. The best conclusion is:
choices: They are associated, but a third variable (e.g., hot weather) may cause both
rationale: Correlation ≠ causation: a third variable (confound) or reverse direction can explain an association.
why: Correct. Correlation does not imply causation; a confound (summer heat) can drive both. Directionality and third variables remain possible.
Correlation alone can't establish that one causes the other.
Reverse causation is equally unsupported by correlation alone.
A real association exists; it's just not necessarily causal.
takeaway: Correlation ≠ causation (watch for confounds / reverse direction).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A survey advertised only on a fitness website over-samples health-conscious people. This threat to a study's validity is a form of:
rationale: Selection/sampling bias = a non-representative sample threatens generalizability.
why: Random error is unsystematic noise, not this systematic skew.
The placebo effect is improvement from expectation, not a sampling issue.
Regression to the mean is a statistical artifact of extreme scores, not sampling bias.
Correct. Selection/sampling bias occurs when the sample isn't representative of the target population, threatening generalizability.
takeaway: Selection bias = unrepresentative sample (hurts generalizability).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In a right-skewed income distribution with a few very high earners, the measure of central tendency pulled MOST toward the high values is the:
rationale: The mean is pulled toward outliers; in a right skew, mean > median > mode.
why: The median resists outliers, staying closer to the bulk of the data.
The mode is the most frequent value, unaffected by extreme values.
Correct. The mean is sensitive to outliers, so a right (positive) skew pulls the mean above the median. The median is more robust.
The range is a measure of spread, not central tendency.
takeaway: Right skew: mean > median > mode (mean chases the outliers).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: A distribution with a long tail extending to the RIGHT (toward high values) is described as:
rationale: Positive/right skew = long tail toward high values (mean pulled up).
why: Correct. A right/positive skew has its tail toward high values (mean > median). Skew is named for the direction of the tail.
A left/negative skew has the tail toward low values.
A normal distribution is symmetric with no skew.
A right tail doesn't make a distribution bimodal.
takeaway: Right skew = tail points right (high values); mean > median.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Standard deviation is a measure of:
choices: The central value of the data
The spread/variability of scores around the mean
rationale: Standard deviation = spread of scores around the mean (dispersion).
why: The central value is captured by the mean/median, not the SD.
The most frequent score is the mode.
Correlation between variables is a separate statistic (r).
Correct. Standard deviation quantifies how dispersed scores are around the mean (larger SD = more spread).
takeaway: SD = how spread out scores are around the mean.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: In null hypothesis testing, a result is typically called 'statistically significant' when the p-value is:
rationale: Statistically significant: p < alpha (commonly 0.05) → reject the null hypothesis.
why: A p-value above 0.05 fails to reach the usual significance threshold.
Correct. A p-value below alpha (often 0.05) leads researchers to reject the null hypothesis and call the result statistically significant.
A p-value of 1.0 indicates no evidence against the null.
The p-value is a probability, unrelated to the raw sample size value.
takeaway: Significant = p < 0.05 (reject the null).

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
tag: Type I vs. Type II error
stem: Rejecting a true null hypothesis (a false positive) is a ______ error; failing to reject a false null (a false negative) is a ______ error.
rationale: Type I = false positive (reject true null); Type II = false negative (miss real effect).
why: Reversed — Type I is the false positive, Type II the false negative.
Random/systematic describe error/bias types, not I/II.
Correct. Type I = false positive (finding an effect that isn't real); Type II = false negative (missing a real effect).
Sampling/measurement are error sources, not the I/II distinction.
takeaway: Type I = false positive. Type II = false negative.

section: Psychological, Social & Biological Foundations of Behavior
stem: Summarizing a dataset with means and standard deviations uses ______ statistics; drawing conclusions about a population from a sample uses ______ statistics.
rationale: Descriptive statistics summarize data; inferential statistics generalize to a population.
why: Correct. Descriptive statistics summarize data; inferential statistics generalize from a sample to a population (hypothesis tests, confidence intervals).
Reversed — summarizing is descriptive, generalizing is inferential.
Nominal/ordinal are levels of measurement, not this pair.
Independent/dependent describe variables, not statistics types.
takeaway: Descriptive = summarize. Inferential = generalize to population.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In DNA, the two-ring nitrogenous bases (purines) are adenine and guanine; the one-ring bases (pyrimidines) are:
rationale: Purines (2 rings) = A, G; pyrimidines (1 ring) = C, T (U in RNA). PURe As Gold = purines; CUT = pyrimidines.
why: Adenine and guanine are purines (two rings), not pyrimidines.
Adenine is a purine; only thymine here is a pyrimidine.
Correct. Pyrimidines (one ring) = cytosine, thymine (and uracil in RNA). Purines (two rings) = adenine, guanine. Mnemonic: PURe As Gold (A, G) are purines; CUT the pie (C, U, T) are pyrimidines.
Guanine is a purine; only cytosine here is a pyrimidine.
takeaway: Purines (2 rings) = A,G. Pyrimidines (1 ring) = C,T,U.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In double-stranded DNA, adenine pairs with thymine via two hydrogen bonds, and guanine pairs with cytosine via:
rationale: A=T (2 H-bonds), G≡C (3 H-bonds). More G–C → higher melting temperature.
why: Correct. G≡C has three hydrogen bonds (stronger); A=T has two. Higher GC content → higher melting temperature.
A–T has two H-bonds; G–C has three.
G–C has three, not one, hydrogen bonds.
Base pairs are held by hydrogen bonds, not covalent bonds.
takeaway: A-T = 2 H-bonds; G-C = 3 H-bonds (G-C stronger → higher Tm).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The two strands of the DNA double helix run antiparallel, meaning one strand runs 5'→3' while its complement runs:
rationale: DNA strands are antiparallel: one 5'→3', the complement 3'→5'.
why: Parallel same-direction strands couldn't base-pair correctly.
Antiparallel means opposite directions, not the same direction.
Antiparallel strands point in opposite directions with opposite polarity.
Correct. The strands are antiparallel — aligned in opposite 5'/3' orientations, which is essential for complementary base pairing and replication.
takeaway: Antiparallel = strands run opposite (5'→3' vs 3'→5').

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Chargaff observed that in any double-stranded DNA sample, the amount of adenine equals thymine and guanine equals cytosine. This reflects:
choices: Complementary base pairing (A pairs with T, G with C)
Equal amounts of all four bases always
rationale: Chargaff's rules: %A=%T and %G=%C (from complementary base pairing).
why: Base composition isn't random; pairing constrains it.
Correct. Because A pairs with T and G with C, %A=%T and %G=%C in double-stranded DNA (Chargaff's rules).
%A=%T and %G=%C, but the four bases aren't necessarily equal to each other.
Chargaff's rules apply to double-stranded DNA.
takeaway: Chargaff: %A=%T, %G=%C (complementary pairing).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The backbone of a DNA strand is formed by covalent phosphodiester bonds linking:
choices: The nitrogenous bases of adjacent nucleotides
The 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' phosphate of the next
The 2' hydroxyl groups of adjacent sugars
rationale: The backbone = phosphodiester bonds from the 3'-OH of one sugar to the 5'-phosphate of the next.
why: Bases pair across strands; they don't form the backbone linkages.
The backbone is sugar–phosphate–sugar, not phosphate–phosphate.
Correct. Phosphodiester bonds connect the 3'-OH of one deoxyribose to the 5'-phosphate of the next, giving the strand 5'→3' polarity.
DNA's deoxyribose lacks a 2'-OH; linkage is 3'–5'.
takeaway: Backbone = 3'→5' phosphodiester bonds (sugar-phosphate).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: DNA's sugar (deoxyribose) differs from RNA's sugar (ribose) in that deoxyribose:
choices: Lacks a hydroxyl group at the 2' carbon
rationale: Deoxyribose lacks the 2'-OH that ribose has (H instead) → DNA is more stable than RNA.
why: Correct. Deoxyribose is missing the 2'-OH present in ribose (it has H instead), making DNA more chemically stable than RNA.
The sugar difference is at the 2' position, not phosphate count.
Uracil is a base, not part of the sugar difference.
Both are five-carbon (pentose) sugars.
takeaway: Deoxyribose = no 2'-OH (RNA's ribose has it). DNA more stable.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The Meselson–Stahl experiment showed DNA replication is semiconservative, meaning each daughter molecule consists of:
choices: One parental (template) strand and one newly synthesized strand
A random mix of old and new fragments in each strand
rationale: Replication is semiconservative: each daughter DNA = one old + one new strand.
why: That would be conservative replication, which was ruled out.
That would leave no new synthesis; both duplexes gain a new strand.
Correct. Semiconservative replication: each new duplex has one conserved parental strand and one new strand.
That describes the dispersive model, which was ruled out.
takeaway: Semiconservative = each new DNA has 1 old + 1 new strand.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: DNA polymerase can only add nucleotides to the ______ end of the growing strand, so synthesis always proceeds:
rationale: DNA polymerase adds to the 3'-OH → synthesis is always 5'→3'.
why: Correct. DNA polymerase adds nucleotides to the free 3'-OH, so the new strand grows 5'→3' (reading the template 3'→5').
Polymerase adds to the 3' end, synthesizing 5'→3'.
Synthesis is 5'→3', not 3'→5'.
Nucleotides are added to the 3' end, not the 5' end.
takeaway: DNA synthesis is always 5'→3' (adds to the 3' end).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At the replication fork, the enzyme that unwinds and separates the two parental DNA strands is:
rationale: Helicase unwinds/separates the parental strands at the replication fork.
why: Ligase seals nicks between fragments, it doesn't unwind DNA.
Primase lays down RNA primers.
Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork but doesn't separate the strands at the fork.
Correct. Helicase unwinds the double helix at the fork; single-strand binding proteins then keep the strands apart.
takeaway: Helicase = unwinds/separates DNA at the fork.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Because synthesis is only 5'→3', the lagging strand is made discontinuously as short segments called:
rationale: The lagging strand is built discontinuously as Okazaki fragments (leading strand is continuous).
why: Introns are non-coding sequences removed from pre-mRNA.
Correct. The lagging strand is synthesized in short Okazaki fragments (away from the fork), later joined by DNA ligase; the leading strand is continuous.
Codons are mRNA base triplets.
Telomeres are repetitive sequences at chromosome ends.
takeaway: Lagging strand = Okazaki fragments (discontinuous); leading = continuous.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: DNA polymerase needs a starting point, so ______ lays down an RNA primer; after synthesis, ______ seals the gaps between fragments.
rationale: Primase makes the RNA primer; DNA ligase seals the gaps between Okazaki fragments.
why: Reversed — primase makes primers, ligase seals gaps.
Helicase/topoisomerase handle unwinding/supercoiling, not priming or sealing.
Correct. Primase synthesizes RNA primers to provide a 3'-OH; DNA ligase joins Okazaki fragments after primers are replaced.
Telomerase extends chromosome ends, not the primer/sealing roles here.
takeaway: Primase = RNA primer. Ligase = seals fragments.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Many DNA polymerases improve fidelity by removing a mismatched nucleotide just added, using their:
rationale: Proofreading = 3'→5' exonuclease activity removes a just-added mismatched base.
why: Correct. Proofreading uses 3'→5' exonuclease activity to excise a wrongly incorporated base, greatly lowering the error rate.
The 5'→3' polymerase activity adds nucleotides; it doesn't remove mismatches.
Helicase unwinds DNA; it isn't a proofreading function.
Ligase seals nicks; it doesn't excise mismatches.
takeaway: Proofreading = 3'→5' exonuclease (removes mismatches).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Because DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the very ends of linear chromosomes, the enzyme that extends these repetitive ends (in germ/stem cells) is:
rationale: Telomerase extends telomeres (repetitive chromosome ends) to offset end-replication shortening.
why: Topoisomerase relieves supercoiling, not end-shortening.
Ligase seals nicks; it doesn't extend telomeres.
Primase makes primers; it doesn't extend chromosome ends.
Correct. Telomerase, a reverse transcriptase with an RNA template, extends telomeres to counter end-replication shortening.
takeaway: Telomerase = extends telomere ends (counters shortening).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Transcription is carried out by RNA polymerase, which — unlike DNA polymerase — :
choices: Does not require a primer to begin synthesis
rationale: RNA polymerase needs no primer, synthesizes 5'→3', and uses uracil instead of thymine.
why: RNA polymerase also synthesizes 5'→3'.
RNA uses uracil, not thymine.
Correct. RNA polymerase can initiate synthesis de novo (no primer needed) and synthesizes RNA 5'→3' using uracil in place of thymine.
Unlike DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase needs no primer.
takeaway: RNA pol: no primer needed; 5'→3'; uses uracil.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: RNA polymerase reads the ______ strand to build an mRNA that is identical (except U for T) to the ______ strand.
rationale: mRNA is built from the template (antisense) strand and matches the coding (sense) strand (U for T).
why: Correct. The template (antisense) strand is read 3'→5'; the resulting mRNA matches the coding (sense) strand sequence with U replacing T.
Reversed — the template is read, and mRNA matches the coding strand.
Leading/lagging are replication terms, not transcription strands.
Leading/lagging are replication terms, not transcription strands.
takeaway: Template strand is read; mRNA = coding strand sequence (U for T).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Transcription begins when RNA polymerase and transcription factors bind a DNA sequence upstream of the gene called the:
choices: Promoter (which often contains a TATA box)
rationale: The promoter (often with a TATA box) is where RNA polymerase binds to start transcription.
why: The terminator signals the END of transcription.
The poly-A tail is added post-transcriptionally to the mRNA 3' end.
The anticodon is on tRNA, unrelated to transcription initiation.
Correct. The promoter is the upstream binding site (eukaryotic promoters often contain a TATA box) that positions RNA polymerase to start transcription.
takeaway: Promoter (TATA box) = transcription start site for RNA pol.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In eukaryotes, the immediate product of transcription — before processing — is:
rationale: Eukaryotic transcription first makes pre-mRNA (hnRNA), later processed into mature mRNA.
why: Mature mRNA results only after processing the pre-mRNA.
Correct. Transcription yields pre-mRNA (hnRNA), which must be processed (cap, tail, splicing) before becoming mature mRNA.
A polypeptide is the product of translation, not transcription.
tRNA is a separate transcript; the mRNA precursor here is pre-mRNA.
takeaway: Transcription → pre-mRNA (hnRNA), then processed to mRNA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In eukaryotes, the RNA polymerase responsible for transcribing protein-coding genes into mRNA is:
rationale: RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA. (Pol I = rRNA; Pol III = tRNA.)
why: RNA polymerase I transcribes most rRNA.
RNA polymerase III transcribes tRNA and 5S rRNA.
Correct. RNA polymerase II transcribes mRNA (protein-coding genes); Pol I makes rRNA and Pol III makes tRNA (and small RNAs).
DNA polymerase III is a replication enzyme, not for transcription.
takeaway: RNA Pol II = mRNA. Pol I = rRNA. Pol III = tRNA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Before a eukaryotic mRNA leaves the nucleus, it receives a 5' 7-methylguanosine cap and a 3' poly-A tail, which together:
choices: Protect the mRNA from degradation and aid export/translation
rationale: The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail protect mRNA and aid export/translation.
why: The start codon (AUG) is within the mRNA sequence, not the cap/tail.
Splicing removes introns; the cap/tail don't.
Correct. The 5' cap and 3' poly-A tail increase mRNA stability and promote nuclear export and ribosome binding.
The ribosome is made of rRNA and protein, not the mRNA cap/tail.
takeaway: 5' cap + poly-A tail = stability + export + translation.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During splicing, the non-coding sequences that are removed from pre-mRNA are ______, and the sequences that remain and are expressed are ______.
rationale: Introns are removed (intervening); exons are expressed (retained).
why: Correct. Introns are intervening sequences spliced OUT; exons are EXpressed sequences retained in the mature mRNA.
Reversed — introns are removed, exons are expressed.
Codons/anticodons are translation terms, not spliced sequences.
Promoters/terminators are transcription signals, not spliced sequences.
takeaway: Introns OUT, exons EXpressed. Splicing removes introns.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Intron removal in eukaryotes is carried out by a complex of small nuclear ribonucleoproteins (snRNPs) called the:
rationale: The spliceosome (snRNPs) removes introns from pre-mRNA.
why: The ribosome translates mRNA into protein.
The proteasome degrades proteins.
A nucleosome is DNA wrapped around histones.
Correct. The spliceosome (snRNPs + associated proteins) recognizes splice sites and excises introns.
takeaway: Spliceosome = removes introns (snRNPs).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: By joining different combinations of exons, a single gene can produce multiple distinct proteins. This is:
rationale: Alternative splicing: one gene → multiple proteins by combining exons differently.
why: A point mutation changes a single base, not exon combinations.
Correct. Alternative splicing lets one gene encode several protein isoforms by including/excluding particular exons.
Semiconservative replication describes DNA copying.
Wobble refers to flexible codon–anticodon pairing.
takeaway: Alternative splicing = one gene → many proteins (different exon combos).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The genetic code is read in units of three mRNA nucleotides, each specifying one amino acid. Each triplet is a:
rationale: A codon = 3 mRNA nucleotides coding one amino acid.
why: The anticodon is the complementary triplet on tRNA.
An exon is a coding mRNA segment, not a single triplet.
Correct. A codon is a three-nucleotide mRNA unit that specifies an amino acid (or a start/stop signal).
An operon is a cluster of prokaryotic genes.
takeaway: Codon = 3-nucleotide mRNA unit → one amino acid.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: With 64 codons but only 20 amino acids, most amino acids are specified by more than one codon. This property is called:
rationale: The code is degenerate: many codons → same amino acid (but each codon is unambiguous).
why: Correct. The code is degenerate/redundant: multiple codons can encode the same amino acid (yet each codon is unambiguous — it codes for only one).
The code is unambiguous, not ambiguous — each codon has one meaning.
The code is non-overlapping; codons don't share nucleotides.
The code is nearly universal, which is a separate property.
takeaway: Degenerate = multiple codons per amino acid (but each codon unambiguous).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Translation begins at the start codon AUG (methionine) and ends at one of three stop codons:
rationale: Start = AUG (Met); stops = UAA, UAG, UGA.
why: Those are alternative start-related codons, not the stop codons.
Those code amino acids, not stop signals.
Those include thymine (DNA); mRNA uses uracil, and these aren't the stop codons.
Correct. The stop (nonsense) codons UAA, UAG, UGA terminate translation; AUG is the start codon coding methionine.
takeaway: Start = AUG (Met). Stops = UAA, UAG, UGA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Flexibility in base pairing at the THIRD codon position — allowing one tRNA to recognize multiple codons — is explained by the:
rationale: Wobble: flexible pairing at the 3rd codon position lets one tRNA read several codons.
why: The central dogma is DNA→RNA→protein, not third-position pairing.
Correct. Wobble allows non-standard pairing at the third codon (first anticodon) position, so fewer tRNAs are needed — and it underlies much of the code's degeneracy.
Chargaff's rules concern DNA base ratios.
The lock-and-key model describes enzyme–substrate specificity.
takeaway: Wobble = flexible 3rd-position pairing (one tRNA, multiple codons).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The genetic code is described as nearly universal and non-overlapping, and it is read:
choices: With codons overlapping by one base
In a fixed reading frame, three bases at a time without gaps
rationale: The code is read 5'→3' in a fixed reading frame, three non-overlapping, commaless bases at a time.
why: mRNA is read 5'→3', not 3'→5'.
The code is non-overlapping; codons don't share bases.
Correct. The code is read continuously (commaless) in a set reading frame, 5'→3', three non-overlapping bases at a time.
The code is commaless; there are no separators between codons.
takeaway: Code is read 5'→3', triplets, non-overlapping, no commas, fixed frame.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Each transfer RNA carries a specific amino acid and recognizes an mRNA codon through its complementary:
rationale: tRNA's anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon to deliver the right amino acid.
why: The codon is on the mRNA; tRNA carries the anticodon.
The promoter is a transcription start site.
Correct. The tRNA anticodon base-pairs with the mRNA codon, ensuring the correct amino acid is delivered.
The poly-A tail is an mRNA modification, not on tRNA.
takeaway: tRNA anticodon pairs with the mRNA codon.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The ribosome, which catalyzes peptide bond formation, is composed of:
choices: rRNA and proteins (with rRNA providing the catalytic activity)
rationale: The ribosome = rRNA + protein; rRNA catalyzes peptide bonds (a ribozyme).
why: Correct. Ribosomes are made of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins; the rRNA is the catalytic component (a ribozyme) forming peptide bonds.
Ribosomes contain no DNA or lipids.
Ribosomes contain rRNA in addition to protein.
mRNA is the message translated, not the ribosome's structure.
takeaway: Ribosome = rRNA + protein; rRNA is catalytic (ribozyme).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The enzyme that attaches the correct amino acid to its matching tRNA ("charging" the tRNA) is:
rationale: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges each tRNA with its correct amino acid (uses ATP).
why: Peptidyl transferase (rRNA) forms peptide bonds in the ribosome.
RNA polymerase transcribes DNA to RNA.
Helicase unwinds DNA during replication.
Correct. Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases charge each tRNA with its correct amino acid, using ATP — a key fidelity step.
takeaway: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase = charges tRNA with the right amino acid.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During elongation, an incoming charged tRNA enters the ______ site, the growing peptide is held at the ______ site, and the empty tRNA leaves from the E site.
rationale: Ribosome sites: A = incoming aminoacyl-tRNA, P = peptidyl (growing chain), E = exit.
why: Reversed — incoming tRNA enters the A site, the chain is at the P site.
Correct. A site = incoming aminoacyl-tRNA; P site = peptidyl-tRNA (growing chain); E site = exit for the deacylated tRNA.
The incoming tRNA enters A, not E; the chain is held at P.
The growing chain is at P, but the incoming tRNA enters A, not P again.
takeaway: A = arrival (aminoacyl), P = peptide (growing), E = exit.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A polypeptide is synthesized from its ______ terminus to its ______ terminus as the ribosome reads mRNA 5'→3'.
rationale: Proteins are built N→C terminus as mRNA is read 5'→3'.
why: Reversed — synthesis goes N→C, not C→N.
5'/3' describe nucleic acids, not polypeptide termini.
Correct. Translation proceeds N-terminus → C-terminus while the ribosome reads mRNA 5'→3'.
5'/3' describe nucleic acids; and the direction would be reversed.
takeaway: Protein synthesis: N→C terminus (mRNA read 5'→3').

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A point mutation that changes a codon but still specifies the SAME amino acid (thanks to code degeneracy) is a:
rationale: Silent mutation: codon changes but the amino acid stays the same (code degeneracy).
why: A missense mutation changes the amino acid.
A nonsense mutation creates a premature stop codon.
Correct. A silent mutation alters the DNA/codon without changing the encoded amino acid — usually at the wobble position.
A frameshift results from insertions/deletions, not a same-amino-acid substitution.
takeaway: Silent = codon changes, same amino acid.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A point mutation that changes one amino acid to a DIFFERENT amino acid is ______; one that changes an amino-acid codon into a STOP codon is ______.
rationale: Missense = different amino acid; nonsense = premature stop codon.
why: Correct. Missense = different amino acid; nonsense = premature stop codon (truncated protein).
Reversed — missense changes the amino acid, nonsense makes a stop.
Silent (no change) and frameshift (indel) are different categories.
Frameshift and silent aren't the substitution types described.
takeaway: Missense = wrong amino acid. Nonsense = premature STOP.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An insertion or deletion of a number of nucleotides NOT divisible by three causes a ______, which alters every codon downstream.
rationale: Frameshift = insertion/deletion not a multiple of 3 → all downstream codons altered.
why: A silent mutation doesn't shift the frame or change the protein.
A point substitution changes one base without shifting the frame.
A transition is a type of substitution, not a frameshift.
Correct. A frameshift shifts the reading frame, garbling all downstream codons (often producing a premature stop).
takeaway: Frameshift = indel not divisible by 3 → downstream codons ruined.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A substitution of one purine for the other purine (or one pyrimidine for the other pyrimidine) is a ______; a purine↔pyrimidine swap is a ______.
rationale: Transition = same base type (purine↔purine / pyrimidine↔pyrimidine); transversion = purine↔pyrimidine.
why: Reversed — same-type swap is a transition.
Correct. Transition = purine↔purine or pyrimidine↔pyrimidine (same type); transversion = purine↔pyrimidine (type switch).
Missense/nonsense describe effects on the protein, not base-type swaps.
Insertions/deletions are indels, not substitutions.
takeaway: Transition = same type swap. Transversion = purine↔pyrimidine.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A thymine dimer caused by UV light is removed and replaced by which repair pathway?
rationale: Nucleotide excision repair removes UV-induced thymine dimers (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum).
why: Replication copies DNA; it isn't the dimer-repair pathway.
Wobble concerns codon–anticodon pairing.
Correct. Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions like UV-induced thymine dimers, then resynthesizes the strand (defective in xeroderma pigmentosum).
Alternative splicing is an RNA-processing mechanism, not DNA repair.
takeaway: Thymine dimers (UV) → fixed by nucleotide excision repair.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An organism's genetic makeup (its alleles) is its ______; the observable trait that results is its ______.
rationale: Genotype = alleles present; phenotype = the observable trait.
why: Reversed — genotype is the genetic makeup, phenotype the observable trait.
Allele/locus describe a gene variant and its position, not this pair.
Correct. Genotype = the alleles present; phenotype = the expressed, observable characteristic.
Dominant/recessive describe allele behavior, not genotype vs. phenotype.
takeaway: Genotype = the alleles. Phenotype = the observable trait.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An individual with two identical alleles for a gene is ______; one with two different alleles is ______.
rationale: Homozygous = two identical alleles; heterozygous = two different alleles.
why: Correct. Homozygous = two identical alleles (AA or aa); heterozygous = two different alleles (Aa).
Reversed — identical alleles = homozygous.
Dominant/recessive describe how alleles are expressed, not zygosity.
Haploid/diploid describe chromosome number, not allele identity.
takeaway: Homozygous = same alleles (AA/aa). Heterozygous = different (Aa).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Mendel's law of segregation states that the two alleles for a trait:
choices: Are inherited only from the father
Separate during gamete formation, so each gamete receives only one
rationale: Law of segregation: the two alleles separate during gamete formation (one per gamete).
why: Alleles separate, not stay together, during gamete formation.
Alleles remain discrete (particulate inheritance), not blended.
Each parent contributes one allele; inheritance isn't paternal-only.
Correct. The two alleles segregate during meiosis so each gamete carries just one allele per gene.
takeaway: Segregation = alleles separate into gametes (one each).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Mendel's law of independent assortment states that alleles of different genes:
choices: Assort into gametes independently of one another (if unlinked)
rationale: Independent assortment: unlinked genes sort into gametes independently → new combinations.
why: Independent assortment produces new combinations, not fixed co-inheritance.
Correct. Genes on different chromosomes assort independently during meiosis, producing new allele combinations (linked genes are an exception).
It specifically enables new combinations.
Assortment occurs in meiosis, not mitosis.
takeaway: Independent assortment = unlinked genes sort independently (meiosis).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: To determine whether an organism showing a dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous, you cross it with an individual that is:
rationale: A test cross uses a homozygous recessive partner to reveal a dominant individual's genotype.
why: A homozygous dominant partner would mask the recessive allele, hiding the answer.
A heterozygous partner complicates interpretation of the ratios.
Correct. A test cross with a homozygous recessive individual reveals the unknown genotype: any recessive offspring means the parent was heterozygous.
Diploid organisms are crossed; 'haploid' isn't the test-cross partner.
takeaway: Test cross = cross with homozygous recessive to find the genotype.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When a heterozygote shows a BLENDED, intermediate phenotype (red × white → pink flowers), the inheritance pattern is:
rationale: Incomplete dominance = blended intermediate heterozygote (red × white → pink).
why: In codominance BOTH alleles are fully and separately expressed, not blended.
Complete dominance masks the recessive allele entirely.
Correct. In incomplete dominance the heterozygote is an intermediate blend of the two homozygous phenotypes.
Epistasis is one gene masking another gene's expression.
takeaway: Incomplete dominance = blended intermediate (pink).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When BOTH alleles are fully and simultaneously expressed in the heterozygote (e.g., AB blood type), the pattern is:
rationale: Codominance = both alleles fully expressed (AB blood type).
why: Correct. In codominance both alleles are expressed distinctly and fully (the AB blood phenotype shows both A and B antigens).
Incomplete dominance blends the phenotypes; codominance shows both fully.
Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
Polygenic inheritance is many genes affecting one trait.
takeaway: Codominance = both alleles fully shown (AB blood).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The human ABO blood group, controlled by three alleles (I^A, I^B, i) in the population, illustrates:
choices: Multiple alleles (with codominance and complete dominance combined)
rationale: ABO = multiple alleles: I^A and I^B codominant, both dominant over i.
why: ABO is governed by three alleles, not one.
I^A and I^B are codominant, not blended (incomplete).
ABO is autosomal, not sex-linked.
Correct. ABO has three alleles: I^A and I^B are codominant to each other and both dominant over the recessive i.
takeaway: ABO = 3 alleles; I^A/I^B codominant, both dominant over i.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: One gene influencing MANY different traits is ______; MANY genes contributing to ONE trait (e.g., height) is ______.
rationale: Pleiotropy = one gene → many traits; polygenic = many genes → one trait.
why: Reversed — pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
Correct. Pleiotropy = one gene, many effects; polygenic = many genes, one (often continuous) trait.
Epistasis/codominance describe different phenomena.
Codominance/epistasis aren't the one-gene-many-traits pair.
takeaway: Pleiotropy = 1 gene, many traits. Polygenic = many genes, 1 trait.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When the expression of one gene MASKS or modifies the expression of a DIFFERENT gene (e.g., an albinism gene hiding coat-color genes), this is:
rationale: Epistasis: one gene masks/modifies the expression of a different gene.
why: Incomplete dominance is an allele interaction within one gene.
Codominance is both alleles of one gene expressed.
Correct. Epistasis is a gene–gene interaction in which one gene's alleles mask the phenotypic effect of another gene.
Independent assortment is how genes sort into gametes.
takeaway: Epistasis = one gene masks another gene.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In humans, biological females are typically ______ and biological males are typically ______.
rationale: Females = XX; males = XY (Y carries SRY).
why: Reversed — females are XX, males XY.
Males are XY, not XX.
Correct. Females are XX (two X chromosomes); males are XY. The Y carries the SRY gene that triggers male development.
Typical human males are XY, not XO.
takeaway: Female = XX, Male = XY (Y has SRY).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: X-linked recessive disorders (e.g., hemophilia, red-green color blindness) affect males more often than females because males:
choices: Have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele is expressed
Cannot inherit the X from their mother
Carry the allele on the Y chromosome
rationale: Males are hemizygous for X — one recessive X allele is expressed (no masking) → X-linked recessive affects males more.
why: Correct. Males are hemizygous for X-linked genes — one recessive allele on their single X is enough to show the trait (no second X to mask it).
Males have one X and one Y, not two X chromosomes.
Males inherit their single X from their mother.
X-linked genes are on the X, not the Y.
takeaway: X-linked recessive hits males more: only 1 X, so no masking allele.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A phenotypically normal mother who carries one copy of an X-linked recessive allele is a ______, and she passes the allele to about half her sons, who will be:
rationale: A carrier mother (heterozygous) passes an X-linked recessive allele to ~half her sons, who are affected.
why: The heterozygous mother is a carrier, not affected.
Sons receiving the allele are affected, not unaffected.
The carrier mother is heterozygous, not homozygous, and her affected sons show the trait.
Correct. A heterozygous carrier mother is unaffected but transmits the allele to ~50% of sons, who (being hemizygous) are affected.
takeaway: Carrier mom → ~50% of sons affected (X-linked recessive).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Meiosis produces gametes that are ______ and genetically ______ from the parent cell.
rationale: Meiosis → haploid, genetically varied gametes (halves chromosome number).
why: Gametes are haploid, not diploid, and vary genetically.
Meiosis creates variation; gametes aren't genetically identical.
Correct. Meiosis halves the chromosome number (diploid → haploid) and generates genetic variation via crossing over and independent assortment.
Gametes are haploid (n), not diploid (2n).
takeaway: Meiosis = haploid + varied gametes (halves 2n→n).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata. This process is:
rationale: Crossing over (prophase I): homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata → recombination.
why: Correct. Crossing over swaps segments between homologous chromosomes in prophase I, creating recombinant chromosomes and genetic variation.
Independent assortment is the random orientation of homolog pairs, a separate variation source.
Nondisjunction is failure of chromosomes to separate properly.
Cytokinesis is the division of the cytoplasm.
takeaway: Crossing over = homologs swap segments in prophase I.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Meiosis I separates ______, reducing the chromosome number (reductional); meiosis II separates ______ (equational), like mitosis.
rationale: Meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes (reductional); meiosis II separates sister chromatids.
why: Reversed — homologs separate in meiosis I, sister chromatids in II.
Meiosis I separates homologs, not chromatids.
The two divisions separate different structures (homologs, then chromatids).
Correct. Meiosis I (reductional) separates homologous chromosomes; meiosis II (equational) separates sister chromatids.
takeaway: Meiosis I = homologs (reductional). Meiosis II = sister chromatids.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Meiosis increases genetic diversity through crossing over and:
rationale: Meiotic variation = crossing over + independent assortment.
why: Semiconservative replication copies DNA faithfully; it doesn't create variation.
Correct. Independent assortment (random orientation of homolog pairs at metaphase I) plus crossing over generate genetic variation in gametes.
Proofreading reduces errors; it doesn't generate diversity.
Binary fission is asexual prokaryotic division.
takeaway: Meiosis variation = crossing over + independent assortment.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Failure of homologous chromosomes or sister chromatids to separate properly during meiosis — producing gametes with abnormal chromosome numbers (e.g., trisomy 21) — is:
rationale: Nondisjunction = chromosomes fail to separate → abnormal chromosome number (e.g., trisomy 21).
why: Crossing over exchanges segments; it doesn't cause aneuploidy by itself.
A translocation moves a segment to a nonhomologous chromosome.
Correct. Nondisjunction is improper chromosome separation, yielding aneuploid gametes (e.g., Down syndrome, trisomy 21).
Independent assortment is normal random orientation, not a separation failure.
takeaway: Nondisjunction = failed separation → aneuploidy (e.g., trisomy 21).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Genes located close together on the SAME chromosome tend to be inherited together and are called:
rationale: Linked genes sit close on the same chromosome and are usually inherited together.
why: Unlinked genes are on different chromosomes and assort independently.
Homologous refers to matching chromosome pairs, not linkage.
Correct. Linked genes are near each other on one chromosome, so they're usually inherited together (violating independent assortment unless crossing over separates them).
Pleiotropy is one gene affecting many traits.
takeaway: Linked genes = close on same chromosome, inherited together.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
