stem: The farther apart two genes are on a chromosome, the ______ the frequency of crossing over between them, which is used to build genetic maps.
rationale: Recombination frequency increases with distance between genes (basis of genetic maps).
why: Correct. Greater distance → more chance a crossover occurs between the genes → higher recombination frequency (measured in map units/centimorgans).
Closer genes have LOWER recombination frequency; farther apart is higher.
Distance changes recombination frequency; it isn't constant.
Recombination frequency is only ~zero for very tightly linked genes.
takeaway: Farther apart genes → higher recombination frequency (map distance).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Two genes that assort essentially independently (far apart or on different chromosomes) show a maximum recombination frequency of about:
rationale: Max recombination frequency ≈ 50% = independent assortment.
why: Recombination frequency cannot exceed ~50%.
0% would mean complete linkage (never separated).
25% indicates linkage, not independent assortment.
Correct. A recombination frequency of ~50% indicates independent assortment — the maximum, because you can't exceed a 1:1 parental-to-recombinant ratio.
takeaway: 50% recombination = independent assortment (the ceiling).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the Hardy-Weinberg model, if p and q are the frequencies of two alleles, then:
rationale: Hardy-Weinberg allele frequencies: p + q = 1.
why: The frequencies sum to 1, not 2.
They sum to 1; their product isn't fixed at 1.
Correct. Allele frequencies for a two-allele gene sum to 1: p + q = 1.
p and q are generally unequal, so p − q isn't necessarily 0.
takeaway: H-W: p + q = 1 (allele frequencies).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The Hardy-Weinberg genotype frequencies are given by:
rationale: H-W genotypes: p² + 2pq + q² = 1 (homo dominant + hetero + homo recessive).
why: Correct. p² (homozygous dominant) + 2pq (heterozygous) + q² (homozygous recessive) = 1.
This omits the 2pq heterozygote term.
That isn't the genotype-frequency equation.
Genotype frequencies sum (not multiply) to 1.
takeaway: H-W genotypes: p² + 2pq + q² = 1.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A population stays in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium (allele frequencies unchanging) only if there is:
choices: No mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, and a large population
rationale: H-W equilibrium needs: no mutation, no migration, no selection, random mating, large population.
why: Selection changes allele frequencies, breaking equilibrium.
Mutation introduces new alleles, breaking equilibrium.
Nonrandom mating disrupts genotype frequencies.
Correct. Equilibrium requires no mutation, no gene flow, no selection, random mating, and a large (no genetic drift) population — rarely all met, so deviations signal evolution.
takeaway: H-W: no mutation/migration/selection, random mating, large N.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: If a recessive disorder affects 1 in 10,000 people (q² = 0.0001), the frequency of the recessive allele (q) is:
why: 0.0001 is q² (the affected frequency), not q.
Correct. q = √(q²) = √0.0001 = 0.01. (Then p = 0.99 and carrier frequency 2pq ≈ 0.0198.)
0.5 doesn't follow from q² = 0.0001.
takeaway: q = √(affected frequency). √0.0001 = 0.01.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Every standard amino acid has a central (alpha) carbon bonded to an amino group, a carboxyl group, a hydrogen, and:
rationale: Amino acid = alpha carbon + amino group + carboxyl group + H + a variable R group.
why: Only acidic amino acids have a second carboxyl; it's not universal.
Correct. The alpha carbon carries an amino group, a carboxyl group, an H, and a distinctive R group (side chain) that defines each amino acid.
Phosphate groups are found in nucleotides, not the amino acid core.
Nitrogenous bases belong to nucleotides, not amino acids.
takeaway: Amino acid: alpha C bonded to -NH2, -COOH, H, and R group.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Amino acids are grouped by their side chains as nonpolar (hydrophobic), polar, acidic, or basic. Amino acids with hydrophobic side chains tend to be found:
choices: On the surface interacting with water
Buried in the interior of a folded protein, away from water
rationale: Hydrophobic (nonpolar) side chains bury in the protein interior; polar/charged face the water.
why: Polar and charged residues, not hydrophobic ones, face the aqueous surface.
Hydrophobic residues aren't restricted to the active site.
Side chains aren't generally phosphate-bonded.
Correct. Hydrophobic (nonpolar) side chains cluster in the protein's interior, away from the aqueous environment; polar/charged residues face the water.
takeaway: Hydrophobic R groups bury inside; polar/charged face water.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At physiological pH, an amino acid exists predominantly as a zwitterion, meaning it has:
choices: A positively charged amino group and a negatively charged carboxyl group (net neutral)
A phosphate and a hydroxyl charge
rationale: A zwitterion: protonated amino group (+) and deprotonated carboxyl (−) → net neutral.
why: Correct. Near neutral pH the amino group is protonated (+) and the carboxyl is deprotonated (−), giving a net-neutral zwitterion.
The zwitterion has one + and one −, not two positives.
It carries charges (one + and one −) that cancel; it's not uncharged.
The charges are on the amino and carboxyl groups, not phosphate/hydroxyl.
takeaway: Zwitterion = +NH3 and -COO− (net neutral, at physiological pH).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The pH at which an amino acid carries no net charge (exists mainly as the zwitterion) is its:
rationale: The isoelectric point (pI) = pH at which the amino acid has no net charge.
why: The pKa of water isn't the amino acid's neutral-charge pH.
Optimal temperature relates to enzyme activity, not charge.
Correct. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH of zero net charge — useful in techniques like electrophoresis.
Melting point isn't the pH of zero net charge.
takeaway: pI = pH of zero net charge (zwitterion).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Amino acids are joined into proteins by peptide bonds, which form between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next via a:
rationale: Peptide bonds form by dehydration (condensation), releasing water (a covalent amide bond).
why: Hydrolysis breaks peptide bonds; it doesn't form them.
Correct. Peptide bond formation is a dehydration/condensation reaction linking a carboxyl to an amino group and releasing water.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, not amino acids.
A peptide bond is a covalent amide bond, not a hydrogen bond.
takeaway: Peptide bond = dehydration reaction (amide bond, releases water).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The specific linear sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, determined by the gene, is its ______ structure.
rationale: Primary structure = the amino acid sequence (peptide bonds).
why: Secondary structure is local folding (helices/sheets).
Tertiary structure is the overall 3D shape of one chain.
Quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple chains.
Correct. Primary structure is the amino acid sequence, held together by peptide bonds.
takeaway: Primary = amino acid sequence.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Alpha helices and beta pleated sheets — local folded patterns stabilized by hydrogen bonds along the backbone — make up a protein's ______ structure.
rationale: Secondary structure = alpha helices & beta sheets (backbone hydrogen bonds).
why: Correct. Secondary structure (alpha helix, beta sheet) arises from hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.
Primary structure is the linear sequence.
Tertiary structure is the overall 3D fold.
Quaternary structure involves multiple subunits.
takeaway: Secondary = alpha helix + beta sheet (backbone H-bonds).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The overall three-dimensional shape of a single polypeptide — stabilized by side-chain interactions (hydrophobic packing, hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bridges) — is its ______ structure.
rationale: Tertiary structure = the 3D shape of one chain (side-chain interactions, disulfide bonds).
why: Secondary structure is local (helices/sheets), not the whole 3D fold.
Primary structure is the sequence.
Correct. Tertiary structure is the 3D conformation of one chain, driven largely by R-group interactions (notably hydrophobic packing and disulfide bonds).
Quaternary structure requires multiple polypeptide chains.
takeaway: Tertiary = 3D shape of one chain (R-group interactions).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When two or more separate polypeptide subunits assemble into a functional protein (e.g., hemoglobin's four chains), that arrangement is the ______ structure.
rationale: Quaternary structure = multiple polypeptide subunits assembled (e.g., hemoglobin).
why: Tertiary structure concerns a single chain's 3D shape.
Correct. Quaternary structure is the assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits into one functional complex.
Secondary structure is local folding within a chain.
Primary structure is the amino acid sequence.
takeaway: Quaternary = multiple subunits assembled (hemoglobin).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Heat, extreme pH, or chemicals can disrupt a protein's shape without breaking peptide bonds, causing loss of function. This is:
rationale: Denaturation = loss of 3D shape/function (heat, pH, chemicals) with the peptide bonds intact.
why: Translation builds a protein; it doesn't unfold one.
Transcription makes RNA from DNA.
Replication copies DNA.
Correct. Denaturation unfolds a protein (disrupting secondary/tertiary/quaternary structure) while leaving the primary sequence intact — often irreversibly abolishing function.
takeaway: Denaturation = protein unfolds/loses function (primary sequence intact).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Enzymes speed up reactions by:
choices: Lowering the activation energy of the reaction
rationale: Enzymes lower activation energy (they don't change ΔG or equilibrium, and aren't consumed).
why: Enzymes don't shift the equilibrium; they speed both directions equally.
Correct. Enzymes are catalysts that lower activation energy, increasing rate without altering the reaction's thermodynamics (ΔG or equilibrium).
Enzymes don't change ΔG; they only lower the activation barrier.
Catalysts are not consumed — they're regenerated.
takeaway: Enzymes lower activation energy (not ΔG, not equilibrium).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An enzyme's specificity comes from the shape and chemistry of its ______, where the substrate binds.
rationale: Enzyme specificity comes from the active site (complementary shape/chemistry).
why: An allosteric site is a regulatory site elsewhere, not the substrate-binding pocket.
The hydrophobic core stabilizes folding, not substrate binding specificity.
A signal peptide targets a protein for transport.
Correct. The active site's complementary shape/chemistry determines which substrate binds, giving enzymes their specificity.
takeaway: Active site = where substrate binds; source of specificity.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The model in which the enzyme's active site changes shape slightly to wrap around the substrate upon binding is the:
rationale: Induced fit: the active site adjusts its shape to embrace the substrate on binding.
why: Correct. In induced fit, substrate binding induces a conformational change that optimizes catalysis (a refinement of the rigid lock-and-key idea).
The lock-and-key model assumes a rigid, pre-fit active site.
Michaelis-Menten describes kinetics, not the binding conformational change.
The second-messenger model is about signal transduction.
takeaway: Induced fit = active site molds around the substrate.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Many enzymes require non-protein helpers for activity: inorganic ions are ______, while organic molecules (often vitamin-derived) are ______.
rationale: Cofactors = inorganic ions; coenzymes = organic helpers (often vitamin-derived).
why: Reversed — inorganic = cofactor, organic = coenzyme.
Substrates/products are reactants, not enzyme helpers.
Correct. Cofactors are inorganic (e.g., Zn²⁺, Mg²⁺); coenzymes are organic (e.g., NAD⁺, FAD, from vitamins).
Inhibitors/activators regulate enzymes; they aren't the cofactor/coenzyme pair.
takeaway: Cofactor = inorganic ion. Coenzyme = organic (vitamin-derived).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Enzyme activity is highest at an optimal temperature and pH; beyond these, activity drops sharply because the enzyme:
rationale: Beyond optimal temperature/pH, enzymes denature and lose activity.
why: Enzyme activity change isn't due to transcription rate.
Correct. Outside optimal temperature/pH, the enzyme denatures (unfolds), disrupting the active site and reducing activity.
Denaturation destroys, not creates, the active site.
The enzyme isn't converted into a substrate.
takeaway: Extreme temp/pH → enzyme denatures → activity drops.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In Michaelis-Menten kinetics, Vmax is the maximum reaction rate, and Km (the Michaelis constant) is the substrate concentration at which the rate is:
rationale: Km = substrate concentration at ½ Vmax (low Km → high affinity).
why: The rate reaches Vmax only at saturating (very high) substrate.
Correct. Km is the substrate concentration giving half-maximal velocity (½ Vmax); a low Km indicates high substrate affinity.
Km is a positive substrate concentration where the rate is ½ Vmax, not zero.
Reaction rate cannot exceed Vmax.
takeaway: Km = [S] at half Vmax. Low Km = high affinity.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: As substrate concentration increases, the reaction rate rises then plateaus at Vmax because:
choices: All enzyme active sites become saturated (occupied)
rationale: Rate plateaus at Vmax when all active sites are saturated.
why: Enzymes are catalysts and aren't consumed.
Substrate doesn't denature; the plateau is from saturation.
Km is a constant for a given enzyme–substrate pair, not ever-increasing.
Correct. At high substrate, active sites are saturated, so adding more substrate can't increase the rate — it levels off at Vmax.
takeaway: Vmax plateau = enzyme active sites saturated.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An enzyme with a LOW Km for its substrate has:
choices: A high affinity for that substrate (reaches half-max at low substrate)
A low affinity for that substrate
rationale: Low Km → high affinity (half-max reached at low substrate).
why: Correct. Low Km means the enzyme reaches half-maximal velocity at low substrate concentration — i.e., it binds substrate tightly (high affinity).
Low Km indicates HIGH affinity, not low.
Km doesn't indicate lack of activity.
Km and Vmax are independent parameters; low Km doesn't set Vmax.
takeaway: Low Km = high substrate affinity.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A competitive inhibitor binds the ______, and its effect can be overcome by adding more substrate — raising the apparent Km while Vmax is unchanged.
rationale: Competitive inhibitor: binds the active site; ↑ apparent Km, Vmax unchanged (overcome by more substrate).
why: Binding an allosteric site describes noncompetitive inhibition.
Correct. Competitive inhibitors bind the active site, competing with substrate; excess substrate outcompetes them, so Vmax is unchanged but apparent Km rises.
A competitive inhibitor binds the enzyme, not the substrate.
It competes at the active site, not by acting as a coenzyme.
takeaway: Competitive: active site; ↑Km, same Vmax (beaten by more substrate).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A noncompetitive inhibitor binds a site OTHER than the active site (an allosteric site) and:
choices: Lowers Vmax and cannot be overcome by adding substrate
rationale: Noncompetitive inhibitor: binds allosterically; ↓Vmax, not overcome by more substrate.
why: Noncompetitive inhibition lowers, not raises, Vmax.
It binds the enzyme's allosteric site, not the substrate.
Its reversibility isn't determined by heating.
Correct. Noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosterically, reducing Vmax; adding substrate doesn't relieve them (Km typically unchanged).
takeaway: Noncompetitive: allosteric site; ↓Vmax, more substrate won't help.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Allosteric enzymes are regulated by molecules that bind a site distinct from the active site, causing a conformational change that:
choices: Either activates or inhibits the enzyme
rationale: Allosteric regulation: a regulator binds a separate site → conformational change that activates OR inhibits.
why: Correct. Allosteric regulators (activators or inhibitors) bind a regulatory site and shift the enzyme's conformation, tuning activity up or down.
Allosteric regulation can inhibit as well as activate.
It changes conformation, not peptide bonds.
It alters shape/activity, not the primary sequence.
takeaway: Allosteric = regulator at a separate site, can activate or inhibit.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In many pathways, the final product inhibits an enzyme early in its own pathway. This self-regulation is:
rationale: Feedback inhibition: the end product inhibits an early pathway enzyme (prevents overproduction).
why: Feedforward activation is the opposite direction of control.
'Competitive activation' isn't a standard regulatory mechanism.
Correct. Feedback inhibition uses the pathway's end product as an allosteric inhibitor of an upstream enzyme, preventing overproduction.
Denaturation is loss of protein shape, not pathway self-regulation.
takeaway: Feedback inhibition = end product shuts off its own pathway.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A reaction with a NEGATIVE change in Gibbs free energy (ΔG < 0) is ______ and proceeds spontaneously; ΔG > 0 is ______.
rationale: ΔG < 0 = exergonic (spontaneous); ΔG > 0 = endergonic (needs energy).
why: Reversed — negative ΔG is exergonic.
Catabolic/anabolic describe breakdown/build-up, not the ΔG sign directly.
Oxidized/reduced describe electron transfer, not spontaneity.
Correct. ΔG < 0 = exergonic (spontaneous, releases free energy); ΔG > 0 = endergonic (nonspontaneous, requires energy input).
takeaway: Exergonic = ΔG<0 (spontaneous). Endergonic = ΔG>0.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: ATP powers cellular work because hydrolysis of its terminal phosphate bond is:
rationale: ATP hydrolysis is exergonic — its released energy is coupled to drive endergonic reactions.
why: ATP hydrolysis releases (not stores) energy.
Correct. ATP hydrolysis (ATP → ADP + Pi) is exergonic; cells couple it to endergonic reactions to drive them.
It is strongly exergonic, not neutral.
ATP hydrolysis occurs throughout the cell, not only the nucleus.
takeaway: ATP hydrolysis = exergonic (drives endergonic reactions via coupling).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Cells drive an unfavorable (endergonic) reaction by coupling it to:
choices: An exergonic reaction such as ATP hydrolysis
rationale: Energy coupling: an exergonic reaction (ATP hydrolysis) drives an endergonic one.
why: Coupling two endergonic reactions can't make the pair spontaneous.
Denaturation destroys enzymes; it isn't an energy source.
Correct. Energy coupling links an exergonic process (e.g., ATP hydrolysis) to an endergonic one so the combined ΔG is negative.
Passive diffusion releases little usable free energy for coupling.
takeaway: Coupling = exergonic (ATP) drives endergonic reaction.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In redox reactions central to metabolism, a molecule that LOSES electrons is ______; one that GAINS electrons is ______.
rationale: Oxidation = lose electrons; reduction = gain electrons (LEO says GER).
why: Correct. LEO the lion says GER: Lose Electrons = Oxidation; Gain Electrons = Reduction. Electron carriers like NAD⁺ are reduced to NADH.
Reversed — losing electrons is oxidation.
Hydrolysis/condensation involve water, not electron transfer.
Phosphorylation adds a phosphate, not electrons.
takeaway: Oxidation = lose e⁻. Reduction = gain e⁻ (LEO GER).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Glycolysis splits one glucose (6 carbons) into two molecules of ______, occurring in the ______.
rationale: Glycolysis: glucose → 2 pyruvate in the cytoplasm (anaerobic-capable).
why: Pyruvate is later converted to acetyl-CoA in the mitochondrion; glycolysis makes pyruvate.
Lactate forms only during fermentation, and glycolysis is cytoplasmic, not nuclear.
Ethanol forms in alcoholic fermentation, not standard glycolysis.
Correct. Glycolysis converts glucose into two pyruvate in the cytoplasm (no oxygen required).
takeaway: Glycolysis = glucose → 2 pyruvate (cytoplasm).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Glycolysis has a net yield per glucose of:
rationale: Glycolysis net: 2 ATP + 2 NADH per glucose.
why: ~30–36 ATP is the total from full aerobic respiration, not glycolysis alone.
Correct. Glycolysis uses 2 ATP and produces 4 (net 2 ATP), plus 2 NADH per glucose.
Glycolysis has a positive net ATP yield (2).
It nets 2 ATP and 2 NADH, not 4 NADH with no ATP.
takeaway: Glycolysis nets 2 ATP + 2 NADH.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Glycolysis itself:
choices: Does not require oxygen (occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic conditions)
rationale: Glycolysis needs no oxygen — it runs in the cytoplasm aerobically or anaerobically.
why: Glycolysis proceeds without oxygen.
Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, not the mitochondria.
Correct. Glycolysis is oxygen-independent; oxygen is needed later (in the ETC), not for glycolysis itself.
No CO2 is released during glycolysis (that happens in later steps).
takeaway: Glycolysis is oxygen-independent (cytoplasm).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Before the citric acid cycle, each pyruvate is oxidized and decarboxylated to form ______, releasing CO2 and generating NADH.
rationale: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (+ CO2 + NADH) by pyruvate dehydrogenase (the link reaction).
why: Lactate forms in fermentation, not the link to the citric acid cycle.
Glucose is the starting fuel, not a product of pyruvate oxidation.
Oxaloacetate combines WITH acetyl-CoA to start the cycle; it isn't made from pyruvate here.
Correct. Pyruvate dehydrogenase converts pyruvate to acetyl-CoA, releasing one CO2 and producing NADH (the link reaction).
takeaway: Pyruvate → acetyl-CoA (+CO2, +NADH) before the Krebs cycle.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The citric acid (Krebs) cycle occurs in the ______ and, per acetyl-CoA, produces NADH, FADH2, and:
choices: Mitochondrial matrix; GTP (or ATP) and CO2
rationale: Krebs cycle (matrix): per acetyl-CoA → 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP, 2 CO2.
why: Pyruvate is a glycolysis product; the cycle is in the matrix, not cytoplasm.
Correct. Each acetyl-CoA in the matrix yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP (≈ATP), and 2 CO2.
The cycle occurs in the matrix and doesn't make DNA.
The ETC is on the inner membrane and consumes O2; the cycle doesn't produce O2.
takeaway: Krebs (matrix): NADH, FADH2, GTP, CO2 per acetyl-CoA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The main purpose of the citric acid cycle for ATP production is to generate ______, which then feed the electron transport chain.
rationale: The Krebs cycle mainly makes NADH & FADH2 to feed the electron transport chain.
why: The cycle makes only 1 GTP per acetyl-CoA directly; most ATP comes later.
The cycle oxidizes fuel; it doesn't synthesize glucose for storage.
Correct. The cycle's chief energetic role is producing NADH and FADH2, which deliver electrons to the ETC where most ATP is made.
The cycle consumes carbon fuel; it doesn't produce oxygen.
takeaway: Krebs cycle's key job: make NADH/FADH2 for the ETC.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the electron transport chain (inner mitochondrial membrane), electrons from NADH and FADH2 are passed down carriers, and the energy released is used to:
choices: Directly phosphorylate ADP at each step
Pump protons (H+) across the membrane, creating a gradient
rationale: The ETC pumps H+ across the inner membrane, storing energy as a proton gradient.
why: ATP is made by ATP synthase using the gradient, not directly at each carrier.
The ETC consumes O2 (forming water); it doesn't split water.
Glucose synthesis is not a function of the ETC.
Correct. The ETC uses electron energy to pump H+ into the intermembrane space, building the proton-motive force used by ATP synthase.
takeaway: ETC pumps H+ → proton gradient (inner membrane).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: ATP is produced when protons flow back down their gradient through ______, a process called:
rationale: Protons flow through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis) → ATP.
why: Glycolysis is a separate cytoplasmic pathway, not proton flow through ATP synthase.
Correct. Protons flow through ATP synthase (chemiosmosis), driving phosphorylation of ADP to ATP — oxidative phosphorylation.
Aquaporins conduct water, not the ATP-generating proton flow.
Pyruvate dehydrogenase makes acetyl-CoA; fermentation is anaerobic.
takeaway: ATP synthase + proton flow = chemiosmosis → ATP.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In aerobic respiration, the FINAL electron acceptor at the end of the electron transport chain is:
rationale: The final electron acceptor in aerobic respiration is oxygen (→ water).
why: CO2 is a waste product of earlier steps, not the final electron acceptor.
NAD+ is an electron carrier that gets reduced earlier, not the terminal acceptor.
Correct. Oxygen accepts the electrons at the end of the ETC and combines with H+ to form water; without O2, the chain backs up and stops.
Pyruvate is a fermentation electron acceptor, not the aerobic terminal acceptor.
takeaway: O2 = final electron acceptor (forms water).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Complete aerobic respiration of one glucose yields approximately how much ATP?
rationale: Aerobic respiration ≈ 30–38 ATP per glucose (mostly from oxidative phosphorylation).
why: Correct. Aerobic respiration yields roughly 30–38 ATP per glucose (estimates vary), most from oxidative phosphorylation.
2 ATP is the net from glycolysis alone.
4 ATP is not the full aerobic yield.
The yield is far below 100 ATP per glucose.
takeaway: Aerobic respiration ≈ 30–38 ATP/glucose (most from oxphos).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When oxygen is unavailable, fermentation allows glycolysis to continue by:
choices: Producing large amounts of ATP directly
Regenerating NAD+ from NADH so glycolysis can keep running
rationale: Fermentation regenerates NAD+ so glycolysis can continue without oxygen.
why: Fermentation yields no extra ATP beyond glycolysis's net 2.
Fermentation doesn't produce oxygen.
It doesn't synthesize glucose; it sustains glycolysis.
Correct. Fermentation reoxidizes NADH to NAD+, replenishing the NAD+ that glycolysis needs — its main purpose (little extra ATP).
takeaway: Fermentation = regenerate NAD+ to keep glycolysis going (no O2).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In humans (and muscle during intense exercise), fermentation converts pyruvate to ______; in yeast, pyruvate is converted to ethanol and ______.
rationale: Human/muscle: pyruvate → lactate. Yeast: pyruvate → ethanol + CO2.
why: Humans make lactate, not ethanol; the pairing is reversed.
Correct. Human/muscle cells perform lactic acid fermentation (pyruvate → lactate); yeast perform alcoholic fermentation (pyruvate → ethanol + CO2).
Fermentation doesn't produce acetyl-CoA/water as its products here.
Fermentation doesn't regenerate glucose or oxygen.
takeaway: Lactic acid ferm (humans) → lactate. Alcoholic (yeast) → ethanol + CO2.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Excess glucose is stored in the liver and muscle as the branched polysaccharide ______; its breakdown to release glucose is glycogenolysis.
rationale: Animals store glucose as glycogen (liver/muscle); glycogenolysis releases it.
why: Starch is the plant storage polysaccharide, not the animal one.
Cellulose is a structural plant polysaccharide, indigestible to humans.
Triglycerides store energy as fat, not as a glucose polymer.
Correct. Animals store glucose as glycogen (glycogenesis); glycogenolysis breaks it down to release glucose.
takeaway: Glycogen = animal glucose storage (liver/muscle).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During prolonged fasting, the body synthesizes new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (lactate, amino acids, glycerol). This pathway is:
rationale: Gluconeogenesis = making new glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors (fasting).
why: Glycolysis breaks glucose down; it doesn't synthesize it.
Correct. Gluconeogenesis makes glucose from non-carbohydrate sources (mainly in the liver) to maintain blood glucose during fasting.
Beta-oxidation breaks down fatty acids, not glucose synthesis.
Glycogenesis stores glucose as glycogen; it doesn't make new glucose from non-carbs.
takeaway: Gluconeogenesis = make glucose from non-carbs (fasting).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: After a meal, high blood glucose triggers ______, which promotes glucose uptake and storage; during fasting, ______ raises blood glucose.
rationale: Insulin lowers blood glucose (fed); glucagon raises it (fasting).
why: Reversed — insulin lowers glucose after a meal, glucagon raises it when fasting.
Cortisol raises glucose but isn't the post-meal lowering hormone; insulin is.
Correct. Insulin (from pancreatic beta cells) lowers blood glucose (uptake/storage); glucagon (from alpha cells) raises it (glycogenolysis, gluconeogenesis).
Both glucagon and epinephrine raise glucose, but the post-meal hormone is insulin.
takeaway: Insulin = lower glucose (fed). Glucagon = raise glucose (fasting).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Fatty acids are broken down to acetyl-CoA (which enters the Krebs cycle) through the process of:
rationale: Beta-oxidation breaks fatty acids into acetyl-CoA for the Krebs cycle.
why: Correct. Beta-oxidation cleaves fatty acids two carbons at a time into acetyl-CoA (yielding NADH/FADH2) for the Krebs cycle.
Glycolysis breaks down glucose, not fatty acids.
Transamination transfers amino groups in amino acid metabolism.
Gluconeogenesis synthesizes glucose.
takeaway: Beta-oxidation = fatty acids → acetyl-CoA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The cell membrane is described by the fluid mosaic model as a:
choices: Phospholipid bilayer with embedded, mobile proteins
rationale: Fluid mosaic: a fluid phospholipid bilayer with embedded, mobile proteins.
why: The membrane is fluid, not a rigid wall.
It's a bilayer (two leaflets), not a single layer.
Correct. The membrane is a fluid phospholipid bilayer with proteins (and cholesterol, carbohydrates) embedded and able to move laterally.
Cholesterol modulates fluidity but doesn't form the sheet itself.
takeaway: Membrane = fluid phospholipid bilayer + embedded proteins.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Phospholipids form a bilayer because each molecule is amphipathic, with:
choices: A hydrophilic (phosphate) head and hydrophobic (fatty acid) tails
A charged core and neutral surface
rationale: Phospholipids are amphipathic: hydrophilic head + hydrophobic tails → bilayer.
why: Correct. The hydrophilic heads face the aqueous exterior/interior and the hydrophobic tails face inward, self-assembling into a bilayer.
A molecule with two hydrophilic ends wouldn't form a stable bilayer.
Two hydrophobic ends wouldn't orient toward water.
The heads (surface) are charged/polar and tails (core) are nonpolar — the opposite of this option.
takeaway: Phospholipid = polar head + nonpolar tails (amphipathic).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In animal cell membranes, cholesterol acts as a fluidity buffer, meaning it:
choices: Keeps the membrane fluid at low temperatures and stable at high temperatures
rationale: Cholesterol buffers membrane fluidity (fluid when cold, stable when hot).
why: Its effect depends on temperature; it doesn't only increase fluidity.
It moderates fluidity rather than making the membrane rigid.
Cholesterol regulates fluidity; it isn't an ion transporter.
Correct. Cholesterol buffers fluidity: at high temperature it restrains movement (stabilizes), at low temperature it prevents tight packing (keeps fluid).
takeaway: Cholesterol = fluidity buffer (fluid when cold, firm when hot).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Movement of a solute DOWN its concentration gradient without energy is ______ transport; movement AGAINST the gradient using ATP is ______ transport.
rationale: Passive = down gradient, no energy; active = against gradient, uses ATP.
why: Reversed — down-gradient is passive, against-gradient is active.
'Bulk/simple' aren't the passive/active pair.
Correct. Passive transport (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis) needs no energy; active transport uses ATP to move against the gradient.
Osmotic/oncotic describe pressures, not this distinction.
takeaway: Passive = down gradient (free). Active = against gradient (ATP).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Osmosis is the passive movement of ______ across a semipermeable membrane from a region of ______ solute concentration to ______ solute concentration.
rationale: Osmosis: water moves from low→high solute (toward the more concentrated side).
why: Correct. Water moves toward the higher solute concentration (lower water concentration) to equalize — i.e., from low to high solute.
Osmosis is the movement of water, not solute.
Water moves toward higher solute (this reverses it).
Osmosis specifically refers to water movement, not ions.
takeaway: Osmosis = water moves toward higher solute concentration.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A red blood cell placed in a HYPOTONIC solution (lower solute outside) will:
choices: Swell and possibly lyse as water moves in
rationale: In a hypotonic solution, water enters the cell → it swells/lyses.
why: Shriveling (crenation) happens in a hypertonic solution, where water leaves.
In a hypotonic solution the cell gains water and changes size.
Water movement here is passive osmosis, not active pumping.
Correct. In a hypotonic solution, water flows into the cell (toward higher internal solute), causing it to swell and potentially burst (lyse).
takeaway: Hypotonic = cell swells (water in). Hypertonic = shrinks.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The Na+/K+ ATPase is a form of active transport that, per cycle, pumps:
choices: 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, using ATP
rationale: Na+/K+ ATPase: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in per ATP (sets up gradients).
why: The ratio is 3 Na+ out and 2 K+ in, not the reverse.
Correct. The Na+/K+ pump uses ATP to export 3 Na+ and import 2 K+, maintaining gradients essential for membrane potential.
It moves Na+ out and K+ in (opposite directions), not both out.
It transports ions, not water.
takeaway: Na+/K+ pump: 3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in (uses ATP).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The organelle that houses the cell's DNA and controls gene expression is the nucleus; within it, the site of ribosome assembly is the:
rationale: The nucleolus (in the nucleus) assembles ribosomes (rRNA synthesis).
why: The Golgi modifies and packages proteins, outside the nucleus.
Lysosomes digest cellular material.
Correct. The nucleolus (inside the nucleus) is where rRNA is transcribed and ribosomal subunits are assembled.
Centrioles organize the mitotic spindle.
takeaway: Nucleolus = ribosome assembly (inside nucleus).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (studded with ribosomes) synthesizes ______, while the smooth ER synthesizes ______ and detoxifies.
rationale: Rough ER = protein synthesis; smooth ER = lipid synthesis + detox.
why: Correct. Rough ER makes and processes proteins (has ribosomes); smooth ER synthesizes lipids/steroids and detoxifies drugs.
Reversed — rough ER makes proteins, smooth ER makes lipids.
The ER doesn't synthesize DNA/RNA (that's the nucleus).
ATP is made in mitochondria, not the ER.
takeaway: Rough ER = proteins. Smooth ER = lipids + detox.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The organelle that modifies, sorts, and packages proteins and lipids for secretion or delivery (like a cellular post office) is the:
rationale: The Golgi apparatus modifies, sorts, and packages proteins/lipids for shipping.
why: The mitochondrion produces ATP, not protein packaging.
Ribosomes synthesize polypeptides; they don't sort/package.
The nucleus stores DNA; it isn't the packaging center.
Correct. The Golgi apparatus modifies (e.g., glycosylation), sorts, and packages molecules into vesicles for their destinations.
takeaway: Golgi = modify + package + ship (cellular post office).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The organelle where most cellular ATP is produced via the citric acid cycle and oxidative phosphorylation is the:
rationale: The mitochondrion makes most ATP (Krebs + oxphos); has its own DNA.
why: Lysosomes digest macromolecules.
Correct. The mitochondrion (with its own DNA and double membrane) is the site of aerobic ATP production — the 'powerhouse' of the cell.
Peroxisomes break down fatty acids and detoxify peroxides.
Vacuoles store water and materials.
takeaway: Mitochondrion = ATP powerhouse (Krebs + oxphos).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The membrane-bound organelles filled with hydrolytic (digestive) enzymes that break down waste, debris, and worn organelles are:
rationale: Lysosomes = digestive organelles (hydrolytic enzymes) for waste and recycling.
why: Ribosomes synthesize proteins; they don't digest.
Centrosomes organize microtubules for cell division.
Correct. Lysosomes contain acidic hydrolytic enzymes that digest macromolecules and recycle cellular components (autophagy).
Golgi vesicles transport materials; the digestive organelle is the lysosome.
takeaway: Lysosome = digestive enzymes (breaks down waste).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The cytoskeleton is built from microfilaments (actin), intermediate filaments, and the largest fibers, which form spindle fibers and the tracks for organelle transport:
rationale: Microtubules = largest cytoskeletal fibers (spindle, cilia/flagella, transport tracks).
why: Ribosomes synthesize proteins; they aren't cytoskeletal fibers.
Cilia are made OF microtubules; the fiber type is microtubules.
Correct. Microtubules (tubulin) are the largest cytoskeletal fibers; they form the mitotic spindle, cilia/flagella cores, and vesicle-transport tracks.
Phospholipids build membranes, not the cytoskeleton.
takeaway: Microtubules = spindle + cilia/flagella + transport tracks.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Eukaryotic cilia and flagella move using a characteristic microtubule arrangement described as:
rationale: Motile cilia/flagella = 9+2 microtubule arrangement (axoneme).
why: Correct. Motile cilia/flagella have a 9+2 axoneme: nine outer microtubule doublets surrounding two central microtubules.
9+0 describes non-motile primary cilia and basal bodies/centrioles, not motile flagella.
2+2 is not the axoneme arrangement.
Cilia/flagella contain many microtubules in the 9+2 pattern, not one.
takeaway: Cilia/flagella = 9+2 microtubule arrangement.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and the mitotic phase. DNA is replicated during:
rationale: DNA is replicated in S phase (G1 = growth, G2 = growth, M = division).
why: G1 is a growth phase before DNA synthesis.
G2 is growth after replication, preparing for mitosis.
Correct. DNA synthesis (replication) occurs in S phase; G1 and G2 are growth phases, and M phase is mitosis/division.
M phase is when the cell divides, after replication.
takeaway: S phase = DNA replication. G1/G2 = growth. M = division.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The correct order of the phases of mitosis is:
rationale: Mitosis order: Prophase → Metaphase → Anaphase → Telophase (PMAT).
why: Correct. PMAT: Prophase (condense), Metaphase (align at the middle), Anaphase (sister chromatids separate), Telophase (nuclei re-form).
Prophase precedes metaphase.
That order is scrambled.
That is the reverse order.
takeaway: Mitosis = PMAT (Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Chromosomes line up along the cell's equator during ______; sister chromatids are pulled to opposite poles during ______.
rationale: Metaphase = chromosomes align at the equator; anaphase = sister chromatids separate.
why: Reversed — alignment is metaphase, separation is anaphase.
Prophase is condensation; telophase is nuclear reassembly.
That pairing is incorrect.
Correct. Metaphase = alignment at the metaphase plate; anaphase = sister chromatids separate toward opposite poles.
takeaway: Metaphase = line up. Anaphase = pull apart.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Progression through the cell cycle is controlled at checkpoints by regulatory proteins called ______ and their partner kinases (CDKs).
rationale: Cyclins + CDKs drive the cell through checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M).
why: Histones package DNA; they aren't the checkpoint regulators.
Correct. Cyclins bind cyclin-dependent kinases (CDKs) to drive the cell past checkpoints (G1/S, G2/M); loss of control can lead to cancer.
Telomeres are chromosome-end sequences, not cycle regulators.
Ribozymes are catalytic RNAs, not cell-cycle proteins.
takeaway: Cyclins + CDKs = cell cycle checkpoint control.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The tumor suppressor protein that halts the cycle for DNA repair (or triggers apoptosis) at the G1/S checkpoint — and is mutated in many cancers — is:
rationale: p53 = tumor suppressor that arrests the cycle for repair or triggers apoptosis (mutated in many cancers).
why: Cyclin D promotes progression; it isn't the guardian tumor suppressor.
Telomerase extends telomeres; it isn't the checkpoint guardian.
Correct. p53 arrests the cycle to allow repair or induces apoptosis if damage is severe; its loss of function permits damaged cells to divide (cancer).
Actin is a cytoskeletal protein, not a cell-cycle regulator.
takeaway: p53 = 'guardian of the genome' (arrest/repair or apoptosis).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Programmed cell death — an orderly, regulated dismantling of a cell (important in development and removing damaged cells) — is:
rationale: Apoptosis = programmed, orderly cell death (vs. necrosis = uncontrolled).
why: Correct. Apoptosis is controlled, programmed cell death (unlike necrosis, which is uncontrolled injury-induced death).
Necrosis is uncontrolled cell death from injury, causing inflammation.
Mitosis is cell division, not death.
Binary fission is prokaryotic asexual reproduction.
takeaway: Apoptosis = programmed cell death (orderly).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The defining feature that distinguishes prokaryotic cells from eukaryotic cells is that prokaryotes:
choices: Lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles
rationale: Prokaryotes lack a membrane-bound nucleus and membrane-bound organelles.
why: Prokaryotes have DNA — it just isn't enclosed in a nucleus.
Correct. Prokaryotes have no membrane-bound nucleus (DNA sits in the nucleoid) and lack membrane-bound organelles; eukaryotes have both.
Prokaryotes are typically single-celled.
Prokaryotes are smaller and lack mitochondria.
takeaway: Prokaryote = no nucleus, no membrane-bound organelles.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gram-positive bacteria stain purple because they have a THICK peptidoglycan cell wall; Gram-negative bacteria stain pink because they have:
choices: A thin peptidoglycan layer plus an outer membrane
rationale: Gram-positive = thick peptidoglycan (purple); Gram-negative = thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane (pink).
why: Gram-negatives do have a (thin) peptidoglycan wall.
Gram-positives, not negatives, have the thicker wall.
Bacteria are prokaryotes and have no nucleus.
Correct. Gram-negatives have a thin peptidoglycan layer and an additional outer membrane (with LPS), so they retain less crystal violet and appear pink.
takeaway: Gram+ = thick wall (purple). Gram− = thin wall + outer membrane (pink).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Prokaryotes reproduce asexually by ______, producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
rationale: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission (asexual, two identical cells).
why: Correct. Binary fission is the asexual division of a prokaryote into two identical cells (no spindle, no mitosis).
Meiosis produces gametes in sexually reproducing eukaryotes.
Mitosis is eukaryotic nuclear division.
Spore budding isn't the standard prokaryotic division mechanism.
takeaway: Binary fission = asexual prokaryotic division (2 identical cells).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Besides the main circular chromosome, many bacteria carry small circular DNA molecules — often bearing antibiotic-resistance genes — called:
rationale: Plasmids = small circular bacterial DNA (often antibiotic-resistance genes).
why: Ribosomes synthesize protein; they aren't DNA molecules.
Lysosomes are eukaryotic digestive organelles.
Correct. Plasmids are small, independently replicating circular DNA molecules that can carry advantageous genes (e.g., antibiotic resistance) and be transferred between cells.
A centromere is a chromosome region, not a separate DNA molecule.
takeaway: Plasmid = extra circular DNA (often resistance genes).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The transfer of DNA (often a plasmid) directly between two bacterial cells through a physical bridge (pilus) is:
rationale: Conjugation = DNA transfer between bacteria via a pilus (direct contact).
why: Transformation is uptake of naked DNA from the environment.
Correct. Conjugation transfers DNA via direct cell-to-cell contact through a sex pilus — a form of horizontal gene transfer.
Transduction is DNA transfer by a bacteriophage.
Binary fission is asexual reproduction, not gene transfer between cells.
takeaway: Conjugation = bacteria transfer DNA through a pilus bridge.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When a bacterium takes up free (naked) DNA fragments directly from its environment, this is:
rationale: Transformation = uptake of naked DNA from the environment.
why: Conjugation requires direct cell-to-cell contact via a pilus.
Transduction uses a virus to move DNA.
Translation is protein synthesis, not gene transfer.
Correct. Transformation is uptake and incorporation of exogenous DNA from the surroundings.
takeaway: Transformation = bacterium grabs free DNA from surroundings.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The transfer of bacterial DNA from one cell to another via a bacteriophage (virus) is:
rationale: Transduction = bacterial DNA moved by a bacteriophage (virus).
why: Correct. In transduction, a bacteriophage accidentally packages host bacterial DNA and injects it into a new host.
Transformation is uptake of naked environmental DNA.
Conjugation is direct transfer via a pilus.
Fermentation is an anaerobic metabolic process, not gene transfer.
takeaway: Transduction = virus carries bacterial DNA to a new cell.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A bacterial growth curve typically follows the order:
rationale: Bacterial growth: lag → log → stationary → death.
why: Lag precedes log; the order is scrambled.
Correct. Growth proceeds through lag (adjusting), log/exponential (rapid division), stationary (nutrients limiting), and death phases.
Lag comes first, not stationary.
That is roughly the reverse order.
takeaway: Growth curve: lag → log → stationary → death.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A microbe that REQUIRES oxygen to survive is an obligate ______; one that is KILLED by oxygen is an obligate ______.
rationale: Obligate aerobe requires O2; obligate anaerobe is killed by O2.
why: Reversed — the oxygen-requiring microbe is the aerobe.
Halophile/thermophile describe salt/heat preferences, not oxygen.
Autotroph/heterotroph describe carbon source, not oxygen use.
Correct. Obligate aerobes need O2; obligate anaerobes are poisoned by it (facultative organisms can use either).
takeaway: Obligate aerobe = needs O2. Obligate anaerobe = killed by O2.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Some bacteria (e.g., Clostridium, Bacillus) survive extreme heat, radiation, and drought by forming dormant, highly resistant structures called:
rationale: Endospores = dormant, resistant bacterial survival structures.
why: Correct. Endospores are dormant, tough survival structures that let certain bacteria persist through harsh conditions and later germinate.
Plasmids are DNA molecules, not survival structures.
Flagella are for motility.
Ribosomes synthesize protein.
takeaway: Endospores = tough dormant survival forms (Clostridium, Bacillus).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A virus consists at minimum of genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat called a:
rationale: A virus = nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) in a protein capsid (± envelope).
why: Viruses lack a cell wall.
Correct. The capsid is the protein shell surrounding the viral genome; some viruses also have a lipid envelope from the host membrane.
Viruses are acellular and have no plasma membrane of their own (some have a host-derived envelope).
The nucleoid is a bacterial DNA region, not a viral coat.
takeaway: Virus = genome + protein capsid (± envelope).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Viruses are not considered fully living cells primarily because they:
choices: Have their own ribosomes and metabolism
Cannot reproduce without hijacking a host cell's machinery
rationale: Viruses are acellular obligate parasites — they need a host cell to replicate.
why: Viruses do contain genetic material (DNA or RNA).
Viruses lack their own ribosomes and metabolism.
Viruses can't divide on their own; they require a host.
Correct. Viruses are obligate intracellular parasites — they lack ribosomes and metabolism and must use a host cell to replicate.
takeaway: Viruses can't reproduce alone — they hijack host cells.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A bacteriophage that immediately replicates and bursts (lyses) the host cell follows the ______ cycle; one that integrates its DNA into the host genome and lies dormant follows the ______ cycle.
rationale: Lytic = replicate + burst the cell; lysogenic = integrate + lie dormant (prophage).
why: Correct. Lytic = immediate replication and cell lysis; lysogenic = viral DNA integrates (as a prophage) and replicates passively until induced.
Reversed — immediate lysis is the lytic cycle.
Lag/log are bacterial growth phases, not phage cycles.
Aerobic/anaerobic describe metabolism, not phage cycles.
takeaway: Lytic = burst now. Lysogenic = integrate + hide (prophage).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Retroviruses like HIV carry RNA and an enzyme that copies their RNA into DNA for host integration. That enzyme is:
rationale: Reverse transcriptase copies retroviral RNA → DNA (e.g., HIV).
why: Helicase unwinds DNA; it doesn't copy RNA into DNA.
RNA polymerase II makes mRNA from DNA, the opposite direction.
Correct. Reverse transcriptase transcribes viral RNA into DNA (reversing the usual flow), which integrates into the host genome.
DNA ligase seals DNA nicks; it isn't a reverse transcriptase.
takeaway: Retrovirus (HIV): reverse transcriptase makes DNA from RNA.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A typical neuron at rest has a membrane potential of about −70 mV, meaning the inside of the cell is:
choices: Equal in charge to the outside
rationale: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV: inside negative relative to outside.
why: The interior is negative, not positive, at rest.
There is a charge separation (potential difference), not equality.
Correct. At rest the interior is negative (~−70 mV) relative to the exterior, maintained by ion gradients and membrane permeability.
There is a measurable potential difference; the membrane is polarized.
takeaway: Resting potential ≈ −70 mV (inside negative).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At rest, the concentration of ______ is high OUTSIDE the neuron, and ______ is high INSIDE, gradients set up by the Na+/K+ pump.
rationale: At rest: Na+ high outside, K+ high inside (set by the Na+/K+ pump).
why: Correct. The Na+/K+ pump keeps Na+ high outside and K+ high inside; the resting membrane is most permeable to K+.
Reversed — Na+ is high outside, K+ is high inside.
Ca2+/Cl− aren't the primary resting-potential gradient pair.
That reverses the relevant ions.
takeaway: Resting gradients: Na+ out, K+ in (Na+/K+ pump).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The resting membrane potential is close to the equilibrium potential for potassium because at rest the membrane is:
choices: Most permeable to K+ (K+ leak channels are open)
rationale: At rest the membrane is most permeable to K+ (leak channels) → potential near E_K.
why: Na+ permeability is low at rest; it rises during an action potential.
The membrane is selectively permeable, not impermeable.
Ca2+ isn't the dominant resting permeability.
Correct. Open K+ leak channels make the resting membrane most permeable to K+, so the resting potential sits near K+'s equilibrium potential.
takeaway: Resting membrane = mostly K+ permeable (leak channels).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During the rising phase of an action potential, voltage-gated ______ channels open, and ______ rushes IN, making the inside more positive.
rationale: Depolarization: voltage-gated Na+ channels open, Na+ rushes in (inside becomes positive).
why: K+ efflux causes repolarization, not the depolarizing rise.
Ca2+ influx triggers neurotransmitter release at the terminal, not the main depolarization.
Correct. Depolarization is driven by voltage-gated Na+ channels opening and Na+ flowing into the cell.
Cl− movement is inhibitory, not the depolarizing current.
takeaway: Depolarization = Na+ in (voltage-gated Na+ channels).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: After the peak, the neuron repolarizes as voltage-gated ______ channels open and ______ flows OUT.
rationale: Repolarization: voltage-gated K+ channels open, K+ flows out.
why: Correct. Repolarization occurs as voltage-gated K+ channels open and K+ exits, restoring the negative interior (often overshooting to hyperpolarization).
Na+ influx causes depolarization, not repolarization.
Ca2+ is not the repolarizing current in the axon.
Cl− isn't the main repolarizing ion here.
takeaway: Repolarization = K+ out (voltage-gated K+ channels).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Once a stimulus reaches threshold, an action potential fires at full amplitude; a stronger stimulus does not make a bigger spike. This is the:
rationale: All-or-none: reaching threshold fires a full-amplitude spike (intensity = frequency, not size).
why: Summation is the adding of graded potentials, not the fixed spike size.
The refractory period concerns the interval before another spike can fire.
Wobble is a genetics/codon concept.
Correct. Action potentials are all-or-none: threshold triggers a full-sized spike; stimulus strength is encoded by firing FREQUENCY, not amplitude.
takeaway: All-or-none = full spike at threshold; intensity coded by frequency.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Immediately after firing, a neuron cannot fire a second action potential no matter how strong the stimulus. This interval — due to inactivated Na+ channels — is the:
rationale: Absolute refractory period: no new spike possible (Na+ channels inactivated).
why: In the relative refractory period a stronger-than-usual stimulus CAN fire a spike.
Correct. During the absolute refractory period, inactivated Na+ channels make another action potential impossible, ensuring one-way propagation.
'Latent period' isn't the standard term for Na+ channel inactivation.
The resting period is the baseline state, not the post-spike block.
takeaway: Absolute refractory = can't fire again (Na+ channels inactivated).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In myelinated axons, the action potential jumps from one node of Ranvier to the next, greatly speeding conduction. This is:
rationale: Saltatory conduction: the impulse jumps between nodes of Ranvier in myelinated axons (fast).
why: Continuous conduction occurs in unmyelinated axons (slower).
Retrograde transport moves materials back toward the soma, not the impulse.
Correct. Saltatory conduction: myelin insulates the axon so the impulse regenerates only at the nodes of Ranvier, jumping node to node (fast).
The impulse is an active, regenerating signal, not passive diffusion.
takeaway: Saltatory conduction = impulse jumps node to node (myelin, fast).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When an action potential reaches the axon terminal, it opens voltage-gated ______ channels, and the influx triggers neurotransmitter vesicle fusion and release.
rationale: At the terminal, Ca2+ influx triggers neurotransmitter vesicle release.
why: K+ efflux repolarizes the membrane; it doesn't trigger release.
Cl− is inhibitory and not the release trigger.
Correct. Ca2+ influx at the terminal triggers synaptic vesicles to fuse with the membrane and release neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft.
Although Na+ carries the axonal impulse, Ca2+ specifically triggers vesicle release at the terminal.
takeaway: Ca2+ influx → neurotransmitter release at the terminal.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Neurotransmitter diffuses across the synaptic cleft and binds ______ on the postsynaptic membrane, altering its membrane potential.
rationale: Neurotransmitter crosses the cleft and binds postsynaptic receptors (often ligand-gated channels).
why: Correct. Neurotransmitters bind postsynaptic receptors (often ligand-gated ion channels), producing excitatory or inhibitory potentials.
Ribosomes synthesize protein; they don't receive neurotransmitters.
The nucleolus assembles ribosomes in the nucleus.
Myelin insulates axons; it isn't the neurotransmitter receptor.
takeaway: Neurotransmitter binds postsynaptic receptors across the cleft.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A neurotransmitter that DEPOLARIZES the postsynaptic cell (making it more likely to fire) produces an ______; one that HYPERPOLARIZES it produces an ______.
rationale: EPSP = depolarizing (excitatory); IPSP = hyperpolarizing (inhibitory).
why: Reversed — depolarizing is excitatory (EPSP).
EPSP/IPSP are graded potentials, not full action/resting potentials.
Both EPSPs and IPSPs are graded signals.
Correct. An excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP) depolarizes; an inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP) hyperpolarizes.
takeaway: EPSP = depolarize (excite). IPSP = hyperpolarize (inhibit).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The neurotransmitter signal is stopped by enzymatic breakdown or by ______, in which the neurotransmitter is transported back into the presynaptic neuron.
rationale: The synaptic signal ends via enzymatic breakdown or reuptake into the presynaptic neuron.
why: Depolarization initiates signaling; it doesn't terminate it.
Correct. Reuptake (via transporters) recycles neurotransmitter back into the presynaptic terminal, terminating the signal (the target of many antidepressants).
Summation combines multiple inputs; it isn't signal termination.
Transduction is converting a stimulus to a neural signal, not termination.
takeaway: Signal ends by enzyme breakdown or reuptake.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Water-soluble peptide hormones bind ______ receptors and act via second messengers; lipid-soluble steroid hormones cross the membrane and bind ______ receptors.
rationale: Peptide hormones → surface receptors + second messengers; steroid hormones → intracellular receptors.
why: Reversed — peptides bind surface receptors, steroids bind intracellular ones.
Peptide receptors are on the surface, not ribosomal.

Correct. Peptide hormones (hydrophilic) bind membrane receptors and use second messengers (fast, short-acting); steroids (lipophilic) diffuse in and bind intracellular/nuclear receptors (slow, long-acting).
Both hormone types have receptors; the difference is their location.
takeaway: Peptide = surface receptor (2nd messenger). Steroid = intracellular receptor.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Because peptide hormones can't cross the membrane, they trigger intracellular signaling molecules such as cyclic AMP (cAMP). These relay molecules are:
rationale: Peptide hormones act through second messengers (e.g., cAMP) inside the cell.
why: Correct. Second messengers (e.g., cAMP, IP3, Ca2+) relay the signal inside the cell after the hormone (first messenger) binds a surface receptor.
The hormone itself is the first messenger; cAMP is the second.
Steroid hormones act directly on intracellular receptors, not via surface-triggered second messengers.
Neurotransmitters act at synapses; here the relay molecule is a second messenger.
takeaway: Second messengers (cAMP) relay peptide-hormone signals intracellularly.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Compared with steroid hormones, peptide hormones generally act:
rationale: Peptide hormones: fast onset, short duration. Steroids: slow onset, long duration.
why: That describes steroid hormones, not peptides.
Peptides act fast but not long-lasting.
Peptides act fast, not slow.
Correct. Peptide hormones act quickly via second messengers but their effects are short-lived; steroids act slowly (altering gene transcription) with longer-lasting effects.
takeaway: Peptide = fast + short. Steroid = slow + long.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The 'master gland' that releases hormones controlling many other endocrine glands — and is itself directed by the hypothalamus — is the:
rationale: The pituitary = master gland (directed by the hypothalamus).
why: The thyroid regulates metabolism but is downstream of the pituitary.
The adrenal gland is regulated by pituitary ACTH.
Correct. The pituitary (anterior and posterior) is the master gland, regulated by the hypothalamus, controlling downstream glands (thyroid, adrenal cortex, gonads).
The pancreas regulates glucose but isn't the master gland.
takeaway: Pituitary = master gland (run by hypothalamus).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The thyroid gland secretes thyroxine (T4/T3), which primarily regulates:
rationale: Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) raises basal metabolic rate.
why: Correct. Thyroid hormones (T3/T4) raise the body's basal metabolic rate; TSH from the pituitary stimulates their release.
Blood glucose is controlled by insulin/glucagon, not thyroxine.
Blood calcium is controlled by calcitonin/PTH, not thyroxine (calcitonin is also from the thyroid but is a different hormone).
Water reabsorption is controlled by ADH.
takeaway: Thyroid (T3/T4) = sets metabolic rate.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The adrenal ______ releases cortisol (a steroid) for longer-term stress; the adrenal ______ releases epinephrine for the rapid fight-or-flight response.
rationale: Adrenal cortex = cortisol (steroid, slow); adrenal medulla = epinephrine (fast).
why: Reversed — cortisol is from the cortex, epinephrine from the medulla.
Anterior/posterior describe the pituitary, not the adrenal gland.
Alpha/beta describe receptors or pancreatic cells, not adrenal regions.
Correct. The adrenal cortex secretes cortisol (steroid, slower); the adrenal medulla secretes epinephrine/norepinephrine (fast). Mnemonic: COTisol from the CORTex.
takeaway: Adrenal cortex = cortisol. Medulla = epinephrine (COTisol from CORTex).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Most hormone axes are regulated by negative feedback, so that rising hormone levels:
choices: Inhibit further release of the stimulating hormones upstream
rationale: Endocrine axes use negative feedback: high hormone → suppress upstream release.
why: That would be positive feedback, which is rarer (e.g., oxytocin in labor).
Correct. Negative feedback: high levels of a downstream hormone suppress the hypothalamic/pituitary signals that drive it, keeping levels in range.
Hormone levels do feed back to regulate their own secretion.
Feedback modulates output; it doesn't permanently disable the gland.
takeaway: Negative feedback = high hormone shuts off its own upstream signals.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
tag: Path of blood through the heart
stem: Deoxygenated blood returns to the right atrium, passes to the right ventricle, and is pumped to the:
rationale: Right heart → lungs (pulmonary); left heart → body (systemic).
why: The aorta carries oxygenated blood from the LEFT ventricle to the body.
Blood reaches the left atrium only after returning from the lungs.
Blood goes to the lungs for oxygenation before systemic distribution.
Correct. The right side pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circuit); the left side then pumps oxygenated blood to the body (systemic circuit).
takeaway: Right side → lungs. Left side → body.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: After returning from the lungs, oxygenated blood enters the LEFT atrium, then the left ventricle, which pumps it to the body through the:
rationale: Left ventricle → aorta → body (oxygenated, systemic circuit).
why: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood to the lungs.
Correct. The left ventricle (the most muscular chamber) pumps oxygenated blood into the aorta for systemic distribution.
The vena cava returns deoxygenated blood to the right atrium.
The pulmonary vein delivers oxygenated blood TO the left atrium; the aorta carries it out.
takeaway: Left ventricle → aorta → body.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The heart's intrinsic pacemaker, which initiates each heartbeat, is the:
rationale: The SA node is the heart's pacemaker (SA → AV → bundle of His → Purkinje).
why: The AV node delays and relays the impulse; it isn't the primary pacemaker.
The bundle of His conducts the impulse to the ventricles.
Correct. The SA node sets the rhythm; the impulse then travels to the AV node, down the bundle of His, and out the Purkinje fibers.
Purkinje fibers spread the impulse through the ventricles.
takeaway: SA node = pacemaker (then AV → His → Purkinje).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The phase of the cardiac cycle when the heart muscle CONTRACTS to eject blood is ______; the phase when it RELAXES and fills is ______.
rationale: Systole = contraction (eject); diastole = relaxation (fill).
why: Correct. Systole = contraction (ejection); diastole = relaxation (filling).
Reversed — contraction is systole.
Depolarization/repolarization describe the electrical events, not the mechanical phases.
Inspiration/expiration are breathing phases, not cardiac phases.
takeaway: Systole = squeeze. Diastole = fill.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Vessels that carry blood AWAY from the heart (usually oxygenated, under high pressure) are ______; vessels that return blood TO the heart are ______.
rationale: Arteries carry blood away from the heart; veins return it.
why: Reversed — arteries carry blood away from the heart.
Capillaries/arterioles aren't the away/toward pair.
Venules are small veins, not the full away/toward contrast.
Correct. Arteries carry blood away from the heart (thick, muscular, high pressure); veins return blood to the heart (thinner, with valves).
takeaway: Arteries = away from heart. Veins = back to heart.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Although arteries usually carry oxygenated blood, the ______ carries DEOXYGENATED blood, and the pulmonary VEIN carries oxygenated blood.
rationale: The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood (pulmonary vein carries oxygenated) — the exception.
why: The aorta carries oxygenated blood.
Correct. The pulmonary artery (heart → lungs) carries deoxygenated blood — the classic exception to 'arteries carry oxygenated blood.'
Coronary arteries carry oxygenated blood to the heart muscle.
The carotid artery carries oxygenated blood to the head.
takeaway: Pulmonary artery = deoxygenated (exception to the rule).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gas, nutrient, and waste exchange between blood and tissues occurs across the thin walls of the:
rationale: Capillaries (thin walls) are the site of gas/nutrient/waste exchange.
why: Arteries are thick-walled distribution vessels, not exchange sites.
Veins return blood; they aren't the main exchange vessels.
Correct. Capillaries have single-cell-thick walls enabling exchange of O2, CO2, nutrients, and wastes with tissues.
The aorta is the largest artery, for distribution, not exchange.
takeaway: Capillaries = exchange site (thin walls).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Oxygen is carried in the blood mainly bound to ______ inside red blood cells.
rationale: O2 is transported bound to hemoglobin in red blood cells.
why: Albumin maintains oncotic pressure and carries some molecules, not the main O2 carrier.
Fibrinogen is a clotting protein.
Platelets are cell fragments for clotting, not O2 carriers.
Correct. Hemoglobin (four subunits, each with an iron-containing heme) binds O2 in red blood cells for transport.
takeaway: Hemoglobin (in RBCs) carries oxygen.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During exercise, increased CO2, lower pH, and higher temperature shift the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve to the RIGHT, which:
choices: Promotes oxygen unloading to active tissues (the Bohr effect)
rationale: Right shift (↑CO2, ↓pH, ↑temp) = Bohr effect → more O2 released to tissues.
why: A right shift DECREASES affinity, aiding unloading.
Correct. A rightward shift (Bohr effect) lowers hemoglobin's O2 affinity, releasing more O2 where metabolically active tissues need it.
The shift enhances, not prevents, O2 release.
It occurs in active tissues, where CO2/H+ are high.
takeaway: Right shift = Bohr effect = O2 unloaded to active tissues.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The formed elements of blood include oxygen-carrying red blood cells, clot-forming platelets, and immune ______.
rationale: Blood formed elements: red cells (O2), platelets (clotting), white cells (immunity).
why: Hepatocytes are liver cells, not blood cells.
Neurons are nerve cells.
Correct. Leukocytes (white blood cells) are the immune formed elements; red cells carry O2 and platelets aid clotting.
Osteocytes are bone cells.
takeaway: Blood cells: RBC (O2), platelets (clot), WBC (immunity).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the lungs, gas exchange between air and blood occurs across the thin walls of the tiny air sacs called:
rationale: Gas exchange occurs in the alveoli (thin-walled air sacs).
why: Bronchi are conducting airways, not the exchange surface.
The trachea conducts air to the bronchi.
Bronchioles conduct air to the alveoli but aren't the exchange surface themselves.
Correct. Alveoli provide a huge, thin surface for O2 and CO2 to diffuse between air and the surrounding capillaries.
takeaway: Alveoli = gas exchange site in the lungs.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gas exchange is driven by partial-pressure gradients: oxygen diffuses from ______ into the blood, and CO2 diffuses from the blood into the ______.
rationale: In the lungs: O2 diffuses alveoli → blood; CO2 diffuses blood → alveoli (down partial-pressure gradients).
why: O2 moves INTO the blood, and CO2 moves OUT of it, in the lungs.
Correct. In the lungs, O2 moves from high-PO2 alveolar air into blood, and CO2 moves from high-PCO2 blood into the alveoli to be exhaled — each down its partial-pressure gradient.
Tissue exchange runs the opposite direction (O2 out of blood).
The gradient is between alveolar air and capillary blood, described by the alveoli.
takeaway: Lungs: O2 in (alveoli→blood), CO2 out (blood→alveoli).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During inhalation, the diaphragm contracts and moves downward, which ______ thoracic volume and ______ intrapulmonary pressure, drawing air in.
rationale: Inhalation: diaphragm down → ↑ volume, ↓ pressure → air in (Boyle's law).
why: That describes exhalation (volume down, pressure up).
Increased volume lowers pressure, not raises it.
Correct. Diaphragm contraction increases chest volume, lowering the pressure inside the lungs below atmospheric, so air flows in (Boyle's law).
Volume increases during inhalation, not decreases.
takeaway: Inhale: diaphragm down → volume up, pressure down → air in.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The immune defenses that are NONspecific, present from birth, and act as a rapid first response (skin, phagocytes, inflammation) make up the ______ immune system.
rationale: Innate immunity = nonspecific, fast, no memory (barriers, phagocytes, inflammation).
why: Adaptive immunity is specific and develops memory over time.
Humoral immunity is a branch of adaptive immunity.
'Memory' is a feature of adaptive, not innate, immunity.
Correct. Innate immunity is nonspecific, immediate, and lacks memory (barriers, phagocytes, complement, inflammation); adaptive immunity is specific and slower.
takeaway: Innate = nonspecific, fast, first line (no memory).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Innate immune cells such as macrophages and neutrophils defend the body by:
rationale: Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) engulf and digest pathogens.
why: Antibody production is done by B cells/plasma cells (adaptive immunity).
Correct. Phagocytes (macrophages, neutrophils) engulf and destroy pathogens and debris — a core innate defense.
Oxygen storage is a red-cell/myoglobin function, not phagocyte activity.
Clot formation is a platelet/coagulation function.
takeaway: Phagocytes = engulf/digest pathogens (innate).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The redness, heat, swelling, and pain at a site of infection or injury — caused by increased blood flow and vascular permeability (mediated by histamine) — is:
rationale: Inflammation = innate response with ↑ blood flow/permeability (redness, heat, swelling, pain).
why: Apoptosis is programmed cell death, not the inflammatory response.
Clonal selection is an adaptive-immunity process.
Correct. Inflammation is an innate response: vasodilation and increased permeability bring immune cells and fluid to the site (histamine is a key mediator).
Opsonization is the tagging of pathogens for phagocytosis, a component but not the whole response.
takeaway: Inflammation = innate response (redness, heat, swelling, pain).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the humoral (antibody-mediated) branch of adaptive immunity, ______ differentiate into plasma cells that secrete antibodies.
rationale: B cells → plasma cells → antibodies (humoral immunity).
why: T cells mediate cell-mediated immunity; they don't secrete antibodies.
Red blood cells carry oxygen, not immunity.
Platelets aid clotting, not antibody production.
Correct. B cells mediate humoral immunity, maturing into plasma cells that secrete antibodies specific to an antigen.
takeaway: B cells = antibodies (humoral immunity).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In cell-mediated immunity, ______ T cells coordinate the immune response by activating other cells, while ______ T cells directly kill infected cells.
rationale: Helper T (CD4+) coordinate; cytotoxic T (CD8+) kill infected cells.
why: Reversed — helper (CD4+) coordinate, cytotoxic (CD8+) kill.
Correct. Helper T cells (CD4+) orchestrate the response; cytotoxic T cells (CD8+) destroy virus-infected or abnormal cells directly.
Plasma/memory are B-cell fates, not the T-cell subsets described.
NK cells are innate; B cells make antibodies.
takeaway: Helper T (CD4) = coordinate. Cytotoxic T (CD8) = kill infected cells.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Adaptive immunity produces long-lived ______ cells, so a second exposure to the same pathogen triggers a faster, stronger response (the basis of vaccination).
rationale: Adaptive immunity forms memory cells → faster secondary response (vaccination).
why: Stem cells are undifferentiated precursors, not immune-memory cells.
Phagocytic cells are innate; they don't provide antigen-specific memory.
Correct. Memory B and T cells persist after an infection, enabling a rapid, robust secondary response — the principle behind vaccines.
Mast cells release histamine in allergy/inflammation, not adaptive memory.
takeaway: Memory cells = faster/stronger second response (vaccines).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
