stem: Chemical digestion of carbohydrates begins in the mouth via salivary ______, while protein digestion begins in the stomach.
rationale: Carb digestion starts in the mouth (salivary amylase); protein digestion starts in the stomach (pepsin).
why: Pepsin digests protein in the stomach, not carbohydrates in the mouth.
Lipase digests fats (mainly in the small intestine).
Correct. Salivary amylase starts carbohydrate (starch) digestion in the mouth; pepsin begins protein digestion in the acidic stomach.
Trypsin digests protein in the small intestine, not carbs in the mouth.
takeaway: Mouth = amylase (carbs). Stomach = pepsin (protein).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The stomach secretes hydrochloric acid, creating a low pH that activates ______, the enzyme that begins protein digestion.
rationale: Stomach HCl activates pepsin (from pepsinogen) to start protein digestion.
why: Correct. Gastric HCl converts pepsinogen to active pepsin (optimal at low pH), which begins breaking down proteins.
Amylase digests carbohydrates and is inactivated by stomach acid.
Bile emulsifies fats; it isn't a stomach protein enzyme.
Insulin is a blood-glucose hormone, not a digestive enzyme.
takeaway: Stomach acid → activates pepsin (protein digestion).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Most nutrient absorption occurs in the ______, whose surface area is hugely increased by villi and microvilli.
rationale: Most nutrient absorption is in the small intestine (villi + microvilli → huge surface area).
why: The stomach mainly digests and stores; little absorption occurs there.
The large intestine mainly absorbs water and forms feces.
The esophagus is a conducting tube; no absorption occurs there.
Correct. The small intestine is the main absorption site; villi and microvilli create an enormous surface area for nutrient uptake.
takeaway: Small intestine = main absorption (villi/microvilli).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Bile, produced by the liver and stored in the gallbladder, aids fat digestion by ______, while the pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and bicarbonate.
rationale: Bile (liver/gallbladder) emulsifies fats; the pancreas supplies enzymes + bicarbonate.
why: Bile emulsifies fat physically; it doesn't cleave peptide bonds.
Correct. Bile emulsifies fats (mechanically increasing surface area for lipase), but it is not an enzyme; the pancreas provides enzymes and neutralizing bicarbonate.
Bile doesn't absorb glucose.
Stomach acid is made by the stomach, not bile.
takeaway: Bile emulsifies fat (not an enzyme); pancreas = enzymes + bicarbonate.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The functional unit of the kidney, where blood is filtered and urine is formed, is the:
rationale: The nephron is the kidney's functional unit (filtration + urine formation).
why: The alveolus is the gas-exchange unit of the lung.
The sarcomere is the contractile unit of muscle.
Correct. The nephron (glomerulus + tubule) filters blood and processes the filtrate into urine.
The villus is an intestinal absorptive projection.
takeaway: Nephron = functional unit of the kidney.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Urine formation involves filtration at the glomerulus, ______ of useful substances back into the blood, and ______ of wastes into the tubule.
rationale: Nephron processes: filtration → reabsorption → secretion.
why: Correct. The three processes are filtration (glomerulus), reabsorption (tubule → blood, recovering water/glucose/ions), and secretion (blood → tubule, adding wastes).
Reversed — useful substances are reabsorbed, wastes are secreted.
Digestion/absorption are gastrointestinal, not renal, processes.
Diffusion/osmosis are mechanisms, not the three named renal processes.
takeaway: Kidney: filter, reabsorb (keep), secrete (dump wastes).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When the body is dehydrated, the posterior pituitary releases antidiuretic hormone (ADH), which causes the kidney to:
choices: Excrete more water, producing dilute urine
Reabsorb more water, producing concentrated urine
rationale: ADH → more water reabsorption → concentrated urine (conserves water).
why: ADH conserves water; excreting more water is the opposite effect.
ADH doesn't halt filtration.
ADH regulates water, not glucose secretion.
Correct. ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting duct (more aquaporins), conserving water and concentrating the urine.
takeaway: ADH = reabsorb water → concentrated urine (when dehydrated).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The adrenal hormone that increases sodium (and thus water) reabsorption in the kidney, raising blood pressure, is:
rationale: Aldosterone → Na+ (and water) reabsorption → ↑ blood pressure.
why: Insulin regulates blood glucose, not renal sodium.
Correct. Aldosterone (from the adrenal cortex) promotes Na+ reabsorption (water follows), increasing blood volume and pressure.
Thyroxine sets metabolic rate.
Calcitonin lowers blood calcium.
takeaway: Aldosterone = reabsorb Na+/water → raise BP.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The production of gametes by meiosis is called gametogenesis: sperm form via spermatogenesis, and eggs form via:
rationale: Oogenesis = egg production (meiosis); spermatogenesis = sperm production.
why: Mitosis produces identical body cells, not haploid gametes.
Fertilization is the fusion of gametes, not their production.
Correct. Oogenesis is the meiotic production of eggs (ova); spermatogenesis produces sperm. Both are forms of gametogenesis.
Ovulation is the release of an egg, not its formation.
takeaway: Oogenesis = eggs. Spermatogenesis = sperm (both meiosis).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A surge in ______ from the anterior pituitary triggers ovulation around the middle of the menstrual cycle.
rationale: A mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation.
why: Correct. A mid-cycle LH surge triggers ovulation (release of the egg from the follicle); FSH drives follicle maturation earlier.
Progesterone (from the corpus luteum) dominates the luteal phase after ovulation; it doesn't trigger it.
ADH regulates water balance, not ovulation.
Insulin regulates blood glucose.
takeaway: LH surge = ovulation trigger (mid-cycle).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: After ovulation, the ruptured follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which secretes ______ to maintain the uterine lining.
rationale: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone to maintain the uterine lining.
why: Testosterone is the principal male androgen, not the corpus luteum's product.
Amylase is a digestive enzyme.
Adrenaline is a fight-or-flight hormone.
Correct. The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (and estrogen), maintaining the endometrium; if no pregnancy occurs, it degenerates and progesterone falls, triggering menstruation.
takeaway: Corpus luteum → progesterone (maintains endometrium).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The fusion of a haploid sperm and a haploid egg produces a diploid ______, which then begins dividing.
rationale: Sperm + egg → diploid zygote (fertilization restores 2n).
why: Gametes are the haploid sex cells that fuse, not the product.
The gastrula is a later stage after gastrulation.
Correct. Fertilization forms a diploid zygote, restoring the full chromosome number; it then undergoes cleavage.
The blastocyst is a later hollow-ball stage.
takeaway: Fertilization: sperm + egg → diploid zygote.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The rapid series of mitotic divisions immediately after fertilization — increasing cell number without increasing overall size — is:
rationale: Cleavage = rapid mitotic divisions after fertilization (more cells, same total size).
why: Correct. Cleavage divides the zygote into many smaller cells (blastomeres) with little growth, forming a morula then a blastula/blastocyst.
Gastrulation forms the germ layers, later than cleavage.
Differentiation is cells becoming specialized.
Implantation is the embryo embedding in the uterine wall.
takeaway: Cleavage = fast early divisions (more cells, no size gain).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gastrulation produces three primary germ layers: ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm. The nervous system and epidermis derive from the:
rationale: Ectoderm → nervous system + epidermis (mesoderm → muscle/bone; endoderm → gut lining).
why: Mesoderm gives rise to muscle, bone, and the circulatory system.
Endoderm forms the gut lining and associated organs.
The blastocoel is the fluid cavity of the blastula, not a germ layer.
Correct. Ectoderm → nervous system and epidermis; mesoderm → muscle, bone, blood, kidneys; endoderm → gut and respiratory linings.
takeaway: Ectoderm = nervous system + skin. (Meso = muscle/bone; Endo = gut.)

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The three types of muscle tissue are skeletal (voluntary, striated), cardiac (involuntary, striated), and:
rationale: Muscle types: skeletal (voluntary/striated), cardiac (involuntary/striated), smooth (involuntary/non-striated).
why: Tendons connect muscle to bone; they aren't a muscle-tissue type.
Ligaments connect bone to bone; they aren't muscle.
Correct. Smooth muscle is involuntary and non-striated (lines organs/vessels); skeletal is voluntary/striated; cardiac is involuntary/striated.
Adipose is fat tissue, not muscle.
takeaway: 3 muscle types: skeletal, cardiac, smooth.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Muscle contracts when ______ filaments slide past ______ filaments, shortening the sarcomere (the sliding filament model).
rationale: Sliding filament: myosin (thick) pulls actin (thin) → sarcomere shortens.
why: Correct. In the sliding filament model, myosin (thick) heads pull actin (thin) filaments inward, shortening each sarcomere and contracting the muscle.
Actin is the thin filament and myosin the thick one (this reverses them).
Collagen/keratin are structural proteins, not sarcomere filaments.
Tubulin forms microtubules, not the contractile filaments.
takeaway: Contraction = actin slides along myosin (sarcomere shortens).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Muscle contraction is triggered when ______ is released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and binds troponin, exposing myosin-binding sites on actin.
rationale: Ca2+ binds troponin → exposes actin sites → myosin binds → contraction.
why: Na+ influx drives the action potential but isn't what binds troponin.
K+ efflux repolarizes membranes; it doesn't trigger the cross-bridge.
Cl− isn't the trigger for the actin–myosin interaction.
Correct. Ca2+ released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum binds troponin, shifting tropomyosin to expose actin's binding sites so myosin can attach and pull.
takeaway: Ca2+ binds troponin → exposes actin → contraction.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Bone is continuously remodeled by ______, which build bone, and osteoclasts, which resorb (break down) bone.
rationale: Osteoblasts build bone; osteoclasts break it down.
why: Osteoclasts resorb bone; the bone-building cells are osteoblasts.
Correct. Osteoblasts build/deposit bone matrix; osteoclasts resorb bone. (Mnemonic: osteoBlasts Build; osteoClasts Carve/Chew.)
Chondrocytes maintain cartilage, not bone deposition.
Myocytes are muscle cells.
takeaway: OsteoBlasts Build, osteoClasts Carve (break down).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At physiological pH, the amino acids with NEGATIVELY charged (acidic) side chains are:
rationale: Acidic (−): aspartate, glutamate. Basic (+): lysine, arginine, histidine.
why: Lysine and arginine are basic (positively charged), not acidic.
Serine and threonine are polar but uncharged.
Correct. Aspartate and glutamate have carboxylate side chains (negative at pH 7). Lysine, arginine, histidine are the basic (positive) ones.
Valine and leucine are nonpolar/hydrophobic.
takeaway: Acidic = Asp, Glu. Basic = Lys, Arg, His.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The three amino acids with basic (positively charged or ionizable-basic) side chains are:
rationale: Basic amino acids: lysine, arginine, histidine.
why: Correct. Lysine, arginine, and histidine have basic side chains (histidine's pKa near physiological pH makes it a common active-site residue).
Aspartate and glutamate are acidic; serine is polar uncharged.
Those are nonpolar/hydrophobic amino acids.
Those are the aromatic amino acids.
takeaway: Basic = Lys, Arg, His (His pKa ~6 → active sites).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: 'Essential' amino acids are those that:
choices: Are made only in the liver
Cannot be synthesized by the body and must come from the diet
rationale: Essential amino acids can't be made by the body — they must come from the diet.
why: 'Essential' refers to dietary necessity, not universal presence in proteins.
Essentiality is about synthesis, not charge.
Nonessential amino acids are synthesized by the body; essential ones must be eaten.
Correct. Essential amino acids (9 in humans) can't be synthesized de novo and must be obtained from food.
takeaway: Essential = must eat them (body can't synthesize).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The amino acids with aromatic (ring-containing) side chains — which absorb UV light at 280 nm — are:
rationale: Aromatic: phenylalanine, tyrosine, tryptophan (absorb UV at 280 nm).
why: Those are small/nonpolar amino acids without aromatic rings.
Correct. Phenylalanine, tyrosine, and tryptophan have aromatic rings; their UV absorbance at 280 nm is used to quantify protein.
Those are charged amino acids.
Those are polar uncharged amino acids.
takeaway: Aromatic = Phe, Tyr, Trp (UV 280 nm).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The smallest amino acid, with just a hydrogen as its side chain (making it achiral and conformationally flexible), is:
rationale: Glycine: side chain = H → smallest, achiral, flexible.
why: Proline is a rigid ring (imino acid), the opposite of flexible.
Cysteine has a thiol side chain that forms disulfides.
Correct. Glycine's side chain is a single H, so it is achiral and provides flexibility in protein backbones (common in turns).
Tryptophan is the largest, aromatic amino acid.
takeaway: Glycine = just H side chain (small, flexible, achiral).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The amino acid whose side chain loops back to bond the backbone nitrogen — forming a rigid ring that disrupts alpha helices and creates kinks — is:
rationale: Proline: rigid ring (imino acid) → kinks, disrupts alpha helices.
why: Correct. Proline's cyclic (imino) structure restricts backbone rotation, introducing kinks and disrupting regular secondary structure.
Glycine adds flexibility; it doesn't create rigid kinks.
Alanine has a simple methyl side chain with no special constraint.
Serine is a small polar residue without ring rigidity.
takeaway: Proline = rigid ring → kinks/helix breaker.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Two cysteine residues can be oxidized to form a covalent ______ that stabilizes tertiary and quaternary protein structure.
rationale: Two cysteines → covalent disulfide bond (–S–S–) stabilizing folded structure.
why: Peptide bonds link the backbone (primary structure), not cysteine side chains.
Disulfides are covalent, unlike hydrogen bonds.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides, not amino acids.
Correct. The thiol (–SH) groups of two cysteines oxidize to form a disulfide (–S–S–) bond — the main covalent bond stabilizing folded structure beyond the backbone.
takeaway: Cysteine + cysteine → disulfide bond (covalent, stabilizes fold).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: For a simple amino acid with only two ionizable groups (pKa1 ≈ 2 for –COOH, pKa2 ≈ 9 for –NH3+), the isoelectric point (pI) is:
choices: The average of the two pKa values (≈ 5.5)
rationale: pI = average of the two pKa values flanking the zwitterion.
why: pKa1 is where –COOH is half-dissociated, not the net-zero point.
The higher pKa alone doesn't give the net-neutral pH.
Correct. For a neutral amino acid, pI is the average of the two flanking pKa values — the pH where the zwitterion (net-zero charge) predominates.
pI depends on the amino acid's pKa values, not a fixed 7.
takeaway: pI = average of the two pKa's around the neutral form.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At a pH BELOW its isoelectric point, an amino acid carries a net ______ charge.
rationale: pH < pI → net positive; pH > pI → net negative.
why: Correct. Below the pI, extra protons are present, so groups are protonated — net positive. Above the pI, net negative.
Net negative occurs ABOVE the pI, not below.
Net zero occurs only AT the pI.
The charge is well-defined by pH relative to pI.
takeaway: Below pI = positive; above pI = negative.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: On a titration curve, an amino acid buffers most effectively (resists pH change) at pH values:
rationale: Buffering is strongest near the pKa (group half-protonated).
why: Buffering isn't tied specifically to pH 7.
Buffering is weakest, not strongest, far from a pKa.
At the pI the amino acid is net-neutral but not maximally buffering.
Correct. Buffering capacity is greatest near a pKa, where the group is ~half-protonated and can absorb added acid or base.
takeaway: Best buffering = pH near a pKa.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In an aqueous environment, the dominant force driving a protein to fold into its tertiary structure is the:
choices: Hydrophobic effect (nonpolar side chains cluster inward)
Covalent bonding of all side chains
rationale: The hydrophobic effect is the main driver of tertiary folding (nonpolar residues bury inward).
why: Peptide bonds define primary structure; they don't drive folding.
Like charges repel; opposite charges attract (salt bridges).
Correct. Burying hydrophobic side chains away from water (the hydrophobic effect) is the primary driver of tertiary folding; H-bonds, ionic, and disulfide bonds refine it.
Most side-chain interactions are noncovalent (only disulfides are covalent).
takeaway: Hydrophobic effect = main driver of protein folding.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Alpha helices and beta sheets are stabilized specifically by:
rationale: Secondary structure = backbone hydrogen bonds (helices, sheets).
why: Correct. Secondary structure is held together by hydrogen bonds between backbone carbonyl oxygens and amide hydrogens.
Disulfides stabilize tertiary/quaternary structure, not secondary.
Peptide bonds form the primary backbone, not the secondary-structure stabilization.
Side-chain ionic bonds contribute to tertiary structure, not secondary.
takeaway: Secondary structure held by backbone H-bonds.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An electrostatic attraction between a positively charged side chain (e.g., lysine) and a negatively charged one (e.g., glutamate) is a:
rationale: A salt bridge = ionic bond between oppositely charged side chains.
why: A disulfide is a covalent bond between cysteine thiols.
A hydrogen bond involves a shared H, not full charges.
Hydrophobic interactions involve nonpolar groups, not charges.
Correct. A salt bridge is an ionic bond between oppositely charged side chains, contributing to tertiary/quaternary stability.
takeaway: Salt bridge = ionic bond (opposite-charged side chains).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Structural proteins like collagen and keratin are ______ proteins; most enzymes and transport proteins like hemoglobin are ______ proteins.
rationale: Fibrous = structural (collagen, keratin); globular = functional (enzymes, hemoglobin).
why: Reversed — structural collagen/keratin are fibrous; enzymes/hemoglobin are globular.
Integral/peripheral describe membrane proteins.
Correct. Fibrous proteins are elongated and structural; globular proteins are compact, water-soluble, and functional (catalysis, transport).
Simple/conjugated describe whether a protein has a non-amino-acid group.
takeaway: Fibrous = structural. Globular = functional/soluble.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The most abundant protein in the human body, a fibrous triple helix rich in glycine and proline that provides tensile strength to connective tissue, is:
rationale: Collagen = most abundant protein; fibrous triple helix (glycine/proline-rich).
why: Correct. Collagen is a fibrous structural protein (triple helix, glycine every third residue) giving strength to skin, bone, and tendon.
Hemoglobin is a globular oxygen-transport protein.
Amylase is a digestive enzyme.
Insulin is a peptide hormone.
takeaway: Collagen = fibrous triple helix (most abundant protein).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal (S-shaped) oxygen-binding curve reflects ______, in which binding of one O2 increases the affinity of the remaining subunits.
rationale: Hemoglobin's sigmoidal curve = cooperative binding (one O2 raises affinity for the next).
why: Competitive inhibition concerns enzymes and substrate, not O2 cooperativity.
Denaturation is loss of structure, unrelated to the binding curve shape.
Feedback inhibition is a metabolic regulation mechanism.
Correct. Hemoglobin's four subunits bind O2 cooperatively (positive cooperativity), producing a sigmoidal curve; myoglobin (one subunit) is hyperbolic.
takeaway: Hemoglobin = cooperative O2 binding (sigmoidal); myoglobin = hyperbolic.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An uncompetitive inhibitor binds ONLY to the enzyme-substrate (ES) complex, and its effect is to:
rationale: Uncompetitive inhibitor: binds ES only → ↓Km and ↓Vmax.
why: Increased Km with unchanged Vmax describes competitive inhibition.
Decreased Vmax with unchanged Km describes noncompetitive inhibition.
Correct. Uncompetitive inhibitors bind only the ES complex, lowering both apparent Km and Vmax (their ratio stays roughly constant).
No inhibitor increases Vmax.
takeaway: Uncompetitive = binds ES only → ↓Km and ↓Vmax.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Which inhibitor type can be overcome (outcompeted) by adding excess substrate?
rationale: Competitive inhibition is the one overcome by excess substrate.
why: Correct. Only competitive inhibition is relieved by excess substrate, because the inhibitor and substrate compete for the same active site.
Noncompetitive inhibitors bind allosterically; extra substrate doesn't displace them.
Uncompetitive inhibitors bind the ES complex, not relieved by more substrate.
Irreversible inhibitors permanently inactivate the enzyme.
takeaway: Only competitive inhibition is beaten by more substrate.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An inhibitor that forms a covalent bond with the enzyme, permanently inactivating it (e.g., aspirin on COX), is a(n):
rationale: Irreversible inhibitor: covalently and permanently inactivates the enzyme.
why: Competitive inhibitors bind reversibly at the active site.
An allosteric activator increases activity, not inhibits it.
A coenzyme assists catalysis; it doesn't inactivate the enzyme.
Correct. Irreversible inhibitors covalently and permanently disable the enzyme; recovery requires synthesizing new enzyme.
takeaway: Irreversible = covalent, permanent inactivation (e.g., aspirin/COX).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: As helicase unwinds DNA, the enzyme that relieves the supercoiling tension building ahead of the replication fork is:
rationale: Topoisomerase/gyrase relieves supercoiling ahead of the fork.
why: Ligase seals nicks between Okazaki fragments; it doesn't relieve supercoiling.
Correct. Topoisomerase (gyrase in bacteria) cuts, relaxes, and reseals DNA to relieve the torsional strain (supercoiling) generated ahead of the fork.
Primase makes RNA primers.
Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase charges tRNAs — unrelated to replication.
takeaway: Topoisomerase = relieves supercoiling (ahead of fork).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: After helicase separates the strands, ______ coat the exposed single strands to keep them apart and prevent reannealing.
rationale: Single-strand binding proteins keep separated strands apart at the fork.
why: Ligase seals fragments; it doesn't coat single strands.
Ribosomes translate mRNA.
Histones package DNA into chromatin, not fork stabilization.
Correct. Single-strand binding proteins stabilize the separated template strands, preventing them from re-pairing before replication.
takeaway: SSBs coat single strands (prevent reannealing).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In bacteria, the main replicative enzyme that synthesizes most new DNA is ______; the enzyme that removes RNA primers and fills the gaps is ______.
choices: DNA polymerase III; DNA polymerase I
DNA polymerase I; DNA polymerase III
rationale: DNA pol III = main synthesis; DNA pol I = removes primers, fills gaps.
why: Correct. DNA pol III does the bulk of synthesis; DNA pol I removes the RNA primers (5'→3' exonuclease) and fills with DNA.
Reversed — pol III is the main synthesizer, pol I replaces primers.
Primase/ligase make primers and seal nicks, not this pair.
Helicase/topoisomerase handle unwinding, not synthesis.
takeaway: Pol III = bulk synthesis. Pol I = replaces primers.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Errors that escape proofreading and leave a mismatched base pair just after replication are corrected by:
rationale: Mismatch repair fixes base-pair mismatches missed by proofreading.
why: Nucleotide excision repair removes bulky lesions like thymine dimers, not simple mismatches.
Correct. Mismatch repair recognizes and removes base-pair mismatches missed by polymerase proofreading, using the newly synthesized strand as the target (defects cause Lynch syndrome).
Transcription makes RNA; it isn't a repair pathway.
Translation makes protein.
takeaway: Mismatch repair = fixes post-replication mismatches.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A single damaged or incorrect base (e.g., from deamination) is removed by a glycosylase and replaced through:
rationale: Base excision repair removes a single damaged base (glycosylase).
why: Nucleotide excision repair removes a segment containing bulky lesions, not a single base.
Replication copies DNA; it isn't a base-repair pathway.
Homologous recombination repairs double-strand breaks.
Correct. Base excision repair removes a single damaged base (via DNA glycosylase) and fills the gap — distinct from removing whole nucleotide stretches.
takeaway: Base excision repair = single damaged base removed.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Double-strand DNA breaks are repaired by non-homologous end joining and, more accurately, by:
choices: Homologous recombination (using a sister chromatid as template)
rationale: Homologous recombination accurately repairs double-strand breaks (template = sister chromatid).
why: Correct. Homologous recombination accurately repairs double-strand breaks using a homologous sequence (sister chromatid) as a template.
Mismatch repair fixes single-base mismatches, not double-strand breaks.
Base excision repair handles single damaged bases.
RNA splicing processes pre-mRNA; it isn't DNA repair.
takeaway: Double-strand breaks → homologous recombination (accurate).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In prokaryotes, a cluster of genes transcribed together from a single promoter under coordinated control is a(n):
rationale: An operon = a cluster of genes under one promoter (coordinated prokaryotic control).
why: An intron is a non-coding sequence removed from pre-mRNA.
Correct. An operon groups functionally related genes under one promoter/operator for coordinated regulation (a hallmark of prokaryotic gene control).
A codon is a three-base mRNA unit.
A nucleosome is DNA wrapped around histones (eukaryotic packaging).
takeaway: Operon = genes co-transcribed from one promoter (prokaryotes).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The lac operon is an INDUCIBLE operon: it is normally OFF and turns ON when ______ is present.
choices: Lactose (the inducer), which inactivates the repressor
rationale: lac operon: inducible — lactose inactivates the repressor → genes turn ON.
why: Glucose actually lowers lac expression (catabolite repression), not induces it.
Tryptophan regulates the trp operon, not the lac operon.
The repressor keeps the operon OFF; it doesn't turn it on.
Correct. Lactose (via allolactose) binds and inactivates the lac repressor, allowing transcription of lactose-metabolism genes — an inducible system.
takeaway: lac operon = inducible (lactose turns it ON).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The trp operon is a REPRESSIBLE operon: it is normally ON and turns OFF when ______ accumulates.
rationale: trp operon: repressible — tryptophan activates the repressor → genes turn OFF.
why: Correct. When tryptophan is abundant, it acts as a corepressor — activating the trp repressor to shut off synthesis of tryptophan-making genes (feedback repression).
Lactose regulates the lac operon, not trp.
Glucose isn't the trp corepressor.
cAMP is involved in catabolite activation of lac, not trp repression.
takeaway: trp operon = repressible (tryptophan turns it OFF).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When glucose is scarce, cAMP rises and binds CAP (catabolite activator protein), which then ______ transcription of the lac operon.
rationale: cAMP-CAP activates lac transcription when glucose is low (positive control).
why: CAP activates rather than blocks transcription.
CAP is a regulatory protein; it doesn't delete DNA.
Correct. Low glucose → high cAMP → cAMP-CAP binds and boosts lac transcription (positive control), so the cell preferentially uses glucose first.
cAMP-CAP has a strong activating effect on lac.
takeaway: Low glucose → cAMP-CAP activates lac (positive control).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In eukaryotes, tightly packed chromatin (heterochromatin) is generally ______, while loosely packed euchromatin is generally ______.
rationale: Condensed heterochromatin = silent; open euchromatin = active.
why: Reversed — condensed chromatin is silent, open chromatin is active.
Correct. Condensed heterochromatin blocks transcription-machinery access (silent); open euchromatin permits transcription (active).
Packing state concerns transcription access, not a replication on/off switch.
Both chromatin states contain histones.
takeaway: Heterochromatin = OFF (packed); euchromatin = ON (open).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Adding acetyl groups to histones (by histone acetyltransferases) loosens DNA–histone binding and generally ______ transcription.
rationale: Histone acetylation loosens chromatin → activates transcription.
why: Acetylation activates rather than silences (deacetylation silences).
Acetylation is an epigenetic mark, not DNA deletion.
Acetylation promotes, rather than prevents, transcription.
Correct. Histone acetylation neutralizes positive charges, loosening histone–DNA interaction and opening chromatin → more transcription.
takeaway: Acetylation = loosen chromatin = ON. Deacetylation = OFF.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In eukaryotes, methylation of cytosines in promoter regions is an epigenetic mark that typically ______ gene expression.
rationale: DNA methylation of promoters typically silences gene expression (epigenetic).
why: Correct. Promoter DNA methylation generally represses transcription — an epigenetic, heritable-but-reversible silencing mark.
Methylation typically silences, not activates.
Methylation clearly affects expression (usually repressive).
Methylation adds a chemical group; it doesn't change the underlying sequence.
takeaway: Promoter methylation = gene silencing (epigenetic).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Regulatory DNA sequences that can be far from a gene yet boost its transcription when bound by activator proteins are:
rationale: Enhancers = distal DNA elements that boost transcription when bound by activators.
why: Introns are non-coding sequences removed from pre-mRNA.
Telomeres are protective chromosome ends.
Correct. Enhancers are distal regulatory elements; bound activators (transcription factors) loop to the promoter and increase transcription.
Codons are mRNA triplets read during translation.
takeaway: Enhancers = distant DNA that boosts transcription (via TFs).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The RNA that carries the genetic message, the RNA that brings amino acids, and the RNA that forms the ribosome are, respectively:
rationale: mRNA = message; tRNA = brings amino acids; rRNA = ribosome.
why: That mislabels each RNA's role.
Correct. mRNA carries the code, tRNA delivers amino acids (anticodon), and rRNA is the structural/catalytic core of the ribosome.
That order is scrambled.
snRNA and miRNA are regulatory/processing RNAs, not the three core players here.
takeaway: mRNA = message, tRNA = amino acids, rRNA = ribosome.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The small nuclear RNAs that combine with proteins to form the spliceosome and remove introns are:
rationale: snRNA (in snRNPs) forms the spliceosome that removes introns.
why: mRNA is the transcript being spliced, not the splicing machinery.
tRNA delivers amino acids in translation.
rRNA builds the ribosome for translation.
Correct. snRNAs (in snRNPs) are core components of the spliceosome that carries out intron removal.
takeaway: snRNA = spliceosome component (removes introns).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Small regulatory RNAs that bind complementary mRNA to block its translation or trigger its degradation (RNA interference) are:
rationale: miRNA/siRNA silence gene expression via RNA interference (target mRNA).
why: Correct. microRNAs and small interfering RNAs mediate RNA interference, silencing gene expression post-transcriptionally.
rRNA and tRNA are translation machinery, not gene silencers.
mRNA is the target; snRNA handles splicing.
mRNA is the message, not a silencing RNA.
takeaway: miRNA/siRNA = RNA interference (silence mRNA).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In a pedigree, a trait that skips generations and often appears in offspring of two unaffected parents is most likely:
rationale: Autosomal recessive: skips generations; unaffected carrier parents → affected child.
why: Autosomal dominant traits usually appear in every generation with an affected parent.
Y-linked traits pass only father-to-son.
Correct. Autosomal recessive traits can skip generations and appear when two heterozygous (carrier) unaffected parents each pass the recessive allele.
Mitochondrial traits pass only from the mother to all offspring.
takeaway: AR = skips generations, carrier parents → affected child.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A trait that appears in every generation, with each affected individual having at least one affected parent, is characteristic of:
rationale: Autosomal dominant: every generation, affected child has an affected parent.
why: Correct. Autosomal dominant traits typically appear in every generation and affect males and females roughly equally, with vertical transmission.
Autosomal recessive traits tend to skip generations.
X-linked recessive traits affect males more and often skip through carrier females.
Mitochondrial inheritance is strictly maternal.
takeaway: AD = every generation, affected parent → affected child.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A trait passed from an affected MOTHER to ALL of her children (but never from an affected father) indicates:
rationale: Mitochondrial inheritance = maternal; affected mother → all children.
why: Y-linked traits pass father-to-son only.
Autosomal dominant traits come from either parent.
X-linked dominant traits can come from either affected parent with distinct sex ratios.
Correct. Mitochondrial DNA is inherited maternally (egg cytoplasm), so an affected mother passes it to all offspring; affected fathers do not transmit it.
takeaway: Mitochondrial = maternal only (mom → all kids).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An abnormal number of chromosomes (e.g., trisomy 21 / Down syndrome), usually resulting from nondisjunction, is called:
rationale: Aneuploidy = abnormal chromosome number (e.g., trisomy 21), often from nondisjunction.
why: Polyploidy is having entire extra chromosome SETS (common in plants).
A translocation moves a segment to a nonhomologous chromosome without necessarily changing count.
Correct. Aneuploidy is an abnormal chromosome count (one extra or missing), commonly from meiotic nondisjunction (e.g., trisomy 21).
A point mutation is a single-base change, not a chromosome-number change.
takeaway: Aneuploidy = wrong chromosome number (e.g., trisomy 21).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A chromosomal rearrangement in which a segment is moved to a NONHOMOLOGOUS chromosome is a:
rationale: Translocation = segment moved to a nonhomologous chromosome.
why: Correct. A translocation relocates a chromosome segment to a nonhomologous chromosome (e.g., the Philadelphia chromosome in CML).
A deletion loses a chromosome segment.
An inversion reverses a segment within the same chromosome.
A duplication copies a segment within the chromosome.
takeaway: Translocation = segment moved to a different chromosome.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Whether nondisjunction occurs in meiosis I versus meiosis II determines whether the resulting error involves ______ failing to separate.
choices: Homologous chromosomes (meiosis I) vs. sister chromatids (meiosis II)
rationale: Nondisjunction: meiosis I = homologs fail; meiosis II = sister chromatids fail.
why: Meiosis I involves homologs, not sister chromatids.
Meiosis II involves sister chromatids, not homologs.
The distinction is about which structures fail to separate, not centromere timing alone.
Correct. Meiosis I nondisjunction = homologs fail to separate; meiosis II nondisjunction = sister chromatids fail to separate.
takeaway: Meiosis I nondisjunction = homologs; II = sister chromatids.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The laboratory technique that amplifies a specific DNA sequence into millions of copies using primers, dNTPs, and a heat-stable polymerase through repeated heating/cooling cycles is:
rationale: PCR amplifies a target DNA sequence (denature–anneal–extend cycles, Taq polymerase).
why: Gel electrophoresis separates DNA by size; it doesn't amplify it.
Cloning inserts DNA into a vector/host, a different process.
Correct. PCR exponentially amplifies a target DNA region through cycles of denaturation, annealing (primers), and extension (Taq polymerase).
Northern blotting detects RNA, not DNA amplification.
takeaway: PCR = amplify DNA (denature/anneal/extend; Taq).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In gel electrophoresis, DNA fragments migrate through the gel toward the positive electrode, and ______ fragments travel farther.
rationale: Gel electrophoresis: DNA moves toward (+); smaller fragments travel farther.
why: Correct. DNA is negatively charged (phosphate backbone) and moves toward the positive electrode; smaller fragments move faster and travel farther.
Larger fragments move more slowly and stay near the wells.
DNA is uniformly negative, so charge doesn't separate fragments — size does.
Both linear and circular DNA can be run; size (and shape) determines migration.
takeaway: Electrophoresis: smaller DNA runs farther (toward +).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: To detect a specific DNA sequence you use a Southern blot; to detect a specific protein you use a:
rationale: Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein (SNoW DRoP).
why: A Northern blot detects RNA, not protein.
A Southern blot detects DNA, the technique already named in the stem.
'Eastern blot' is not a standard core technique for protein detection.
Correct. Southern = DNA, Northern = RNA, Western = protein (mnemonic: SNoW DRoP — Southern/Northern/Western → DNA/RNA/Protein).
takeaway: Southern=DNA, Northern=RNA, Western=protein (SNoW DRoP).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The gene-editing system that uses a guide RNA to direct a nuclease to a specific DNA sequence for a targeted cut is:
rationale: CRISPR-Cas9 = guide-RNA-directed nuclease for targeted DNA editing.
why: PCR amplifies DNA; it doesn't edit the genome.
Correct. CRISPR-Cas9 uses a guide RNA to target Cas9 nuclease to a precise DNA site, enabling targeted edits (knockouts, insertions).
Gel electrophoresis separates fragments by size.
Gram staining classifies bacteria by cell-wall type.
takeaway: CRISPR = guide RNA directs Cas9 to cut a specific DNA site.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Inserting a gene of interest into a plasmid vector and introducing it into bacteria to produce many copies (or a protein product) is:
rationale: Molecular cloning: insert a gene into a plasmid vector → bacteria make copies/protein.
why: PCR amplifies DNA in vitro without a host cell.
Karyotyping visualizes chromosome number/structure.
Correct. Recombinant DNA technology inserts a gene into a vector (plasmid) that bacteria replicate, enabling gene copies or protein production (e.g., recombinant insulin).
Electrophoresis separates fragments; it doesn't clone genes.
takeaway: Cloning = gene into plasmid → bacteria copy it (recombinant DNA).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The key rate-limiting (committed-step) enzyme of glycolysis, which is allosterically inhibited by ATP and activated by AMP, is:
rationale: PFK-1 is the rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis (inhibited by ATP, activated by AMP).
why: Hexokinase catalyzes the first step but is not the main committed regulatory point; PFK-1 is.
Pyruvate kinase is regulated but not the primary rate-limiting enzyme.
Lactate dehydrogenase acts in fermentation, not the committed glycolytic step.
Correct. PFK-1 catalyzes the committed step (fructose-6-P → fructose-1,6-bisP) and is the main regulatory point — inhibited by ATP/citrate, activated by AMP.
takeaway: PFK-1 = committed/rate-limiting step of glycolysis.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Glycolysis is divided into an energy-INVESTMENT phase that USES 2 ATP and a payoff phase that PRODUCES:
rationale: Glycolysis: invest 2 ATP, produce 4 ATP + 2 NADH → net 2 ATP + 2 NADH.
why: The payoff phase yields 4 ATP (net 2), plus 2 NADH.
Correct. The investment phase spends 2 ATP; the payoff phase produces 4 ATP + 2 NADH, for a net of 2 ATP and 2 NADH per glucose.
36 ATP is the full aerobic total, not glycolysis's payoff.
The payoff phase makes ATP as well as NADH.
takeaway: Glycolysis: −2 ATP invest, +4 ATP +2 NADH payoff (net +2 ATP).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Glucose is not the only sugar entering glycolysis; fructose and ______ (from milk) can also be funneled into the pathway.
rationale: Fructose and galactose can feed into glycolysis (after conversion).
why: Cellulose is indigestible to humans (no cellulase).
Glycogen must first be broken down to glucose units.
Correct. Monosaccharides like fructose and galactose feed into glycolysis after conversion; humans can't digest cellulose.
Sucrose is a disaccharide that must be hydrolyzed to glucose + fructose first.
takeaway: Fructose & galactose feed into glycolysis.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Building glycogen from glucose is ______; breaking glycogen down to release glucose is ______.
rationale: Glycogenesis = build glycogen; glycogenolysis = break it down.
why: Reversed — building is glycogenesis, breakdown is glycogenolysis.
Gluconeogenesis/glycolysis are different pathways (new glucose / glucose breakdown).
Lipogenesis/lipolysis concern fat, not glycogen.
Correct. Glycogenesis stores glucose as glycogen; glycogenolysis breaks glycogen back down to glucose-1-phosphate.
takeaway: Glycogenesis = store; glycogenolysis = break down glycogen.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: ______ promotes glycogen synthesis (storage) after a meal, while glucagon and epinephrine promote glycogen breakdown.
rationale: Insulin → glycogen storage; glucagon/epinephrine → glycogen breakdown.
why: Glucagon promotes breakdown, not storage.
Correct. Insulin drives glycogen synthesis (fed state); glucagon (fasting) and epinephrine (stress) drive glycogenolysis.
Cortisol affects glucose but isn't the primary glycogen-synthesis signal.
Thyroxine sets metabolic rate, not this specific control.
takeaway: Insulin stores glycogen; glucagon/epi break it down.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the ______ and makes glucose from precursors such as lactate, glycerol, and glucogenic amino acids.
rationale: Gluconeogenesis occurs mainly in the liver (lactate, glycerol, amino acids → glucose).
why: The brain consumes glucose; it doesn't perform net gluconeogenesis.
Red blood cells rely on glycolysis and lack mitochondria for it.
The small intestine absorbs nutrients; it isn't the main gluconeogenic organ.
Correct. The liver (and some kidney) performs gluconeogenesis, synthesizing glucose from non-carbohydrate precursors during fasting.
takeaway: Gluconeogenesis = liver makes glucose from non-carbs.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gluconeogenesis is not just glycolysis run backward because it must bypass the three irreversible glycolytic steps using:
choices: The exact same enzymes in reverse
Different enzymes (e.g., PEP carboxykinase, fructose-1,6-bisphosphatase, glucose-6-phosphatase)
rationale: Gluconeogenesis uses unique enzymes to bypass glycolysis's three irreversible steps.
why: The irreversible steps can't simply run backward; unique enzymes are needed.
Correct. Gluconeogenesis uses distinct enzymes to bypass the three irreversible (highly exergonic) glycolytic steps.
Multiple bypass enzymes are required, not one.
Enzymes are required; the pathway is enzyme-catalyzed.
takeaway: Gluconeogenesis ≠ reverse glycolysis (bypass enzymes needed).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The pentose phosphate pathway runs parallel to glycolysis and generates two key products:
rationale: Pentose phosphate pathway → NADPH + ribose-5-phosphate.
why: ATP and pyruvate are glycolysis products, not the PPP's signature outputs.
FADH2/CO2 are associated with the Krebs cycle.
Lactate/NAD+ relate to fermentation.
Correct. The PPP produces NADPH (for biosynthesis/antioxidant defense) and ribose-5-phosphate (for nucleotide synthesis).
takeaway: PPP = NADPH (biosynthesis) + ribose-5-P (nucleotides).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Unlike NADH (which fuels ATP production), NADPH is mainly used for:
choices: Reductive biosynthesis (e.g., fatty acid synthesis) and antioxidant defense
rationale: NADPH powers reductive biosynthesis and antioxidant defense (not ATP production).
why: NADH, not NADPH, feeds the ETC for ATP.
Correct. NADPH provides reducing power for anabolic reactions (fatty acid/cholesterol synthesis) and maintains glutathione for antioxidant defense.
Glycolysis uses NAD+, not NADPH.
DNA replication uses dNTPs/ATP, not NADPH as its energy source.
takeaway: NADPH = biosynthesis + antioxidant (NADH = ATP).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Fatty acids are transported into the mitochondrion and broken down by beta-oxidation into ______, which enters the Krebs cycle.
rationale: Beta-oxidation: fatty acids → acetyl-CoA (+ NADH/FADH2) for the Krebs cycle.
why: Fatty acids aren't converted to glucose in humans (no net conversion).
Beta-oxidation produces acetyl-CoA, not pyruvate.
Lactate is a fermentation product, not a beta-oxidation product.
Correct. Beta-oxidation cleaves fatty acids two carbons at a time into acetyl-CoA (generating NADH and FADH2), yielding far more ATP per gram than carbohydrate.
takeaway: Beta-oxidation = fatty acids → acetyl-CoA (mitochondria).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: During prolonged fasting or low-carbohydrate states, the liver converts excess acetyl-CoA into ______, which the brain can use as an alternative fuel.
rationale: Fasting: liver makes ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA (alternative brain fuel).
why: Glycogen is a glucose store, not made from surplus acetyl-CoA in fasting.
Correct. Ketogenesis produces ketone bodies from acetyl-CoA when carbohydrate is scarce; the brain adapts to use them, sparing glucose.
Lactate comes from anaerobic glycolysis, not ketogenesis.
Cholesterol synthesis uses acetyl-CoA but isn't the fasting brain fuel.
takeaway: Ketone bodies = fasting fuel (from acetyl-CoA, used by brain).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Cholesterol and triglycerides are carried in the blood by lipoproteins; ______ delivers cholesterol to tissues ('bad'), while ______ returns it to the liver ('good').
rationale: LDL delivers cholesterol to tissues ('bad'); HDL returns it to liver ('good').
why: Reversed — LDL delivers to tissues, HDL returns to liver.
Chylomicrons/VLDL mainly carry dietary/endogenous triglycerides.
Correct. LDL ('bad') deposits cholesterol in tissues/arteries; HDL ('good') carries cholesterol back to the liver (reverse transport).
Albumin/globulin are plasma proteins, not the LDL/HDL cholesterol carriers.
takeaway: LDL = bad (to tissues); HDL = good (to liver).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Transferring an amino group from an amino acid to a keto acid is ______; removing an amino group as ammonia is ______.
rationale: Transamination = transfer amino group; deamination = remove it as ammonia.
why: Reversed — transferring an amino group is transamination.
Beta-oxidation/glycolysis are fuel-breakdown pathways, not amino-group handling.
Ketogenesis/lipolysis concern lipids.
Correct. Transamination moves an amino group (via aminotransferases); deamination removes it as ammonia, which must be detoxified.
takeaway: Transamination = move amino group; deamination = remove as NH3.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Toxic ammonia produced from amino acid breakdown is converted in the liver into the less-toxic, excretable molecule ______ via the urea cycle.
rationale: The urea cycle (liver) converts toxic ammonia into excretable urea.
why: Glucose is a fuel, not the nitrogen-excretion product in humans.
Correct. The urea cycle (liver) converts ammonia into urea, which the kidneys excrete — preventing toxic ammonia buildup.
Uric acid handles purine breakdown (and is the main nitrogen waste in birds/reptiles), not the human urea cycle product.
Creatine is a muscle energy molecule, not urea-cycle output.
takeaway: Urea cycle = ammonia → urea (liver, then kidney excretes).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Amino acids broken down into pyruvate or Krebs-cycle intermediates (feeding glucose synthesis) are ______; those broken down into acetyl-CoA/acetoacetate are ______.
rationale: Glucogenic → glucose precursors; ketogenic → acetyl-CoA/ketones.
why: Reversed — those yielding glucose precursors are glucogenic.
Essential/nonessential concern dietary need, not this metabolic fate.
Correct. Glucogenic amino acids can be used to make glucose; ketogenic amino acids yield acetyl-CoA/ketone bodies (some are both).
Polar/nonpolar describe side chains, not catabolic fate.
takeaway: Glucogenic = →glucose; ketogenic = →acetyl-CoA/ketones.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The anterior pituitary SYNTHESIZES and releases its own hormones (e.g., ACTH, TSH, FSH, LH, GH, prolactin), while the posterior pituitary:
choices: Stores and releases hormones (ADH, oxytocin) made by the hypothalamus
rationale: Anterior pituitary makes its hormones; posterior stores hypothalamic ADH & oxytocin.
why: ADH and oxytocin are made in the hypothalamus, not the posterior pituitary.
The posterior pituitary does release hormones (ADH, oxytocin).
Correct. The posterior pituitary stores/releases ADH and oxytocin produced by hypothalamic neurons; the anterior pituitary makes its own hormones.
Growth hormone is from the anterior pituitary, not posterior.
takeaway: Anterior = makes hormones; posterior = stores hypothalamic ADH/oxytocin.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Anterior pituitary hormones like TSH and ACTH are 'tropic' because they:
choices: Stimulate other endocrine glands to release their hormones
Act directly on the pituitary itself
rationale: Tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH) stimulate other endocrine glands.
why: Correct. Tropic hormones target other endocrine glands (TSH → thyroid, ACTH → adrenal cortex), which then release their own hormones.
Tropic hormones act on downstream glands, not on the pituitary itself.
Pituitary hormones are peptides, not steroids.
Their effects extend well beyond bone.
takeaway: Tropic hormones = tell other glands to secrete (TSH→thyroid, ACTH→adrenal).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary by secreting releasing/inhibiting hormones into a:
choices: Direct nerve axon into the gland
Portal blood vessel system connecting the two
rationale: The hypothalamus controls the anterior pituitary via a portal blood system.
why: Direct axonal control applies to the posterior pituitary, not the anterior.
Endocrine glands are ductless; they secrete into blood, not ducts.
Salivary ducts are exocrine and unrelated.
Correct. The hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal system carries releasing hormones directly to the anterior pituitary; the posterior lobe is controlled by direct neural connection.
takeaway: Hypothalamus → anterior pituitary via portal blood vessels.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When blood calcium is LOW, the parathyroid glands release ______, which raises blood calcium (bone resorption, kidney reabsorption, vitamin D activation).
rationale: PTH raises blood calcium (bone, kidney, vitamin D).
why: Calcitonin LOWERS blood calcium, the opposite of PTH.
Insulin regulates glucose, not calcium.
Correct. PTH raises blood calcium by stimulating osteoclasts, renal Ca2+ reabsorption, and vitamin D activation (which boosts gut absorption).
Aldosterone regulates sodium/water, not calcium.
takeaway: Low Ca → PTH raises it (bone/kidney/vit D).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When blood calcium is HIGH, the thyroid releases ______, which lowers blood calcium (opposing PTH).
rationale: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium (opposes PTH).
why: Correct. Calcitonin (from thyroid C cells) lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts — the counter-regulator to PTH.
PTH raises calcium; calcitonin lowers it.
Thyroxine sets metabolic rate, not calcium balance.
Cortisol is a stress/glucose hormone.
takeaway: High Ca → calcitonin lowers it (calciTONIN tones it down).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Thyroid hormone (T3/T4) release is stimulated by TSH from the pituitary, which is itself stimulated by ______ from the hypothalamus.
rationale: Thyroid axis: TRH → TSH → T3/T4 (with negative feedback).
why: ADH regulates water balance, not the thyroid axis.
Insulin regulates glucose.
Calcitonin regulates calcium, not the TSH axis.
Correct. The axis is TRH (hypothalamus) → TSH (pituitary) → T3/T4 (thyroid), with negative feedback from thyroid hormone.
takeaway: TRH → TSH → T3/T4 (thyroid axis).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The adrenal cortex secretes three classes of steroid hormones: mineralocorticoids (aldosterone), glucocorticoids (cortisol), and:
rationale: Adrenal cortex steroids: mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and androgens.
why: Epinephrine is from the adrenal MEDULLA, not the cortex.
Insulin is from the pancreas.
Correct. The cortex makes mineralocorticoids, glucocorticoids, and androgens (all steroids); epinephrine is from the medulla.
Thyroxine is from the thyroid.
takeaway: Cortex = aldosterone + cortisol + androgens (all steroids).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Cortisol, released in response to stress (via ACTH), raises blood glucose and:
rationale: Cortisol: raises blood glucose + suppresses immune/inflammatory response.
why: Correct. Cortisol (a glucocorticoid) increases blood glucose (gluconeogenesis) and suppresses immune/inflammatory activity — the basis of steroid anti-inflammatory drugs.
Cortisol raises, not lowers, blood glucose.
Cortisol suppresses inflammation rather than stimulating it.
Cortisol is a slow-acting steroid, not a fast peptide.
takeaway: Cortisol = ↑glucose + immune suppression (steroid).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The adrenal medulla, part of the sympathetic nervous system, secretes ______ for the rapid fight-or-flight response.
rationale: Adrenal medulla = epinephrine/norepinephrine (fast fight-or-flight).
why: Aldosterone is a cortical mineralocorticoid.
Cortisol is a cortical glucocorticoid.
Thyroxine is from the thyroid.
Correct. The medulla releases catecholamines (epinephrine, norepinephrine) for fast sympathetic 'fight-or-flight' effects.
takeaway: Medulla = epinephrine (fast); cortex = steroids (slow).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the pancreatic islets of Langerhans, beta cells secrete ______ and alpha cells secrete ______.
rationale: Islets: beta cells → insulin; alpha cells → glucagon.
why: Reversed — beta cells make insulin, alpha cells make glucagon.
Cortisol/aldosterone are adrenal hormones.
Correct. Beta cells release insulin (lowers glucose); alpha cells release glucagon (raises glucose).
Amylase/lipase are exocrine digestive enzymes, not islet hormones.
takeaway: Beta = insulin (lower glucose); alpha = glucagon (raise).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The pancreas is a dual gland: its ENDOCRINE islets secrete hormones into the blood, while its EXOCRINE tissue secretes ______ into a duct.
rationale: Exocrine pancreas → digestive enzymes + bicarbonate (into a duct); endocrine → hormones.
why: Correct. The exocrine pancreas releases digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, proteases) and bicarbonate into ducts leading to the small intestine.
Insulin is the endocrine (hormonal) secretion, not exocrine.
Bile is made by the liver, not the pancreas.
Adrenaline is an adrenal hormone.
takeaway: Pancreas: endocrine = insulin/glucagon; exocrine = enzymes + HCO3−.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The ______ nervous system drives 'fight-or-flight' (increased heart rate, dilated pupils); the ______ system drives 'rest-and-digest.'
rationale: Sympathetic = fight-or-flight; parasympathetic = rest-and-digest.
why: Reversed — fight-or-flight is sympathetic.
Somatic controls voluntary muscle; autonomic is the broader category.
Correct. Sympathetic = fight-or-flight (mobilize energy); parasympathetic = rest-and-digest (conserve energy).
Central/peripheral is an anatomical division, not this functional pair.
takeaway: Sympathetic = fight/flight; parasympathetic = rest/digest.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Most parasympathetic effects are mediated by ______, while most sympathetic target-organ effects are mediated by ______.
rationale: Parasympathetic → acetylcholine; sympathetic (target) → norepinephrine.
why: Correct. Parasympathetic postganglionic neurons release acetylcholine; most sympathetic postganglionic neurons release norepinephrine (sweat glands are a cholinergic exception).
Reversed — parasympathetic is cholinergic, sympathetic mostly adrenergic.
Dopamine/serotonin aren't the primary autonomic effectors here.
GABA/glutamate are central nervous system transmitters.
takeaway: Parasympathetic = ACh; sympathetic = norepinephrine (mostly).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The simplest neural pathway — sensory neuron → (interneuron) → motor neuron producing an automatic response without waiting for the brain — is a:
rationale: A reflex arc = sensory → (interneuron) → motor for a rapid automatic response.
why: A second messenger cascade is an intracellular signaling process.
Negative feedback is a homeostatic regulatory concept.
The resting potential is a membrane state, not a pathway.
Correct. A reflex arc processes a stimulus through the spinal cord for a rapid, involuntary response (e.g., knee-jerk), bypassing conscious brain processing.
takeaway: Reflex arc = fast automatic response via spinal cord.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Along the nephron, the segment responsible for the BULK of reabsorption of glucose, amino acids, and most ions/water is the:
rationale: The proximal convoluted tubule does the bulk reabsorption (glucose, amino acids, ions, water).
why: The loop of Henle establishes the medullary osmotic gradient (concentrating urine).
The distal convoluted tubule handles fine-tuned, hormone-regulated reabsorption/secretion.
The collecting duct adjusts final water reabsorption under ADH.
Correct. The proximal convoluted tubule reabsorbs most filtered glucose, amino acids, and the majority of Na+/water.
takeaway: PCT = bulk reabsorption (glucose, amino acids, most water/ions).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The loop of Henle establishes a concentration gradient in the medulla so the kidney can produce concentrated urine. This is the:
rationale: The loop of Henle's countercurrent multiplier builds the medullary gradient (concentrated urine).
why: The Bohr effect concerns hemoglobin's oxygen release.
Correct. The loop of Henle's countercurrent arrangement (descending limb permeable to water, ascending limb pumping salt) builds the medullary osmotic gradient enabling water conservation.
Chemiosmosis is ATP synthesis via a proton gradient.
The Frank-Starling mechanism relates to cardiac output.
takeaway: Loop of Henle = countercurrent multiplier (medullary gradient).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the loop of Henle, the descending limb is permeable to ______, while the ascending limb is permeable to (pumps out) ______.
rationale: Descending limb = water out; ascending limb = salt out.
why: Reversed — the descending limb handles water, the ascending limb handles salt.
Glucose is reabsorbed proximally; protein isn't normally filtered.
Correct. The descending limb loses water (permeable to water, not salt); the ascending limb pumps out salt (impermeable to water) — the basis of the countercurrent gradient.
Air/blood aren't nephron contents.
takeaway: Descending = water leaves; ascending = salt pumped out.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The body regulates blood pH through two systems: the ______ adjust CO2 rapidly, and the ______ adjust bicarbonate (HCO3−) more slowly.
rationale: Lungs adjust CO2 fast; kidneys adjust bicarbonate slowly (acid-base balance).
why: Reversed — lungs handle CO2 quickly, kidneys handle bicarbonate slowly.
Liver/spleen aren't the primary acid-base regulators.
Heart/brain don't directly regulate blood pH balance.
Correct. Lungs alter CO2 (fast, via breathing rate); kidneys alter bicarbonate reabsorption/excretion (slow) — together buffering blood pH.
takeaway: Lungs = CO2 (fast); kidneys = bicarbonate (slow).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Because CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3 ⇌ H+ + HCO3−, hypoventilation (retaining CO2) will push blood pH ______.
rationale: Retaining CO2 → more H+ → lower pH (respiratory acidosis).
why: Retaining CO2 acidifies (lowers pH), it doesn't raise it.
Correct. Retaining CO2 shifts the equilibrium toward more H+, lowering pH (respiratory acidosis); hyperventilation does the reverse (alkalosis).
Blood pH is normally ~7.4, not driven to 7.0 by this.
CO2 changes clearly shift the equilibrium and pH.
takeaway: ↑CO2 → ↓pH (acidosis); ↓CO2 → ↑pH (alkalosis).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Most carbon dioxide is transported in the blood in the form of:
rationale: Most CO2 is carried as bicarbonate (HCO3−) in plasma.
why: Only ~20–30% of CO2 is carried bound to hemoglobin.
Only a small fraction travels as dissolved CO2 gas.
Carbon monoxide is a toxic gas, not the form of CO2 transport.
Correct. The majority of CO2 travels as bicarbonate (formed via carbonic anhydrase in red cells); smaller amounts bind hemoglobin (carbaminohemoglobin) or dissolve as gas.
takeaway: Most CO2 travels as bicarbonate (HCO3−).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The enzyme in red blood cells that rapidly converts CO2 and water into carbonic acid (which dissociates to bicarbonate) is:
rationale: Carbonic anhydrase converts CO2 + H2O → bicarbonate (in red cells).
why: Hemoglobin carries O2 (and some CO2), but it isn't the CO2-hydrating enzyme.
Correct. Carbonic anhydrase speeds CO2 + H2O → H2CO3 → H+ + HCO3−, enabling efficient CO2 transport and acid-base buffering.
Amylase digests carbohydrates.
DNA polymerase replicates DNA.
takeaway: Carbonic anhydrase = CO2 + H2O → HCO3− (fast).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Fetal hemoglobin (HbF) has a ______ oxygen affinity than adult hemoglobin, allowing the fetus to pull oxygen from maternal blood.
rationale: Fetal hemoglobin has HIGHER O2 affinity → pulls O2 from maternal blood.
why: A lower affinity would prevent the fetus from extracting maternal O2.
The affinities differ; HbF is higher.
Correct. HbF binds O2 more tightly (higher affinity, left-shifted curve) than adult HbA, so oxygen transfers from mother to fetus across the placenta.
HbF certainly binds oxygen — with higher affinity.
takeaway: Fetal Hb = higher O2 affinity (pulls O2 from mom).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: An antibody (immunoglobulin) is Y-shaped, with constant regions and variable regions; the ______ regions at the tips determine which antigen it binds.
rationale: An antibody's variable regions determine antigen specificity (constant region = class).
why: The constant region defines the class (IgG, IgM, etc.), not antigen specificity.
'Hydrophobic regions' isn't the antigen-binding determinant.
Antibodies are secreted/soluble; 'transmembrane region' doesn't define binding.
Correct. The variable regions (at the Fab tips) form the antigen-binding site and give each antibody its specificity; the constant region determines the antibody class/effector function.
takeaway: Variable region = antigen binding; constant region = antibody class.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: MHC class I molecules (on all nucleated cells) present ______ antigens to cytotoxic T cells; MHC class II (on antigen-presenting cells) present ______ antigens to helper T cells.
rationale: MHC I = endogenous → cytotoxic (CD8) T cells; MHC II = exogenous → helper (CD4) T cells.
why: Reversed — MHC I presents endogenous, MHC II presents exogenous antigens.
Correct. MHC I displays endogenous (e.g., viral) peptides to CD8+ cytotoxic T cells; MHC II displays exogenous (engulfed) peptides to CD4+ helper T cells.
Both present peptides that can be self or foreign; the key distinction is endogenous vs. exogenous.
Both MHC classes present antigens; that's their function.
takeaway: MHC I = inside antigens → CD8; MHC II = outside antigens → CD4.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A group of plasma proteins that, when activated, punch holes in pathogen membranes and tag them for destruction is the:
rationale: The complement system = plasma proteins that lyse and tag pathogens.
why: The clotting cascade forms blood clots, not pathogen lysis.
The renin-angiotensin system regulates blood pressure.
Correct. The complement system enhances (complements) immune defense by lysing pathogens (membrane attack complex), opsonizing them, and promoting inflammation.
The lymphatic system transports lymph/immune cells but isn't this protein cascade.
takeaway: Complement = plasma proteins that lyse/tag pathogens.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The hormone released by the small intestine that stimulates the pancreas to release bicarbonate (neutralizing stomach acid) is:
rationale: Secretin → pancreatic bicarbonate release (neutralizes stomach acid).
why: Gastrin stimulates gastric acid secretion (in the stomach), not bicarbonate.
Insulin regulates blood glucose.
Correct. Secretin (from the duodenum, triggered by acidic chyme) stimulates pancreatic bicarbonate release to neutralize acid.
Aldosterone regulates sodium/water in the kidney.
takeaway: Secretin = pancreatic bicarbonate (neutralize acid).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When fats enter the small intestine, ______ is released to stimulate gallbladder contraction (bile release) and pancreatic enzyme secretion.
rationale: CCK → gallbladder contraction (bile) + pancreatic enzymes (triggered by fat).
why: Correct. CCK, triggered by fats/proteins in the duodenum, causes gallbladder contraction (bile) and pancreatic enzyme release, plus satiety signaling.
Gastrin drives gastric acid secretion, not gallbladder contraction.
Glucagon raises blood glucose.
ADH regulates water reabsorption.
takeaway: CCK = bile + pancreatic enzymes (fat trigger).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Protein digestion involves pepsin in the stomach and, in the small intestine, pancreatic enzymes such as:
rationale: Protein digestion: stomach pepsin → small intestine trypsin/chymotrypsin.
why: Amylase and lipase digest carbohydrates and fats, not protein.
Pepsin works in the acidic stomach, not the small intestine.
Bile salts emulsify fat; they aren't protein enzymes.
Correct. Trypsin and chymotrypsin (pancreatic proteases) continue protein digestion in the small intestine after stomach pepsin.
takeaway: Protein: pepsin (stomach) → trypsin/chymotrypsin (small intestine).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The hypothalamus releases GnRH, stimulating the anterior pituitary to release FSH and LH, which act on the gonads. This is the:
rationale: HPG axis: GnRH → FSH/LH → gonads (sex hormones).
why: The renin-angiotensin system controls blood pressure.
The countercurrent system concerns the kidney.
Correct. The HPG axis (GnRH → FSH/LH → gonadal sex hormones) controls reproduction, regulated by feedback.
The complement cascade is part of immunity.
takeaway: HPG axis = GnRH → FSH/LH → gonads.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The menstrual cycle's first half, when a follicle matures and estrogen rises, is the ______ phase; after ovulation, the ______ phase is dominated by progesterone from the corpus luteum.
rationale: Menstrual cycle: follicular (estrogen, pre-ovulation) → luteal (progesterone, post-ovulation).
why: Correct. Follicular phase = follicle maturation + rising estrogen (FSH-driven); luteal phase = corpus luteum + progesterone after ovulation.
Reversed — the follicular phase comes first, the luteal phase after ovulation.
Systole/diastole are cardiac phases.
Cleavage/gastrulation are embryonic stages.
takeaway: Follicular = estrogen (before); luteal = progesterone (after ovulation).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Rising estrogen from the maturing follicle ultimately triggers a mid-cycle surge of ______, causing ovulation — an example of positive feedback.
rationale: High estrogen → positive feedback → LH surge → ovulation.
why: Progesterone dominates AFTER ovulation; it isn't the ovulation trigger.
Insulin regulates glucose.
Calcitonin regulates calcium.
Correct. High estrogen switches to positive feedback at mid-cycle, triggering the LH surge that causes ovulation.
takeaway: Estrogen → LH surge → ovulation (positive feedback).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons trigger muscle contraction by releasing the neurotransmitter:
rationale: At the neuromuscular junction, motor neurons release acetylcholine.
why: Dopamine is a central neurotransmitter, not the NMJ transmitter.
GABA is inhibitory in the central nervous system.
Correct. Motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, depolarizing the muscle fiber to initiate contraction.
Norepinephrine acts at sympathetic targets, not the skeletal NMJ.
takeaway: NMJ neurotransmitter = acetylcholine.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: When a muscle contracts (sliding filament), the ______ shortens and the H zone and I band narrow, but the length of the ______ (thick filaments) stays constant.
rationale: Contraction: sarcomere/H zone/I band shorten; A band stays constant.
why: Correct. During contraction the sarcomere, H zone, and I band shorten, while the A band (thick-filament length) stays constant.
The A band stays constant; the sarcomere shortens — reversed here.
Filament lengths don't change; they slide past each other.
Bone/tendon aren't sarcomere structures.
takeaway: Contraction: sarcomere/H/I shorten; A band constant.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Muscle fibers rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, resistant to fatigue and used for endurance, are ______ fibers; fibers built for rapid, powerful, quickly-fatiguing contractions are ______ fibers.
rationale: Slow-twitch (I) = endurance (aerobic); fast-twitch (II) = power (anaerobic).
why: Reversed — endurance fibers are slow-twitch.
Cardiac/smooth are other muscle tissue types, not the twitch distinction.
Fibrous/globular describe proteins.
Correct. Slow-twitch (type I) fibers are aerobic, fatigue-resistant (endurance); fast-twitch (type II) are anaerobic, powerful, quick to fatigue.
takeaway: Slow-twitch = endurance; fast-twitch = power.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The brief delay in electrical conduction at the AV node is important because it allows:
choices: The ventricles to contract before the atria
The heart to stop between beats
The atria to finish contracting and fill the ventricles before they contract
rationale: The AV node delay lets the atria empty into the ventricles before ventricular contraction.
why: Atria contract before ventricles; the delay preserves that order.
The heart doesn't stop; the delay is a brief pause in conduction.
Correct. The AV nodal delay ensures atrial contraction completes and ventricles fill before ventricular contraction begins.
The delay helps forward filling, not backward flow.
takeaway: AV delay = atria fill ventricles before they contract.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Unlike skeletal muscle, cardiac muscle can generate its own rhythmic contractions without nervous input because it is:
rationale: The heart is myogenic: the SA node self-generates the beat (nerves only modulate rate).
why: Correct. The heart is myogenic — the SA node spontaneously depolarizes, setting the rhythm; autonomic input only modulates the rate.
A neurogenic heart would need nerve signals to beat; the heart is myogenic.
Cardiac muscle is involuntary, not voluntary.
Cardiac muscle is highly contractile.
takeaway: Heart is myogenic (SA node self-fires; nerves just modulate).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Rapid, moment-to-moment blood pressure regulation is handled by ______ in the carotid arteries and aorta that sense stretch and trigger reflex adjustments.
rationale: Baroreceptors (carotid/aorta) sense pressure and drive rapid reflex adjustments.
why: Chemoreceptors sense blood gases/pH, not primarily pressure.
Osmoreceptors sense blood osmolarity (water balance).
Correct. Baroreceptors detect arterial stretch (pressure) and drive autonomic reflexes to adjust heart rate and vessel tone.
Nociceptors sense pain.
takeaway: Baroreceptors = sense BP (stretch) → reflex adjustment.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: For longer-term blood pressure control, low pressure triggers the kidney to release renin, activating a cascade that produces angiotensin II and aldosterone to:
rationale: RAAS: renin → angiotensin II + aldosterone → raise BP (vasoconstriction + Na+/water retention).
why: Correct. The renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system raises blood pressure via angiotensin II (vasoconstriction) and aldosterone (Na+/water retention).
RAAS raises, not lowers, blood pressure.
RAAS promotes Na+/water RETENTION (less urine), raising volume.
RAAS regulates blood pressure/volume, not glucose breakdown.
takeaway: RAAS = raise BP (angiotensin II vasoconstricts; aldosterone retains Na+/water).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The simple sugars glucose, fructose, and galactose are all ______ with the formula C6H12O6, differing only in structural arrangement.
rationale: Monosaccharides (glucose, fructose, galactose) = single-sugar hexoses, C6H12O6 isomers.
why: Disaccharides are two sugar units joined together.
Polysaccharides are many sugar units.
Correct. Glucose, fructose, and galactose are monosaccharides (single sugar units, six-carbon hexoses) that are isomers of one another.
Amino acids are protein monomers, not sugars.
takeaway: Monosaccharides = single sugars (glucose/fructose/galactose).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Two monosaccharides join to form a disaccharide through a ______ bond, formed by a dehydration reaction.
rationale: Sugars are linked by glycosidic bonds (formed by dehydration).
why: Correct. A glycosidic bond links sugars (via dehydration/condensation); hydrolysis breaks it.
Peptide bonds link amino acids.
Phosphodiester bonds link nucleotides.
Disulfide bonds link cysteine residues in proteins.
