takeaway: Glycosidic bond = links sugars (dehydration).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The disaccharide formed from glucose + fructose is sucrose (table sugar); the one formed from glucose + galactose is:
rationale: Lactose = glucose + galactose; sucrose = glucose + fructose; maltose = glucose + glucose.
why: Maltose is glucose + glucose, not glucose + galactose.
Starch is a polysaccharide, not a disaccharide.
Cellulose is a structural polysaccharide.
Correct. Lactose (milk sugar) = glucose + galactose; sucrose = glucose + fructose; maltose = glucose + glucose.
takeaway: Lactose = glucose+galactose; sucrose = glucose+fructose.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Plants store glucose as starch and animals store it as glycogen; both use ______ glycosidic linkages that humans can digest.
rationale: Storage polysaccharides (starch, glycogen) use digestible α linkages.
why: β linkages (as in cellulose) can't be digested by humans.
Correct. Starch and glycogen use α-1,4 (and α-1,6 branch) linkages, which human enzymes can hydrolyze.
Peptide bonds link amino acids, not sugars.
Ester bonds appear in fats, not the glucose–glucose sugar linkage.
takeaway: Starch/glycogen = α linkages (digestible).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Humans cannot digest cellulose (dietary fiber) even though it is made of glucose, because cellulose uses ______ glycosidic linkages.
rationale: Cellulose = β linkages → indigestible to humans (fiber); starch = α (digestible).
why: α linkages (starch/glycogen) ARE digestible; cellulose is β.
Peptide bonds are in proteins.
Correct. Cellulose's β-1,4 linkages resist human digestive enzymes (which only cleave α linkages), so it passes as fiber.
Phosphodiester bonds are in nucleic acids.
takeaway: Cellulose = β (indigestible fiber); starch = α (digestible).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A fatty acid with NO carbon-carbon double bonds (straight chains that pack tightly, solid at room temp) is ______; one with double bonds (kinked, liquid) is ______.
rationale: Saturated = no double bonds (solid); unsaturated = double bonds/kinks (liquid).
why: Reversed — no double bonds = saturated.
Fatty acid tails are nonpolar regardless; this isn't the saturation distinction.
Correct. Saturated fatty acids (no double bonds) pack tightly and are solid (fats); unsaturated ones have kinks and are liquid (oils).
Essential/nonessential concerns dietary need, not double bonds.
takeaway: Saturated = no double bonds (solid); unsaturated = kinked (liquid).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The main form of long-term energy storage in animals, consisting of glycerol bonded to three fatty acids via ester bonds, is a:
rationale: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (main energy storage).
why: Correct. Triglycerides (glycerol + 3 fatty acids) are the primary energy-storage lipids, yielding more energy per gram than carbohydrates.
Phospholipids have two fatty acids + a phosphate head (membranes), not three fatty acids.
Steroids have a four-ring structure, not glycerol + fatty acids.
Proteins are amino acid polymers.
takeaway: Triglyceride = glycerol + 3 fatty acids (energy storage).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Phospholipids form cell membranes because they are amphipathic: a phosphate head plus ______ fatty acid tail(s).
rationale: Phospholipids = phosphate head + 2 fatty acid tails (amphipathic → bilayer).
why: Three fatty acids describes a triglyceride (a storage lipid), not a phospholipid.
Four rings describes steroids, not phospholipid tails.
Phospholipids do have fatty acid tails (two of them).
Correct. A phospholipid has a hydrophilic phosphate head and two hydrophobic fatty acid tails, driving bilayer formation.
takeaway: Phospholipid = phosphate head + 2 tails (membrane).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Cholesterol and the steroid hormones share a characteristic structure of:
choices: A glycerol backbone with three tails
rationale: Steroids = four fused carbon rings (cholesterol, steroid hormones).
why: A single long chain describes fatty acids, not steroids.
Correct. Steroids (cholesterol, cortisol, testosterone, estrogen) share a four-fused-ring core; cholesterol is the precursor of steroid hormones.
Glycerol + 3 tails is a triglyceride.
A phosphate head describes phospholipids.
takeaway: Steroids = four fused rings (cholesterol → steroid hormones).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Unlike carbohydrates, proteins, and nucleic acids, lipids are:
choices: Not true polymers (not built from repeating monomer units)
rationale: Lipids are defined by hydrophobicity, not by being polymers (unlike carbs/proteins/nucleic acids).
why: Glycerol is a component of some lipids but they aren't glycerol polymers.
Nucleotide polymers are nucleic acids.
Correct. Lipids are a diverse group defined by hydrophobicity, not by being polymers of a repeating monomer.
Amino acid polymers are proteins.
takeaway: Lipids = hydrophobic, NOT polymers.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Natural selection acts on heritable variation so that individuals with traits better suited to the environment leave more offspring. The measure of an individual's reproductive success is its:
rationale: Fitness = reproductive success; natural selection favors higher-fitness heritable traits.
why: Genetic drift is random allele-frequency change, not a measure of reproductive success.
Mutation rate is the rate of new variation, not reproductive success.
Correct. Fitness quantifies reproductive success; natural selection increases the frequency of alleles that raise fitness.
Ploidy is the number of chromosome sets.
takeaway: Fitness = reproductive success (what selection acts on).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Selection that favors one extreme phenotype, shifting the population mean, is ______ selection; selection favoring the average and against extremes is ______ selection.
rationale: Directional = favors one extreme; stabilizing = favors the average; disruptive = both extremes.
why: Correct. Directional selection shifts toward one extreme; stabilizing selection favors intermediate phenotypes; disruptive selection favors both extremes.
Reversed — favoring one extreme is directional.
Artificial/natural describes the selector, not the phenotype pattern.
Sexual/kin selection are different concepts.
takeaway: Directional = one extreme; stabilizing = the middle; disruptive = both ends.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Random change in allele frequencies due to chance — which has a larger effect in SMALL populations (e.g., bottleneck, founder effects) — is:
rationale: Genetic drift = random allele-frequency change (strongest in small populations).
why: Natural selection is non-random, based on fitness.
Gene flow is allele movement between populations (migration).
Directional selection is a non-random, fitness-based process.
Correct. Genetic drift is random (non-adaptive) allele-frequency change, most pronounced in small populations.
takeaway: Genetic drift = random change (big effect in small populations).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The formation of a new species generally requires ______ between populations, preventing gene flow so they diverge genetically.
rationale: Speciation requires reproductive isolation (blocks gene flow → divergence).
why: Increased gene flow homogenizes populations, opposing speciation.
Correct. Reproductive isolation (geographic or otherwise) stops gene flow, allowing populations to diverge into separate species.
Mutation alone doesn't produce a new species without isolation.
Population size isn't the defining requirement for speciation.
takeaway: Speciation = reproductive isolation → divergence.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A population that is EVOLVING at a given gene will show allele/genotype frequencies that:
rationale: Deviation from Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium signals evolution is occurring.
why: Matching H-W predictions indicates no evolution at that locus.
p = q is a special case, not a signature of evolution.
Correct. Hardy-Weinberg describes a NON-evolving population; deviation from its predicted frequencies is evidence of evolutionary change (selection, drift, migration, etc.).
Populations have alleles; evolution changes their frequencies.
takeaway: Evolving population = deviates from Hardy-Weinberg.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Gel electrophoresis with SDS (SDS-PAGE) separates proteins primarily by:
rationale: SDS-PAGE separates proteins by size (SDS gives uniform charge).
why: SDS masks native charge so size, not charge, drives separation.
SDS denatures proteins, removing native shape as the variable.
Correct. SDS coats proteins with uniform negative charge and denatures them, so migration through the gel depends on size (smaller = faster).
Electrophoresis separates by physical properties, not function.
takeaway: SDS-PAGE = separate proteins by size.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A technique that separates proteins along a pH gradient, with each protein migrating until it reaches the pH equal to its ______, is isoelectric focusing.
rationale: Isoelectric focusing separates proteins by pI (each stops where pH = pI).
why: Correct. In isoelectric focusing, a protein stops migrating where the pH equals its pI (net charge zero).
Size-based separation is SDS-PAGE, not isoelectric focusing.
Optimal temperature is an enzyme-activity parameter.
Km is an enzyme-kinetics constant.
takeaway: Isoelectric focusing = separate by pI (pH gradient).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A separation method in which a protein mixture passes through a column and components separate based on properties like size, charge, or affinity is:
rationale: Chromatography separates proteins by size, charge, or affinity (column methods).
why: Centrifugation separates by density/mass under spinning force, not column interaction.
Titration measures acid-base quantities.
PCR amplifies DNA.
Correct. Column chromatography (size-exclusion, ion-exchange, affinity) separates proteins by differential interaction with the stationary phase.
takeaway: Chromatography = separate by size/charge/affinity (column).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Cell junctions that form a watertight seal between adjacent cells, preventing molecules from leaking between them (e.g., in the gut lining), are:
rationale: Tight junctions = watertight seal between cells (no leakage).
why: Gap junctions form communication channels, not watertight seals.
Correct. Tight junctions seal neighboring cells to block paracellular leakage, controlling what crosses an epithelial layer.
Desmosomes provide mechanical anchoring, not sealing.
Plasmodesmata connect plant cells, not animal epithelia.
takeaway: Tight junction = seal (no leakage between cells).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Channels that directly connect the cytoplasm of adjacent cells, allowing ions and small molecules to pass for communication (e.g., coordinating heart-muscle contraction), are:
rationale: Gap junctions = channels connecting cytoplasm for communication (ions/small molecules).
why: Tight junctions seal cells rather than connect their cytoplasm.
Desmosomes anchor cells mechanically, without a communicating channel.
Peroxisomes are organelles, not cell junctions.
Correct. Gap junctions are intercellular channels enabling rapid electrical/chemical communication (important in cardiac and smooth muscle).
takeaway: Gap junction = communication channel (ions/molecules pass).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Junctions that act like rivets, anchoring adjacent cells together to resist mechanical stress (e.g., in skin), are:
rationale: Desmosomes = anchoring junctions (mechanical strength, like rivets).
why: Correct. Desmosomes provide strong mechanical adhesion between cells, distributing tension across a tissue.
Gap junctions communicate; they don't primarily anchor.
Tight junctions seal; desmosomes anchor.
Ribosomes synthesize protein, not a junction.
takeaway: Desmosome = anchor/rivet (mechanical strength).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The four basic tissue types in animals are epithelial, connective, nervous, and:
rationale: Four tissue types: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.
why: Bone is a TYPE of connective tissue, not a separate primary category.
Blood is a specialized connective tissue, not a fourth primary type.
Correct. The four primary tissue types are epithelial (covering/lining), connective (support), muscle (movement), and nervous (signaling).
Adipose is a connective tissue, not a primary category.
takeaway: 4 tissues: epithelial, connective, muscle, nervous.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A stem cell that can give rise to ANY cell type in the body plus extra-embryonic tissue (placenta) is ______; one that can become any body cell but not placenta is ______.
rationale: Totipotent = any cell + placenta; pluripotent = any body cell; multipotent = limited.
why: Reversed — totipotent is the most versatile (includes placenta).
Correct. Totipotent (e.g., zygote) → any cell + placenta; pluripotent (embryonic stem cells) → any body cell; multipotent → a limited range; unipotent → one type.
Multipotent/unipotent are more restricted than the stem-cell types described.
That reverses the restriction order.
takeaway: Toti = everything+placenta; pluri = any body cell; multi = limited.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: As a cell differentiates into a specialized type, it does so mainly by:
choices: Losing its nucleus in all cases
Selectively expressing different genes (not by losing DNA)
rationale: Differentiation = selective gene expression, not loss of DNA.
why: Cells retain their full genome; they don't delete unused genes.
Differentiation doesn't add new chromosomes.
Most differentiated cells keep their nucleus (red blood cells are an exception).
Correct. Differentiated cells keep the same genome but express different subsets of genes; DNA is generally not lost (with rare exceptions).
takeaway: Differentiation = different genes expressed (same DNA).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The stage at which a cell becomes committed to a particular fate — even before it visibly specializes — is:
rationale: Determination = commitment to a cell fate (before visible differentiation).
why: Correct. Determination is commitment to a fate; differentiation is the subsequent visible specialization.
Denaturation is loss of protein structure.
Translation is protein synthesis.
Transduction is signal conversion (or viral gene transfer).
takeaway: Determination = committed to a fate (before specializing).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Dense bone forming the hard outer shell is ______ bone; the porous inner bone containing red marrow is ______ bone.
rationale: Compact bone = dense outer shell; spongy bone = porous inner (marrow).
why: Reversed — the dense outer layer is compact bone.
Correct. Compact (cortical) bone is the dense outer layer; spongy (trabecular) bone is the porous interior housing marrow.
Cartilage is a separate connective tissue, not the outer shell here.
Tendons/ligaments connect tissues; they aren't bone types.
takeaway: Compact = dense outer; spongy = porous inner (marrow).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: The flexible, avascular connective tissue that cushions joints and forms structures like the ear and nose is:
rationale: Cartilage = flexible, avascular connective tissue (joints, ear, nose).
why: Compact bone is rigid and vascularized, unlike cartilage.
A tendon connects muscle to bone.
Nerve tissue conducts signals.
Correct. Cartilage is a flexible, avascular (no direct blood supply) connective tissue; it cushions joints and serves as a template for bone.
takeaway: Cartilage = flexible, avascular (cushions joints).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Bone is continuously remodeled: ______ deposit new bone matrix, while osteoclasts resorb it, and mature ______ maintain the tissue.
rationale: Osteoblasts build, osteoclasts resorb, osteocytes maintain bone.
why: Correct. Osteoblasts build bone, osteoclasts break it down, and osteocytes (mature, embedded cells) maintain it.
Osteoclasts resorb; the builders are osteoblasts.
Chondrocytes/myocytes maintain cartilage/muscle, not bone.
Neurons/glia are nervous-tissue cells.
takeaway: Osteoblast = build, osteoclast = break, osteocyte = maintain.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: Beyond structure, the skeleton serves as the body's main reservoir for:
rationale: The skeleton is the body's main calcium/phosphate reservoir (hormone-regulated).
why: Glucose is stored as glycogen in liver/muscle, not bone.
Oxygen is carried by hemoglobin, not stored in bone.
Correct. Bone stores most of the body's calcium and phosphate, releasing or storing it under hormonal control (PTH, calcitonin, vitamin D).
Sodium is regulated mainly by the kidney, not bone reservoir.
takeaway: Bone = calcium/phosphate reservoir (PTH/calcitonin).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: From outermost to innermost, the layers of the skin are the epidermis, the ______ (containing blood vessels, nerves, glands), and the hypodermis.
rationale: Skin layers: epidermis → dermis → hypodermis.
why: 'Cortex' refers to outer regions of organs like kidney/adrenal, not skin.
Correct. The skin's layers are epidermis (outer barrier), dermis (vessels, nerves, glands, follicles), and hypodermis (fat/insulation).
'Medulla' is an inner region of organs, not a skin layer.
An alveolus is a lung air sac.
takeaway: Skin: epidermis (barrier), dermis (vessels/nerves), hypodermis (fat).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: To COOL the body when overheated, the skin responds by ______ and increasing sweat production.
choices: Vasodilating (widening) blood vessels near the surface
rationale: Cooling: skin vasodilates + sweats. Warming: vasoconstrict, shiver, piloerection.
why: Vasoconstriction conserves heat (a warming response), not cooling.
Shivering generates heat to warm the body.
Piloerection traps insulating air to warm the body.
Correct. Cooling: surface vasodilation radiates heat away and sweating evaporates heat. Warming responses are the opposite (vasoconstriction, shivering, piloerection).
takeaway: Cool = vasodilate + sweat; warm = vasoconstrict + shiver.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A primary function of the skin in the immune system is to serve as:
choices: A physical barrier (first line of innate defense) against pathogens
rationale: The skin is a physical barrier — innate immunity's first line of defense.
why: Correct. The skin is a physical/chemical barrier — part of innate immunity's first line of defense against pathogen entry.
Antibodies are made by plasma cells (B cells), not the skin.
Gas exchange occurs in the lungs.
The pituitary, not skin, is the endocrine master gland.
takeaway: Skin = physical barrier (innate first line of defense).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: A key function of the lymphatic system is to collect excess interstitial fluid that leaks from capillaries and return it to the:
rationale: The lymphatic system returns excess interstitial fluid to the bloodstream (prevents edema).
why: Lymph returns to the venous blood, not directly to the kidneys.
Correct. The lymphatic system returns filtered interstitial fluid (lymph) to the venous blood, maintaining fluid balance; blockage causes edema.
It doesn't drain into the digestive tract.
It doesn't return fluid via the lungs.
takeaway: Lymphatics return interstitial fluid to blood (prevent edema).

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: As lymph passes through lymph nodes, it is filtered and screened for pathogens by resident:
rationale: Lymph nodes filter lymph using immune cells (lymphocytes, macrophages).
why: Red blood cells carry oxygen; they don't screen lymph.
Osteocytes are bone cells.
Nephrons are kidney filtration units, not lymph filters.
Correct. Lymph nodes house immune cells that filter lymph and mount responses against pathogens/antigens.
takeaway: Lymph nodes = filter lymph + immune screening.

section: Biological & Biochemical Foundations of Living Systems
stem: In the small intestine, specialized lymphatic vessels called ______ absorb dietary fats (as chylomicrons).
rationale: Lacteals = intestinal lymphatic vessels that absorb dietary fat (chylomicrons).
why: Correct. Lacteals are lymphatic capillaries in intestinal villi that absorb fats (chylomicrons), which enter lymph before the bloodstream.
Nephrons are kidney units, not fat absorbers.
Alveoli are lung air sacs.
Fat absorption uses lacteals (lymphatic), not arteries.
takeaway: Lacteals = absorb dietary fat (chylomicrons) via lymph.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Distance and speed are scalars (magnitude only); displacement and velocity are ______ because they also include direction.
rationale: Vectors (displacement, velocity) have direction; scalars (distance, speed) don't.
why: Displacement and velocity carry direction, making them vectors, not scalars.
'Units' aren't a category of quantity type.
Correct. Displacement and velocity are vectors (magnitude + direction); distance and speed are scalars (magnitude only).
They aren't constants; they can vary.
takeaway: Displacement/velocity = vectors; distance/speed = scalars.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Acceleration is defined as the rate of change of:
rationale: Acceleration = change in velocity over time (Δv/Δt).
why: Correct. Acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime; it is nonzero whenever speed OR direction changes.
Rate of change of position is velocity, not acceleration.
Rate of change of force isn't the definition of acceleration.
Mass is generally constant and isn't part of the definition.
takeaway: Acceleration = Δvelocity / Δtime.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Near Earth's surface, in the absence of air resistance, all objects fall with the same acceleration of approximately:
choices: A value proportional to their mass
rationale: Free-fall acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s², the same for all masses.
why: Free-fall acceleration is independent of mass.
Objects in free fall accelerate; g is not zero.
g is an acceleration (m/s²), not a velocity (m/s).
Correct. Gravitational acceleration g ≈ 9.8 m/s² is the same for all masses in free fall (a heavy and light object fall together in a vacuum).
takeaway: g ≈ 9.8 m/s², independent of mass.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In projectile motion (ignoring air resistance), the horizontal and vertical components of motion are:
choices: Independent of each other (horizontal velocity constant, vertical accelerates at g)
rationale: Projectile motion: horizontal (constant velocity) and vertical (accelerates at g) are independent.
why: The components are generally not equal.
Correct. Horizontal and vertical motions are independent: horizontal velocity is constant (no horizontal force), while vertical motion accelerates due to gravity.
There is no horizontal acceleration (ignoring air resistance).
The vertical component accelerates, so both aren't constant.
takeaway: Projectile: horizontal constant, vertical accelerates — independent.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Newton's second law states that the net force on an object equals:
rationale: Newton's 2nd law: F_net = ma.
why: Mass times velocity is momentum (p), not force.
That inverts the relationship incorrectly.
Correct. F_net = ma; net force and acceleration are directly proportional (and in the same direction).
Weight times height relates to potential energy, not this law.
takeaway: F = ma (net force = mass × acceleration).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Newton's third law states that for every action force, there is an equal and opposite reaction force, acting on:
choices: A different object (the two forces act on different bodies)
rationale: Newton's 3rd law: equal and opposite forces on two different objects.
why: Correct. Action-reaction pairs are equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and act on DIFFERENT objects (so they don't cancel on one object).
The pair acts on two different objects, not the same one — that's why they don't cancel.
Both objects experience the force regardless of size.
The forces are real and act on the two interacting bodies.
takeaway: 3rd law: equal/opposite forces on DIFFERENT objects.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Mass is the amount of matter (constant everywhere); weight is the ______ on that mass and changes with location.
rationale: Weight = mg (a force that varies with g); mass is constant.
why: Weight and mass are different quantities (force vs. amount of matter).
Volume is space occupied, not weight.
Density is mass per volume, not weight.
Correct. Weight = mg (a force, in newtons) and varies with g; mass (in kg) is invariant.
takeaway: Mass = matter (constant); weight = mg (force, varies).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The friction force that must be overcome to START a stationary object moving is generally ______ the friction once it is already sliding.
choices: Greater than (static friction max > kinetic friction)
rationale: Max static friction > kinetic friction (harder to start than to keep moving).
why: Static (max) friction is greater, not less, than kinetic.
Correct. Maximum static friction is typically greater than kinetic friction, which is why it takes more force to start motion than to maintain it.
They differ; static max generally exceeds kinetic.
Static friction isn't zero — it can be substantial.
takeaway: Static friction (max) > kinetic friction.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In physics, work is done on an object only when a force causes:
choices: Any force to be applied, even without motion
Displacement in the direction of the force (W = Fd·cosθ)
rationale: Work = F·d·cosθ — requires displacement along the force.
why: Holding an object still (no displacement) does zero physical work.
Work relates to force and displacement, not mass change.
Correct. Work = F·d·cosθ; if there is no displacement (or force is perpendicular to motion), no work is done.
Work is energy transfer via force×displacement, not defined by temperature.
takeaway: Work = force × displacement × cosθ (needs motion).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The kinetic energy of a moving object is given by:
rationale: Kinetic energy = ½ mv² (scales with speed squared).
why: Correct. Kinetic energy = ½ mv²; it scales with the SQUARE of speed (doubling speed quadruples KE).
mgh is gravitational potential energy.
mv is momentum, not kinetic energy.
½ kx² is spring (elastic) potential energy.
takeaway: KE = ½ mv² (double speed → 4× KE).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a closed system with only conservative forces, as an object falls, its gravitational potential energy is:
choices: Converted into kinetic energy (total mechanical energy conserved)
rationale: Falling: PE → KE, total mechanical energy conserved (no friction).
why: Energy is conserved, not destroyed.
Energy isn't converted to mass in classical mechanics problems.
Gravitational PE decreases as the object falls, not increases.
Correct. Energy is conserved: PE converts to KE as the object falls, keeping total mechanical energy constant (without friction).
takeaway: Energy conserved: PE converts to KE as it falls.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Power is the rate at which work is done, given by:
rationale: Power = Work / time (rate of doing work).
why: Power is work per unit time, not work times time.
Correct. Power = work/time (watts); it measures how quickly energy is transferred.
Force times displacement is work, not power.
Mass times acceleration is force.
takeaway: Power = work / time (watts).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The momentum of an object is defined as:
rationale: Momentum = mass × velocity (p = mv), a vector.
why: ½ mv² is kinetic energy, not momentum.
Mass times acceleration is force.
Correct. Momentum p = mv is a vector quantity (direction matters); it's conserved in isolated systems.
Force times distance is work.
takeaway: Momentum p = mv (vector).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Impulse equals the change in momentum, and also equals:
choices: Force times the time it acts (J = F·Δt)
rationale: Impulse = F·Δt = Δp (longer time → smaller force).
why: Correct. Impulse = F·Δt = Δp; extending the time of a collision (e.g., airbags) reduces the force for a given momentum change.
Force times distance is work, not impulse.
That isn't the impulse relationship.
Work times time isn't impulse.
takeaway: Impulse = F·Δt = change in momentum.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In an isolated system (no external forces), the total momentum before a collision:
choices: Equals the total momentum after the collision
rationale: Momentum is conserved: total before = total after (isolated system).
why: Total momentum is conserved, not increased.
Total momentum need not be zero; it's simply conserved.
Kinetic energy (not momentum) can convert to heat in inelastic collisions.
Correct. Momentum is conserved in isolated systems: total p before = total p after, whether the collision is elastic or inelastic.
takeaway: Momentum conserved: p(before) = p(after).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a perfectly ELASTIC collision, both momentum and ______ are conserved; in an INELASTIC collision, only momentum is.
rationale: Elastic: momentum + kinetic energy conserved. Inelastic: only momentum.
why: Mass is conserved in both, so it doesn't distinguish them.
Correct. Elastic collisions conserve kinetic energy; inelastic collisions conserve momentum but lose kinetic energy (to heat/deformation).
Force isn't a conserved quantity here.
Temperature isn't the conserved quantity that defines elastic collisions.
takeaway: Elastic = KE conserved too; inelastic = KE lost.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: An object is in translational equilibrium (not accelerating) when:
choices: The net force on it is zero (ΣF = 0)
rationale: Translational equilibrium: net force = 0 (ΣF = 0).
why: Equilibrium includes constant-velocity motion, not only rest.
Zero net torque is ROTATIONAL equilibrium, a separate condition.
Correct. Translational equilibrium requires ΣF = 0; the object may be at rest OR moving at constant velocity.
Mass isn't zero; the forces simply balance.
takeaway: Translational equilibrium = ΣF = 0 (rest or constant velocity).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Torque, the rotational equivalent of force, is calculated as:
rationale: Torque = rF·sinθ (force × lever arm).
why: Correct. Torque = rF·sinθ; a longer lever arm or perpendicular force produces more rotational effect.
Force times mass isn't torque.
Torque is force times distance, not divided by it.
Mass times velocity is momentum.
takeaway: Torque = r × F × sinθ (lever arm matters).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: For an object to be in complete equilibrium, the net force AND the net ______ must both be zero.
rationale: Complete equilibrium: ΣF = 0 and Στ = 0.
why: Mass isn't a balance condition for equilibrium.
Velocity can be constant (nonzero) in equilibrium.
Density isn't an equilibrium condition.
Correct. Complete (static) equilibrium requires ΣF = 0 AND Στ = 0 (no linear or rotational acceleration).
takeaway: Full equilibrium = net force AND net torque both zero.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The restoring force of an ideal spring is proportional to its displacement from equilibrium, given by:
rationale: Hooke's law: F = −kx (restoring force proportional to displacement).
why: F = ma is Newton's second law, not the spring force law.
½ kx² is spring potential energy, not force.
Correct. Hooke's law: F = −kx; the negative sign shows the force opposes (restores toward) the displacement.
mgh is gravitational potential energy.
takeaway: Hooke's law: F = −kx (spring restoring force).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: For a simple pendulum (small angles), the period depends on the length and gravity but is INDEPENDENT of:
choices: The mass of the bob and the amplitude
The string material's rigidity aside, everything
rationale: Pendulum period depends on length and g, NOT mass or amplitude.
why: Correct. Period T = 2π√(L/g) depends only on length and g — not on the bob's mass or (for small swings) the amplitude.
Period DOES depend on length.
Period DOES depend on g.
Period specifically depends on L and g; it's mass/amplitude that don't matter.
takeaway: Pendulum T = 2π√(L/g): independent of mass & amplitude.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In simple harmonic motion (like a mass on a spring), speed is MAXIMUM at the ______ and zero at the ______.
rationale: SHM: speed max at equilibrium, zero at turning points.
why: Reversed — speed is zero at the turning points, max at equilibrium.
SHM speed varies with position along the whole path, not just top/bottom.
Speed changes continuously in SHM.
Correct. In SHM, speed peaks at equilibrium (max KE) and is zero at the extremes (max PE), where the object momentarily stops.
takeaway: SHM: fastest at equilibrium, stops at the extremes.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Pressure is defined as:
rationale: Pressure = Force / Area (P = F/A).
why: Pressure is force divided by area, not multiplied.
Correct. Pressure = F/A; the same force over a smaller area produces greater pressure.
Force times distance is work.
Mass per volume is density, not pressure.
takeaway: Pressure = F/A (force per area).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The pressure in a static fluid increases with depth according to P = ρgh, so pressure depends on:
choices: The surface area of the fluid
Fluid density and depth (not the container's shape)
rationale: Hydrostatic P = ρgh: depends on density and depth, not container shape.
why: Container shape doesn't change pressure at a given depth.
Surface area alone doesn't set the pressure at depth.
Depth, not total volume, determines the pressure.
Correct. Hydrostatic pressure P = ρgh depends on density and depth; container shape and total volume don't affect pressure at a given depth.
takeaway: Fluid pressure = ρgh (density × g × depth).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Pascal's principle — the basis of hydraulic lifts — states that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is:
choices: Transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid
rationale: Pascal's principle: applied pressure transmits equally throughout an enclosed fluid.
why: Correct. Pascal's principle: applied pressure transmits equally throughout an enclosed fluid, letting a small force on a small area lift a large load on a large area.
The pressure transmits fully, not lost as heat.
It is felt throughout the fluid, not only at the top.
It isn't determined by container weight.
takeaway: Pascal: pressure transmits equally through a fluid (hydraulics).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The buoyant force on a submerged or floating object equals:
choices: The weight of the fluid displaced
rationale: Buoyant force = weight of fluid displaced (Archimedes).
why: The buoyant force equals the displaced fluid's weight, not the object's weight (unless floating).
Correct. Archimedes' principle: buoyant force = weight of displaced fluid (F_b = ρ_fluid · V_displaced · g).
Volume isn't a force.
Atmospheric pressure isn't the buoyant force.
takeaway: Buoyancy = weight of displaced fluid.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: An object floats if its average density is ______ the fluid's density, and sinks if it is ______.
rationale: Float if density < fluid; sink if density > fluid.
why: Reversed — lower density floats.
Equal density gives neutral buoyancy, not the float/sink pair.
Density isn't zero; it's compared to the fluid's density.
Correct. Less dense than the fluid → floats; more dense → sinks; equal → neutrally buoyant (suspended).
takeaway: Less dense = float; more dense = sink.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: For an incompressible fluid in a pipe, the continuity equation (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) means that where the pipe NARROWS, the fluid:
rationale: Continuity (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂): narrower pipe → faster flow.
why: Fluid speeds up, not slows down, in a narrower section.
Correct. Continuity: flow rate (A·v) is constant, so a smaller cross-sectional area forces a higher velocity.
It doesn't stop; it accelerates.
Incompressible fluid density stays constant.
takeaway: Continuity: narrow pipe = faster flow (A·v constant).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Bernoulli's principle states that in a flowing fluid, where the velocity is HIGH, the pressure is:
rationale: Bernoulli: high fluid velocity → low pressure.
why: High velocity corresponds to LOW pressure, not high.
Pressure changes with velocity per Bernoulli.
Pressure is lower but not necessarily zero.
Correct. Bernoulli: faster-moving fluid exerts lower pressure (energy conservation) — the basis of lift and the Venturi effect.
takeaway: Bernoulli: fast flow = low pressure.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The ideal gas law relating pressure, volume, moles, and temperature is:
rationale: Ideal gas law: PV = nRT.
why: It uses moles (n), not mass (m), with R.
Correct. PV = nRT relates pressure, volume, moles (n), and absolute temperature; R is the gas constant.
That form isn't the ideal gas law.
That arrangement isn't correct.
takeaway: PV = nRT (P, V, moles, temperature).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: At constant temperature, if the volume of a gas DECREASES, its pressure will:
choices: Increase (P and V are inversely proportional)
rationale: Boyle's law: at constant T, P and V are inversely related.
why: Pressure rises when volume falls, not decreases.
Pressure changes; it doesn't stay constant.
Pressure increases but doesn't go to zero.
Correct. Boyle's law: at constant T, P ∝ 1/V — compressing a gas raises its pressure.
takeaway: Boyle: ↓volume → ↑pressure (constant T).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: According to kinetic molecular theory, the average kinetic energy of gas molecules is directly proportional to:
rationale: Average kinetic energy of gas molecules ∝ absolute temperature.
why: Correct. Average molecular kinetic energy ∝ absolute temperature; heavier molecules move slower at the same temperature but have the same average KE.
Pressure alone doesn't set average kinetic energy.
Volume alone doesn't set it.
At a given temperature, KE is the same regardless of molar mass.
takeaway: Gas KE ∝ Kelvin temperature.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a mixture of non-reacting gases, the total pressure equals:
choices: The pressure of the largest gas only
The sum of the partial pressures of each gas
rationale: Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of partial pressures.
why: Every gas contributes, not just the largest.
It's the sum, not the average.
Correct. Dalton's law: total pressure = sum of each gas's partial pressure (each contributes independently).
It's the sum, not the product.
takeaway: Dalton: P_total = sum of partial pressures.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The electrostatic force between two charges is proportional to the product of the charges and inversely proportional to:
choices: The square of the distance between them
rationale: Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² (inverse-square with distance).
why: The dependence is on distance SQUARED, not distance to the first power.
It depends on the product of charges, not their sum, and on r².
Correct. Coulomb's law: F = kq₁q₂/r² — an inverse-square relationship with distance (like gravity).
It's an inverse-square (r²), not inverse-cube, law.
takeaway: Coulomb: F ∝ q₁q₂/r² (inverse square).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Two charges of the SAME sign will ______, while opposite charges will ______.
rationale: Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
why: Correct. Like charges repel; opposite charges attract.
Reversed — same-sign charges repel.
Same-sign charges repel, so not both attract.
Opposite charges attract, so not both repel.
takeaway: Like repel, opposite attract.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Electric potential difference (voltage) is the ______ per unit charge between two points.
rationale: Voltage = work (energy) per unit charge (V = W/q).
why: Force per charge is the electric field, not voltage.
Current is charge flow rate, not energy per charge.
Resistance opposes current; it isn't energy per charge.
Correct. Voltage = work (energy) per unit charge (V = W/q); it drives charge flow in a circuit.
takeaway: Voltage = energy per charge (W/q).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Ohm's law relates voltage, current, and resistance as:
rationale: Ohm's law: V = IR.
why: That inverts the relationship incorrectly.
That inverts it incorrectly.
Correct. Ohm's law: V = IR (voltage = current × resistance).
The quantities multiply (I×R), they don't add.
takeaway: V = IR (voltage = current × resistance).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Resistors connected in SERIES have a total resistance equal to:
choices: The sum of the individual resistances (R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ...)
The reciprocal of the sum of reciprocals
Always less than the smallest resistor
rationale: Resistors in series add: R_total = R₁ + R₂ + ...
why: Correct. Series resistances add directly; total resistance is greater than any single resistor.
Reciprocal-of-reciprocals is the PARALLEL formula, not series.
Series total is larger than the largest resistor, not smaller than the smallest.
Series resistance isn't zero.
takeaway: Series resistors add (R_total = R₁+R₂+...).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Adding resistors in PARALLEL causes the total resistance to:
rationale: Resistors in parallel: total resistance DECREASES (more current paths).
why: Parallel resistance decreases, not increases.
It changes as branches are added.
It doesn't simply double.
Correct. Parallel resistors provide more paths for current, lowering total resistance below the smallest branch (1/R_total = 1/R₁ + 1/R₂ + ...).
takeaway: Parallel resistors: total R decreases (more paths).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The power dissipated by an electrical device can be calculated as:
rationale: Electrical power P = IV (= I²R = V²/R).
why: That isn't the power relationship.
Correct. Electrical power P = IV (also I²R or V²/R); it's the rate of energy transfer.
That isn't correct either.
Power is a product (IV), not a sum.
takeaway: P = IV (electrical power).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A capacitor is a device that stores ______ in the electric field between two separated conductors.
rationale: A capacitor stores charge/energy in an electric field (Q = CV).
why: Capacitors store charge, not a flow of current itself.
Resistance is stored by resistors, not capacitors.
Correct. A capacitor stores charge/energy (Q = CV) in the field between its plates; it opposes changes in voltage.
Magnetic flux is associated with inductors, not capacitors.
takeaway: Capacitor = stores charge/energy (Q = CV).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A magnetic field is produced by ______, and a magnetic force acts on a charge only when the charge is:
rationale: Magnetic fields come from moving charges; magnetic force acts only on moving charges.
why: Correct. Moving charges (currents) create magnetic fields, and magnetic force acts only on charges that are MOVING (F = qvB·sinθ).
Stationary charges create electric, not magnetic, fields and feel no magnetic force.
Neutral atoms and heating aren't the source described.
Magnetism relates to moving charge, not insulators specifically.
takeaway: Magnetism = moving charges (force only on moving charge).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The speed of a wave equals its:
rationale: Wave speed v = fλ (frequency × wavelength).
why: Speed is the product of f and λ, not the quotient.
Amplitude relates to energy/intensity, not wave speed.
That isn't the wave-speed relationship.
Correct. v = fλ; for a fixed wave speed, frequency and wavelength are inversely related.
takeaway: v = fλ (speed = frequency × wavelength).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Sound waves are ______ waves, in which particles oscillate parallel to the direction of energy propagation.
rationale: Sound = longitudinal (parallel oscillation); light = transverse.
why: Transverse waves oscillate perpendicular to propagation (e.g., light), unlike sound.
Correct. Sound is a longitudinal (compression) wave — particle motion is parallel to propagation; light is transverse.
Sound is mechanical, not electromagnetic.
Standing waves are a special pattern, not the basic sound-wave type.
takeaway: Sound = longitudinal; light = transverse.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Unlike light, sound cannot travel through:
choices: A vacuum (it requires a material medium)
rationale: Sound requires a medium — it can't travel through a vacuum (light can).
why: Sound travels through air.
Sound travels through water (even faster than air).
Correct. Sound is a mechanical wave requiring a medium (air, water, solids); it can't propagate through a vacuum. Light (EM) can.
Sound travels through solids (fastest of the three).
takeaway: Sound needs a medium (no sound in vacuum).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: As an ambulance siren approaches you, the perceived pitch (frequency) is ______; as it moves away, the pitch is ______.
rationale: Doppler: approaching → higher pitch; receding → lower pitch.
why: Correct. The Doppler effect: approaching source → waves compressed → higher perceived frequency; receding → stretched → lower.
Reversed — approaching raises the pitch.
The perceived pitch changes with relative motion.
Pitch shifts up or down, not to zero/maximum.
takeaway: Doppler: approaching = higher pitch, receding = lower.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Visible light, X-rays, radio waves, and microwaves are all forms of electromagnetic radiation that travel through a vacuum at:
rationale: All EM radiation travels at c in a vacuum (differing in frequency/wavelength).
why: All EM radiation travels at c in a vacuum, regardless of type.
EM waves travel far faster than sound.
EM waves travel at c, not zero.
Correct. All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum; they differ in frequency/wavelength (and thus energy), not vacuum speed.
takeaway: All EM waves travel at c in vacuum (differ in λ/f).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When light passes into a denser medium (higher index of refraction), it slows down and bends:
rationale: Into a denser medium: light slows and bends toward the normal.
why: Bending away from the normal occurs going to a LESS dense medium.
Correct. Entering a denser (higher-n) medium, light slows and bends toward the normal; entering a less dense medium, it bends away.
Refraction is transmission with bending, not reflection.
The bending angle depends on the indices, not always 90°.
takeaway: Denser medium → light bends toward the normal (slows).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A converging (convex) lens focuses parallel light rays to a point and can form a ______ image of a distant object.
rationale: A converging lens focuses light and forms a real, inverted image of a distant object.
why: It forms real inverted images for distant objects (virtual upright only when object is within f).
It does form images.
Correct. A converging lens brings parallel rays to a real focal point and forms a real, inverted image of an object beyond its focal length.
The image isn't always magnified or upright.
takeaway: Converging lens = focuses rays; real inverted image (distant object).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When light travels from a denser to a less dense medium beyond the critical angle, it undergoes:
choices: Total internal reflection (the basis of fiber optics)
rationale: Total internal reflection: beyond the critical angle, light fully reflects (fiber optics).
why: Correct. Beyond the critical angle, light hitting a boundary to a less dense medium is entirely reflected back — total internal reflection (used in fiber optics).
Beyond the critical angle, light is reflected, not transmitted.
This is reflection, not diffraction.
This is reflection, not polarization.
takeaway: TIR = full reflection beyond critical angle (fiber optics).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The atomic number of an element equals its number of ______, while the mass number equals protons plus ______.
rationale: Atomic number = protons; mass number = protons + neutrons.
why: Reversed — atomic number counts protons.
Atomic number counts protons, not electrons.
Correct. Atomic number = number of protons (defines the element); mass number = protons + neutrons.
Mass number adds neutrons, not electrons (electrons have negligible mass).
takeaway: Atomic # = protons; mass # = protons + neutrons.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but DIFFERENT numbers of neutrons are:
rationale: Isotopes = same protons, different neutrons.
why: Correct. Isotopes differ in neutron number (and thus mass number) but share the same atomic number (element identity).
Ions differ in electron number (charge), not neutrons.
Isomers are molecules with the same formula but different structure.
Allotropes are different structural forms of an element (e.g., graphite vs. diamond).
takeaway: Isotopes = same element, different neutron count.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: An atom that has LOST electrons becomes a ______ (positive ion), while one that has GAINED electrons becomes a ______ (negative ion).
rationale: Cation = lost electrons (positive); anion = gained electrons (negative).
why: Reversed — losing electrons makes a cation (positive).
Those are neutron-count/structure terms, not charge.
Protons/neutrons are nuclear particles, not ion types.
Correct. Losing electrons → net positive = cation; gaining electrons → net negative = anion.
takeaway: Cation = + (lost e−); anion = − (gained e−).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Electronegativity generally INCREASES as you move ______ across a period and ______ up a group.
rationale: Electronegativity increases toward the upper-right (max at fluorine).
why: It increases toward the right and up, not left and down.
It increases going up, not down.
Correct. Electronegativity increases toward the upper right of the periodic table (fluorine is the most electronegative).
It increases going right, not left.
takeaway: Electronegativity: increases right and up (F highest).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Atomic radius generally ______ across a period (left to right) and ______ down a group.
rationale: Atomic radius: decreases across a period, increases down a group.
why: Correct. Across a period, more protons pull electrons in tighter (smaller radius); down a group, added shells make atoms larger.
Reversed — radius decreases across a period, increases down a group.
It decreases across a period.
It increases down a group.
takeaway: Radius: shrinks left→right, grows top→bottom.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Ionization energy (the energy to remove an electron) generally follows the ______ trend as electronegativity.
choices: Same (increases up and to the right)
rationale: Ionization energy increases up and to the right (same direction as electronegativity).
why: It follows the same, not opposite, trend as electronegativity.
The trends are related, both reflecting nuclear pull.
The trend is systematic, not random.
Correct. Ionization energy increases toward the upper right (like electronegativity) — electrons are held more tightly there.
takeaway: Ionization energy increases up/right (like electronegativity).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In radioactive decay, an ______ particle is a helium nucleus (heavy, low penetration), while a ______ particle is a high-energy electron.
rationale: Alpha = helium nucleus; beta = electron; gamma = photon.
why: Reversed — the helium nucleus is the alpha particle.
Gamma is a photon, not the helium nucleus.
Correct. Alpha = helium nucleus (2p + 2n); beta = electron (or positron); gamma = high-energy photon (most penetrating).
Gamma is a photon, not an electron.
takeaway: Alpha = He nucleus; beta = electron; gamma = photon.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time required for:
choices: Half of the radioactive nuclei to decay
rationale: Half-life = time for half the radioactive nuclei to decay.
why: Correct. Each half-life reduces the remaining radioactive quantity by half (exponential decay), regardless of the starting amount.
One half-life decays half, not all, of the sample.
Radioactive decay reduces the quantity; it doesn't double the mass.
Half-life concerns quantity decayed, not halving the atomic number.
takeaway: Half-life = time for half the sample to decay.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Ranked from LEAST to MOST penetrating, the three types of radiation are:
rationale: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma (gamma most penetrating).
why: That's the reverse — gamma is most penetrating.
Alpha is the least penetrating, not in the middle.
Gamma is most penetrating, so it comes last, not middle.
Correct. Alpha (stopped by paper) < beta (stopped by aluminum) < gamma (needs lead/concrete). Heavier, more-charged particles penetrate less.
takeaway: Penetration: alpha < beta < gamma.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Water is an excellent solvent for ionic and polar substances because the water molecule is:
rationale: Water is polar (bent + partial charges) → dissolves ions/polar solutes.
why: Water is bent, not linear, and it is polar.
Water has distinct partial charges (δ− on O, δ+ on H), not a uniform sphere.
Correct. Water's bent geometry and O–H electronegativity difference make it polar, so it dissolves ions and polar molecules ('like dissolves like').
Water has partial charges that make it polar.
takeaway: Water = polar (bent) → great solvent for ionic/polar.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Many of water's unusual properties (high boiling point, high specific heat, cohesion) arise from:
rationale: Water's special properties come from hydrogen bonding between molecules.
why: Correct. Hydrogen bonds between water molecules give water high specific heat, high boiling point, surface tension, and cohesion/adhesion.
The bonds WITHIN a water molecule are covalent; between molecules they're hydrogen bonds.
Water molecules aren't held together by ionic bonds.
Hydrogen bonding (not just weak dispersion) dominates water's behavior.
takeaway: Water's properties = hydrogen bonding (high specific heat, cohesion).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: By the Brønsted-Lowry definition, an acid is a proton (H+) ______ and a base is a proton ______.
rationale: Brønsted-Lowry: acid = proton donor, base = proton acceptor.
why: Reversed — the acid donates the proton.
Electron donor/acceptor is the Lewis definition, not Brønsted-Lowry.
Correct. Brønsted-Lowry: acid donates H+, base accepts H+. (Lewis definition uses electron pairs instead.)
Those aren't the Brønsted-Lowry roles.
takeaway: B-L acid = H+ donor; base = H+ acceptor.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When an acid donates a proton, what remains is its:
rationale: An acid minus H+ = its conjugate base (differ by one proton).
why: Correct. An acid loses H+ to become its conjugate base; a base gains H+ to become its conjugate acid (they differ by one proton).
Gaining a proton (base → conjugate acid) is the reverse relationship.
The product is the conjugate base, not necessarily a neutral salt.
It's the same species minus a proton, not a different element.
takeaway: Acid − H+ = conjugate base.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A STRONG acid differs from a weak acid in that a strong acid:
rationale: A strong acid dissociates completely; a weak acid only partially.
why: Partial dissociation describes a WEAK acid.
Acids by definition donate H+; strong ones do so completely.
Strength refers to degree of dissociation, not concentration.
Correct. Strong acids ionize ~100% in water; weak acids only partially dissociate (described by Ka).
takeaway: Strong acid = fully dissociates; weak = partial (Ka).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: pH is defined as:
choices: The negative log of the hydrogen ion concentration (pH = −log[H+])
rationale: pH = −log[H+] (log scale; each unit = 10×).
why: It's the NEGATIVE log, so lower pH = higher [H+].
pH is a log scale, not the raw concentration.
Correct. pH = −log[H+]; each unit change in pH is a 10-fold change in [H+].
pH tracks [H+], not directly [OH−].
takeaway: pH = −log[H+] (each unit = 10× change).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: At 25°C, for any aqueous solution, pH + pOH equals:
rationale: At 25°C, pH + pOH = 14.
why: Correct. Because Kw = [H+][OH−] = 10⁻¹⁴ at 25°C, pH + pOH = 14.
7 is neutral pH, not the sum of pH and pOH.
The sum is 14, not 0.
The sum is 14, not 100.
takeaway: pH + pOH = 14 (at 25°C).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A solution with pH < 7 is ______, pH = 7 is neutral, and pH > 7 is ______.
rationale: pH < 7 = acidic; pH = 7 neutral; pH > 7 = basic.
why: Reversed — below 7 is acidic.
Only pH exactly 7 is neutral.
Saturated/dilute describe concentration, not pH.
Correct. pH below 7 = acidic (more H+); pH above 7 = basic (more OH−); 7 = neutral.
takeaway: pH<7 acidic, =7 neutral, >7 basic.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A buffer solution, which resists changes in pH, is typically made of:
choices: A strong acid and a strong base
A weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base + conjugate acid)
rationale: A buffer = weak acid + its conjugate base (resists pH change).
why: Strong acid + strong base neutralize to a salt; that isn't a buffer.
Pure water has negligible buffering capacity.
Correct. Buffers pair a weak acid with its conjugate base, neutralizing added acid or base to hold pH nearly constant.
Two strong acids don't form a buffer.
takeaway: Buffer = weak acid + conjugate base.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When a buffer contains equal concentrations of weak acid and conjugate base, the pH equals:
rationale: When [acid] = [conjugate base], pH = pKa (Henderson-Hasselbalch).
why: Correct. Henderson-Hasselbalch: pH = pKa + log([base]/[acid]); when [base] = [acid], the log term is 0, so pH = pKa (maximum buffering).
pH equals pKa here, not necessarily 7.
pH isn't zero.
It equals the pKa, not the pKb.
takeaway: Equal acid/base → pH = pKa (best buffering).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In an acid-base titration, the equivalence point is where:
choices: Moles of added base exactly neutralize the moles of acid
rationale: Equivalence point: moles of titrant = moles of analyte (fully neutralized).
why: The indicator is added at the start, not the equivalence point.
Equivalence pH is 7 only for strong acid + strong base; weak systems differ.
Correct. At the equivalence point, added titrant has reacted stoichiometrically with the analyte (moles acid = moles base).
The endpoint is detected, not spontaneous.
takeaway: Equivalence point = moles acid = moles base.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: On a weak-acid titration curve, at the half-equivalence point (half the acid neutralized), the pH equals:
choices: The pKa of the weak acid
rationale: At the half-equivalence point, pH = pKa (buffer region).
why: Correct. At half-equivalence, [acid] = [conjugate base], so pH = pKa — a useful way to read pKa from a titration curve.
pH = pKa here, not necessarily 7.
pH isn't zero at half-equivalence.
The half-equivalence pH (pKa) differs from the equivalence-point pH.
takeaway: Half-equivalence: pH = pKa.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: For a titration of a STRONG acid with a STRONG base, the pH at the equivalence point is:
rationale: Strong acid + strong base: equivalence pH = 7.
why: Equivalence pH > 7 applies to weak acid + strong base, not strong-strong.
Equivalence pH < 7 applies to strong acid + weak base.
It's 7, not 0.
Correct. Strong acid + strong base yields a neutral salt and water, so the equivalence point is pH 7. (Weak-acid titrations give equivalence pH > 7.)
takeaway: Strong-strong titration: equivalence pH = 7.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The solubility product constant (Ksp) describes the equilibrium for:
choices: A slightly soluble ionic solid dissolving into its ions
rationale: Ksp = equilibrium constant for a sparingly soluble salt dissolving into ions.
why: Gas solubility is described by Henry's law, not Ksp.
Proton donation is described by Ka.
Correct. Ksp is the equilibrium constant for the dissolution of a sparingly soluble salt into its constituent ions; a larger Ksp means greater solubility.
Redox equilibria use cell potentials, not Ksp.
takeaway: Ksp = dissolution equilibrium of a solid (bigger Ksp = more soluble).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Adding an ion already present in a saturated salt solution will ______ the solubility of that salt.
rationale: Common ion effect: a shared ion decreases a salt's solubility (Le Chatelier).
why: Correct. The common ion effect shifts the dissolution equilibrium backward (Le Chatelier), decreasing solubility.
A common ion decreases, not increases, solubility.
It shifts equilibrium and changes solubility.
It suppresses dissolution, it doesn't remove the ion.
takeaway: Common ion → less soluble (equilibrium shifts back).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A bond formed by the TRANSFER of electrons (typically metal + nonmetal) is ______; a bond formed by SHARING electrons (nonmetal + nonmetal) is ______.
rationale: Ionic = electron transfer; covalent = electron sharing.
why: Reversed — electron transfer is ionic, sharing is covalent.
Correct. Ionic bonds transfer electrons (forming cations/anions); covalent bonds share electron pairs.
Metallic bonding is a different type (delocalized electrons), not electron transfer here.
Hydrogen 'bonds' are intermolecular attractions, not the electron-sharing bond type.
takeaway: Ionic = transfer e−; covalent = share e−.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A covalent bond between atoms of DIFFERENT electronegativities, creating partial charges, is a:
rationale: Polar covalent = unequal sharing (electronegativity difference → partial charges).
why: Nonpolar covalent bonds share electrons equally (similar electronegativity).
A large enough difference becomes ionic; a moderate difference is polar covalent.
Metallic bonds involve delocalized electrons among metal atoms.
Correct. Unequal sharing (electronegativity difference) makes a bond polar covalent, with δ+ and δ− ends.
takeaway: Polar covalent = unequal e− sharing (δ+/δ−).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A molecule is nonpolar overall if its bond dipoles ______, even if individual bonds are polar (e.g., CO2).
rationale: A molecule is nonpolar if symmetric geometry makes bond dipoles cancel (e.g., CO2).
why: Symmetric dipoles cancel rather than adding.
Correct. Symmetric geometry can cancel bond dipoles, making the whole molecule nonpolar (CO2 is linear/symmetric despite polar C=O bonds).
Polar covalent bonds aren't ionic.
In a nonpolar molecule the dipoles oppose/cancel, not point the same way.
takeaway: Symmetric molecule = dipoles cancel = nonpolar (CO2).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape based on the idea that electron pairs around a central atom:
choices: Repel and arrange to maximize their separation
rationale: VSEPR: electron pairs repel and spread out to set molecular geometry.
why: Electron pairs repel, they don't cluster.
Electron-pair arrangement determines shape.
Angles vary by geometry (e.g., 109.5° tetrahedral, 120° trigonal), not always 90°.
Correct. VSEPR: electron pairs (bonding and lone) repel, arranging to minimize repulsion (maximize separation), which sets the molecular geometry.
takeaway: VSEPR = electron pairs repel → determine shape.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Ranked from WEAKEST to STRONGEST, the intermolecular forces are:
rationale: IMF strength: London dispersion < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding.
why: That's reversed — hydrogen bonding is strongest.
Correct. London dispersion (weakest, present in all) < dipole-dipole < hydrogen bonding (strongest IMF, a special strong dipole force). Ion-dipole is even stronger.
London dispersion is weakest, not in the middle.
The forces differ substantially in strength.
takeaway: IMF: dispersion < dipole-dipole < H-bonding.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Hydrogen bonding (the strongest normal IMF) occurs when H is bonded to:
choices: N, O, or F (highly electronegative atoms)
rationale: Hydrogen bonding requires H bonded to N, O, or F.
why: C–H bonds are not polar enough for true hydrogen bonding.
H bonded to a metal isn't the hydrogen-bonding scenario.
H2 has no hydrogen bonding.
Correct. Hydrogen bonds form when H is bonded to N, O, or F and interacts with a lone pair on another N, O, or F.
takeaway: H-bonding = H on N, O, or F.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A substance with STRONGER intermolecular forces will generally have a ______ boiling point.
rationale: Stronger intermolecular forces → higher boiling point.
why: Correct. Stronger IMFs require more energy to separate molecules into the gas phase, raising the boiling point.
Stronger IMFs raise, not lower, the boiling point.
Boiling point varies with IMF strength.
Boiling points aren't zero for molecules with IMFs.
takeaway: Stronger IMFs = higher boiling point.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A reaction that RELEASES heat has a ______ enthalpy change (ΔH < 0); one that ABSORBS heat has ΔH ______.
rationale: Exothermic: ΔH < 0 (releases heat); endothermic: ΔH > 0 (absorbs heat).
why: Reversed — releasing heat is ΔH < 0 (exothermic).
ΔH isn't zero for these reactions.
Correct. Exothermic reactions release heat (ΔH < 0); endothermic reactions absorb heat (ΔH > 0).
Endothermic ΔH is positive, not negative.
takeaway: Exothermic ΔH<0 (releases); endothermic ΔH>0 (absorbs).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Entropy (S) is a measure of ______, and it tends to INCREASE when a solid melts or a gas forms.
rationale: Entropy (S) = disorder; increases with melting, vaporization, dissolving.
why: Correct. Entropy measures disorder; it increases as substances become more dispersed/random (solid → liquid → gas, dissolving).
Heat content relates to enthalpy, not entropy.
Rate is a kinetics concept, not entropy.
Mass is conserved and isn't entropy.
takeaway: Entropy = disorder (increases: solid→liquid→gas).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A reaction is spontaneous (thermodynamically favorable) when its Gibbs free energy change is:
rationale: Spontaneous when ΔG < 0 (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS).
why: ΔG > 0 is nonspontaneous.
ΔG = 0 is equilibrium, not spontaneity.
ΔG equals ΔH only if TΔS = 0.
Correct. ΔG = ΔH − TΔS; ΔG < 0 means spontaneous, ΔG > 0 nonspontaneous, ΔG = 0 at equilibrium.
takeaway: Spontaneous = ΔG < 0 (ΔG = ΔH − TΔS).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: For a reaction that is endothermic (ΔH > 0) but increases entropy (ΔS > 0), spontaneity is favored at:
rationale: ΔH>0, ΔS>0 → spontaneous at high temperature (−TΔS dominates).
why: Low temperatures keep ΔG positive here.
Correct. When ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, raising T makes the −TΔS term more negative, eventually making ΔG < 0 (spontaneous at high T).
Spontaneity depends on temperature in this case.
It becomes spontaneous once T is high enough.
takeaway: ΔH>0, ΔS>0: spontaneous at high T.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The minimum energy required for a reaction to proceed (the barrier reactants must overcome) is the:
rationale: Activation energy (Ea) = the barrier reactants must overcome to react.
why: Gibbs free energy determines spontaneity, not the kinetic barrier.
Bond dissociation energy is for breaking a specific bond, not the overall barrier.
Correct. Activation energy (Ea) is the energy barrier for a reaction; a lower Ea means a faster rate.
Entropy measures disorder, not the reaction barrier.
takeaway: Activation energy = reaction barrier (lower = faster).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A catalyst speeds up a reaction by ______ without being consumed, and it does NOT change:
choices: Lowering the activation energy; the equilibrium position or ΔG
Raising the activation energy; the rate
rationale: A catalyst lowers activation energy (faster rate) but doesn't change ΔG/equilibrium.
why: Correct. A catalyst provides a lower-Ea pathway (faster rate) but doesn't alter ΔG, the equilibrium position, or the reaction's thermodynamics.
A catalyst LOWERS activation energy and speeds the rate.
It doesn't supply net energy or change the products.
It doesn't change ΔG.
takeaway: Catalyst = lower Ea (faster), no change to ΔG/equilibrium.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Increasing the temperature of a reaction generally ______ the reaction rate because molecules collide more frequently and energetically.
rationale: Higher temperature → faster rate (more energetic, frequent collisions).
why: Higher temperature increases, not decreases, rate.
Temperature strongly affects rate.
Reactions speed up, not stop, at higher temperature.
Correct. Higher temperature raises molecular speed and collision energy/frequency, increasing the fraction of collisions that exceed Ea → faster rate.
takeaway: ↑Temperature = ↑rate (more/harder collisions).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Le Chatelier's principle states that a system at equilibrium, when disturbed, will shift to:
rationale: Le Chatelier: a disturbed equilibrium shifts to counteract the change.
why: The system counteracts, not amplifies, the stress.
It re-establishes equilibrium; it doesn't stop.
Correct. Le Chatelier: an equilibrium responds to a stress (concentration, pressure, temperature) by shifting in the direction that relieves it.
The shift direction depends on the stress, not always toward products.
takeaway: Le Chatelier: system shifts to oppose the stress.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: If more reactant is added to a system at equilibrium, the equilibrium will shift:
rationale: Adding reactant shifts equilibrium toward products.
why: Correct. Adding reactant stresses the system, so it shifts toward products to consume the excess (Le Chatelier).
Adding reactant pushes toward products, not back toward reactants.
It does shift to relieve the added reactant.
The shift is toward products, not necessarily a solid.
takeaway: Add reactant → shift toward products.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A large equilibrium constant (Keq >> 1) indicates that at equilibrium the reaction favors:
rationale: Large Keq (>>1) → products favored at equilibrium.
why: A small Keq (<< 1) would favor reactants.
A large Keq clearly favors one side (products).
Keq magnitude reflects product/reactant ratio, not precipitation specifically.
Correct. Keq = [products]/[reactants]; a large Keq means products dominate at equilibrium.
takeaway: Keq >> 1 = products favored.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a redox reaction, the species that LOSES electrons is ______ and the species that GAINS electrons is ______.
rationale: Oxidation = lose electrons; reduction = gain (OIL RIG).
why: Reversed — losing electrons is oxidation.
Redox is about electron transfer, not acid-base neutralization.
Correct. OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain (of electrons). The oxidized species is the reducing agent.
Those describe solubility changes, not redox.
takeaway: OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In any electrochemical cell, oxidation occurs at the ______ and reduction occurs at the ______.
rationale: Oxidation at the anode; reduction at the cathode (An Ox, Red Cat).
why: Correct. Oxidation always occurs at the anode; reduction always at the cathode ('An Ox' and 'Red Cat').
Reversed — oxidation is at the anode.
An electrolyte isn't where a half-reaction occurs; electrodes are.
The salt bridge balances charge; it isn't a reduction site.
takeaway: Anode = oxidation; cathode = reduction.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A ______ (voltaic) cell uses a spontaneous redox reaction to GENERATE electricity, while an ______ cell uses electricity to DRIVE a nonspontaneous reaction.
rationale: Galvanic = spontaneous (makes current); electrolytic = driven by electricity.
why: Reversed — the spontaneous, current-generating cell is galvanic.
Anode/cathode are electrodes, not cell types.
Series/parallel describe circuit wiring, not cell types.
Correct. Galvanic cells: spontaneous (ΔG < 0, produces current). Electrolytic cells: nonspontaneous (require an external power source).
takeaway: Galvanic = spontaneous (battery); electrolytic = forced by power.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A carbon double-bonded to one oxygen AND single-bonded to a hydroxyl (–COOH) is the ______ group, found in carboxylic acids.
rationale: Carboxyl (–COOH) = carboxylic acids (acidic).
why: A hydroxyl is just –OH (alcohol).
An amino group is –NH2.
A lone carbonyl (C=O) without the –OH is an aldehyde/ketone, not a carboxyl.
Correct. The carboxyl group (–COOH) defines carboxylic acids; it's acidic because the conjugate base is resonance-stabilized.
takeaway: Carboxyl = –COOH (carboxylic acid, acidic).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The –OH group defines an ______, while a C=O group defines a ______ (aldehyde or ketone).
rationale: –OH = alcohol; C=O = carbonyl (aldehyde/ketone).
why: Amino defines amines; carboxyl (not carbonyl alone) defines carboxylic acids.
Correct. Hydroxyl (–OH) = alcohol; carbonyl (C=O) = aldehyde (terminal) or ketone (internal).
Ester/ether are other oxygen groups, not –OH and C=O.
Alkane/alkene describe C–C saturation, not these functional groups.
takeaway: Hydroxyl (–OH) = alcohol; carbonyl (C=O) = aldehyde/ketone.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A carbonyl carbon bonded to at least one HYDROGEN (carbonyl at the end of a chain) is an ______; a carbonyl bonded to two carbons (internal) is a ______.
rationale: Aldehyde = terminal carbonyl (–CHO); ketone = internal carbonyl.
why: Reversed — the terminal carbonyl is an aldehyde.
Ester/ether aren't the carbonyl-position distinction.
Correct. Aldehydes have the carbonyl at a chain END (–CHO); ketones have it between two carbons.
Alcohol/acid aren't defined by carbonyl position.
takeaway: Aldehyde = end carbonyl; ketone = middle carbonyl.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Molecules with the same molecular formula but DIFFERENT connectivity (bonding order) are ______ isomers; those with the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement are ______.
rationale: Structural = different connectivity; stereoisomers = same connectivity, different 3D.
why: Reversed — different connectivity is structural isomerism.
Enantiomers/diastereomers are subtypes of stereoisomers, not the top-level pair.
Cis/trans are a subtype of stereoisomers.
Correct. Structural (constitutional) isomers differ in connectivity; stereoisomers share connectivity but differ in 3D arrangement.
takeaway: Structural = different bonds; stereo = same bonds, different 3D.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Two stereoisomers that are non-superimposable MIRROR IMAGES of each other are:
rationale: Enantiomers = non-superimposable mirror images.
why: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images.
Correct. Enantiomers are non-superimposable mirror images (like left/right hands); they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions.
Structural isomers differ in connectivity, not mirror-image relationship.
Conformers interconvert by bond rotation; they aren't distinct configurations.
takeaway: Enantiomers = mirror images (non-superimposable).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A carbon atom bonded to FOUR different groups — giving the molecule handedness — is a:
rationale: A chiral center = carbon with four different groups (source of handedness).
