why: A carbonyl carbon is C=O, not necessarily chiral.
The anomeric carbon is a specific sugar case, not the general definition.
Correct. A chiral center is a carbon with four different substituents; it makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image.
An achiral carbon lacks four different groups.
takeaway: Chiral center = C with 4 different groups.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A solution of a single enantiomer is 'optically active,' meaning it:
rationale: Optically active = rotates plane-polarized light (chiral, single enantiomer).
why: Correct. Chiral molecules (single enantiomers) rotate plane-polarized light; a racemic (50/50) mixture shows no net rotation.
Optical activity is about rotating polarized light, not absorbing all light.
Optical activity is unrelated to water solubility.
Optical activity requires a stereocenter, not the absence of one.
takeaway: Optical activity = rotates polarized light (chiral).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In organic reactions, an electron-RICH species that attacks is a ______; an electron-POOR species that accepts electrons is an ______.
rationale: Nucleophile = electron-rich (attacks); electrophile = electron-poor (accepts).
why: Reversed — the electron-rich attacker is the nucleophile.
Acid/base (proton transfer) isn't the same framing as nucleophile/electrophile.
Oxidant/reductant concern electron transfer in redox, a different context.
Correct. Nucleophiles ('nucleus-loving,' electron-rich) donate electrons to electrophiles (electron-poor).
takeaway: Nucleophile = electron-rich; electrophile = electron-poor.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: An SN2 reaction occurs in a single concerted step with backside attack (causing inversion) and is fastest with ______ substrates; SN1 goes through a carbocation and is favored by ______ substrates.
rationale: SN2 favors primary (backside attack, inversion); SN1 favors tertiary (carbocation).
why: Reversed — SN2 favors primary, SN1 favors tertiary.
Correct. SN2 needs an accessible carbon (primary, less steric hindrance); SN1 forms a carbocation, stabilized best at tertiary carbons.
Aromatic/aliphatic isn't the SN1/SN2 substrate distinction.
Polar/nonpolar describes solvents/bonds, not the substrate order here.
takeaway: SN2 = primary (inversion); SN1 = tertiary (carbocation).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Oxidizing a PRIMARY alcohol gives an aldehyde and then a ______; oxidizing a SECONDARY alcohol gives a ______.
rationale: Primary alcohol → carboxylic acid; secondary → ketone (oxidation).
why: Reversed — secondary alcohols give ketones, primary give acids.
Oxidation here adds oxygen/removes hydrogen, not forming ethers/esters.
Correct. Primary alcohol → aldehyde → carboxylic acid; secondary alcohol → ketone; tertiary alcohols resist oxidation.
These are oxygenation products, not alkane/alkene.
takeaway: 1° alcohol → acid; 2° alcohol → ketone (oxidation).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Infrared (IR) spectroscopy is used primarily to identify ______ by the characteristic vibrations of their bonds (e.g., a broad O–H peak, a strong C=O near 1700 cm⁻¹).
rationale: IR spectroscopy identifies functional groups (bond vibrations).
why: Molecular mass is determined by mass spectrometry.
Proton counting/environments is NMR.
Optical rotation is measured by a polarimeter.
Correct. IR detects bond vibrations, revealing functional groups (O–H broad, C=O ~1700 cm⁻¹, etc.).
takeaway: IR = functional groups (C=O ~1700, broad O–H).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Nuclear magnetic resonance (¹H NMR) spectroscopy provides information about:
choices: The number and environment of hydrogen atoms (molecular structure)
rationale: NMR reveals hydrogen number/environment → molecular structure.
why: Molecular weight is from mass spectrometry.
Correct. ¹H NMR reveals how many hydrogens are present and their chemical environments (via shifts, splitting, integration), building up the structure.
Boiling point isn't determined by NMR.
Optical rotation is measured by polarimetry.
takeaway: NMR = H environments (structure).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Mass spectrometry determines a compound's ______ by ionizing it and measuring the mass-to-charge ratio of the fragments.
rationale: Mass spectrometry gives molecular mass (and fragments) via m/z.
why: Bond-vibration identification of functional groups is IR.
Hydrogen environments come from NMR.
Correct. Mass spec ionizes and fragments molecules, measuring m/z to give molecular mass and structural clues from the fragments.
pH is an acid-base property, not a mass-spec output.
takeaway: Mass spec = molecular mass + fragments (m/z).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is accelerating because its ______ is constantly changing, and the net force points:
choices: Velocity (direction); toward the center of the circle
rationale: Uniform circular motion: velocity direction changes; net force points toward the center (centripetal).
why: Speed is constant; it's the velocity direction that changes, and the force points inward.
Mass doesn't change; the force is centripetal (inward), not tangential.
Correct. In uniform circular motion, speed is constant but velocity's DIRECTION changes, so there is centripetal acceleration and a net (centripetal) force toward the center.
Speed is constant here; the changing quantity is velocity direction.
takeaway: Circular motion: centripetal force points to the center.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The centripetal force required to keep an object of mass m moving at speed v in a circle of radius r is:
rationale: Centripetal force F = mv²/r.
why: Correct. Centripetal force F = mv²/r (from a = v²/r); it increases sharply with speed and decreases with larger radius.
That omits the square on v.
That isn't the centripetal force relationship.
That inverts the relationship.
takeaway: F_centripetal = mv²/r.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The outward 'centrifugal force' you seem to feel in a turning car is:
choices: A fictitious (apparent) force — really your inertia resisting the inward acceleration
rationale: Centrifugal force is fictitious — it's inertia; the real force is centripetal (inward).
why: It is not a real force; it's an inertial effect.
It isn't gravity.
It's the opposite of the (real, inward) centripetal force.
Correct. Centrifugal force is a fictitious force in a rotating frame; the only real force is the inward (centripetal) one, and inertia makes you feel pushed outward.
takeaway: Centrifugal = fictitious (inertia); real force is inward.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The centripetal force keeping a planet in orbit or a car turning is not a new force — it is PROVIDED by:
choices: An existing force (gravity, friction, tension, etc.) directed toward the center
rationale: Centripetal force is a ROLE filled by gravity, friction, or tension (whatever points inward).
why: There is no separate 'centripetal force' — an ordinary force plays that role.
Correct. 'Centripetal' names the ROLE, not a new force — gravity (orbits), friction (turning car), or tension (whirled object) supplies the inward force.
Centrifugal force is fictitious and points outward.
Air resistance opposes motion; it isn't the centripetal source.
takeaway: Centripetal = role played by gravity/friction/tension (inward).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The gravitational force between two masses is proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to:
choices: The square of the distance between them (F = Gm₁m₂/r²)
rationale: Gravitation: F = Gm₁m₂/r² (inverse-square).
why: The dependence is on r squared, not r.
It depends on the PRODUCT of masses, not their sum.
Correct. Universal gravitation F = Gm₁m₂/r² is an inverse-square law (like Coulomb's law for charges).
It's inverse-square, not inverse-cube.
takeaway: Gravity: F ∝ m₁m₂/r² (inverse square).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A satellite stays in circular orbit because the gravitational force acts as the ______ force, continuously pulling it toward the planet.
rationale: In orbit, gravity is the centripetal force pulling the satellite inward.
why: Correct. Gravity supplies the centripetal force for orbital motion, constantly redirecting the satellite toward the planet's center.
Centrifugal force is fictitious.
There is no normal (contact) force in orbit.
There is no friction in the vacuum of orbit.
takeaway: Orbit: gravity = centripetal force.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Astronauts in orbit feel 'weightless' not because gravity is absent, but because they are:
choices: Moving too fast for gravity to act
Shielded from gravity by the spacecraft
In continuous free fall around the Earth
rationale: Orbital 'weightlessness' = continuous free fall (gravity is still present).
why: Gravity is still strong in low orbit; it hasn't disappeared.
Speed doesn't turn off gravity; free fall causes weightlessness.
Spacecraft don't shield gravity.
Correct. Orbiting astronauts (and their craft) are in free fall together, so there's no normal force — producing apparent weightlessness though gravity is still substantial.
takeaway: Weightless in orbit = free fall (gravity still acts).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Viscosity is a fluid's:
rationale: Viscosity = a fluid's resistance to flow (internal friction).
why: Floating is buoyancy, not viscosity.
Density is mass per volume, a separate property.
Correct. Viscosity measures a fluid's internal resistance to flow; honey is more viscous than water.
Pressure transmission is Pascal's principle, not viscosity.
takeaway: Viscosity = resistance to flow (honey > water).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Smooth, orderly fluid flow in parallel layers is ______ flow; chaotic, mixing flow (at high velocity) is ______ flow.
rationale: Laminar = smooth layered flow; turbulent = chaotic (high velocity).
why: Correct. Laminar flow is smooth and layered; turbulent flow is chaotic and occurs at high velocity/high Reynolds number.
Reversed — smooth layered flow is laminar.
Ideal/viscous describe fluid types, not this flow pattern.
Static/dynamic isn't the laminar/turbulent distinction.
takeaway: Laminar = smooth; turbulent = chaotic (fast).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In laminar flow through a tube, the flow rate is extremely sensitive to the tube's radius — proportional to the radius raised to the:
rationale: Poiseuille: flow rate ∝ r⁴ (tiny radius changes hugely affect flow).
why: The dependence is r⁴, far stronger than linear.
It's r⁴, not r².
Flow strongly depends on radius, not independent of it.
Correct. Poiseuille's law: flow rate ∝ r⁴, so even a small narrowing of a vessel drastically reduces flow (clinically important for blood vessels).
takeaway: Flow ∝ r⁴ (radius dominates; Poiseuille).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The electric field at a point is the force per unit ______ that a small positive test charge would experience there.
rationale: Electric field E = F/q (force per unit charge).
why: Force per mass is a gravitational field, not electric.
Field isn't force per distance.
Correct. Electric field E = F/q (force per unit charge); it points away from positive charges and toward negative charges.
Field isn't force per area.
takeaway: E = F/q (field = force per charge).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Electric field lines point ______ from a positive charge and ______ a negative charge.
rationale: Field lines: away from +, toward −.
why: Correct. By convention, field lines emanate from positive charges and terminate on negative charges (direction a positive test charge would move).
Reversed — lines point away from positive charges.
Lines point toward negative charges, not away.
Lines point away from positive charges, not toward.
takeaway: Field lines: out of +, into −.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Electric potential (voltage) is potential energy per unit ______; it exists in space whether or not a charge is present.
rationale: Electric potential = potential energy per charge (V = PE/q).
why: Per mass would relate to gravitation, not electric potential.
Potential isn't energy per distance.
Potential isn't energy per time (that's power).
Correct. Electric potential = potential energy per unit charge (V = PE/q); a charge placed at that potential then has PE = qV.
takeaway: Potential (V) = PE per charge.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The decibel scale for sound intensity is ______, so a 10 dB increase represents a ______ increase in intensity.
rationale: Decibels are logarithmic: +10 dB = 10× intensity.
why: The dB scale is logarithmic, not linear.
+10 dB is a 10×, not 2×, change.
Correct. Decibels are logarithmic: every +10 dB is a 10× increase in intensity (so +20 dB is 100×).
The scale is logarithmic; +10 dB is 10×, not a doubling.
takeaway: dB is logarithmic: +10 dB = 10× intensity.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When a driving frequency matches an object's natural frequency, the amplitude grows dramatically. This is:
rationale: Resonance: driving at the natural frequency → large amplitude.
why: Correct. Resonance is the large-amplitude response when a system is driven at its natural frequency (e.g., a pushed swing, a shattered glass).
Refraction is the bending of waves entering a new medium.
Diffraction is bending around obstacles/openings.
Attenuation is the loss of amplitude, the opposite of resonance.
takeaway: Resonance = drive at natural frequency → big amplitude.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: On a string fixed at both ends, only certain wavelengths produce standing waves; these allowed frequencies are the:
rationale: Standing waves occur at harmonics (fundamental × integer multiples).
why: Beats arise from two close frequencies interfering, not from a single string's modes.
Allowed frequencies are set by length, not unrelated.
Only specific (quantized) frequencies are allowed, not random ones.
Correct. A fixed string supports standing waves at the fundamental frequency and integer multiples (harmonics), set by the string's length.
takeaway: Standing waves = harmonics (integer multiples of fundamental).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A converging (convex) lens has a ______ focal length; a diverging (concave) lens has a ______ focal length.
rationale: Converging = positive f; diverging = negative f.
why: Reversed — converging is positive.
Focal lengths are finite nonzero values here.
Correct. Sign convention: converging lenses/mirrors have positive focal length; diverging ones have negative focal length.
Those values are incorrect for these lens types.
takeaway: Converging f > 0; diverging f < 0.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The thin lens (and mirror) equation relating focal length f, object distance o, and image distance i is:
rationale: Thin lens/mirror equation: 1/f = 1/o + 1/i.
why: Correct. 1/f = 1/o + 1/i governs image formation for thin lenses and mirrors.
That isn't the thin lens equation.
That isn't correct either.
The terms add (1/o + 1/i), not subtract.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A real image (which can be projected on a screen) forms where light rays actually converge and has a ______ image distance; a virtual image has a ______ image distance.
rationale: Real image = positive i (projectable, inverted); virtual = negative i (upright).
why: Reversed — real images have positive image distance.
Real images have positive, not zero, image distance.
Those values are incorrect.
Correct. Real images (rays actually meet) have positive image distance and are inverted; virtual images (rays only appear to diverge from) have negative image distance and are upright.
takeaway: Real image = +i (projectable); virtual = −i (upright).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Electrons fill orbitals from lowest to highest energy, one orbital type at a time. This is the:
rationale: Aufbau principle: electrons fill lowest-energy orbitals first.
why: The uncertainty principle concerns position/momentum, not filling order.
Le Chatelier concerns equilibrium shifts.
Correct. The Aufbau ('building up') principle: electrons occupy the lowest-energy orbitals first.
Pauli exclusion limits electrons per orbital (2, opposite spins), a related but different rule.
takeaway: Aufbau = fill lowest-energy orbitals first.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The Pauli exclusion principle states that a single orbital can hold at most ______ electrons, which must have ______.
rationale: Pauli exclusion: max 2 electrons per orbital, opposite spins.
why: Correct. Each orbital holds a maximum of two electrons with opposite (paired) spins.
Paired electrons must have OPPOSITE spins, not the same.
An orbital holds two electrons, not eight (a shell may hold more).
An orbital can hold two electrons, not just one.
takeaway: Pauli: 2 e− per orbital, opposite spins.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The electrons in the outermost shell, which determine an atom's chemical bonding behavior, are the:
rationale: Valence electrons (outermost shell) determine bonding.
why: Core electrons are inner and don't drive bonding.
'Free electrons' describes conduction, not the general bonding electrons.
Delocalized electrons are a special (metallic/aromatic) case.
Correct. Valence electrons (outermost shell) govern bonding and reactivity; core electrons are shielded and generally inert.
takeaway: Valence electrons = outer shell (drive bonding).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: When filling degenerate (equal-energy) orbitals, electrons occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing up. This is:
rationale: Hund's rule: fill degenerate orbitals singly (parallel spins) before pairing.
why: Aufbau sets the order of orbital energies, not single-filling within a subshell.
Correct. Hund's rule: electrons spread out singly across equal-energy orbitals (minimizing repulsion) before doubling up.
Ohm's law concerns circuits.
Raoult's law concerns vapor pressure of solutions.
takeaway: Hund's rule: one electron per orbital first (then pair).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency, given by:
rationale: Photon energy E = hf (higher frequency = higher energy).
why: E = mc² is mass-energy equivalence, not photon energy.
½ mv² is kinetic energy of a mass.
Correct. Photon energy E = hf (h = Planck's constant); higher frequency (e.g., UV) means higher energy per photon.
That isn't Planck's relation.
takeaway: E = hf (photon energy ∝ frequency).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Atoms emit light at specific discrete wavelengths (line spectra) because their electrons can only occupy:
rationale: Line spectra arise from quantized energy levels (discrete electron transitions).
why: Correct. Electrons occupy quantized energy levels; light is emitted at discrete wavelengths when an electron drops between levels (line spectrum).
Energies are quantized (discrete), not continuous.
Electrons occupy multiple discrete levels, not a single one.
Electrons occupy orbitals around, not within, the nucleus.
takeaway: Emission lines = quantized energy-level transitions.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In the photoelectric effect, electrons are ejected from a metal only when the light exceeds a threshold ______, demonstrating light's particle (photon) nature.
rationale: Photoelectric effect: ejection needs a threshold frequency (photon nature of light).
why: Below the threshold frequency, more intensity still ejects no electrons.
It's a minimum frequency (maximum wavelength) threshold, framed by frequency.
Temperature isn't the threshold variable in the photoelectric effect.
Correct. A minimum photon FREQUENCY (energy) is needed to eject electrons; increasing intensity below threshold frequency does nothing — evidence for photons.
takeaway: Photoelectric: needs threshold frequency (not just intensity).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Molarity, the most common concentration unit, is defined as:
choices: Moles of solute per liter of solution (mol/L)
Moles of solute per kilogram of solvent
rationale: Molarity (M) = moles solute / liters solution.
why: Grams per liter is a mass concentration, not molarity.
Correct. Molarity (M) = moles solute / liters of solution.
Moles per kilogram of solvent is MOLALITY, not molarity.
That inverts the definition.
takeaway: Molarity = mol solute / L solution.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: To calculate concentrations when diluting a stock solution, use:
rationale: Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (moles conserved).
why: That isn't the dilution relationship.
Concentrations and volumes don't add in dilution.
The subscripts must match (M₁V₁ = M₂V₂).
Correct. In dilution, moles of solute are conserved, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
takeaway: Dilution: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Unlike molarity (per liter of solution), molality is moles of solute per kilogram of solvent and is preferred when ______ matters.
choices: Temperature (mass doesn't change with temperature; volume does)
rationale: Molality (mol/kg solvent) is temperature-independent (mass, not volume).
why: Correct. Molality uses mass (temperature-independent), so it's preferred for temperature-dependent work like colligative properties; molarity's volume changes with temperature.
Color is irrelevant to the concentration unit choice.
Molality's advantage is temperature independence, not pressure.
Catalysis isn't the reason to choose molality.
takeaway: Molality = mol/kg solvent (temp-independent).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Colligative properties (like freezing point depression) depend on the ______ of solute particles, not their chemical identity.
rationale: Colligative properties depend on the NUMBER of particles, not identity.
why: It's particle number, not mass, that matters.
Correct. Colligative properties depend only on the NUMBER of dissolved particles, not what they are.
Color is irrelevant to colligative behavior.
Shape/identity don't matter — only particle count.
takeaway: Colligative = depends on particle count (not identity).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
tag: Freezing point depression & boiling point elevation
stem: Dissolving a solute (like salt in water) ______ the freezing point and ______ the boiling point.
rationale: Solute: lowers freezing point, raises boiling point.
why: Reversed — solute lowers freezing point, raises boiling point.
Boiling point rises, not falls.
Freezing point falls, not rises.
Correct. Solutes depress freezing point and elevate boiling point (why salt melts ice and pasta water boils hotter).
takeaway: Solute: ↓freezing point, ↑boiling point.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The pressure needed to stop water from flowing across a semipermeable membrane into a more concentrated solution is the ______, a colligative property.
rationale: Osmotic pressure = pressure resisting water flow into a concentrated solution.
why: Correct. Osmotic pressure is the colligative property driving water across membranes toward higher solute concentration (key in cell biology).
Vapor pressure concerns evaporation, not osmosis.
Atmospheric pressure is the ambient air pressure.
Partial pressure concerns gas mixtures.
takeaway: Osmotic pressure = colligative (drives water across membranes).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The direct transition of a solid to a gas, without passing through the liquid phase (e.g., dry ice), is:
rationale: Sublimation = solid → gas directly (deposition is the reverse).
why: Condensation is gas → liquid.
Correct. Sublimation is solid → gas directly; deposition is the reverse (gas → solid).
Vaporization is liquid → gas.
Deposition is gas → solid (the reverse of sublimation).
takeaway: Sublimation = solid → gas (dry ice).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: On a heating curve, temperature stays CONSTANT during a phase change (a plateau) because added energy goes into:
choices: Breaking intermolecular forces (latent heat), not raising temperature
rationale: Phase-change plateaus: energy breaks IMFs (latent heat), temperature constant.
why: Temperature is constant during the plateau, not rising.
Phase changes break intermolecular forces, not chemical bonds.
The energy goes into the phase change, not pressure.
Correct. During a phase change, absorbed energy (latent heat) breaks intermolecular attractions rather than increasing kinetic energy, so temperature is constant.
takeaway: Phase change = latent heat (temp constant, breaks IMFs).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: On a phase diagram, a substance with stronger intermolecular forces will require ______ to boil.
rationale: Stronger IMFs → higher boiling temperature.
why: Correct. Stronger IMFs hold molecules together more tightly, so more thermal energy (higher temperature) is needed to vaporize them.
Stronger IMFs raise, not lower, the boiling temperature.
Boiling still requires heat energy.
Temperature (not only pressure) determines boiling for a given pressure.
takeaway: Stronger IMFs = higher boiling point.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The heat absorbed or released when a substance changes temperature (without a phase change) is:
rationale: q = mcΔT (heat = mass × specific heat × temperature change).
why: mgh is gravitational potential energy.
Correct. q = mcΔT, where m is mass, c is specific heat, and ΔT is the temperature change.
½ mv² is kinetic energy.
Pt is electrical energy (power × time).
takeaway: q = mcΔT (heating without phase change).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Water resists temperature change and stabilizes climate/organisms because it has an unusually ______ specific heat.
rationale: Water has a high specific heat (resists temperature change).
why: Water's specific heat is high, not low.
Specific heat isn't zero.
Specific heat is a positive quantity.
Correct. Water's high specific heat (from hydrogen bonding) means it absorbs a lot of heat for a small temperature change — buffering temperature.
takeaway: Water = high specific heat (temperature buffer).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Because enthalpy is a state function, the total enthalpy change of a reaction is the same regardless of the pathway taken. This is:
rationale: Hess's law: ΔH is path-independent (enthalpy is a state function).
why: Correct. Hess's law: ΔH is path-independent, so reaction enthalpies can be summed from steps.
Le Chatelier concerns equilibrium shifts.
Hund's rule concerns orbital filling.
Raoult's law concerns vapor pressure of solutions.
takeaway: Hess's law: ΔH independent of path (sum the steps).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A rate law such as rate = k[A]²[B] expresses the reaction rate as a function of:
choices: Reactant concentrations (each raised to an experimentally determined order)
rationale: Rate laws depend on reactant concentrations to experimentally determined orders.
why: Orders are found experimentally, not simply read from coefficients.
Correct. Rate laws are determined experimentally; the exponents (orders) are NOT necessarily the stoichiometric coefficients.
Rate depends on concentrations (and k, which depends on temperature), not temperature alone.
The equilibrium constant describes equilibrium, not the rate law.
takeaway: Rate law orders = experimental (not the coefficients).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In the rate law rate = k[A]²[B], the OVERALL reaction order is:
rationale: Overall order = sum of exponents (2 + 1 = 3).
why: 2 is the order in A alone, not the overall order.
1 is the order in B alone.
The exponents are summed (2+1=3), not multiplied.
Correct. Overall order = sum of the exponents = 2 + 1 = 3.
takeaway: Overall order = sum of exponents.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a multi-step reaction, the overall rate is controlled by the:
rationale: The rate-determining step is the slowest step (the bottleneck).
why: Correct. The slowest step is the bottleneck (rate-determining step) that sets the overall reaction rate.
The fastest step doesn't limit the rate.
The slowest step limits it, which isn't always the first.
Exothermicity (thermodynamics) doesn't set the kinetic bottleneck.
takeaway: Rate-determining step = slowest step.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: One mole of any substance contains Avogadro's number of particles, which is approximately:
rationale: One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number).
why: 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s is the speed of light, not Avogadro's number.
Correct. A mole = 6.022 × 10²³ particles (Avogadro's number); it links the atomic and macroscopic scales.
9.8 is g (m/s²).
1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C is the elementary charge.
takeaway: 1 mole = 6.022×10²³ particles.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: In a reaction, the limiting reagent is the reactant that:
choices: Is present in the greatest amount
Runs out first, limiting how much product can form
rationale: The limiting reagent runs out first and caps product formation.
why: The most abundant reactant is usually in excess, not limiting.
Cost is irrelevant to which reagent limits.
The limiting reagent sets the yield, not necessarily the rate.
Correct. The limiting reagent is completely consumed first and caps the amount of product; the others are in excess.
takeaway: Limiting reagent = runs out first (caps yield).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Percent yield is calculated as:
rationale: Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%.
why: Correct. Percent yield = (actual / theoretical) × 100%; it's usually below 100% due to side reactions and losses.
That inverts the ratio.
Yields aren't multiplied.
Percent yield is a ratio, not a difference.
takeaway: % yield = actual/theoretical × 100.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: The formula giving the SIMPLEST whole-number ratio of atoms (e.g., CH₂O) is the ______ formula; the actual number of atoms (e.g., C₆H₁₂O₆) is the ______ formula.
rationale: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual atom counts.
why: Reversed — the simplest ratio is the empirical formula.
Structural/condensed describe how formulas are drawn, not this ratio distinction.
Correct. Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual counts (a whole-number multiple of the empirical formula).
Ionic/covalent describe bonding, not formula types here.
takeaway: Empirical = simplest ratio; molecular = actual counts.

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: Hydrocarbons with only single C–C bonds are ______; those with a carbon-carbon double bond are ______; those with a triple bond are alkynes.
rationale: Alkanes = single bonds; alkenes = double; alkynes = triple.
why: Reversed — single-bond hydrocarbons are alkanes.
Correct. Alkanes (single bonds, saturated), alkenes (C=C), alkynes (C≡C).
Aromatic/aliphatic is a different classification.
Esters/ethers are oxygen-containing groups, not hydrocarbons.
takeaway: Alkane (single), alkene (double), alkyne (triple).

section: Chemical & Physical Foundations of Biological Systems
stem: A 'saturated' hydrocarbon is one that:
rationale: Saturated hydrocarbon = only single bonds (max hydrogens).
why: Double/triple bonds make a hydrocarbon UNsaturated.

stem: The author's central thesis is that:
choices: a flawless forgery is aesthetically equal to the original it copies
the higher price paid for originals reflects snobbery rather than reason
a painting's worth lies partly in its history and not solely in its appearance
the visible appearance of a painting contributes nothing to its true value
rationale: The passage builds to the "modest thesis" of the last two paragraphs: appearance carries most of a painting's value, but not all — the remainder comes from historical, causal contact.
why: This is the skeptic's position, which the author spends the passage arguing against.
The author explicitly rejects the charge that the preference is "mere snobbery."
Correct. Appearance carries "much"/"most," but history supplies a real remainder (¶4–5).
Overstated — the author concedes appearance carries "the larger share" of the value.
takeaway: The CARS main idea is usually the qualified thesis the author settles on, not the strongest-sounding claim in the passage.
passage: Suppose a forger produces a copy of a painting so exact that no expert, however equipped, could tell it from the original. Most of us would still prefer to own the original, and would pay vastly more for it. This preference is easy to mock as mere snobbery — a fetish for provenance that adds nothing to what the eye receives. If two canvases are visually identical, the skeptic asks, how can one be aesthetically superior to the other? Whatever we are paying for, it cannot be the look of the thing.

The skeptic assumes that the value of a painting must reside entirely in its present visual surface. But this assumption is far from obvious. When I stand before a canvas that Rembrandt himself touched, I am in physical, causal contact with the very object his hand shaped. The forgery, however exquisite, offers no such contact; it is the terminus of a different causal chain, one that runs back not to Rembrandt but to a clever imitator in a rented studio. To value the original is to value that lineage, and there is nothing irrational about caring where a thing comes from.

An analogy makes the point. A letter in a beloved's handwriting is treasured over a flawless photocopy, though the copy conveys every word. We do not think the person who keeps the original has made a perceptual error, as though they had failed to notice that the words are the same. They are responding to something the photocopy lacks: a direct trace of the writer's presence. Paintings, on this view, are less like texts, whose value is exhausted by their content, and more like relics, whose value depends on their history.

Yet the analogy should not be pressed too far. Relics are valued almost wholly for contact and hardly at all for how they look; the point of a saint's bone is not its appearance. Great paintings are not like this. Their history matters, but so, undeniably, does what they show — the very composition and color the forger has reproduced. A defender of originals need not deny that appearance carries much of a painting's worth. The claim is only that appearance does not carry all of it, and that the remainder, however hard to name, is not nothing.

This more modest thesis is also the more defensible one. It grants the skeptic everything plausible in the skeptical position — that the visible work is most of what we prize — while denying the further, unargued step from "most" to "all." The forger's triumph, if it is one, is to have captured the larger share of a painting's value. It is not to have shown that the smaller share was an illusion all along.

section: Critical Analysis & Reasoning Skills
idea: History — the press and the Reformation
stem: The author's primary purpose is to:
choices: argue that the printing press played no role in the Reformation
show that the press was a contributing condition of the Reformation rather than its cause
defend the claim that Luther would certainly have failed without printing
trace the technical history of movable type in Europe
rationale: The passage repeatedly separates "shaped / made easier / necessary instrument" from "caused / sufficient." Paragraphs 4–5 land on print as one condition among several, not the cause.
why: Too strong — the author says print "shaped" the movement and "lowered the cost of dissent."
Correct. The thesis is condition-not-cause: "a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation."
The author undercuts single-cause stories and notes Wyclif and Hus gained followings without print.
The technology is discussed only to serve the causation argument, not as the subject.
takeaway: Purpose questions want the author's argumentative aim, not an incidental detail like technical history.
passage: It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

The appeal of the simpler story is easy to understand. Causes that can be named and dated — a machine, an invention — are more satisfying than a tangle of politics, literacy, and timing. But history rarely obliges us with single causes, and the historian's task is often to resist the tidy explanation in favor of the true one.

passage: It is often said that the printing press caused the Protestant Reformation. Luther's theses, the story goes, would have died as a local academic dispute had the new technology not broadcast them across Europe within weeks. There is something to this. Print did carry Luther's words farther and faster than any scribe could, and the reformers themselves marveled at the machine — one called it "God's highest act of grace." But "the press caused the Reformation" claims more than the evidence will bear.

Consider what the same presses were printing. In the decades before Luther, Europe's workshops turned out indulgences, devotional manuals, and papal bulls in enormous numbers; the technology served the old church at least as eagerly as it later served its critics. A tool that amplifies whatever message it is given cannot, by itself, explain why one message rather than another swept the continent. To credit the press with the Reformation is to mistake a multiplier for a cause.

The point can be sharpened. Earlier reformers — Wyclif in England, Hus in Bohemia — had advanced doctrines close to Luther's a full century before movable type, and had won substantial followings without it. Their movements were contained, but by armies and inquisitions, not by any shortage of copyists. What differed in Luther's case was not merely the speed of transmission but a constellation of circumstances: a fractured German political landscape in which sympathetic princes could shield him, a literate urban public primed by grievance, and a message pitched to that public's discontents.

None of this makes the press irrelevant. Technologies shape the movements that use them, and a Reformation conducted by pamphlet was bound to differ from one conducted by sermon and manuscript. The press lowered the cost of dissent and widened the circle of those who could join it. But "shaped" is not "caused," and "made easier" is not "made inevitable." The most we can say is that print was among the conditions that allowed the Reformation to spread as it did — a necessary instrument, perhaps, but not a sufficient explanation.

idea: Philosophy — can we learn from fiction?
stem: The central claim of the passage is that:
choices: novels can prove general truths about human psychology
fiction offers a kind of understanding — of what experiences are like — distinct from the general facts science provides
fiction and science are ultimately in competition
emotional responses to fiction carry no cognitive value
rationale: Paragraphs 2–5 distinguish "knowing that" (general facts, science's domain) from "knowing what something is like" (fiction's domain), and the last paragraph frames this as a division of labor.
why: The author explicitly denies fiction can prove general facts.
Correct. This is the "knowing what it is like" thesis, complementary to science.
The final paragraph says the two "divide the labor... rather than compete."
The author argues the opposite: imaginative grasp is doing "cognitive work."
takeaway: The main idea is the distinction the author builds, not either extreme claim the passage sets up in order to reject.
passage: Can a novel teach us anything true about the world? The doubt is old and not unserious. A novel, after all, is by definition a made-up story; its characters never lived, its events never happened. Whatever a novelist asserts through the tale is unsupported by evidence — the author simply stipulates that things are so within the fiction. If I want to know how grief works, or how power corrupts, it seems I should consult a psychologist or a historian, not a storyteller who has invented her data.

This objection has force against one kind of knowledge but not another. It is true that fiction cannot establish general facts: no number of novels about ambitious men could prove that ambition corrupts, since the novelist controls the outcome. But not all knowledge is knowledge of general facts. There is also knowing what something is like — what it would be to face a certain choice, to bear a certain loss. And here fiction has resources the treatise lacks: it can place us, in imagination, inside a situation and let us try it on.

Consider the difference between being told that jealousy distorts perception and following, page by page, a character's jealous misreadings of an innocent scene. The first hands us a proposition to file away; the second rehearses the experience, and may leave us better able to recognize the distortion in ourselves. The novelist need not prove that jealousy works this way. It is enough that she renders it so vividly that we recognize it — the recognition, not the proof, is the point.

A skeptic may reply that this "knowledge" is merely emotional, not cognitive — that we have been moved, not taught. But the line is not so clean. To grasp what a situation is like is often a precondition for judging it well; the person who cannot imagine another's suffering will reason poorly about how to treat them. If fiction cultivates that imaginative grasp, it is doing cognitive work, even if it proves no theorems.

The modest conclusion is that fiction and science divide the labor of understanding rather than compete for it. Science tells us that things are so and why; fiction shows us what their being so is like from the inside. To ask a novel to furnish general laws is to misunderstand the kind of knowledge it offers — and to conclude, from its failure to do so, that it offers none, is to make the same mistake twice.

stem: The passage is primarily concerned with:
choices: exposing invented traditions as frauds that ought to be abandoned
arguing that a tradition's meaning and function do not depend on the antiquity of its origins
proving that all traditions are in fact recent inventions
tracing the specific history of the Scottish tartan
rationale: The third and fifth paragraphs make the core point: invented origins do not negate present function, and a practice's authority rests not on antiquity but on "what work it does."
why: The third paragraph explicitly rejects the cynical "frauds" reading.
Correct. Origin-age is severed from present meaning and function.
The fourth paragraph says most traditions are "refashioned inheritances," not pure inventions.
Tartan is one recurring example, not the subject of the passage.
takeaway: A passage's subject is the thesis it argues, not the illustrative example it happens to open with.
passage: Many customs that present themselves as immemorial are surprisingly young. The Scottish clan tartan, worn as a badge of ancient lineage, was largely codified in the nineteenth century; the elaborate ceremonial of certain monarchies, apparently the residue of centuries, was substantially devised within living memory of those who first performed it. Historians have given such practices a name: invented traditions — rituals that claim continuity with a distant past to which their actual connection is tenuous or fabricated.

Why manufacture a past? Invented traditions tend to appear, scholars note, at moments of rapid change, when older bonds have frayed and new institutions must secure loyalty quickly. A ritual that feels ancient lends the present an air of inevitability; what looks as though it has always been done is harder to question than what is admittedly new. The invention, in other words, does work: it stabilizes, legitimizes, binds.

It would be easy to draw a cynical moral — that such traditions are frauds, and that exposing their recent origins deflates them. But this conclusion moves too fast. That a practice was invented at a datable moment does not show that it is meaningless to those who observe it. A wedding ritual devised a century ago may bind a community as tightly as one a millennium old; the bonds are real even if the pedigree is not. To confuse the falsity of a tradition's origin story with the falsity of its present function is to misjudge what such traditions are for.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.

Nor is the category as tidy as it first appears. Few traditions are either wholly ancient or wholly invented; most are refashioned inheritances — old materials put to new use. The nineteenth-century codifiers of tartan did not conjure it from nothing: they systematized and embellished a genuine, if looser, prior practice. "Invented" is thus better read as a matter of degree than as a verdict of pure fabrication.

The value of the concept, then, is not that it unmasks tradition as a lie. It is that it dissolves a false assumption: that the authority of a practice depends on the antiquity of its origins. Once we see how readily a sense of the ancient can be manufactured, we are freed to ask a better question — not how old a tradition is, but what work it does, and for whom.
